[Page 81]

﴿Alif. Lam. Ra.﴾ The discussion of the letters that occur at the openings of some surahs was already given at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah. They are like a numbered list of items: they have no place in i'rab (grammatical case-analysis), and they are pronounced only in the state of *sakt* (a brief pause without breath, between words). The state of *sakt* is treated like *waqf* (stopping at the end of a word). For this reason the name *را* is not elongated in the verse, although in the language it ends with a *hamza*. With *sakt* the *hamza* is dropped, just as it is dropped in *waqf*, because pausing on a *hamza* is burdensome in both *waqf* and *sakt*. Thus the word becomes two letters, and so it is not elongated. For the same reason, the reciters (*qurra'*) agreed on not elongating the letters *را*, *ها*, *يا*, *طا* and *حا* that occur at the beginnings of surahs, even though these names are elongated in ordinary usage of the language.

* * *

﴿These are the verses of the Wise Book.﴾ The demonstrative *tilka* may refer to all the verses of the Qur'an that were revealed before this surah, since those verses are present in people's minds, both believers and others. They are as if visible and observed. Therefore pointing to them is correct, since they are recited and preserved. Whoever wishes to hear them and reflect upon them can do so. Moreover, discussion of them is the subject of people's gatherings, their evening talk, their concerns and their disputes. So they come readily to mind when they are indicated.

The demonstrative explains its intended meaning through its predicate, which is *āyātu al-Kitābi al-Ḥakīmi* (the verses of the Wise Book), just as it does in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Rum: 56], and His saying: ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾ [al-Kahf: 78]. In al-Kashshaf it is said: he imagined a separation between them that would soon occur, so he pointed to it with "this."

Something of this meaning has already been mentioned at His saying: ﴿That is the guidance of Allah; He guides with it whom He wills of His servants﴾ [al-An'am: 88], in Surah al-An'am. The purpose of the demonstrative is either to urge reflection on the verses of the Qur'an, so that it becomes clear to them that it is from Allah and they know the truthfulness of the one who brought it. Or it is to convince them, by the verses of the Wise Book, of the signs that demonstrate the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ). For they would ask the Prophet for a sign of his truthfulness, as His saying in this surah indicates: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who do not expect to meet Us say: "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it."﴾ [Yunus: 15]. So it was said to them: ﴿These are the verses of the Wise Book﴾, meaning: it is not one single sign but many verses, for the inimitability is present in every surah of it.

Moreover, it contains lofty truths, guidance to the truth and wisdom. A man who is unlettered, who grew up among an ignorant people, could not bring the like of this guidance and wisdom except that he was inspired with a divine revelation. This is what His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿You did not recite before it any book, nor did you write it with your right hand; otherwise the falsifiers would have doubted﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 48].

On this basis, the demonstrative is the subject (*mubtada'*) and *āyātu* is its predicate (*khabar*). The genitive construction *āyātu al-Kitābi* (verses of the Book) is similar to the explanatory genitive (*idafah bayaniyyah*), although the Book stands in the position of a container for the verses according to a different consideration; this is what the explanatory genitive means on close examination.

It is also permissible to make the demonstrative *tilka* refer to the letters ﴿Alif. Lam. Ra.﴾. For the preferred view regarding the disjoined letters at the openings of surahs is that the purpose of enumerating them is the challenge to inimitability, so they are like spelling for the learner. Thus ﴿Alif. Lam. Ra.﴾ may be placed as a subject (*mubtada'*), and the demonstrative is its predicate. The meaning is: those letters

[Page 82]

are the verses of the Wise Book; that is, the letters of the Wise Book are of their kind, i.e. all its compositions are of the kind of those letters.

The aim is to record their inability to match it, by the fact that all the verses of the Wise Book are of the kind of the letters of their speech. So why are you unable to match it with its like, if you deny that the Book is sent down from Allah? For if it were not from Allah, its being specifically this inimitable arrangement, rather than their speech, would be impossible, since it is composed of the letters of their speech.

*Al-Kitāb* means the Qur'an. The definite article in it is for previous reference (*'ahd*). It is also permissible to take the definite article as indicating perfection in the genus, as you say: "You are the man."

*Al-Ḥakīm* is a descriptive adjective, which may be understood in one of several ways. It may mean the agent (*fā'il*), i.e. the one who judges over the books by distinguishing its sound parts from its altered parts, like His saying: ﴿and a guardian over it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48], and His saying: ﴿And He sent down with them the Book in truth, to judge between people concerning what they differed about﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213].

It may mean the pattern *mufa'al* with an open 'ayn, i.e. *muhkam* (firmly established), like *'atīd* meaning *mu'idd* (prepared).

It may mean one possessing wisdom (*dhū al-ḥikmah*), because it includes wisdom, truth and lofty realities. For wisdom is hitting upon the truth in speech and action. So it is described with the description of a wise person among people, by way of the extended usage that arises from eloquence, as in the words of al-A'sha:

*And a strange, wise (word) that comes to kings; I have said it so that it may be said: "Who said it?"*

It may also be that it is described with the description of the One who sent it down, the One who speaks it, as al-Kashshaf adopted in his explanation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ya-Sin﴾ [Ya-Sin: 1], ﴿By the Wise Qur'an, indeed you are among the messengers﴾ [Ya-Sin: 2–3]. The choice of the description *al-Ḥakīm* among the descriptions of perfection that belong to the Qur'an is because this description is especially fitting to the context of showing the inimitability in terms of meaning, after showing the inimitability in terms of wording with His saying: ﴿Alif. Lam. Ra.﴾ ﴿These are the verses of the Wise Book﴾, and because of what the surah contains of proofs of monotheism and refutation of polytheism.

[Page 83]

This meaning is alluded to by His saying after this: ﴿Say: "Had Allah willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made you aware of it. I had already lived among you a lifetime before it. Will you not then reason?"﴾ [Yunus: 16].

[Page 84]

This clause is a resumed sentence (*isti'naf*) of explanatory type (*istinaf bayani*, a clause that answers an implied question), because the sentence ﴿These are the verses of the Wise Book﴾ [Yunus: 1], with its vagueness about who is calling people to attend to the verses of the Wise Book, raises a question about that caller. So this clause came to explain that the reason for it is that the people regard the revelation made to a man from among themselves as far-fetched, as if it were impossible. It came in this structure, which combines the identification of the caller with the denial of the cause that prompted him and the declaring of ignorant those who brought it about. You may also take it as an initial resumption, since it is the starting point of the purpose for which the surah came, which is to argue for the truthfulness of the Messenger and to establish the Resurrection.

So the *hamzah* is for interrogation used to express denial. That is, how can they be astonished at this with the astonishment of one who deems it impossible?

The benefit of placing the denying interrogation before *kana* ("was") rather than saying "the people were amazed" is to show that their astonishment is itself an object of wonder, since their astonishment is aimed at declaring revelation to a human being impossible.

The meaning is: astonishment at Our revelation has come into being and become established among them, because the verb *kana* indicates stability and firm establishment. When it is used, it implies that this is something not expected to occur.

The phrase ﴿لِلنّاسِ﴾ ("for the people") is connected to *kana* in order to add emphasis to the establishment of this astonishment among them, since the basic function of the *lam* is to indicate ownership, and this is borrowed to express firm possession. That is, the existence of this as an amazement has become firmly fixed in their souls.

﴿عَجَبًا﴾ ("an amazement") is the predicate of *kana*, placed before its subject for the sake of emphasis, because it is the locus of the denial.

﴿أنْ أوْحَيْنا﴾ ("that We revealed") is the subject of *kana*. It is expressed with *an* and the verb rather than with the explicit verbal noun *wahyunā*, in order to convey through the verb what it indicates of renewal, and through the past-tense form what it indicates of established occurrence, affirming that the revelation they are astonished at did occur and was renewed. This increases their distress.

The word *ʿajab* is the verbal noun of ʿ*ajiba*, used when one regards a thing as outside the familiar and rare in occurrence. Since astonishment was the starting point of their denial, and they had already denied the revelation to him and did not limit themselves to calling it strange, the denial came against them in the form of denying their astonishment at inspiration to a man from among mankind. This is because denying the astonishment at this implies, a fortiori, denying the denial, and uproots denial from its roots.

It is also possible that *ʿajab* is a metonymy (*kinaya*, an expression in which the literal meaning implies something else) for the impossibility of the event occurring, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿She said, "Woe to me! Shall I bear a child while I am an old woman and this my husband is an old man? Indeed, this is an amazing thing." They said, "Do you wonder at the decree of Allah?"﴾ [Hud: 72] in Surat Hud, and His saying: ﴿Or do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, to warn you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 63] in Surat al-A'raf. The narration of their astonishment came with the insertion of what conveys a rebuttal of them, namely that revelation was sent to a man from among the people, and this is the case with all the messages, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed﴾ [Yusuf: 109], and He said: ﴿And if We had made it an angel, We would have made it a man﴾ [al-An'am: 9], and He said: ﴿Say, "If there were in the earth angels walking securely, We would have sent down upon them from the heaven an angel as a messenger."﴾ [al-Isra': 95].

The term ﴿النّاسُ﴾ ("the people") is applied to a group of human beings, and what is meant is the polytheists of Makkah, because they are the intended audience of this speech. This usage is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, the people have gathered against you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173]. From Ibn ʿAbbas: a group of the Arabs denied the message of Muhammad (ﷺ) and said, "Allah is too great for a messenger to be a human being." So Allah, exalted is He, sent down: ﴿Is it a wonder for the people that We revealed to a man from among them, "Warn the people"?﴾

The *an* in His saying ﴿أنْ أنْذِرِ النّاسَ﴾ ("that warn the people") is explanatory (*tafsiriyya*, introducing an explanation of what precedes) with respect to the verb ﴿أوْحَيْنا﴾, because revelation here carries the meaning of speech.

The second ﴿النّاسُ﴾ ("the people") encompasses all human beings who can be warned, so it is a customary (*ʿurfi*) generality. And because the word "people" in its second occurrence refers to something other than what it referred to the first time, it is repeated in its apparent form rather than saying "warn them."

When the command to give good news to those who believed was joined by conjunction to the command to warn, the "people" to whom warning applies remained restricted to those who were not believers.

[Page 85]

The object of the warning is omitted, for the sake of making it awesome, and because its substance is known from its contrast with His saying: ﴿and give good news to those who believed that they will have a sure footing (qadam sidq) with their Lord﴾. The verb "to give good news" is transitive by means of the preposition *bi*, so the implied sense is: "and give good news to those who believed *that* they have a sure footing." The preposition was omitted together with *anna*, following the usual practice.

*Qadam* is a noun for what has gone before and preceded, so it can be used for good and for merit, and also for its opposite. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*For you is a footing that people do not deny,*
*along with an inherited nobility that has overflowed the sea.*

Al-Mazari mentioned in *al-Mu'allim* from Ibn al-A'rabi that *qadam* is only used to express the meaning of precedence, but in the sense of honour and eminence. It is the form *faʿal* in the sense of *faʿil*, like *salaf* and *thaql*. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: From this word is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the description of Hell: "until the Lord of Might places His foot (*qadamahu*) in it, and it says, 'Enough, enough.'" This refers to the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Jahannam will not cease saying, 'Is there more?' until the Lord of Might (in another narration: the Compeller) places His foot (*qadamahu*) in it, and it says, 'Enough, enough, by Your might.' And parts of it are drawn in to others." This is one of two interpretations of the meaning of "*qadamahu*." The origin of this is in al-Mazari's *al-Mu'allim* on Sahih Muslim, and he attributed it to al-Nadr ibn Shumayl.

The intended meaning of ﴿قَدَمَ صِدْقٍ﴾ ("a sure footing") in the verse is a footing of goodness. The annexation of *qadam* to *sidq* is an annexation of the qualified to its qualifier. Its original form is *qadamun sidqun*, meaning *sadiq* (true, sound), and it is a description using a verbal noun. According to the majority view, the description *sidq* applied to *qadam* is a restrictive description. According to Ibn al-A'rabi's view, it is a descriptive, revealing description.

*Sidq* (truthfulness) is the agreement of a thing with the belief of the one who believes, and it is well known in the sense of the correspondence of a statement. A thing may be annexed to *sidq* in the sense of its meeting what is hoped for from it, approved, and that the hope of the one who hopes is not disappointed, as in His saying: ﴿And We had certainly settled the Children of Israel in a good settlement﴾ [Yunus: 93], and His saying: ﴿In a seat of truth in the presence of a Sovereign, Omnipotent﴾ [al-Qamar: 55].

His saying ﴿أنْ أنْذِرِ النّاسَ﴾ is an explanation of the verb ﴿أوْحَيْنا﴾. He restricted himself to mentioning this revealed content only because it is what moved them to deny, since it confronted their turning away from his error from their religion, and they heard from him the preference of believers over them. Also, in the mention of the explanation there is an insertion (*idmaj*, weaving one thing into another) of good news for the believers regarding this distinction.

[Page 86]

﴿The disbelievers said, "Indeed, this is clearly magic."﴾

This sentence is a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*, where the substitute includes the substituted element in meaning) for the sentence ﴿Is it a wonder for the people...﴾ and so on. The reason for this substitution is that their saying this indicates that their astonishment at the claim of revelation and messengerhood reached from their souls the extreme of impossibility and denial, until they came to say ﴿Indeed, this is clearly magic﴾ [Yunus: 76] or ﴿Indeed, this is clearly magic﴾. The demonstrative ﴿this﴾ refers to what is contained in the clause ﴿that warn the people and give good news to those who believed﴾.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿لَسِحْرٌ﴾ ("is magic") with a kasra on the *sin* and a sukun on the *ha*, meaning by it the product of the verbal noun, i.e. that this speech is the speech of magic, that is, it is speech by which one is bewitched. Among the methods of magic in their minds was that the magician would say words not understood by people, which give them the impression that these words contain properties and names unknown except to magicians. So the demonstrative refers to the revelation.

Ibn Kathir, ʿAsim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿لَساحِرٌ﴾ ("is a magician"). Then the demonstrative refers to "a man" in His saying "from among them, a man," who is the Prophet (ﷺ). Their description of him as a magician indicates that they denied that he was from Allah, and they could not claim that he was speaking nonsense and falsehood, so they hastened to claim he was a magician. Among their misguided beliefs was that one of the methods of magic is that the magician says statements that draw in the minds of the bewitched. This is from their inability to attack the Qur'an with criticisms of its wording and meanings.

*Sihr* (magic) is the imagining of what is not existent as existent. It was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They taught people magic﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102] in Surat al-Baqarah.

*Mubin* is the active participle of *abana*, which is in the sense of *bana*, meaning "became manifest," that is, clear and evident magic. This description is a fabrication and slander on their part, because it is not clear in that regard. Rather, it is the manifest truth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 3:

Page 87
﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days and then established Himself above the Throne, arranging [every] affair. There is no intercessor except after His permission. That is Allah, your Lord, so worship Him. Then will you not be reminded?﴾ This is a fresh, independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i) serving as an argument for the sole divinity of Allah, exalted is He. It was placed here because the strongest thing that moved the polytheists to claim that what the Prophet brought was sorcery is that he negated partners with Allah in divinity and denied them from their gods whom they associated with Him. They said: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾ [Sad: 5]. Therefore, the denial of their deeming this impossible was followed by establishing the proof of its truth.

The address is to the polytheists, and for this reason the statement is emphasized with a particle of emphasis, and it is followed by "Then will you not be reminded?" This is an iltifat (shift) from the third person in His saying: ﴿Is it a wonder for the people?﴾ [Yunus: 2] and His saying: "The disbelievers said." The discussion of the similar opening of this verse has already passed in Surat al-A'raf up to His saying: ﴿then established Himself above the Throne﴾.

His saying "Allah" (Allah) is the predicate of "inna" (indeed), as indicated by His saying after it: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord, so worship Him﴾.

The clause "arranging the affair" (yudabbiru al-amr) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the Name of Majesty, or a second predicate about "your Lord".

Tadbir (arrangement): considering the outcomes of decreed matters and their obstacles, with the aim of bringing them to completion in what they are intended for, with praiseworthy outcome.

The purpose of tadbir is creation and acting in accordance with what has been arranged. Allah's arranging of affairs is an expression of perfect knowledge of what He creates them upon, because the word tadbir is the most comprehensive of linguistic terms in approximating the perfection of creation.

Al-amr (the affair): a genus encompassing all matters and conditions in the world. It has already occurred in His saying: ﴿and they turned over matters for you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 48] in Surat Bara'a.

In attributing these qualities to Allah, exalted is He, there is an implicit rebuttal of the polytheists, who made for themselves gods that create nothing and know nothing, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They create nothing, while they themselves are created﴾ [al-Nahl: 20].

Page 88
For this reason the sentence ﴿There is no intercessor except after His permission﴾ falls well after the full clause "who created". Because the polytheists made their gods intercessors, when they are warned of Allah's anger they say: ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾ [Yunus: 18], meaning our protectors from His anger. So after the true God was described by what is absent from their gods, the attribute of intercession with Allah and protection of those upon whom anger is directed was denied of their gods.

The negation is emphasized with "min" (from), which comes after the negative particle, to emphasize the negation and the absence of the attribute from all members of the genus whose name it precedes, such that no particularity remains for their gods.

The addition of ﴿except after His permission﴾ is a precaution (ihtiras) to establish the intercession of Muhammad (ﷺ) by Allah's permission. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28]. The purpose of this is the negation of intercession for their gods insofar as they are partners with Allah in divinity; for their intercession with Him would be effective, like the intercession of a peer with his peer. Intercession was discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48] in Surat al-Baqarah. Likewise, the intercessor was discussed at His saying: ﴿Do we have any intercessors?﴾ [al-A'raf: 53] in Surat al-A'raf.

The position of the clause "there is no intercessor" is like the position of the clause "arranging the affair".

The clause "That is Allah, your Lord" is an independent sentence, a summary (fadhlaka) of the clauses preceding it and a consequence of them. It is interposed between those clauses and the clause derived from it, which is "so worship Him", and it is an emphasis of the content of the original clause, which is "Indeed, your Lord is Allah".

The use of the demonstrative at its beginning serves to distinguish Him most completely; because they doubted the attribute of divinity and went astray in it with manifest error, they were deserving of being awakened by means of the demonstrative. It also serves to alert that the one indicated deserves what is mentioned after the demonstrative, insofar as He is characterized by those attributes for which He is pointed out. For the Creator of the worlds with utmost perfection and power, the owner of their affair, the arranger of their conditions, and the absolute disposer, is worthy of worship, like the demonstrative in His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5], after His saying: ﴿for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2], ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3], up to His saying: (﴿and they are certain﴾ [al-Baqarah: 4]).

Page 89
The command to worship Him is derived from His being their Lord; the derived matter is the purpose of the clause, and what precedes it emphasizes the clause "Indeed, your Lord is Allah" with a summarizing and conclusive emphasis. The estimate is: "Indeed, your Lord is Allah" up to His saying "so worship Him," like His saying: (﴿Say: By the bounty of Allah and His mercy, so let them rejoice in that﴾ [Yunus: 58]), since His saying "in that" (fa-bi-dhalika) comes as an emphasis of the clause "by the bounty of Allah and His mercy." The derived element, which is "so let them rejoice," is placed after it. The estimate is: "Say: By the bounty of Allah and His mercy, so let them rejoice in that."

The intended worship is the true worship in which no other is associated with Him, by the indication of the command to it being derived from the attributes exclusive to Allah, not their worshipped beings.

The clause "Then will you not be reminded?" is an independent clause for rebuke. This is a new purpose, so it was not conjoined. The interrogation is a denial of their failure to remember, since they associated others with Him and did not reflect that He alone creates the worlds, owns them, and arranges their affairs.

Tadhakkur (remembrance) means reflection. In this form it is used only for the mind recalling its intelligibles, i.e., its movement among its known matters. It is close to tafakkur (reflection); however, since tadhakkur is derived from the root dhikr, which originally means the flow of a word over the tongue, and which is also used for a known thing coming to mind after forgetting and absence, it indicates the movement of the mind among matters already fixed in it beforehand.

For this reason, it is preferred here over "that perhaps you may reflect" (la'allakum tatafakkarun), to indicate that the argument for the oneness of Allah, exalted is He, has already been established in souls by innate nature and by the call and proofs previously presented to them; so mere bringing these proofs to mind suffices for the argument.

[Page 90]

﴿To Him is your return, all of you. The promise of God is true. He originates creation, then repeats it, that He may recompense with justice those who believe and do righteous deeds. As for those who disbelieve, for them is a drink of boiling water and a painful punishment, because they used to disbelieve.﴾

Their being commanded to worship Him came right after the mention of recompense, as a warning and a glad tiding. So the sentence serves as evidence for the obligation of worshipping Him, and it stands in the position of a result arising from affirming His creation of the heavens and the earth. The One who created such worlds from no prior existence is not incapable of re-creating some of the existents in those worlds as a second creation. Among what points to this is His saying: ﴿Indeed He originates creation, then repeats it.﴾ The origination of creation is what was mentioned earlier, and its repetition is what His saying ﴿To Him is your return, all of you﴾ conveys. Therefore it is separated (fasl) from the preceding sentence because of the near-complete connection between them, though it may also be another predicate (khabar) of His saying "Indeed your Lord," or of His saying "That is God, your Lord."

This sentence includes the affirmation of the Gathering (ḥashr) which they denied, and for which they denied the Prophet (ﷺ).

In the fronting of the prepositional phrase in His saying "To Him is your return" there is an indication of restriction (qasr), meaning not to other than Him. This cuts off the hopes of some of them who say about their gods: ﴿These are our intercessors with God﴾ [Yunus: 18], meaning they are intercessors on the assumption that the resurrection for recompense occurs. So when the return is to Him and not to other than Him, He is worthy of worship, and the worship of other than Him is false.

Al-marji‘ (the return) is a mimi noun (maṣdar mīmī) meaning "return." It was discussed earlier in His saying: ﴿To God is your return, all of you, and He will inform you of what you used to do﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 105], in Surat al-'Uqud.

"Jamī‘an" (all of you) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun of the addressees, which is the object-complement (muḍāf ilayhi) of the maṣdar that governs it.

"Wa‘d Allāh" (the promise of God) is in the accusative as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq) emphasizing the content of the equivalent sentence. Grammarians call this "emphasizing itself" (mu’akkid li-nafsihi), because the content of "To Him is your return" is the promise of their being returned to Him, which is what "the promise of God" conveys. An elided verb is assumed for it, since an emphasizing sentence cannot govern it. The estimate is: "God promised you a promise, true."

"Ḥaqqan" (truly) is in the accusative as an absolute object emphasizing the content of "the promise of God," by way of the elided verb. Grammarians call this "emphasizing something else" (mu’akkid li-ghayrihi), meaning it emphasizes one of two meanings that the emphasized sentence may bear.

The sentence "Indeed He originates creation" stands in the position of evidence for the occurrence of the resurrection and its possibility, in that He has already begun the creation of people. The beginning of their creation indicates the possibility of re-creating them after non-existence, and affirming its possibility repels the polytheists' denial of it. So its possibility is evidence for His saying "To Him is your return, all of you." The inference about its possibility comes from first mentioning the origination of the heavens and the earth, like His saying: ﴿He it is who originates creation, then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27].

The position of "inna" (indeed) is to emphasize the predicate, given their denial of the resurrection. The emphasis arises from His saying "then repeats it," since they do not deny that He originated creation.

On recitation: the majority read ﴿innahu yabda'u al-khalq﴾ with a kasra on the hamza of "innahu." Abu Ja‘far read it with a fatha on the hamza, on the assumption of an elided lam of causation, meaning: "His promise of the resurrection is true, because He originates creation and then repeats it, so repetition after the first creation does not defeat Him." Or the maṣdar (the verbal noun formed from "anna") is an absolute object governed by what governs "wa‘d Allāh," meaning God promised a promise of the beginning of creation and then its repetition. In that case it would be a substitute for "wa‘d Allāh," either an identical substitute (badal muṭābiq) or an explanatory apposition (‘aṭf bayān).

It is also permissible that the maṣdar formed from "anna" and what follows it be in the nominative, governed by the elided verb for which "ḥaqqan" was put in the accusative by its elision. The estimate is: "It has become true, truly, that He originates creation," meaning "His beginning creation and then its repetition is true."

The causal clause "that He may recompense those who believe" and so on shows the wisdom of the resurrection, which is recompense for deeds committed in the worldly life. For if people were sent back according to their deeds without recompense for good and evil, the doer of good and the doer of evil would be equal. Perhaps some evildoers were in better circumstances in this world than the good-doers. So it is part of wisdom that every doer meet the recompense of his deed. This world was not fit to manifest that, because its order was established on the principle of generation and corruption, admitting the occurrence of what opposes the truth, the diversion of good things away from the righteous and their pouring upon the corrupters, and the reverse, for causes and effects that suit the life ordained in this world. So wisdom requires another world, exclusively for permanence and survival, in which every category is placed in what befits it and does not exceed to another, since there is no room in it for dispositions and causations that oppose truth and merit.

The recompense of those who believe and do righteous deeds is mentioned first, for its nobility and its fitness for that world, and because they followed in the worldly life what God created people for, and did not dispose of it by favoring corruption over righteousness.

The bā’ in "bil-qisṭ" (with justice) can indicate the transitivity of the verb of recompense and also the meaning of exchange (‘iwaḍ). Qisṭ means justice: equalizing two things in an attribute, and recompensing with what equals the one recompensed. Its earlier discussion occurred in His saying: "(standing firm in justice)" [Al ‘Imran: 18], at the beginning of Surat Al ‘Imran. So the bā’ indicates that they are recompensed with what equals their righteous deeds, so their recompense there is righteousness, which is the ultimate bliss. And that this recompense is a reward for their equity (qisṭ) in their deeds, in their justice in them, by doing what equals the righteousness intended by the order of this world.

The ambiguity here between the two meanings of the bā’ serves to magnify the status of the recompense of those who believe and do righteous deeds, with an indication that it is a recompense matching the righteousness of their deeds.

The recompense of the believers is singled out, though all recompense is justice. Rather, the increase in the believers' reward may be an extra favor beyond justice, for two reasons. The first is to comfort and honor the believers, by informing them that their recompense is what they have earned by their deeds, as in His saying: ﴿Enter the Garden for what you used to do﴾ [al-Nahl: 32]. Among the greatest generosity is that the generous one gives the impression that what he bestows upon the honored one is his due, and that he has no favor in it.

The second reason is the indication that the recompense of the disbelievers falls short of what justice requires, so there is favor in it by way of a kind of lightening. For if they were requited according to the measure of their crime, their punishment would be more severe. For this reason the style was changed in mentioning the recompense of those who disbelieve. It came explicitly, encompassing the states of punishment, in His saying: ﴿For them is a drink of boiling water and a painful punishment.﴾ The drink of boiling water was singled out from among the kinds of painful punishment because it is the most hateful kind of punishment to ordinary souls.

The drink of boiling water was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Those are they who were delivered to ruin for what they earned; for them is a drink of boiling water and a painful punishment, for what they used to disbelieve﴾ [al-An‘am: 70], in Surat al-An‘am. The bā’ in His saying "bimā kānū yakfurūn" (for what they used to disbelieve) indicates exchange.

The clause "And those who disbelieve..." to its end is an explanatory resumption (istinʾāf bayānī). When the mention of the believers' recompense came as the reason for everyone's return to Him, and what is the recompense of all was not mentioned in that reason, the listener is naturally eager to know the recompense of the disbelievers. So the resumption came to inform him of it.

The wisdom of changing the style, by not conjoining the recompense of the disbelievers to the recompense of the believers (so that it would say "and He recompenses those who disbelieve with punishment..."), as in His saying: ﴿to warn of a severe punishment from Him and to give glad tidings to the believers﴾ [al-Kahf: 2], is an indication of concern for the recompense of the believing righteous, that it is what is announced first. The recompense of the disbelievers is fit for turning away from mentioning it, were it not for the questions of the listeners.

[p. 94]

This is also an initiatory resumption (*isti'naf ibtida'i*, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic). The pronoun in *huwa* ("It is He") refers to the Name of Majesty (Allah) in His words: "Indeed your Lord is Allah." This is another argument for His sole right to dispose of the creatures, and another kind of proof of divinity, mixed with a reminder of favour toward those being addressed by the proof. The previous proof included the great matter of creation and the vastness of knowledge and power, by mentioning things in which the addressees have no share of enjoyment. This proof includes things from which the addressees take a great share of benefit, namely the creation of the sun and the moon in their forms, and the precise determination of their movements, which Allah inspired in humankind so that they might benefit from it in many matters of their lives.

[p. 95]

Making the sun a *ḍiyā'* (a bright, intense light) serves people's benefit by its light, in seeing what concerns them to see, by which the affairs of their lives are sustained, during the times of their occupations. Making the moon a *nūr* (light) serves the benefit of its light, a benefit suited to the need that may arise to see things in the time of darkness, which is the night. For this reason its light was made weaker, so that people benefit from it only to the extent of the need of the one who benefits. Whoever is not compelled to benefit from it does not notice its light, and that light does not distract him from his rest, for which the darkness of the night was made. Had the sun been made constantly visible to people, they would all be equal in continuous benefit from its light, and that would distract them from the rest by which they regain the strength of their nerves, through which their vigour and the completeness of their life are maintained.

*Ḍiyā'* (ضِياءٌ): the strong, shining, intense light, because it illuminates for the one who sees. It is a derived noun from *ḍaw'* (ضَوْءٌ), which is the light that makes things clear; so *ḍiyā'* is stronger than *ḍaw'*.

The *yā'* in *ḍiyā'* (ضِياءٍ) is changed from a *wāw*, because the *wāw* came after a *kasrah* on the *ḍād*, so it was changed to a *yā'* for lightness.

*Nūr* (نُورٌ): a ray, and it is derived from the name of fire. It is more general than *ḍiyā'*; it applies to both a weak ray and a strong ray. Thus the sun's *ḍiyā'* is also a *nūr*, but the moon's *nūr* is not *ḍiyā'*. This is the original basis for the use of these names, but in the speech of the Arabs some of these words are commonly used in the place of others, in a way that is difficult to regulate.

Since *nūr* was placed in contrast with *ḍiyā'*, it became clear that the intended meaning of *nūr* here is a particular kind of light.

His words *ḍiyā'an* (ضِياءً) and *nūran* (نُورًا) are two *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusatives, describing the state of the object at the time of the action), indicating the wisdom and blessing in their creation. The sense is: He made things according to a measure when He fashioned them.

The pronoun in the accusative in *qaddarahu* (قَدَّرَهُ) either refers to the light, in which case *manāzil* (مَنازِلَ, "stations") means "degrees," namely the degrees of the moon's light in strength and weakness, which follow what appears to people as luminous from the moon's sphere, as in His words: ﴿And the moon—We have determined for it stations until it returns like an old palm-stalk﴾ (Yā-Sīn 36:39). That is, until its light diminishes night after night, and it becomes like a withered palm-stalk.

[p. 96]

In this case *manāzil* is in the position of a *ḥāl* of the pronoun in the accusative in *qaddarahu*, and so it is a *ẓarf mustaqarr* (a settled adverbial complement, describing a fixed state or place). That is, a measure according to the stations, so the light in each station has a measure different from its measure in another station. Or the pronoun refers to the moon, with an omitted word understood: "and He determined its course," in which case *manāzil* is in the accusative as an adverb of place.

*Manāzil* (مَنازِلُ) is the plural of *manzil*, which is the place of alighting. What is meant here is the positions in which the moon appears in its direction each night of the month. There are twenty-eight stations, according to the number of nights of the lunar month. Calling them "stations" is a metaphor by resemblance; they are actually points of the sky (*sumūt*) where the moon appears each night in a certain point of them, as if it alights there. Human beings have observed them and found that they do not vary.

Those among them who were guided knew that they came into existence in this order only through the making of the Wise Creator.

The signs of these stations are groups of stars gathered in a shape that does not change, and the early scholars gave them names. These are their names in Arabic, in their order of rising at dawn through the seasons of the year. The Arabs begin their mention of them with *al-Sharṭān*, and so on. This is with regard to the moon's arrival each night at the point of one of these stations, so the first night of the crescent is *al-Sharṭān*, and so on. These names are arranged according to their division among the seasons of the solar year. They are: *al-'Awwā'*, *al-Simāk al-A'zal*, *al-Ghafr*, *al-Zubānā*, *al-Iklīl*, *al-Qalb*, *al-Shawlah*, *al-Na'ā'im*, *al-Balda*, *Sa'd al-Dhābiḥ*, *Sa'd Bula'*, *Sa'd al-Su'ūd*, *Sa'd al-Akhbiyah*, *al-Far' al-A'lā*, *al-Far' al-Asfal*, *al-Ḥūt*, *al-Sharṭān*, *al-Biṭayn*, *al-Thurayyā*, *al-Dabarān*, *al-Hāq'ah*, *al-Han'ah*, *Dhirā' al-Asad*, *al-Nathrah*, *al-Ṭarf*, *al-Jabhah*, *al-Zubrah*, *al-Ṣarfah*.

These stations are distributed over the twelve *burūj* (zodiacal constellations, "mansions") in which the sun resides through the seasons of the year, so each of the twelve *burūj* has two and a third stations. This is a method for knowing their stars, and it has no connection with considering them as stations of the moon.

Allah has informed us of the reason He determined the moon into stations: that people might know the number of years and the reckoning, that is, the number of years by the completion of each year through the gathering of twelve [lunar months].

[p. 97]

*Al-ḥisāb* (الحِسابُ): the verbal noun of *ḥasiba* in the sense of "counted." It is conjoined with *'adad* (عَدَدَ), meaning: "and that you might know the reckoning." Its definiteness is for a known reference: the well-known reckoning. What is meant by it is the reckoning of days and months, because the reckoning of years has already been mentioned specifically. Since in this verse the knowledge of the number of years alone was restricted, it became clear that what is meant by the reckoning is the reckoning of the moon, because the legal year is lunar, and because the pronoun in *qaddarahu* refers to the moon, even though the sun has another reckoning, which is the reckoning of the seasons. This was mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿The sun and the moon [move] by a precise reckoning﴾ (al-An'ām 6:96).

From knowing the nights, one knows the months, and from knowing the months, one knows the year. In this there is ease for people in regulating their affairs, their journeys, and their financial dealings, and this is the basis of civilization. In this verse there is an indication that knowledge of the regulation of chronology is a blessing which Allah bestowed on humankind.

His words ﴿Allah did not create that except in truth﴾ form a resumed sentence, like a conclusion to the whole preceding sentence, because when He informed that He is the One who made the sun a *ḍiyā'* and the moon a *nūr*, and mentioned the wisdom of some of that, it led to the purpose of mentioning it, which is to draw attention to the wisdom in it, so that by this one may infer that their Creator is an agent who chooses and is wise, and so that the polytheists may awaken from their heedlessness of those wisdoms, as He said in this surah: ﴿And those who are heedless of Our signs﴾ (Yūnus 10:7).

The *bā'* (بِ) is for accompaniment (*mulābasah*). *Al-ḥaqq* (الحَقُّ) here is the opposite of *al-bāṭil* ("falsehood, vanity"). It means wisdom and benefit, because one of the usages of *al-bāṭil* is to apply it to what is pointless and devoid of wisdom, and likewise *al-ḥaqq* applies to its opposite. In this there is a refutation of the polytheists who were not guided to the wisdom in that, which indicates the Oneness [of Allah], and that its Creator is not their gods. He said: ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve﴾ (Ṣād 38:27). And He said: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play. We did not create them except in truth, but most of them do not know﴾ (al-Dukhān 44:38–39).

Therefore He followed this reminder with the sentence ﴿We detail the signs for a people who know﴾ (al-A'rāf 7:32). This sentence is a new, initiatory sentence, brought for the sake of expressing favour through the blessing, and to record the blame upon those who were not guided by these proofs to what they contain of clarification. It is also possible that the sentence is in the position of a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause) of the Name of Majesty in His words: ﴿Allah did not create that except in truth﴾.

[p. 98]

Thus, according to the reading of *nufaṣṣilu* (نُفَصِّلُ) with the *nūn* (first person plural), which is that of Nāfi' and the majority, and a transmission from Ibn Kathīr, there is an *iltifāt* (shift in grammatical person) in the pronoun of the subject of the *ḥāl*. According to the reading of *yufaṣṣilu* (يُفَصِّلُ) with the *yā'* (third person), which is that of Ibn Kathīr in the well-known transmission from him, and of Abū 'Amr, Ibn 'Āmir, and Ya'qūb, its meaning is clear.

*Tafṣīl* (التَّفْصِيلُ): explanation, clarification, because clarification extends to all the parts of a thing. It was mentioned earlier at His words: ﴿And thus We detail the signs, so that the way of the criminals may become clear﴾ (al-An'ām 6:55), in Sūrat al-An'ām.

The use of the present-tense verb indicates recurrence.

The detailing is made for the sake of "a people who know," meaning those whose nature is knowledge, in what the present tense indicates of renewed knowledge. Knowledge is renewed only in one whose habit and constant practice it is, because scholars, people of sound reason, are the ones who benefit from evidences and proofs.

The mention of the word "people" (*qawm*) is an allusion to the fact that the attribute of knowledge is firmly established in them, so that it became one of the constituents of their peoplehood, as was mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:164), in Sūrat al-Baqarah. In this there is an implicit indication that those who did not benefit from the detailing of the signs are not among those who know, nor among those in whom knowledge is firmly established.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 6:

﴿Indeed, in the alternation of the night and the day, and in what Allah has created in the heavens and the earth, there are signs for a people who are mindful of Allah.﴾

This is another argument for Allah's exclusive creation and determination (infirad Allah bil-khalq wal-taqdir, the sole-ness of Allah in creating and ordaining). It is an argument from the conditions of light and darkness and the succession of night and day, and in this there is a great lesson. By its conjunction of His saying, ﴿and what Allah has created in the heavens and the earth﴾, it is more general than the first proof, because it encompasses more than the creation of the sun and the moon, more than the creation of night and day, and more than everything in the earth and the sky that human knowledge reaches in its various eras, and in accordance with the varying degrees to which people's minds can draw inferences.

The emphasis of this argument by the particle (inna) is in order to place those addressed by it, who have not been guided by those evidences to monotheism, in the position of one who denies that there are signs of divine oneness in that, by their not acting in accordance with the requirement of knowledge.

The discussion of a verse similar to this one has already preceded: His saying, ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day, and the ship that runs in the sea﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164], in Surat al-Baqarah and at the end of Surat Al 'Imran.

His saying "and what Allah has created" includes bodies and all conditions.

The signs here are attributed to "a people who are mindful of Allah" (qawm yattaquna), whereas in the verse of al-Baqarah they are attributed to "a people who reason" (qawm ya'qilun), and in the verse of Al 'Imran to "people of understanding" (ulu al-albab). This is because the context here is an allusion to the polytheists who have not been guided by the signs, so that they may know that their distance from taqwa (God-consciousness, mindfulness) is the cause of their deprivation of benefit from the signs, and that its benefit is attained by those who are mindful, that is, who beware of error. The muttaqun (the God-conscious) are those characterized by guarding against what leads to loss, which moves them to seek the causes of success, so that thought turns to looking and reasoning by means of the evidences. The explanation of this has passed at His saying, ﴿a guidance for the mindful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] at the beginning of al-Baqarah, given that His saying in the verse before it, ﴿We detail the signs for a people who know﴾ [al-A'raf: 32], has already preceded. As for the verse of al-Baqarah and the verse of Al 'Imran, they occur in a context addressed to people alike. The mention of the word qawm (people) has preceded in the verse before this one.

This is a resumptive threat (istinaf wa'id) addressed to those who did not believe in the Resurrection, did not reflect on the Hereafter, and did not consider the signs. It follows from the argument from evidence (istidlal) concerning what they disbelieved in. The commentary combines argument suited to people of intellect with a threat suited to those who turn away from the truth. This indicates that these people are not benefited by the proofs, which benefit only those who have knowledge and fear God. As for these people, they remain persistently in their obstinacy until they encounter the punishment. Since the return to Him for recompense has been established, the threat came to be directed at those who deny the Resurrection, "who do not hope for the meeting with their Lord and the return to Him."

Because this sentence occupies the position of a threat, one that people in general, believers and disbelievers alike, can know, the discourse shifts from the pronoun to the explicit noun (al-idhhar) in place of the pronoun (al-damir). The relative form (al-mawsuliyya) is used to indicate that the relative clause (al-sila) is the cause of the outcome stated in the predicate (al-khabar).

The phrase "those who do not hope for our meeting" has been made a mark by which they are identified, since it recurs frequently in the Qur'an. Among its occurrences is one where the relative form cannot be sustained except by fame through the relative clause, as we will mention at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them as clear evidences, those who do not hope for Our meeting say, "Bring us a Qur'an other than this"﴾ [Yunus: 15] in this surah.

Al-raja' (hope, expectation) means the supposition that something will occur, without specifying that the thing supposed is desired, although that is common in their speech; it is not, however, a necessary condition. Thus the meaning of ﴿do not hope for Our meeting﴾ is that they do not suppose it and do not expect it.

The meaning of ﴿and were content with the life of this world﴾ is that they did not exercise their reflection on another life, which is higher and more enduring. This is because contentment with the life of this world, and being satisfied that it is sufficient, diverts attention from the evidences for the Hereafter. People of guidance, however, see the life of this world as a deficient life, so they feel a need to seek a life that is purer than its troubles. Soon there appear to them evidences of its existence, and it suffices to have the report of the Truthful One concerning it and the establishment of proofs for its certain occurrence. For this reason, contentment with the life of this world is made a blameworthy trait and a cause of falling into the abyss of loss.

The verse contains an indication that the delight in and contentment with the life of this world is proportionate to the extent of one's immersion in them, in proportion to what diverts one from preparing for the Hereafter. This does not, however, require turning away from the life of this world, for God has bestowed upon His servants many blessings in it, and it is obligatory to acknowledge His favour through them, to thank Him for them, and to advance through them toward higher levels, which are the levels of another life, and to take provision for it. In this there are stations and degrees, in proportion to what the lofty souls are prepared for of the delights of spiritual perfections. The highest of these is the station of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "I said: What have I to do with the world?"

Al-iṭmi'nan (tranquillity, being at rest) means stillness, which occurs in the body and in the soul, and the latter is more common. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿O soul at peace﴾ [al-Fajr: 27]. The conjugation of this verb has already been discussed at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿But that my heart may be at rest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260] in Surat al-Baqarah.

[Page 100]

The meaning of ﴿and were at rest therein﴾ is that their souls were settled and they directed their resolve toward obtaining its benefits, and did not strive to obtain what would benefit them in the Hereafter, because stillness at a thing requires not moving toward anything else. It is reported from Qatadah: "If you wish, you may see this described person as a man of the world: he is pleased with it, angered by it, rejoices in it, and is concerned and grieved over it."

Those who are heedless (alladhina hum ghafilun) are the very same as those who do not hope for the meeting, but the relative pronoun is repeated for the sake of emphasis on the relative clause, and to indicate that it alone is sufficient to merit what is mentioned after it as the predicate. The relative pronoun was not repeated in His words ﴿and were content with the life of this world﴾ because contentment with the life of this world is part of the completion of the meaning of the relative clause in His words ﴿Indeed, those who do not hope for Our meeting﴾.

By heedlessness (al-ghaflah) is meant the neglect of reflection on the signs altogether, as indicated by the context and the setting, and by what the nominal sentence used in the relative clause, ﴿they are heedless of Our signs﴾, implies, since it signifies permanence. Also, by placing the prepositional phrase before the verb in ﴿heedless of Our signs﴾, their heedlessness is restricted to the signs of God in particular, not to other things. Thus they are not among those who are heedless of other things. Taken together, this indicates that their heedlessness of God's signs is a habit and a disposition for them, and that they persist in it, so that it amounts to turning away from God's signs and refusing to consider them, out of obstinacy and arrogance. The intended meaning is not one who is occasionally overcome by heedlessness of some signs at some times.

This is followed by the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) in order to increase the presence of their attributes in the minds of the listeners, and because the use of the demonstrative as a subject after a series of descriptions indicates that the one referred to is worthy of the predicate because of those attributes, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-ma'wa (the abode) is the name of a place of shelter, that is, the place of their return, their destination and their final place of return.

The bā' (in bi-ma) is causal (li-l-sababiyya). The use of the relative particle "mā" in His words "for what they earned" (bi-ma kasabu) indicates the cause of the ruling, that is, that what they earned is the reason for their destination to the Fire. It thus confirms the causality conveyed by the bā'.

The use of "kāna" (was) indicates that this earning is their habitual practice.

The use of the imperfect verb indicates repetition, so that their habit is the repeated doing of that which they earned.

The relative pronoun was not repeated in His words ﴿and were content with the life of this world﴾ because contentment with the life of this world is part of the completion of the meaning of the relative clause in His words ﴿Indeed, those who do not hope for Our meeting﴾.

By heedlessness (al-ghaflah) is meant the neglect of reflection on the signs altogether, as indicated by the context and the setting, and by what the nominal sentence used in the relative clause, ﴿they are heedless of Our signs﴾, implies, since it signifies permanence. Also, by placing the prepositional phrase before the verb in ﴿heedless of Our signs﴾, their heedlessness is restricted to the signs of God in particular, not to other things. Thus they are not among those who are heedless of other things. Taken together, this indicates that their heedlessness of God's signs is a habit and a disposition for them, and that they persist in it, so that it amounts to turning away from God's signs and refusing to consider them, out of obstinacy and arrogance. The intended meaning is not one who is occasionally overcome by heedlessness of some signs at some times.

This is followed by the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) in order to increase the presence of their attributes in the minds of the listeners, and because the use of the demonstrative as a subject after a series of descriptions indicates that the one referred to is worthy of the predicate because of those attributes, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-ma'wa (the abode) is the name of a place of shelter, that is, the place of their return, their destination and their final place of return.

The bā' (in bi-ma) is causal (li-l-sababiyya). The use of the relative particle "mā" in His words "for what they earned" (bi-ma kasabu) indicates the cause of the ruling, that is, that what they earned is the reason for their destination to the Fire. It thus confirms the causality conveyed by the bā'.

The use of "kāna" (was) indicates that this earning is their habitual practice.

The use of the imperfect verb indicates repetition, so that their habit is the repeated doing of that which they earned.

[Page 101]

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, their Lord guides them by their faith. Rivers flow beneath them in Gardens of Bliss.﴾ ﴿Their call therein is: "Glory be to You, O Allah." And their greeting therein is: "Peace." And the last of their call is: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾

This sentence came as a resumptive clause (istinaf bayani, a clause that answers an implied question) so that the states of the believers would be mentioned independently and not grammatically subordinate to the states of the disbelievers. This is one of the methods of emphasizing the news. The reason for mentioning it is to contrast the states of those who deny the meeting with Allah with their opposites, as an honoring of its people and as a vexation to the disbelievers.

The definiteness of the subject (al-musnad ilayhi) by the relative pronoun (al-mawsuliyyah), rather than by the definite article (al-lam), here indicates, through the relative pronoun, the cause of the predicate's construction: that their faith and their deeds are the cause of the occurrence of the content of the predicate for them.

Guidance (al-hidayah) is directing toward the beneficial goal and indicating it. So the meaning of ﴿their Lord guides them﴾ is that He directs them to what is good for them. The intended guidance is creational (al-irshad al-takwini), meaning that He creates in their souls the knowledge of beneficial deeds and facilitates their increase in them. As for guidance that is indication by speech and instruction, Allah addresses it to both believers and disbelievers.

The bāʾ in (بِإيمانِهِمْ, "by their faith") is causal (lil-sababiyyah), such that faith is a cause of the content of the predicate, which is guidance. Thus the bāʾ serves to affirm the causality derived from the definiteness by the relative pronoun, similar to His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us﴾ [Yunus: 7] through ﴿for what they used to earn﴾ [Yunus: 8]. This is in the formation of their guidance to good things by Allah's making: Allah makes for faith a light that is placed in the heart of the believer, and this light has luminous rays connecting the believer's soul with the realms of holiness (ʿawalim al-quds). These rays become a magnetic cause for the soul's being moved toward goodness and perfection, which continually increases day by day. Therefore, the believer draws nearer to correct perception, protected from error, in proportion to the degrees of faith and righteous deeds.

In a hadith: "Among the nations there have been muhaddathun (those spoken to, i.e., inspired), and if there is one in my community, it is ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab." Ibn Wahb said: the interpretation of muhaddathun is mulhamun (inspired), the correct understanding.

[Page 102]

And in a hadith: "Beware the insight of the believer, for he looks with the light of Allah." Because of this light, the companions of the Prophet ﷺ were the most complete of people in faith, since when they received faith from the Prophet ﷺ, his radiant lights in their souls were stronger and more extensive.

In the shift from the proper name of Allah (ism al-jalalah) to the description of lordship (al-rububiyyah), attached to the pronoun of (those who believe), there is an honoring of the believers and of the status of their guidance, that it is the granting of a Master to His allies. Therefore its nature is to be a complete gift, mixed with mercy and honor.

The use of the present tense (al-mudari') indicates that this guidance continually recurs and renews itself.

In this sentence there is a mention of the readiness of their souls in this world for ascending the degrees of perfection.

The clause ﴿rivers flow beneath them in Gardens of Bliss﴾ is a second predicate, mentioning what they obtain of bliss in the Hereafter as a result of their guidance obtained in this world. The discussion of its counterpart (tajri min tahtiha al-anhar) was previously made in Surat al-Baqarah. What is meant by "beneath them" is beneath their dwellings. Al-jannat (the Gardens) was previously discussed, and al-naʿim (bliss) was discussed in His saying: ﴿therein for them is enduring bliss﴾ [al-Tawbah: 21] in Surat Bara'ah.

The clause ﴿their call therein is "Glory be to You, O Allah"﴾ and what is conjoined to it are states (ahwal) of the pronoun in (those who believe).

Al-da'wa here means supplication (du'a'). It is said: daʿwah with the ending (ha'), and daʿwa with the feminine alif.

Subhan is a verbal noun meaning glorification (al-tasbih), that is, declaring Allah free of imperfections (al-tanzih). It was previously discussed at His saying: ﴿They said: "Glory be to You, we have no knowledge"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 32] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Allahumma is a vocative address to Allah, so applying the term supplication to this glorification is because it is intended as an address to Allah to produce His declaration of transcendence. Thus supplication in it is in its linguistic sense. It may also be that calling this glorification a supplication is because it is a praise directed toward seeking the bestowal of mercies and bliss, as Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"When a man praises you one day, the praise suffices him from having to ask."

Know that restricting their call therein to the phrase (Glory be to You, O Allah) indicates that they have no other call in Paradise besides this utterance, because restriction in a context of explanation indicates exclusivity (al-qasr). Although it is not one of the standard methods of restriction, it is derived from the context. However, His saying: ﴿and the last of their call is: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds"﴾ indicates that this praise is among their calls, so it follows that they have a call and a final call.

The reason for mentioning this among the states of the believers is that it shows that what they are in of bliss is the ultimate goal of those who desire it, such that if they wish to enjoy the station of calling upon their Lord, which is the station of nearness, they find themselves not longing for anything to ask for, so they substitute praise of their Lord for requests. They are thus inspired to adhere to glorification, because it is the most indicative expression of exaltation and transcendence, and so it comprehends the expression of all perfections.

Al-tahiyyah (greeting) is a generic noun for the words of honor with which one opens a meeting. Its origin is derived from the verbal noun of (hayyahu), when one says to him at meeting: "May Allah give you life." Then it came to predominate over every expression said at meeting, just as the word al-salam did, so it includes such phrases as: "Hayyaka Allah" (May Allah give you life), "ʿImm sabahan" (Good morning), "ʿImm masaʾan" (Good evening), "Sabbahaka Allah bi-khayr" (May Allah greet you with good), and "Bit bi-khayr" (Spend the night in goodness). The discussion of these was previously made at His saying: ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, respond with one better than it﴾ [al-Nisa': 86] in Surat al-Nisa'.

For this reason, He informed about their greeting that it is "peace" (salam), meaning the word salam, reporting about the genus by one of its individuals; that is, Allah made the word salam a greeting for them.

The apparent meaning is that the greeting among them is the phrase "salam," and that it is quoted here in its own wording rather than the wording "al-salamu ʿalaykum" or "salamun ʿalaykum," because if that were intended it would have said "wa tahiyyatuhum fiha al-salam" with the definite article, so that the definite article would make it immediately clear that it refers to the well-known salam in Islam, which is the phrase "al-salamu ʿalaykum." Likewise, Allah's greeting upon them is in this wording: ﴿"Peace," a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58]. As for His saying: ﴿and the angels will enter upon them from every gate, "Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23], this is a gentle address to them with the greeting that Islam brought to them.

[Page 104]

The reason for omitting the word ʿalaykum (upon you) in the greeting of the people of Paradise among themselves is that their greeting among themselves is merely companionship and honoring. Therefore it resembled good wishes and gratitude more than supplication and invoking amen. It is as though they rejoice in the complete safety they enjoy in Paradise, so their tongues spontaneously express at meeting what is in their hearts. This contrasts with the greeting of the people of this world, which often occurs between those who meet and do not know one another, so in it there remains a trace of the meaning for which humankind instituted salam, which is the meaning of securing the one met from anticipated harm among many strangers. Therefore the widespread wording is the word "salam," which means safety, and so it is appropriate to explicitly state that safety is upon the addressee, in order to achieve the meaning of calming his fear. That is an ancient practice: one who intends harm to the one he meets does not open with salam. For this reason, salam was made the emblem of Muslims at meeting, to generalize security among the community, which is one of the effects of Islamic brotherhood. Likewise was the custom of hospitality in ancient civilization: if the visitor is a visitor of evil or war, the host refrains from offering hospitality, as Allah related about Ibrahim: ﴿When he saw their hands not reaching toward it, he disliked them and felt fear of them﴾ [Hud: 70].

In this there is an honoring of the status of this word, which is the emblem of Muslims when they meet, because of the comprehensive meanings of honor it contains, for it is a supplication for safety from everything that disturbs. It is therefore more eloquent than "Ahyaka Allah" (May Allah give you life), because that is a supplication for life, which may not be good, whereas salam comprises life and the purity from the afflictions that occur within it.

The attachment of tahiyyah to the pronoun (hum) means the greeting that proceeds from them, that is, from some of them to others.

The reason for mentioning their greeting in this verse is to indicate that they are in companionship and joy, and that is among the greatest pleasures of the soul.

The clause (and the last of their call) is the remainder of the circumstantial clauses (al-jumal al-haliyyah). The praise of Allah is made part of their supplication, as demanded by (an, the explanatory an) which is explained by "the last of their call," because "their call" contains the meaning of speech, since it is made the last of their utterances.

The meaning of "the last of their call" is that they conclude their supplication with it. Thus they repeat "Glory be to You, O Allah," and when they wish to move to another state of bliss, they terminate their supplication with the clause ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾.

[Page 105]

The context and arrangement of the speech indicate that they call upon Allah while gathered together, which is why the mention of their call is joined with the mention of their greeting. Perhaps when they see one another, they hasten to supplication with glorification, and when some of them draw near to others, some greet others. Then when they wish to separate, they conclude their supplication with praise. Thus (an) is explanatory for "the last of their call," and it indicates that the last of the supplication is the very phrase ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2].

The virtue of these two phrases is indicated by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Two words are beloved to the All-Merciful, light upon the tongue, heavy in the scale: Subhan Allah wa bihamdihi, Subhan Allah al-ʿAzim (Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him; Glory be to Allah the Mighty)."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 11:

﴿And if Allah were to hasten for the people the evil as they hasten (for) the good, their term would surely have been decreed for them. So We leave those who do not expect meeting Us in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾

The coming of the conjunctive particle (harf al-'atf) at the beginning of this verse implies, in the science of rhetoric (ilm al-balagha), a particularity in its conjoining to what precedes it and a greater connection with what precedes it. Therefore, it is necessary to clarify the relevance of its placement. The apparent meaning is that the polytheists, out of their delusion, used to reckon God's actions like the actions of people, rushing to retaliation when angered with a swift rush, and they reckoned the Messengers to have been sent only to manifest extraordinary signs and to vanquish their opponents, and they equated them with charlatans and those who challenge with feats of valour and marvels. So when they denied the Prophet ﷺ and persisted obstinately, and no calamities from a comprehensive punishment or a general pestilence befell them as a result, they increased in delusion regarding their falsehood and in deeming it impossible that the Messenger ﷺ was sent by God the Exalted. Many verses of the Qur'an indicate this, such as His saying: ﴿And when they said, "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment."﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], and His saying: ﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 54], and His saying: ﴿So indeed for those who wronged is a portion like the portion of their companions, so let them not ask Me to hasten﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 59]. We have explained this in Surah al-An'am and in Surah al-Anfal.

Page 106
The believers sometimes wished for the descent of punishment upon the polytheists and were slow to see the arrival of victory for the Prophet - upon him be prayers and peace - and his companions, as came in the hadith: "that the Muslims said: Will you not seek victory?" Some of them sometimes marvelled that God provides sustenance to the polytheists while they disbelieve in Him. So when the verses of this surah came with the thunderbolts of threat for the polytheists, they were followed by that which removes their doubts and reassures the hearts of the believers, by what His saying encompasses: ﴿And if Allah were to hasten for the people the evil as they hasten (for) the good, their term would surely have been decreed for them.﴾

This is a general statement that indicates that God established the order of this world upon gentleness towards creatures and the preservation of kinds until terms He willed, and He made for this continuance the means of provision with blessings by which the life endures. So the goods poured out upon creatures in this world are many, and the afflictions that arise are rare, and most of them are caused by causes set into the order of the cosmos and by the actions of its people. Among them is what comes contrary to custom at the place of their terms, which God the Exalted determined by His saying: ﴿For every nation is a term﴾ [Yunus: 49] and His saying: ﴿For every term is a Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 38].

This sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿Indeed, those who do not expect meeting Us﴾ [Yunus: 7], the verse. Since their punishment, to which they are bound to return, was mentioned, it was fitting to explain to them the reason for deferring the punishment from them in this world, so that the shubha of their delusion may be uncovered, and so that those who believe may know one of the wisdoms of God's governance of this cosmos. The indication that this sentence is connected to the sentence ﴿Indeed, those who do not expect meeting Us﴾ [Yunus: 7] is His saying at the end of this: ﴿So We leave those who do not expect meeting Us in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾

This verse makes clear that God made gentleness continuous upon His servants, not cut off from them, because He established upon it the order of the world, since He willed the stability of its structure, and that He did not decree the equalling of evil with good in this world, out of kindness and gentleness from Him. God is Subtle with His servants, and in that is a great favour upon them. And that those who deserve evil, if it were hastened for them as they deserve, the order upon which the world was founded would be nullified.

And "the people" (al-nas) is a general term for all people. But since the discourse concerns refuting the doubt of the polytheists, and they were the ones deserving evil, they were the first to come to mind from the generality of people, as His saying ﴿So We leave those who do not expect meeting Us in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ further clarifies.

Page 107
The composition of the verse is in a firm, wondrous concision. In the side of evil is mentioned ﴿yu'ajjilu﴾ (hastens), which indicates the root of the category of hastening, even with the least that its meaning is realized in. And the hastening of God's good to them is expressed with the word ﴿isti'jalahum﴾ (their seeking haste), which indicates exaggeration in hastening, by what the addition of the sin and the ta' (for other than seeking) conveys, since seeking does not appear here. It is like their saying: ista'akhara (delayed), istaqdama (advanced), istajlaba (brought), istaqama (went straight), istaban (became clear), istajaba (responded), istamta'a (enjoyed), istakbara (was arrogant), istakhfa (hid), and His saying: ﴿and they covered themselves with their garments﴾ [Nuh: 7]. Its meaning: their hastening towards good, as al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) took it, to indicate that the hastening of good is from Him.

So the hasting here is not in the sense of seeking hastening, because the polytheists did not ask for the hastening of good, nor did they ask for it so that it occurred; rather it means abundant hastening, as in the saying of Sulami ibn Rabi'a:

"And when the maidens were veiled with smoke, and hastened the setting of the pots, and grew weary"
(i.e., they hastened), and in this usage it is like the other usage, transitive to an object, as in the verse and as in the hadith "so he hastened death."

The phrase ﴿isti'jalahum﴾ is in the absolute object construction (maf'ul mutlaq) indicating resemblance, and its governing verb is ﴿yu'ajjilu﴾, and the meaning: "And if God were to hasten for the people the evil as He hastens for them the good abundantly." So His saying ﴿isti'jalahum﴾ is a verbal noun (masdar) annexed to its object, not to its subject, and the subject of the hastening is God the Exalted, as indicated by His saying ﴿And if Allah were to hasten﴾.

The preposition bi- in His saying ﴿bil-khayr﴾ is for emphasis of attachment, like that in His saying ﴿and wipe over your heads﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 6]. Its origin is: isti'jalahum al-khayr, so the exaggeration conveyed by the sin and the ta' and the emphasis of attachment indicate the grace that good for them is abundant and firmly established. The attaching of the object of the verb of hastening with this preposition is frequent, and they did not draw attention to it in its many occurrences. It will come in Surah al-Nahl.

The answer of "law" (lau) is made His saying ﴿laqudiya ilayhim ajaluhum﴾ (their term would surely have been decreed for them), and the answer of "law" is by nature in the realm of impossibility, meaning: and that is impossible, because God determined for the terms of their annihilation a specific appointed time: ﴿No nation can precede its term, nor can they delay﴾ [al-Hijr: 5].

Page 108
Al-qada' means decree.
Al-ajal means the specified duration for the survival of a people. The meaning: "their term would surely have come to them." Since qudiya is construed with the sense of "reached" and "arrived," it takes ila. This is the aspect of the tafsir of the verse and the secret of its composition, and one should not turn to other than it in understanding it. This meaning is like the meaning of ﴿Say: If what you seek hastily were with me, the matter would surely have been decided between me and you﴾ [al-An'am: 58] in Surah al-An'am.

The sentence ﴿So We leave those who do not expect meeting Us﴾ etc. is a consequence (mufarra'a) of the sentence ﴿And if Allah were to hasten for the people﴾ through its end.

The majority read ﴿laqudiya﴾ in the passive voice, and ﴿ajaluhum﴾ is raised as the deputy subject. Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read it with fath on the qaf and the dad, and ﴿ajaluhum﴾ in the accusative, on the basis that in qada there is a pronoun referring back to the divine name in His saying ﴿And if Allah were to hasten for the people the evil﴾ etc.

The sentence ﴿So We leave those who do not expect meeting Us﴾ is a consequence of the sentence of "law" and its answer, which conveys the negation of God hastening evil for the people, by the negation of its necessary consequence, which is the arrival of their term to them. That is: since the hastening is negated, "We leave those who do not expect meeting Us wandering," that is, We leave them during the period of deferring punishment from them, while engaged in their transgression, that is, the excess of their arrogance and pride.

And al-'ama (wandering) is the lack of sight.

The verb was not put in the subjunctive after the fa' because the subjunctive occurs in answer to a pure negation, whereas the negation derived from "law" is achieved by implication. And because the nature of an answer to a negation is that it be caused by the negated thing, not by the negation itself, and the consequence here is built upon something derived from the negation.
