As for the negated thing, it is the hastening of evil, and it does not cause that He leave the unbelievers wandering. By this you know that His saying ﴿So We leave﴾ is not conjoined to an implied speech; rather the estimation is an estimation of meaning, not an estimation of grammatical parsing, meaning: "So We leave those who deny the resurrection in their misguidance, as a respite for them."

His saying ﴿in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ has a parallel that preceded in His saying ﴿and He extends them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-Baqara: 15] in Surah al-Baqara. And al-tughyan is disbelief.

Page 109
The use of the relative form in defining the unbelievers indicates that the most severe of their transgression is their denial of resurrection, and because it has become like a sign upon them, as has preceded just now.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 12:

﴿When harm touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side, or sitting, or standing. But when We remove his harm from him, he passes on as though he had never called upon Us against a harm that touched him. Thus is what they used to do made attractive to the wasteful.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) with the phrase ﴿And if God were to hasten for people the evil...﴾ [Yunus: 11] and what follows it, because the most important purpose of both is taking heed (i'tibar) from the blameworthy conditions of the polytheists, to denounce their state and to warn against falling into the like of it, as indicated by the concluding of this verse with the sentence ﴿Thus is what they used to do made attractive to the wasteful.﴾ Since the previous verse explained the reason for delaying the punishment of annihilation (istisal) from them and deferring their recompense to the Hereafter, this verse explains their condition when some harm touches them and when harm is removed from them.

The word al-insan (man) is intended as a genus, and the definite article (al-) here indicates customary totality (al-istighraq al-ʿurfi), i.e., the disbelieving man, because the majority of people at that time were disbelievers, since the Muslims before the Hijra did not exceed some seventy-odd men together with their women and children who were their followers. In this sense, those considered in this judgment are the disbelievers, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And man says, "When I have died, will I really be brought forth alive?"﴾ [Maryam: 66] and His words: ﴿O man, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾ [al-Infitar: 6] ﴿Who created you and proportioned you﴾ [al-Infitar: 7]. The Muslims take from this judgment what suits the measure of the remnants of this jahili condition in each of them, so that each one awakens from his heedlessness.

The pronoun referring back to "people" in His words ﴿And if God were to hasten for people the evil﴾ [Yunus: 11] is replaced here by the word insan, because mentioning the word insan contains an allusion to reminding them of God's blessing upon them in making them among the noblest kinds existing on earth. Some exegetes made the definite article in insan indicate a specific reference (al-ʿahd) and took the intended person to be Abu Hudhayfa ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, whose name was Muhashshim, who was a polytheist and had been afflicted with an illness.

The word al-ḍurr (harm) has been mentioned previously in His words ﴿And if God touches you with harm﴾ [Yunus: 107] in Surat al-An'am.
The word al-du'a' (calling upon) here means request and asking with humility.

The preposition lam in His words ﴿li-janbihi﴾ (lying on his side) has the meaning of ʿala (upon), as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿They fall down upon their chins﴾ [al-Isra: 107] and His words: ﴿and He laid him down upon his brow﴾ [al-Saffat: 103]. Do you not see that in the place of lam the particle ʿala came in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Remember God standing, sitting, and upon your sides﴾ [al-Nisa: 103] and His words: ﴿Those who remember God standing, sitting, and upon their sides﴾ [Al 'Imran: 191]. Similar to this is the statement of Jabir ibn Jinni al-Taghlabi:

He struck him with the spear, then turned it in him, and he fell prostrate upon the two hands and upon the mouth.

That is, upon the two hands and upon the mouth. It arises from the meaning of exclusivity (al-ikhtisas), which is the most general of the meanings of lam, because the exclusivity of a thing occurs in many modes, among them its being above it.

The particle of exclusivity was used here only to indicate that the side is specifically associated with calling upon God at the time of harm and is connected to it, so the rest is a fortiori. This usage is considered in the verse of Jabir and the two other verses, as becomes apparent upon reflection; this is the aspect of the difference between the two usages.

The position of the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and for this reason ﴿sitting or standing﴾ is conjoined in the accusative. The side was made genitive by lam and was not put in the accusative, so that one would not say, for example, "lying down, or sitting, or standing," in order to depict the firmness of his state of ease by mentioning a part of his body, because that is more evident in his firmness, just as the mention of giving in the two other verses and the verse of Jabir was more evident in depicting the state, by combining the mention of the limbs with the mention of the actions that indicate the root meaning, to show that he calls upon God in the most intimate of conditions, which is the state of seeking ease and constant calm. For this reason the side was mentioned first. As for the addition of ﴿sitting or standing﴾, it is for the purpose of generalizing and completing the states, because the context is one of elaboration to increase the depiction of states, meaning: he calls upon Us in all conditions, nothing diverts him from calling upon Us.

The janb (side) is the singular of junub (sides). It was mentioned previously in His words: ﴿so their foreheads and their sides will be branded﴾ [al-Tawba: 35] in Surat Bara'a.

al-qu'ud (sitting) is sitting down.
al-qiyam (standing) is erecting oneself. It was mentioned previously in His words: ﴿And when it grows dark for them, they stand﴾ [al-Baqara: 20] in Surat al-Baqara.

Idha (when) here is merely for temporal sense and for specifying the time of its response with its condition, and it is not for the future as is its usual case, because the intent here is to narrate the state of the polytheists in calling upon God when distressed and turning away from Him to worshipping their gods in times of ease, as indicated by His words: ﴿Thus is what they used to do made attractive to the wasteful﴾, since He made it a circumstance for the wasteful. Since He expressed their action with the word kanu (they used to), which indicates that it was their action in the past times, for this reason the verbs of the past tense were used in its condition, its response, and what is conjoined to them, because that being their state in the past is more fitting to record against them than if it were supposed to be their state in the future, since perhaps among them there are those who will be admonished by this verse and cease that action or be led to consider the truth.

For this reason the sentence ﴿So when We remove from him his harm, he passes on﴾ is made a consequence of it, because this consequence is the purpose of the speech, since the first state, which is the one made a consequence of, is a praiseworthy state were it not for what follows it.

Al-kashf (removal): its literal meaning is the manifestation of something that has a covering or veil over it. Its application to mere removal became common, either by way of metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal) through the relation of generality, or by way of metaphor (al-istiʿara) by likening the removed thing to a covering over something.

al-murur (passing on) here is figurative, in the sense of exchanging one state for another. The exchange is likened to moving from one place to another, because movement is an exchange; that is, he moved to a state like that of one who had never called upon Us before, meaning he forgot the state of his distress and need for Us, so he became as though he had never fallen into that need.

Ka'anna is the light form of ka'anna, and its subject is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-shan), which has been omitted, as is usual. The verb "call upon" was made transitive with the preposition ila (to) in His words: ﴿to a harm﴾, not with lam as is usual in such as His words:

I called upon Miswar for what befell me

by way of the metaphor of the subsequent kind (al-istiʿara al-tabiʿiyya), likening harm to a sudden enemy who calls out to someone who surprised him, seeking help to repel it.

Making ila mean lam is a departure from the eloquence of this composition and a confusion of the rhetorical considerations.

The sentence ﴿Thus is what they used to do made attractive to the wasteful﴾ is a concluding sentence (tadhyil) that encompasses what came before and other things, meaning: in this same way Satanic adornment made attractive to them the actions they used to perform in their past times, in calling upon God and other of their errors.

The discussion of the meaning and position of "thus" (kadhalika) in verses like this has been given previously at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqara: 143] in Surat al-Baqara, and at His words: ﴿Thus We made attractive to every nation their deeds﴾ [al-An'am: 108] in Surat al-An'am. So the reference here is to the adornment that is derived here, which is the adornment of their turning away from calling upon God in times of ease, meaning: such a wondrous adornment was made attractive to every wasteful person as his deed.

al-israf (wastefulness): excess and abundance in something not praiseworthy. Therefore the intended "the wasteful" here are the disbelievers. The word ﴿al-musrifin﴾ [Yunus: 83] was chosen for its indication of their exaggeration in disbelief, and the definite article in al-musrifin is for totality, to include those spoken of and others.

The verb of adornment was attributed to the passive voice because the Muslims know that the one who adorns for the wasteful is their Satanic impulses, for the verb of adornment has been attributed to Satan on more than one occasion; or because knowing who adorns for them is not important here, but what matters is the lesson and admonition from their considering their blameworthy deeds good with a Satanic approval.

The meaning is that it is the nature of blameworthy and ugly deeds, when they are repeated by their doers, that they become a habit for them which makes their ugliness appear good to them, so they hardly feel its ugliness, so how would they abandon them, as it is said:

A man is judged in the days of his trial, until he sees as good what is not good.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 13:

﴿And We certainly destroyed the generations before you when they did wrong, and their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they were not going to believe. Thus do We recompense the criminal people.﴾

The address returned to the polytheists, resuming from its beginning at His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah﴾ [Yunus: 3] up to His saying: ﴿that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ [Yunus: 5], on account of the parallel between them and the nations before them in being deluded by the postponement of punishment from them, until destruction befell them suddenly. This verse is both a threat and an admonition with what befell their likes.

The sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿And if Allah were to hasten for people the evil﴾ [Yunus: 11], through what it contains of warning that evil may descend upon them, but the punishment of Allah is not hastened. So He set forth for them an example from what befell the nations before them, and their term of punishment was decreed for them, though they knew of nations among them who suffered total annihilation, such as 'Ad, Thamud and the people of Noah.

To emphasize the threat and warning, the sentence is reinforced with the oath particle (lam al-qasam) and (qad), which is for affirmation.

Al-ihlak (destruction): uprooting and annihilation.

Al-qurun: plural of qarn, originally a long period of time; what is meant here is the peoples of the generations. Its explanation has preceded at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did they not see how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ [al-An'am: 6] in Surat al-An'am.

His saying ﴿from before you﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (hal) describing al-qurun.

Lamma is a noun of time meaning "when," in the verified view, and it is followed by a sentence.

The Arabs frequently placed lamma at the beginning of its clause, so the flavor of the conditional was imparted to it by this placement, and it resembled conditionals, because it is followed by a sentence resembling the conditional clause, and because its governing element is a past-tense verb; thus it required two clauses and resembled the conditional particles.

The meaning: We destroyed them when they did wrong, that is, they associated partners with Allah, and their messengers came to them with clear proofs, such as Hud and Salih, but they did not believe.

The clause ﴿and their messengers came to them﴾ is conjoined to the clause "they did wrong."

Al-bayyinat: plural of bayyinah, which is the proof of truthfulness. Its explanation has preceded at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There has come to you a clear proof from your Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 157] in Surat al-An'am.

The clause ﴿and they were not going to believe﴾ is conjoined to it. The three clauses together are what the destruction is timed by: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the cities until He sent to their mother [city] a messenger﴾ [al-Qasas: 59].

The negation of their faith is expressed with the form of the lam of denial, for emphasis in its negation, indicating despair of their faith.

The clause ﴿Thus do We recompense the criminal people﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil). The definite article in ﴿the criminal people﴾ is for comprehensiveness, so it encompasses the past generations and encompasses the addressees, and thus it was a warning to Quraysh that they would suffer what those suffered. What is meant by criminality is its utmost degree, which is polytheism.

The discussion of ﴿Thus do We recompense the criminal people﴾ is like the discussion of its counterpart just before. Likewise the mention of the word "people" is as it is in its counterpart in this surah and in al-Baqarah.

Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 14:

﴿Then We made you successors (khalā'if) in the land after them, so that We might see how you would act.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on "We destroyed (ahlaknā)," and the particle "thumma" (then) indicates a considerable interval between the two periods, meaning: "Then We made you replace them in the land." The use of "thumma" here to conjoin one clause to another implies a sequence of rank (tarākhī al-rutbī), because their being made successors is more important than the destruction of the generations before them, owing to the favour (minna) it contains for them, and because it gave them something in exchange for those who were destroyed.

Khalā'if is the plural of khalīfa (successor). It was discussed earlier in His words: ﴿And it is He who made you successors of the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 165], in Surat al-An'am.

The "land" (al-arḍ) here means the lands of the Arabs, so the definite article in it is for a known referent (al-ʿahd), because those addressed had succeeded ʿĀd, Thamūd, Ṭasm, Jadīs and Jurhum in their dwellings, generally speaking.

[p. 115]

Al-naẓar (looking/seeing) is used here for certain knowledge, since naẓar is the strongest path to knowledge. Thus the meaning of ﴿so that We might see﴾ is "so that We might know," that is, so that We might know with a knowledge connected to your deeds. The intended knowledge is therefore its connection in the sense of actual realisation (al-taʿallug al-tanjīzī).

Kayfa is an interrogative noun that suspends (muʿallaq) the verb of knowing from the action; it is in the accusative governed by naẓara. The meaning in such a construction is: "so that We might know the answer to how you act." Iyas ibn Qabisa said:

"I came forward while the spear swayed between us, so that I might know which of its (the battle's) men were cowards and which were brave."

That is: so that I might know the answer to which of its men were cowards.

Ibn 'Ashur made their being installed as successors in the land the cause of God's knowledge of their deeds as a metaphor (kināya) for the manifestation of their deeds in reality, whether they were of the kind that pleases God or of the kind that does not. When their deeds become manifest, God knows them with the knowledge of existing things, even though He knows eternally (ʿilman azalīyan) that this will occur. Likewise, the meaning of Iyas ibn Qabisa's verse is "so that the coward might become manifest from the brave." The purpose of giving the advance as the cause is not that He acquires knowledge of the coward and the brave, but He uses that as a metaphor for the manifestation of the coward and the brave. A parallel to this was already mentioned in His words, exalted is He: ﴿and that God may know those who believe and take from among you martyrs﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 140], in Surat Āl ʿImrān.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (*al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*) on surah 10, verse 15:

﴿When Our clear verses are recited to them, those who do not hope for meeting Us say, "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it." Say, "It is not for me to change it on my own accord. I follow only what is revealed to me. Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous day."﴾

This is a conjunction ('atf) with the clause ﴿And if God were to hasten evil for people...﴾ [Yunus: 11] and what follows, because that clause arises from their saying, ﴿O God, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], as was mentioned earlier. That is one of the methods of denial. Then this verse relates another method of their denial of the Prophet ﷺ, namely that the Qur'an is revealed to him from God, the Exalted. They imagine that the Prophet ﷺ composed the Qur'an on his own accord, and for this reason they made part of their denial that they say to him, ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it,﴾ offering him the hope that they would believe in it if it were different or altered to suit their desires.

The meaning of ﴿other than this﴾ is "contrary to it." What is intended is opposition to the entire Qur'an, by turning away from it and producing another book with different styles, like the books of Persian stories and epics, since their words allow no other meaning. Their intent is not that he should bring other surahs different from those already revealed, because that already exists, and they have no purpose in that if its meaning is of the same kind as what came before it.

He described the verses as ﴿clear﴾ to intensify the astonishment at their request to change them, not at a request for him to change it, since there is no hope of anything better than it.

Al-tabdil (change) means alteration. It may apply to essences, as when you say, "I exchanged the dinars for dirhams," and it may apply to attributes, as when you say, "I changed the ring into a seal." Since they had already mentioned bringing something other, it is determined that the intended meaning of change is the other sense, namely changing the attributes. Thus the intended meaning of "other" in their saying ﴿other than this﴾ is words other than what he had brought before, which would not contain what they dislike and what angers them. What is meant by change is that he would deliberately take the existing Qur'an and alter the verses containing expressions that condemn polytheism by praising it, expressions that condemn their idols by praising them, expressions about resurrection and rising by their opposites, and threats against them by expressions of good news.

They called what they asked him to bring a Qur'an because it is a substitute for that which is named the Qur'an, for the Qur'an is the proper name of the book brought by Muhammad ﷺ. That is, "Bring something other than this, which you call a Qur'an."

The pronoun in ﴿change it﴾ refers to the demonstrative, meaning "or change this."

The change was left general in the verse because it is known to the listeners.

Furthermore, their statement may be meant seriously, or they may intend it as mockery. In either case, God commanded His Prophet ﷺ to answer them in a way that removes their doubt from their souls if they are serious, or from the souls of those who hear them among their common people, so that those people might take their words seriously and wait for a change to the Qur'an.

The third-person pronoun in ﴿when it is recited to them﴾ refers either to the people, meaning the polytheists, or to ﴿those who do not hope for meeting Us﴾ [Yunus: 7] in His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who do not hope for meeting Us﴾ [Yunus: 7].

Placing the adverbial phrase ﴿when it is recited﴾ before its governing verb ﴿say those who do not hope for meeting Us﴾ serves to emphasize that time in which the verses are recited to them, and at which they utter this statement, in order to express astonishment at their words and the weakness of their reasoning.

Because the governing verb of the adverbial phrase is a past-tense verb, it is known that their statement belongs to the past. Hence the adverbial phrase is attached to a clause whose verb is present, ﴿is recited﴾, which indicates that this present tense is not meant to refer to the present or the future, since the past cannot be taken to occur in the present or the future. Therefore it is determined that the use of the present verb is solely to indicate repetition and recurrence, meaning: this is what they say whenever the verses are recited to them.

The referent of ﴿those who do not hope for meeting Us﴾ [Yunus: 7] is the same as the referent of the pronoun in ﴿to them,﴾ so the context called for a pronoun. The use of the relative construction was only because those who do not hope for meeting God became known for the polytheists, so this description became like a proper name for them, as we pointed out earlier at His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who do not hope for meeting Us and are content with the life of this world﴾ [Yunus: 7]. There is no causal relationship here between the relative clause and the predicate, so the relative form does not indicate the reason for the predicate's construction.

Since their request has an explicit meaning, namely bringing another Qur'an or changing the verses of the existing Qur'an, and an implied, allusive meaning, namely that it is not sent down from God and that the one who brought it was not sent by God, the answer to their saying has two parts. The first is what God taught him in His saying, ﴿Say, "It is not for me to change it on my own accord,"﴾ which answers their explicit request. The second is what He taught him in His saying, ﴿Say, "If God had willed, I would not have recited it to you,"﴾ [Yunus: 16], which answers the necessary implication of their words.

It is reported from Mujahid that he named some people who made this statement, who were five: 'Abd Allah ibn Umayya, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Mikraz ibn Hafs, 'Amr ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Qays, and al-'As ibn 'Amir. They said to the Prophet ﷺ, "Bring a Qur'an that does not contain abandoning the worship of idols, al-Lat, al-'Uzza, Manat, and Hubal, and does not contain criticism of them."

The answer to their request came as a comprehensive statement, fulfilling the right of wondrous brevity, and relying on the principle that the question clarifies the intended meaning of the answer. They sensed the impossibility of changing the Qur'an on the part of the Messenger ﷺ. This is a sufficient answer, because change includes bringing something other than it and altering some of its structures. Moreover, if changing it, which is altering some of its words and purposes, is impossible, then nullifying all of it and bringing something other is even more clearly impossible.

The answer came in the most emphatic form of negation, ﴿It is not for me﴾, meaning that changing it is not something within my possession.

The word ﴿on my own accord﴾ (tilqa') is a verbal noun of the pattern tif'al. The common pattern of tif'al is with a open tā' (tafʿāl), but tilqā' is an anomaly in this regard, as are tibyān and timthāl, meaning meeting, clarification, and standing before, and they came with a kasra on the tā', with no fourth example. Then tilqā' was applied to the direction of meeting, and then applied generally to direction and place, as in His saying, ﴿And when he turned toward (tilqā') Madyan﴾ [al-Qasas: 22]. So the meaning of ﴿from my own accord﴾ is "from my own direction." This prepositional phrase functions as a circumstantial qualifier that emphasizes the clause ﴿It is not for me to change it,﴾ and such a qualifier is called emphasizing for the other, since change can only come from the one who changes. So this circumstantial qualifier is not restrictive, for it is not possible to suppose that he would change, from God's direction, the change they desire. The meaning is that he is a conveyer, not one who disposes freely.

The clause ﴿I follow only what is revealed to me﴾ gives the reason for the clause ﴿It is not for me to change it,﴾ meaning: I follow only the revelation, and I have no right to alter it. The particle ma is verbal (masdariyyah). Following the revelation means conveying what has been obtained through it, which is what has been entrusted.

The word "following" (ittiba') is used metaphorically for not exercising discretion, based on the resemblance to the literal following, which means not going beyond tracing one's steps in walking.

The negative in and the exceptive particle establish a restriction on the scope of following to what God has revealed, and this is a relative restriction (qasr idafi), meaning: I convey only what has been revealed to me, not something invented that I could then alter and change. The evidence that it is relative is that it comes as an answer to the rejection of their request.

Therefore, whoever seeks to use this restriction as proof that the Prophet ﷺ was not permitted to exercise ijtihad (independent reasoning, meaning the scholarly exertion of judgment) has departed from the speech's proper course.

The clause ﴿Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord﴾ and so on stands as a reason for the clause ﴿I follow only what is revealed to me,﴾ and for this reason it is separated from it. It is joined with the particle inna for emphasis, and inna indicates causation.

His saying ﴿if I disobey my Lord﴾ means: if I disobey Him by bringing another Qur'an and changing it on my own accord.

The context of the speech indicates that bringing another Qur'an other than this means nullifying this Qur'an and replacing it with something else, and that changing it means altering the meanings and realities of what it contains, which is impossible.

For this reason the Messenger ﷺ was not instructed to say here, "Except what God wills," or anything similar.

This is an answer to the necessary implication of their demand, and to its implicit accusation that they charged the Messenger (ﷺ) with lying about God in his claim to have been sent and to have had the Qur'an revealed to him, as was mentioned in the answer before it. Because it is an independent answer to a meaning they intended in their speech, the command concerning it came separated from the first, not conjoined to it, to signal its independence and that it is not a completion of the first answer.

[Page 120]

In this answer there is an argument (istidlal) that he is sent from God Most High, and that he did not fabricate the Qur'an from himself. Within its folds lie many proofs. The argument is organized by negating the contradictory of the desired conclusion in order to establish the desired conclusion. His saying ﴿If God had willed, I would not have recited it to you﴾ has the estimate: if God had willed that I not recite it to you, I would not have recited it. The object of the verb of willing is often omitted in the conditional clause, because the consequent indicates it. The argument was built on negating God's willing, through negating the recitation of the Qur'an, because that is the claim of the disbelievers, who assumed it is not from God. Thus the argument was a refutation of their claim at the outset and an affirmation of his claim in its outcome. This combination of the two matters is among the wondrous forms of argument. That is: if God had willed that I not bring you this Qur'an, He would not have sent me with it, and I would have remained in the state I was in from the beginning of my life.

The second proof is implicit, namely the implication of the answer of the conditional particle lau. The answer of lau requires a consistent implied reversal in meaning, by affirming the contradictory of the answer. It may be omitted, and it may be mentioned, as in the saying of Ubayy ibn Sulma ibn Rabi'a:

"Had any hooved creature flown before her, she would have flown; but it did not fly."

Its estimate here is: If God had willed that I not recite it, I would not have recited it, but I recited it to you. Its recitation is the proof of the messengerhood, because its recitation includes its inimitability (i'jaz) in knowledge, since it came from one who was not among the people of knowledge and wisdom, and its inimitability in eloquence, since it came as a speech that defeated all the people of the language despite their combined efforts in eloquence and the differences in their ranks. It is not the nature of any created being to be superior to all of them, nor is it the nature of his speech that none of them could produce its like.

Therefore the clause ﴿So I have indeed dwelt among you a lifetime before it. Will you not then reason?﴾ was made to branch from the argument, as a reminder to them of his well-known past state among them, which was the state of being unlettered (ummiyya). That is: I had indeed been among you for a long period, forty years, while you watched the stages of my upbringing, and you saw in them no state resembling the state of greatness and utmost perfection that he reached when God revealed the message to him. Nor did you see in him any eloquence of speech, or any renown for debating the people of eloquence, oratory and poetry, resembling the eloquence of the speech he uttered from the revelation of the Qur'an. For if his state after the revelation had been a customary state, and the eloquence of the speech he brought likewise customary, then he would have had, from the beginnings of his upbringing, the preparations that lead to this end, and the acquiring of that would have been in stages and gradually. Undoubtedly, then, the dissimilarity of the two states shows that this latter state is purely a divine state, and that this speech is revealed to him from God, with no action of his own in it.

This speech would not have been a proof against the polytheists, nor a refutation of their claim, except insofar as it is built upon the recitation of the Qur'an. Thus mention of the Qur'an is the axis of the argument. Then, when the clause ﴿So I have indeed dwelt among you a lifetime before it﴾ branched from it, it was a reminder to them of his state before he recited the Qur'an to them. Were it not for these two matters, the argument would have reverted to begging the question (muṣādara), that is, an argument by the very claim itself, because they could then say: God did not send you to us, since He willed not to send you to us, but you fabricated against God what He did not say.

This is the explanation of how this argument is organized from this verse.

The argument has thus led, in this manner, to proving to them the inimitability of the Qur'an and the unlettered state of the Prophet. The word ﴿I recited it﴾ has a force that no other word has, because it includes a reciter of speech, a recited speech, and the one who causes that recitation to be made.

By the first, it points to the miracle of the capacity to recite the Book together with the established fact of his being unlettered, since the style of religious books is different from the style that the Arabs knew from their poets and orators.

By the second, it points to the Qur'an itself, which is a miracle indicating the truthfulness of the one who brings it, because of what it contains of truths and religious guidance, which is the nature of the prophets of religions and their scholars. As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you did not recite before it any book, nor did you write it with your right hand; otherwise the falsifiers would have doubted﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 48]. ﴿Rather, it is clear signs in the breasts of those who have been given knowledge; and none rejects Our signs except the wrongdoers﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 49].

By the third, it points to the fact that it is a speech from God Most High. Thus through this argument, the indication of the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ) in his messagehood from God Most High was organized.

Recitation (tilawa) is reading what is written or reciting what is memorized. It therefore implies the conveying of speech from someone other than the one conveying it. It was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Solomon﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102], in Surat al-Baqarah, and at His saying: ﴿And when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith﴾ [al-Anfal: 2], in Surat al-Anfal.

﴿Adrakum﴾ means "made you know" or "informed you". The verb of knowing (diraya), when it relates to a thing, takes its object directly at times and with the preposition bi at other times. One says darraytuhu and darraytu bihi. It came in this verse in the second usage, which is the more common in Sibawayh's report.

The majority read ﴿nor would He have made you know of it﴾ with the negative particle (wa-la), conjoined to ﴿what I recited to you﴾. That is: if God had willed, He would not have commanded me to recite the Qur'an to you, nor would He have informed you of it. Al-Bazzi transmitted from Ibn Kathir, in one of his two narrations, an initial lam in place of the negative particle la, that is, without an alif after the lam. Then it is conjoined to the answer of lau, and the lam is an extra lam for emphasis, as is its role in the answer of lau. The meaning on this reading is: if God had willed, I would not have recited it to you; and if He had willed, He would have made you understand its meanings, so you would not lie.

The branching of the clause ﴿So I have indeed dwelt among you﴾ is a branching of the proof from the conditional clause and its inseparability from its two sides.

Al-'umr (lifetime) is life. It is derived from 'umran (civilization), because the duration of life is the period in which the living populate the worldly realm. 'Umr is also applied to a long period which, if a person lived its measure, he would have taken his share of endurance. This is what is meant here, as shown by the indefiniteness of ﴿'umuran﴾. The meaning is not "I dwelt for the duration of my life," because his life had not ended. Rather, what is meant is a period whose measure is that of a customary lifetime, that is, the lifespan of any one of the people. The meaning is: I dwelt among you forty years before the descent of the Qur'an.

﴿'Umuran﴾ is in the accusative as a substitute for a time adverb, since a measure of time is intended.

Al-lubth (remaining) is staying in a place for a period. It was discussed at His saying: ﴿He said, "How long have you remained?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 259], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The locative sense in ﴿fikum﴾ means "among your community," that is, among you.

Qabl and ba'd, when attached to entities, refer to some state of the entity indicated by the context, that is, before its descent. The pronoun in ﴿qablihi﴾ refers to the Qur'an.

The branching of the clause ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ from the conditional clause and what branches from it is a branching of rebuke and wonder at the establishment of the argument against them, since their condition has shown that they are like one who does not reason.

Therefore the word ta'qilun (you reason) was chosen, because reason is the first degree of perception. Its object is either omitted, since the preceding discourse indicates it. The estimate: will you not reason that such a combination of unlettered-ness with bringing this wondrous Book in its eloquence and meanings can only be the state of one upon whom God has bestowed His message? For such a thing is not normally achievable for anyone, and nothing approaching it is achievable except after lengthy study with scholars, reading earlier books, debating scholars, and conversing with the people of eloquence, orators and poets, over a long time and a great lifespan. How then could what is greater than that customary attainment be achieved all at once by one who spent his life among them in their lands, whom they watched morning and evening, and whose land was not known for the pursuit of the sciences? Nor was there among them any People of the Book, except those who devoted themselves to worship and cut themselves off from mixing with people.

Or ta'qilun may be taken as intransitive, so no object is estimated, meaning: will you not be people who reason, so that you would know that such a state can only come from the revelation of God.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 17:

﴿Who does greater wrong than one who invents a lie against Allah or denies His signs? Indeed, the criminals will not succeed.﴾

When the proof had been established against them, with what they had no means of disowning, the verse follows it with a consequence drawn from their fabrication of lies, which was already known from their conduct: their taking partners besides Him, as indicated by His words: ﴿And We destroyed the generations before you when they did wrong﴾ [Yunus: 13], meaning they associated partners, down to His words: ﴿so that We may see how you will act﴾ [Yunus: 14]; and their denial of the signs of Allah in their saying: ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it﴾ [Yunus: 15]. In this there is also a directing of the speech toward its suitability to be taken as an even-handed judgment between Him and them, since they had implicitly charged Him with fabrication against Allah when they said: ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this﴾ [Yunus: 15], and openly denied that the Qur'an is from Allah. So when He had established the proof against them that it is from Allah, and that it is not for him to bring it from his own accord, He drew the consequence that the one who invents a lie against Allah and the ones who deny His signs are both the greatest of people in wrongdoing, and that there is no one more wrong than either of them. This is a form of matching the opponent so that he stumbles: the speech appears to him to be even-handed between the two, but when the meaning becomes clear, its thrust is found to fall upon the opponent alone.

Page 124

The division (tafriʿ) is suitable for both meanings, and it is a consequence of what came before it, which contained that they associated partners with Allah and denied the Qur'an.

The place of "aw" (or) under both readings is that of division (taqsim), which is either a division of states (taqassum ahwal) or a division of types (taqassum anwaa').

The interrogation is one of denial (istifham inkari). Injustice (zulm) here means transgression (i'tida'). That either of the two matters is the greatest wrong is because it is a transgression against the Creator through lying about Him and denying His signs.

The clause ﴿Indeed, He, the criminals will not succeed﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyil), and its position requires that its generality include those mentioned in the preceding speech, which is concluded (with the letter ya pointed from below, i.e., the verb is in the passive form), so it implies that those people are criminals and that they will not succeed.

Success (falah) has been discussed in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And those are the successful﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah.

The emphasis of the clause with the emphatic particle (inna) looks to the inclusiveness of the general term "the criminals" to include the addressees, because they deny being among the criminals.

Opening the clause with the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n) is for the purpose of emphasizing its content.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 18:**

﴿They worship besides Allah what neither harms them nor benefits them, and they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah." Say, "Do you inform Allah of what He does not know in the heavens or on earth?" Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾

This is a conjunction (*'atf*) with the sentence ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾ [Yunus: 15], a conjunction of one narrative to another. This is another narrative about the forms of their disbelief: they said, ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this﴾ [Yunus: 15] when the verses of the Qur'an are recited to them. And among their disbelief is that they worship idols and say, "They are our intercessors with Allah."

The connection between the two narratives is that both contain a disbelief they displayed in the form of mockery and derision, and the suggestion that they have an excuse for persisting in disbelief. Perhaps (just as they implied that if a Qur'an other than the one recited to them came, or if what they wished to alter were altered, they would believe), whenever the Prophet (ﷺ) warned them of the punishment of Allah, they said, "Our gods will intercede for us with Allah." It is narrated that al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said it, on the basis of supposing what does not occur: "If it is the Day of Resurrection, al-Lat and al-'Uzza will intercede for me." This is like the statement of al-'As ibn Wa'il, who was a polytheist, to Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, who was a Muslim, when he demanded from him payment for a sword he had made: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, which your companion (meaning the Prophet (ﷺ)) reports, I will have wealth, and I will pay you from it."
Concerning this, Allah, the Exalted, revealed His saying: ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our verses and said, "I will surely be given wealth and children"?﴾ [Maryam: 77], and so on.

It is also permissible for the sentence ﴿they worship...﴾ etc. to be a conjunction with the sentence ﴿Who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah?﴾ [Yunus: 17], since their worship of what neither harms them nor benefits them is a form of invention (*iftira'*).

The choice of the relative pronoun in ﴿what neither harms them nor benefits them﴾ serves the alert implied by the relative clause, that they are mistaken in worshipping what neither harms nor benefits. It also prepares for the conjunction of ﴿and they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah"﴾, to belittle their opinion that they may hope for intercession from those idols, since they have no power to harm or benefit in this world, so they are even less capable in the Hereafter.

The choice of the present tense in ﴿they worship﴾ and ﴿they say﴾ is to evoke the strange state of their continuing to worship them, meaning: they worshipped the idols and continue to worship them, in wonder at their determination in their error, and at their saying ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾, whereby they acknowledged that the one who disposes of affairs is Allah.

The mention of the negation of harm is placed before the negation of benefit because what is demanded of the polytheists is that they abandon worship of the idols. The custodians of the idols used to frighten their worshippers that the idols would inflict harm upon them and their children, just as the wife of Tufayl ibn 'Amr al-Dawsi said when he informed her that he had embraced Islam and invited her to embrace it: "Are you not afraid for the little ones from Dhu al-Shara?" So the beginning with the negation of harm was intended to remove the illusions of the polytheists on this point, which prevent many of them from abandoning the worship of idols.

Allah commanded His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to respond to them with a mockery of them: that they have informed Allah that they have intercessors with Him. The meaning of this is that since this was something they had invented, and it does not occur, its invention was treated as though they had informed Allah of it while He did not know it. This became a metonymy (*kinaya*) for its falsehood, because what Allah does not know to occur is non-existent. From this is the saying of one who wishes to deny something about himself: "Allah did not know this of me." And in its opposite is their saying to affirm the occurrence of something: "Allah knows that such-and-such," until it became among the Arabs one of the formulas of oath.

﴿In the heavens or on earth﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) from the omitted pronoun after ﴿يَعْلَمُ﴾ (ya'lamu, "He knows"), which refers back to *ma* ("what"). The estimated sense is: "what He does not know," that is, existing in the heavens or on earth. The purpose of mentioning both is to generalize the places, as is the usage of combining opposites such as "the east and the west."

The negative particle is repeated after the conjunctive particle to increase the emphasis on the negation.

The interrogative in ﴿Do you inform﴾ is for denial and rebuke, and *al-inba'* means informing.

The sentence ﴿Glory be to Him, and exalted is He﴾ is an expression of declaration of transcendence (*tanzih*). It is disconnected from what precedes it, which is why it is separated (*fasl*). The discussion of its counterpart was previously made at His saying: ﴿And they attributed to Him sons and daughters without knowledge. Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they describe﴾ [al-An'am: 100], in Surat al-An'am.

The *ma* in His saying ﴿above what they associate﴾ is a verbal-noun (*masdariyya*) particle, meaning: "above their association," that is, exalted is He above that being established for Him.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read ﴿تُشْرِكُونَ﴾ (tushrikun, "you associate") with the second-person (*ta'*), on the basis that it is part of what is being said. The rest (the other readers) read it with the third-person (*ya'*), on the basis that it is a continuation of the address with the phrase ﴿Say﴾. On both readings, it deserves to be separated (*fasl*) because of the complete disconnection.

[Page 127]

This is a parenthetical clause (*jumla mu'tarida*) placed between the clause *wa-ya'budūna* (and they worship) and the clause ﴿And they say: "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ [Yunus: 20]. The reason for the parenthesis is the earlier statement ﴿Do you inform God of what He does not know in the heavens or on the earth?﴾ [Yunus: 18]. The worship of idols and the invention of the idea that they intercede is part of the division that the misguided among mankind introduced into the sound creed in which God created people at the beginning of their existence. It therefore falls within the rebuke contained in that statement.

The form of restriction (*qasr*, an exclusive construction that limits a predicate to a subject) is used to intensify the assertion, because it is an important and remarkable report, and it belongs to the highest rank among the civilizational wisdoms and historical realities. The restriction is an emphasis upon emphasis, since it contains two forms: an affirmation of what is affirmed and a negation of everything else. It is therefore stronger than the emphasis that answers a denial, and so it indicates a response to a strong denial.

The restriction is made appropriate here by its occurring directly after the dispute with those who changed the true religion and promoted their sect with false excuses, such as their saying ﴿These are our intercessors with God﴾ [Yunus: 18] and their saying ﴿We worship them only so that they may bring us nearer to God in closeness﴾ [al-Zumar: 3]. This contrasts with the verse in Surat al-Baqara ﴿People were one community﴾ [al-Baqara: 213], which occurs in the context of a dispute with the People of the Book, in accordance with the statement ﴿Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them﴾ [al-Baqara: 211]. The People of the Book do not deny that people were once one community. The verse of this surah therefore points to unity in belief, and for this reason it expresses the division that arose afterward through the notion of *ikhtilaf* (divergence), which implies blame and is followed by a warning in the statement ﴿Had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord...﴾ up to its end. The verse of Surat al-Baqara points to unity in law, which is gathered together by the natural *hanifiyya* (pure monotheistic disposition, *fitra*). For this reason it expresses the division that befell it by saying that God sent prophets as bearers of good news and as warners. Then the mention of divergence comes incidentally after that, in the statement ﴿And He sent down with them the Book with truth, to judge between people concerning that over which they differed﴾ [al-Baqara: 213]. By this is meant the divergence among followers of the various laws, in accordance with the statement ﴿None differed over it except those who had been given it﴾ [al-Baqara: 213].

The discussion of ﴿People were one community﴾ [al-Baqara: 213] has already been given in Surat al-Baqara.

*Al-nās* (the people, mankind) is a collective noun for humanity, and its definite article is for comprehensiveness (*istighraq*, encompassing all members). *Umma* (community) is a great group that has one state in some matter.

[Page 128]

What is meant here is one community in religion. The context indicates that what is meant is that they were one in the true religion, which is monotheism, because the truth is that over which the agreement of humanity is possible, since it arises from the soundness of belief free of error and distortion. When man was created, he was created upon a complete *fitra*, far from artificiality. This is conceivable only in the knowledge of God, the Exalted, and not in deeds, since deeds vary according to different needs. If error and mistake can occur among humans, then error is not universal over their minds. It is therefore established that people, in the knowledge of God, the Exalted, were one community agreed upon monotheism, because when God created man He made him upon sound reason that accords with reality, and He placed in his reason the awareness of a Creator and that He is One, as an innate placement, just as He placed instinctive inspirations in the species of animals. This was confirmed by revelation to the father of humanity, Adam, peace be upon him.

Then humanity introduced into their minds the far-reaching divergence from the truth, through false divergence, imagination and illusions, and through corrupt analogies. This falls within the meaning of His statement, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We created man in the best of stature﴾ [al-Tin: 4] ﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tin: 5] ﴿Except for those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Tin: 6]. It is therefore established that what is meant in this verse by the people being one community is unity in the truth, and that the intended purpose is to praise that state, because the purpose of this verse is to show the corruption of polytheism and to demonstrate the error of its adherents, by showing that their first ancestor was not like them in corruption of mind. The addressees held their ancestors in high esteem, and the form of restriction indicates that the intention is to nullify the claim of anyone who claims otherwise.

Its placement after the mention of those who worship besides God idols that neither harm them nor benefit them indicates that they are the ones intended for nullification, since they used to suppose that what they were upon of error was the religion of truth. For this reason, [it is reported that] they depicted Abraham and Ishmael casting divining arrows in the Ka'ba. The Prophet ﷺ said on the day of the Conquest: "They lied, by God; they never cast lots with them at all." He then recited: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a *hanif*, a Muslim, and he was not of the polytheists﴾ [Al 'Imran: 67]. In this way the definite article in *al-nās* is taken as comprehensive.

It is also permissible that by *al-nās* is meant specifically the Arabs, by the indication of the address, and the intention would be to remind them of the covenant of their father Abraham, peace be upon him, when he and his sons and descendants were upon the *hanifiyya* and monotheism, as He said, the Exalted: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am free of what you worship, except He who created me, for He will guide me"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 26] ﴿And He made it a lasting word among his descendants that they might return﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 28]. That is, among his descendants from among the Arabs. In this case the definite article is for a known covenant (*'ahd*, specific reference).

[Page 129]

The clause ﴿Had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾ is a report that the truth is one, that this divergence is blameworthy, and that had it not been that God willed to give mankind respite until the Day of Recompense, He would have shown them the decisive resolution of their divergence by annihilating the falsifier and preserving the one who is right. This word was left general here and was indicated in Surat al-Shura by His statement: ﴿Had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, for a specified term, the matter would have been decided between them﴾ [al-Shura: 14].

The term (*ajal*) is the term of the survival of nations, and that is at the extinction of the world. The judgment between them is therefore postponed until the Day of Reckoning. Clearer than this in explaining the meaning of (the word) is His statement in Surat Hud: ﴿Had your Lord willed, He would have made people one community, but they will continue to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy; and for that He created them﴾ [Hud: 118–119] ﴿And the word of your Lord was fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together"﴾ [Hud: 119]. Its explanation will come later.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in His statement ﴿concerning that over which they differ﴾ is for the sake of rhyme with the verse-ending (*fāṣila*, the rhyming end of a verse).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 20:

﴿They say, "Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "The unseen belongs only to Allah, so wait; indeed, I am with you among those who wait."﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) on the clause ﴿And they worship, besides Allah, that which neither harms them nor benefits them﴾ [Yunus: 18]. Having mentioned their fabrication concerning divinity, He then negates their slander concerning prophethood.

The pronoun in ʿalayhi ("to him") refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), even though he has not been mentioned before it in the verse, for knowledge of what is meant by the pronoun makes mention of its referent unnecessary. The mention of the Prophet (ﷺ) among them in their assemblies and private conversations, during his residence among them after the Prophethood, was their preoccupying concern, so the third-person pronoun was used in their speech without a prior referent, and the addressees knew that he was the one intended. Many similar instances occur in the Qur'an.

In His saying, ﴿Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾, lawlā (why not) is a particle of urging (taḥḍīḍ). The nature of urging is that it is addressed to the one being urged, since urging is a form of demand, and the nature of demand is that it is addressed to the one demanded. For this reason the attachment of the verb "sent down" to a third-person pronoun in this verse is interpreted in one of two ways:

Either it is an iltifāt (shift of grammatical person), the original wording being "Why has not a sign been sent down to you?", and it is part of reporting speech by its meaning, like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Tell My servants who have believed to establish prayer﴾ [Ibrahim: 31], meaning, "Tell them: establish." The purpose of this is the purpose of iltifāt, to renew the listener's attentiveness.

Or this statement was made among themselves, so that some of them might display to others a doubt about the non-existence of the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ); or it was said to the Muslims in hope that they would turn them back to disbelief.

The sign (āyah) is the mark of truthfulness. They wanted a miracle that breaks habit, according to their own proposals, like their saying, ﴿Or you ascend into the sky﴾ [al-Isra: 93], and their saying, ﴿Why has he not been given the like of what was given to Musa?﴾ [al-Qasas: 48]. This arises from their ignorance of the realities of things, and their submitting imagination and illusion to judge the realities of things. They suppose that Allah is eager to manifest the truthfulness of His Messenger (ﷺ), and that their denial provokes Him so that He becomes angry and hastens to accommodate their obstinacy in order to be rid of them. If He does not do so, they have silenced Him and rendered Him powerless, while He is the Able. Thus they imagined that the one claiming the mission on His behalf is not truthful in his claim, and they did not realize that Allah has measured the order of affairs with precise measure, established realities and their causes, caused events to proceed according to the order He has determined, and made matters reach their appointed times that He has set. The denial of deniers or the obstinacy of the ignorant does not harm Him, for He has set for them what befits them of deterrents in the Hereafter without doubt, and in this world some [warnings]. All of this proceeds according to systems that wisdom requires, which the question of a questioner does not move Him to change, nor the folly of a fool. He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing.

Thus they made the Messenger's (ﷺ) persistence in calling them with the proofs that Allah commanded him to call them with, and his not replacing that with other signs according to their desire, into evidence that he is not supported by Allah. They inferred from this the negation that Allah sent him, for had He sent him, He would have supported him with what necessitates acceptance from him among those to whom he was sent. But the wretched ones did not realize that Allah sent the Messenger (ﷺ) only as a mercy to them and a seeking of their welfare, and that their not accepting His mercy and guidance does not harm him.

For this reason, in reporting their speech, He departed from the name Allah to the word "Lord" joined to the pronoun of the Messenger (ﷺ), in His saying "from his Lord," as an allusion to the lordship specific to the connection with the Messenger (ﷺ): the lordship of the one who chooses (in the form of the active participle) over the chosen one (in the form of the passive participle) from among the rest of creation, which requires anger for his anger. They supposed that Allah's anger is like the anger of creatures, requiring haste toward retribution, and they did not know the secrets of divine wisdom, the divine judgment, and the sublime knowledge.

Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to answer their proposal with what is the guiding reality, even though it is higher than their perceptions: an answer containing an implicit threat to them, which is His saying, ﴿So say, "The unseen belongs only to Allah."﴾ The conjunction fā' of consequence was used here, and not in some of its counterparts, to indicate that their speech is followed by the answer, as is the manner of one firmly established in his state and steadfast in his matter.

Al-ghayb (the unseen) is what is hidden from people's senses among things. What is meant here is what comes into being of created things not customary in the worldly realm, of miracles. The explanation of this is His saying, ﴿Say, "The signs are only with Allah"﴾ [al-An'am: 109].

The lam is for ownership, meaning the hidden matters are not within the power of anyone except Allah. The statement came in the form of restriction (qaṣr) to refute them in their belief that it is within the capacity of the true Messenger to bring what his people ask of him of extraordinary things. They made the non-occurrence of their proposal a sign that he is not a messenger from Allah. Therefore He replied to them with the form of restriction, which indicates that the Messenger has no control over bringing about what they asked for, so that they would know that by their question they are casting themselves into audacity against Allah, Exalted is He, by way of silencing Him.

The clause ﴿So wait; indeed, I am with you among those who wait﴾ is a consequence of the clause ﴿The unseen belongs only to Allah﴾, meaning: my practice and your practice are nothing but waiting for what Allah brings, if He wills, like the saying of Nuh to his people: ﴿Only Allah will bring it to you, if He wills, and you will not be able to escape﴾ [Hud: 33].

This is an implicit threat to them, that what Allah brings they expect only as evil for themselves, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they said, "Why has not an angel been sent down to him?" Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and then they would not be reprieved﴾ [al-An'am: 8].

The "with" (maʿiyyah) in His saying "with you" is metaphorical, used for sharing in the general act of waiting.

[Page 133]

When he had related the rebellion of the polytheists, he explained here that they were heedless of it, lost in their arrogance and self-admiration because of the blessing and ease they enjoyed. Their enjoyment of blessings made them forget to expect the arrival of its opposite, so they varied their ways of denying God's threat with every kind of mockery, as He - may He be exalted - said: ﴿Leave Me with those who deny, the people of plenty, and give them a little respite﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11].

The discourse is in the manner of relating their state, and the one addressed is the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers. It also contains an indirect reminder to the disbelievers of the state of calamities that befell them, so that perhaps they would remember, and prepare the means of fear against the arrival of the punishment with which he warned them in His saying: ﴿Wait, then﴾, as in the hadith: "Get to know God in ease, and He will know you in hardship."

Thus, by ﴿the people﴾ is meant the people known and spoken of, by the context's indication, in the two senses previously mentioned in His saying - may He be exalted: ﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side﴾ [Yunus: 12].

It has been said that the verse alludes to what afflicted the Quraysh of famine for seven years, by the supplication of the Prophet (ﷺ). Then God removed the famine from them and sent down rain upon them. When they revived, they began to slander the signs of God, oppose the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and plot against him. The famine that afflicted the Quraysh is the one mentioned in Surat al-Dukhan, where they were warned of the "great seizing." Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the seizing of the Day of Badr. Thus this verse would have been revealed after the passing of the seven years, which were like the years of Joseph, and after they had been revived. So it would have been revealed after the tenth or eleventh year of the Prophethood.

The word ﴿made to taste﴾ (al-idhāqa) is used in the general sense of perception, either as a metaphor or figuratively, as previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿that he may taste the consequence of his affair﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 95], in Surat al-'Uqud.

[Page 133 ends]

[Page 134]

The word ﴿mercy﴾ (raḥma) here is applied to the effect of mercy, which is blessing and benefit, as in His saying: ﴿and spreads His mercy﴾ [al-Shura: 28].

The word ḍarrā' means harm (ḍurr). The word "touch" (mass) is used for afflicting. The meaning is: when a blessing reaches people after harm, such as rain after drought, safety after fear, and health after sickness.

The word idhā in His saying ﴿then, when they have a scheme﴾ is for suddenness (al-mufājaʾa), and it links the response of the conditional idhā, because the response is a nominal sentence, which cannot be connected to the conditional idhā that is usually followed by verbs, if it occurs as an adverbial clause; and if it occurs as a condition, it cannot be a response to it. Therefore the particle of suddenness (idhā al-fujā'iyya) was introduced upon the response clause, because the particle of suddenness indicates haste and speed in the content of the sentence. It thus gives the function of the particle fa of consequence, which is used to link the response of the condition to its condition. When the particle of suddenness comes, it dispenses with it.

The word makr (scheming) in its true sense is concealing harm and displaying it in the form of peace. It has been discussed before at His saying: ﴿And they schemed, and God schemed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54], in Surat Al 'Imran.

The word "in" (fī) in His saying ﴿concerning Our signs﴾ is for figurative containment, whose intended meaning is accompaniment, i.e., their scheming accompanying Our signs. The meaning of their scheming concerning the signs is that they scheme in a manner connected with them. That is because they give the impression that the signs of the Qur'an do not indicate the truthfulness of the Messenger, and they claim that if another sign were sent down upon him, they would believe in it. They are lying in that, and they only deny him out of obstinacy, arrogance, and preserving their religion of polytheism.

Since the discourse implicitly contained a warning to them, He commanded the Messenger to admonish them that God is swifter in scheming, i.e., swifter than you. So He made God's scheming against them swifter than their scheming against God's signs.

The superlative form (ism al-tafḍīl) indicates that the scheming of the disbelievers is also swift, because of what the particle of suddenness indicates of haste, which is speed. The meaning is: God is quicker in scheming against you than you are in scheming with respect to God's signs.

The word "aswa'" (swifter) is derived either from "asra'a," the augmented form used irregularly, or from "sara'a," the unaugmented form, based on its occurrence in speech, as reported by al-Farisi.

[Page 134 ends]

And the delay of God's punishment for them is called by the name "scheming," by way of the metaphor of representation (al-isti'āra al-tamthīliyya), because the form of that delay, in its concealment from them, is like the form of the act of the schemer. The reciprocity (al-mushākala) made it fitting, as previously mentioned in the verse of Al 'Imran.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Our messengers record what you scheme﴾ is a resumptive address (istiʾnāf) directed at the polytheists themselves, as a threat from God. Therefore it is separated from the preceding clause because the addressee differs. The emphasis of the clause is because the addressees believe otherwise, since they used to suppose that they were scheming against the Prophet (ﷺ), and that their scheme was proceeding against him without his perceiving it. So God informed them that the angels appointed to count the deeds record that. The purpose of this is that it is counted and reckoned against them and is not neglected, and it is a warning of punishment for it. This implies God's knowledge of that - may He be exalted.

He used the present tense in ﴿record﴾ (yaktubūna) and ﴿scheme﴾ (tamkurūna) to indicate recurrence, i.e., their recording recurs whenever their scheming recurs. So in His saying ﴿what you scheme﴾ there is no shift (iltifāt) from the third person to the second person, because the referents of the two pronouns differ.

The majority of readers recited ﴿what you scheme﴾ with the second-person ta. Rawh on the authority of Ya'qub recited (mā yamkurūna) with the third-person ya, the pronoun referring to ﴿the people﴾ in His saying ﴿And when We make the people taste mercy﴾. On this reading, the discourse is directed to the Prophet (ﷺ).

This sentence is a *badal ishtimal* (an apposition of inclusion, a grammatical term for a phrase that is a part of the thing it follows) of the preceding clause ﴿And when We let people taste mercy﴾ [Yunus: 21] to its end, because transgression on earth is included in the plotting against God's signs. The purpose of this clause is His saying:

[Page 135]
﴿Then when He has delivered them, behold, they commit transgression on earth﴾ [Yunus: 23], and what precedes it is a preparation and an incorporation of a reminder of favour. He follows the threat against ingratitude for the blessing with a mention of some of God's blessings upon them, then the harm that follows the blessing as a test and a reminder of their Creator, then how relief is granted to them out of mercy, yet a group of them rejects both blessings and does not take heed. So the purpose is that in this there are the greatest signs of God's oneness. How, then, can they say ﴿Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ [Yunus: 20], when everything has a sign? In all of this there is a reminder of favour upon them, a recording of their ingratitude for it, a sequence of signs coming upon them, and so that they are not deceived by the respite and do not suppose it to be approval of their disbelief or incapacity to seize them. This is a very elegant placement for this Qur'anic verse.

The attribution of causing them to travel (*taysir*) to God, may He be exalted, is on the basis that He is its cause, since He is the creator of the inspiration of thought and the powers of mental and physical movement. Thus the attribution is a rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*), and the restriction (*qasr*) conveyed by the clause ﴿He is the One who causes you to travel﴾ is an assertive restriction (*qasr idda'i*). The speech is used for reminding of favour and for an implicit rebuke of their failure in the duty of thankfulness.

*Ḥattā* here is inceptive (*ibtida'iyyah*), and it is an end point (*ghaya*) of the causing to travel specifically at sea. It is an end point with respect to what is conjoined to its complement, namely His saying ﴿they called upon God﴾ up to His saying ﴿without right﴾ [Yunus: 23]. What is being ended (*al-mughayya*) is what is in His saying "causes you to travel", namely the favour that implies it is a gentle and agreeable travel for people. So what comes after *ḥattā* and its conjoined clauses is the limit of that gentleness, because the state after *ḥattā*, at which the favoured travel ends, is the state in which they enter into adversity and harm. This arrangement is a wonderful weaving among the varieties of speech.

Among the fine points of style in the verse: since it is concerned with mentioning the blessing, it uses pronouns of address that are suitable for all listeners. When it was prepared for the transition to mentioning harm, there occurs a shift from pronouns of address to the pronoun of absence, to vary the style in a way that leads to what pertains specifically to the polytheists. So it says ﴿and they were carried along with them﴾ (*wa jarayna bihim*) in the manner of *iltifat* (shift of person), meaning "and they were carried along with you". Thus the pronouns were arranged to include both groups, until He said ﴿Then when He has delivered them, behold, they commit transgression on earth without right﴾ [Yunus: 23]. This is not among the qualities of believers, so the pronoun of absence here became purely for the polytheists. He excluded from the statement everyone other than those who transgress on earth without right, relying on the context, because those who transgress on earth without right do not include the Muslims.

This is a type of *iltifat* that the scholars of rhetoric (*ahl al-ma'ani*) did not point out, and it is like specification by way of allusion (*takhsis bi tariq al-ramz*).

[Page 136]
This verse has been counted among the examples of *iltifat* from address to absence in all its pronouns of absence, following al-Zamakhshari in *al-Kashshaf*, on the basis that the pronouns of address are for the polytheists and the pronouns of absence are also for them. What I have inclined to is more appropriate.

The use of the pronoun of absence began from the end of the mention of the blessing, at His saying ﴿and they were carried along with them by a good wind﴾, to make clear that the blessing enveloped them, and to indicate that the suddenness of the violent storm in the state of joy is intended to test and frighten them. It is thus a preparation for His saying ﴿and the waves came upon them from every place﴾.

Travel on land is well known to the Arabs, and likewise travel at sea. They used to sail the sea to Yemen and to the lands of Abyssinia. The Quraysh had the winter journey to Yemen, and they sometimes sailed the sea for that. Ṭarafa ibn al-'Abd described ships and their sailing, and 'Amr ibn Kulthum mentioned them in his *Mu'allaqa*, and al-Nabigha in his *Daliyya* (ode rhyming in d).

The majority of readers recite *yusayyirukum* with a *ya'* (taḥtiyya) at its beginning, with a damma, then an unpointed *sin*, followed by a *ya'*, then a *ra'*, from *al-sayr* (travel), meaning "makes you travel". Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read (*yanshurukum*) with a *ya'* with a fatḥa at its beginning, followed by a *nun*, then a dotted *shin*, then a *ra'*, from *al-nashr* (dispersal), which is scattering, in the manner of His saying ﴿then, behold, you are human beings dispersing﴾ [al-Rum: 20] and His saying ﴿then disperse throughout the land﴾ [al-Jumu'a: 10]. Ibn 'Atiyya said, citing 'Awf ibn Abi Jamila and Abu al-Zaghal: they (i.e., the people of Kufa) used to read "yanshurukum", then they looked into the Mushaf of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan and found it written *yusayyirukum* (i.e., with a *ya'*, an unpointed *sin*, and a *ya'*). The first one to write it thus was al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, meaning he ordered it to be written so in the Mushafs of the people of Kufa.

*Ḥattā* is an end point of the travel. Here it is inceptive, followed by the particle of surprise (*idha al-fuja'iyya*) and its answer. The clause and the end point are what the answer of *idha* conveys, namely His saying ﴿there came upon it a violent wind﴾. So the coming of the violent wind is the end point of the pleasant and favoured travel, since at that time the travel turns into calamity and disaster.

*Al-fulk* is a noun for the sea vessel and a collective noun for it in a single form. It has already been discussed at His saying ﴿and the ships that run in the sea with what benefits people﴾ [al-Baqara: 164] in Surat al-Baqara. Here it is intended as a plural.

[Page 137]
*Al-jary* is rapid movement on land or at sea. He, may He be exalted, said ﴿In the name of God is its course﴾ [Hud: 41], and the apparent meaning is that it is literal in both.

*Al-rih* (wind) is feminine in the speech of the Arabs, and this was discussed at His saying ﴿And He it is who sends the winds as heralds before His mercy﴾ [al-A'raf: 57] in Surat al-A'raf. *Al-tayyiba* means that which is agreeable and gentle to the riders.

*Al-tayyib* is that which is described as very good. The original meaning of *al-tayyib* is suitability in what is intended from a thing, as in His saying ﴿We shall surely give him a good life﴾ [al-Nahl: 97], and one says "the stay pleased him in such-and-such a place" (*taba lahu al-maqam*). From it, a thing that has a pleasant scent and fragrance is called *ṭīb*.

The clause ﴿there came upon it a violent wind﴾ is the answer to *idha*. In mentioning their being carried along by a good wind and their joy in it, there is an indication that the coming of the violent squall happened suddenly, without anticipation from the signs known to sailors, as is usually the case. In this there is also an indication that this was by a decree intended by God, may He be exalted, in order to frighten them and remind them of His oneness.

The pronoun in *jā'athā* refers back to *al-fulk*, because the plural of non-rational things is treated as a feminine singular.

*Al-'aṣif* is a description specific to wind, meaning very swift. The feminine ta' is not attached to it because it is specific to the description of wind, so it has dispensed with the feminine marker, like *nāfis*, *ḥā'iḍ* and *mur'id*. Its usage became common in this way, and when it is mentioned as a description of wind, it remains without the ta'. They said the ta' was not attached because it has the sense of a relative adjective (*nisba*), like *lābin* and *tāmir*, but there is room for examination in this.

The meaning of ﴿from every place﴾ is from every direction of the ship, so the beginning that *min* conveys is the beginning of the places oriented toward the ship.

The meaning of ﴿they were encompassed﴾ (*uḥīṭa bihim*) is that they were seized and destroyed. The Arabs say "the enemy encircled the tribe" when he gained control over it and overcame it, because encircling it indicates surrounding and besieging it. Since that is defeat and taking possession of it, the phrase ﴿they were encompassed﴾ became a figurative metaphor for destruction, as has been discussed at His saying ﴿and God encompasses the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqara: 19], His saying ﴿unless you are surrounded﴾ [Yusuf: 66], and His saying ﴿and his fruit was encompassed﴾ [al-Kahf: 42], meaning it was destroyed. So the meaning of ﴿and they thought that they were encompassed﴾ is that they thought destruction.

[Page 138]
The clause ﴿they called upon God, sincere to Him in religion﴾ is the answer to *idha*. The meaning of ﴿sincere to Him in religion﴾ is devoting worship to Him exclusively in their supplication, meaning they called upon Him and did not call upon their idols along with Him. It is not meant that they ceased from associating partners in all their circumstances; rather, that is their condition in supplication at times of hardship. This is an establishment of proof against them by means of some of their circumstances, like His saying ﴿Is it other than God you call upon, if you are truthful?﴾ [al-An'am: 40] and ﴿Rather, it is Him you call upon﴾ [al-An'am: 41].

The clause ﴿if You deliver us from this﴾ explains the clause "they called upon", because its content is supplication.

The demonstrative *hādhihi* (this) refers to a present state for them, namely the state of being on the verge of drowning, so what is pointed to is the state visible to them.

He has affirmed their promise of thankfulness with three emphatics: the lam of preparation for the oath, the *nun* of emphasis, and the expression in the form ﴿of the thankful﴾ rather than "we shall surely be thankful", because of what it conveys of their being of this company whose habit is thankfulness, as the explanation of the particularity of this structure has already been given at His saying ﴿Indeed I would then be astray, and I would not be of the guided﴾ [al-An'am: 56] in Surat al-An'am.
