He used the sudden particle *idha* in the answer to *lammā* to indicate their hastening to transgression on earth immediately after deliverance.

*Al-baghy* is aggression. It has been discussed at His saying ﴿and sin and transgression without right﴾ [al-A'raf: 33] in Surat al-A'raf. What is meant by it here is polytheism, as is stated explicitly in its parallel ﴿Then when He delivers them to the land, behold, they associate partners﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 65]. Polytheism was called *baghy* because it is aggression upon the right of the Creator, and it is the greatest aggression, just as it is called *ẓulm* (wrongdoing) in many verses, among them His saying ﴿Indeed, associating partners with God is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13]. It is not fitting to interpret *baghy* here as wrongdoing and corruption on earth, because that is not the condition of all of them, for among them are the wise ones of their people; and because it does not fit His saying after it ﴿Your transgression is only against yourselves﴾ [Yunus: 23]. There are parallels to the meaning of this verse in the Qur'an, like His saying ﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance; then when He bestows upon him a favour from Himself, he forgets what he had been calling upon before and sets up rivals to God to mislead from His way﴾ [al-Zumar: 8], and the verse continues.

The addition of ﴿on earth﴾ is merely to emphasise their capacity to be saved. It is like His saying ﴿Then when He delivers them to the land, some of them are moderate﴾ [Luqman: 32], meaning they made the place of the trace of the blessing of deliverance into a place for transgression.

[Page 139]
Likewise His saying ﴿without right﴾ [Yunus: 23] is a qualifying restriction that reveals the meaning of *baghy*, since transgression is never by right. It is like the qualification in His saying ﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from God?﴾ [al-Qasas: 50].

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 23:**

﴿O mankind, your transgression is only against yourselves—the enjoyment of the worldly life. Then to Us is your return, and We will inform you of what you used to do.﴾

This is a resumed address (istinaf) to the polytheists, who are the ones who transgress in the earth without right.

The address opens with ﴿O mankind﴾ to draw in their attention. Its purpose is to warn the polytheists and then to threaten them.

The construction that restricts transgression to its being harmful to them, as conveyed by the particle of elevation (ḥarf al-isti'la', "ʿalā"), serves as a reminder of a real fact and as an admonition to them, so that they know that the warning against shirk and the threat for it are for the sake of their own welfare, not because they could harm Him, as in His saying: ﴿And they will not harm Him at all﴾ [al-Tawbah: 39]. Thus the meaning of ʿalā here is figurative elevation, used as a metaphor for harm, because the one who is elevated and dominant harms the one who is overcome and placed beneath him. For this reason it is common to say: "This thing is ʿalayka (against you)," and in its opposite: "This thing is laka (for you)," as in His saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own soul; and whoever does evil, it is against it﴾ [Fussilat: 46]. And the one who acknowledges a debt says: "Laka ʿalayya kadhā (I owe you such-and-such)."

Tawbah ibn al-Humayyir said:

*"Layla has claimed that I am a wicked man;*
*her piety is for herself, or her wickedness is against her."*

And al-Samaw'al the Jew said:

*"Is the superiority mine, or against me, if I am reckoned?*
*Indeed I am one who will be held to account."*

That is because ʿalā indicates obligation and imposition, while al-lām (la-) indicates entitlement.

In the hadith: "The Qur'an is a proof for you or against you."

The word "al-anfus" (the selves) here means the selves of the transgressors, taking into account the distribution among the individuals referred to by the plural pronoun addressed in His saying "baghyukum (your transgression)," and among the individual selves, as in their saying "rakiba al-qawmu dawabbahum (the people rode their animals)," meaning each one rode his own animal. The meaning is therefore: the transgression of each person is only against his own self, because shirk harms only the polytheist's own self, by corrupting his thinking and his action, and then by his falling into punishment.

The word matāʿun is in the nominative in the reading of the majority, as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is the enjoyment of the worldly life." Hafs from ʿĀṣim read it in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial state) of "baghyukum." It may also be in the accusative as a ẓarf (adverb of time) of "al-baghy," since al-baghy is a verbal noun derived from a verb, so it functions like a verb; the verbal noun thus stands in place of the adverb of time, being annexed to what carries the sense of duration. The specification of the transgression by this duration is in view of its being mentioned in the context of divine anger against them. So the meaning is that He gave them a long respite. Would that you remembered! Then do not reckon the respite as approval of your deeds, nor as incapacity on His part; He will call you to account for it in the Hereafter. Both readings have other aspects beyond what we have mentioned.

Al-matāʿ is that which is benefited from in a non-lasting way. It was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place and enjoyment for a time﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 24], in the surah of al-Aʿraf. The meaning under both readings is one: We gave you respite in your polytheism only for the duration of life, and nothing more; then We will call you to account for your transgression at your return to Us.

The clause ﴿then to Us is your return﴾ is conjoined with "thumma" to indicate a gradual, rank-based sequence (al-tarākhī al-rutbī), because the content of this clause is a more explicit threat than the content of the clause ﴿your transgression is only against yourselves﴾.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in ﴿to Us is your return﴾ serves to indicate exclusivity (ikhtiṣāṣ), meaning: you return to Us, not to anyone else. This treats the addressees as one who thinks he will return to other than God, because their state, in denying His signs, turning away from His worship and toward worshipping idols, is like the state of one who thinks he will be gathered to idols, even though the polytheists deny resurrection altogether.

The consequence ﴿so We will inform you﴾ following the clause ﴿to Us is your return﴾ is a consequence of warning that follows a threat, and it is a consequence of menace. The word "inbā'" (informing) is used metonymically for requital, because informing entails knowledge of their evil deeds, and one who knows of the evil conduct of his servant is not prevented from punishing him by any obstacle. The mention of "kuntum" (you were) together with the present-tense verb indicates the recurrence of their deeds and their firm hold over them. And although the threat that this verse brings concerns the greatest transgression, every instance of transgression has a share of this threat.

[p. 141]

﴿Indeed, the likeness of the worldly life is only like water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it, [vegetation] of which men and livestock eat. Until, when the earth takes on its adornment and becomes beautified, and its people think that they have power over it, Our command comes to it by night or by day, and We make it into stubble, as if it had not flourished yesterday. Thus do We detail the signs for a people who give thought.﴾

This verse serves as an explanation (bayan) of the phrase ﴿the enjoyment of the worldly life﴾ [Yunus: 23], which indicates that their enjoyment of this world is only for a short period. So this verse makes clear that enjoyment is headed toward extinction. It elaborates by likening the condition of worldly enjoyment for its people to the condition of crops in their freshness and then in their going toward harvest.

Al-mathal (the likeness) is a state that is depicted in a particular form. Here the comparison is a comparison of a composite state with a composite state. This is expressed by the word "mathal," which is common in the composite simile (al-tashbih al-murakkab), as was mentioned earlier at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

The form of restriction (qasr) serves to emphasize the purpose of the comparison, which is the swiftness of passing away. It also serves to treat the listeners as though they assume the worldly life's brightness will last, because their state of absorption in the pleasures of this world is like the state of one who assumes its permanence and denies that it could have a swift and sudden end. The meaning is: the state of the worldly life is restricted to resembling the state of the described vegetation. Thus the restriction is a qasr qalb (inverted restriction, correcting a belief held by the addressees), built on treating the addressees as those who believe the opposite of that state.

The state of life is compared, in the swiftness of its passing and the disappearance of its delights after their brightness, and in the increase of its freshness, to the state of the vegetation of the earth in its becoming debris and its ending as stubble.

Among the excellence of this comparison is that it includes separate comparisons drawn from the stages of the two similar states, such that every part of this composite comparison is suitable to compare a part of the two similar states. For this reason, the description of the two states was lengthened from its beginning.

[p. 142]

His words, ﴿like water which We sent down from the sky﴾, compare to it the beginning of life's stages, from the time of youth, when there is nothing but hope for the pleasures of living and its freshness. That hope resembles the state of rain descending from the sky, in that it is the cause of what is hoped for from it: the adornment and freshness of the earth.

His words, ﴿and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it﴾, compare to it the stage of the beginning of the freshness of life and the emergence of life's blossom. That resembles the emergence of crops shortly after the rain, in what is observed of the first signs of what is hoped for. For this reason it is joined with the fa' of sequence (fa' al-ta'qib), to indicate the swiftness with which vegetation appears right after rain, and so it indicates the swiftness of life's growth in the first of its stages. He expressed this by "mingling with the water," so that it appeared before the water dried up. That is, the vegetation mingled with the water, meaning it bordered it and accompanied it.

His words, ﴿of which men and livestock eat﴾, are a description of the vegetation of the earth, of which there are kinds that men eat, such as vegetables and herbs, and kinds that livestock eat, such as grass and pasture. This is used as a likeness for what people enjoy in life of pleasures, and for what animals enjoy, since the animal has a share in the enjoyment of life in proportion to the scope of its life.

Since this includes both the eaten and the eater, it is correct to liken to it people's desires for taking the delights of life according to differences in the ranks of aspirations. This includes likening the lofty matters of worldly blessings, which high aspirations strive for, to the vegetation that people live on, and likening the base matters to the vegetation that livestock eat. It also includes likening those who incline toward those base matters to livestock, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as livestock eat﴾ [Muhammad: 12].

The discussion of ﴿until, when the earth takes its adornment﴾ is like the discussion of His statement ﴿until, when you were in the ship﴾ [Yunus: 22]. It is a limit (ghayah) to which the comparison is made: the attainment of benefit from the goods of this world reaches its utmost point, its ripening and completion, the multiplication of its kinds, people's total absorption in taking them, and their forgetting of the destination toward annihilation.

The command of Allah is His decree and His bringing into being. His coming to it is the striking of that land with calamities that quickly bring it to dryness and destruction.

[p. 143]

Within the meaning of the limit derived from "hatta" (until) is something indicating that between the beginning of the appearance of life's pleasures and their end there are many ranks and numerous stages. This is implicit within the meaning of "hatta."

His words, ﴿by night or by day﴾, are an alternation regarding the time, to arouse the expectation of the possibility that life's freshness may disappear at any time, because a thing specified by a particular time makes people feel secure from its occurrence at other times.

Al-zukhruf (adornment) is the name for gold, and it is applied to whatever one adorns oneself with, of clothing and jewelry, in which there is gold and coloring.

Attributing to the earth the taking of its adornment, meaning the appearance of beauty in it, is an implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah). The earth is likened to a woman when she wants to adorn herself and brings out her finest clothes of jewelry and colors. The Arabs apply the term "taking" to that act, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of worship﴾ [al-A'raf: 31], and Bashshar ibn Burd said:

"And take garments of adornment and dyed fabrics, and they are the most splendid."

The mention of "izzayyanat" (it became beautified) after "zukhrufahā" is a tarshih (a supporting detail) for the metaphor, because a woman takes her adornment in order to beautify herself.

"Izzayyanat" originally was "tazayyanat," but the ta' was changed into a zay in order to be assimilated into the following zay, so it was made sukoon and assimilated, and a hamzat al-wasl (connecting hamzah) was brought in for the sake of pronouncing the sukoon.

Know that in His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Our command came to it by night or by day, so We made it into stubble﴾, there is an indication of the cycle of uprooting. So it warns of threat to the disbelievers and makes the likeness more tightly bound to their lives, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and they were then in despair﴾ [al-An'am: 44]. Especially since this likeness was struck for the enjoyment of the disbelievers through their transgression and the respite granted to them in it. And His statement, ﴿and its people thought that they had power over it﴾, which indicates that its people are the intended target of that striking, makes this indication clearer.

The meaning of ﴿that they had power over it﴾ is that they continue to benefit from it and achieve its fruits. So the term "power" (qudrah) is applied to the capacity to benefit from it and its continuance, by way of metaphor (isti'arah).

[p. 144]

Al-hasid (stubble) means the harvested, which is the crop cut from its roots. Describing the earth as "stubble" is in the manner of the rational metaphor (al-majaz al-'aqli), since what is harvested is in fact its vegetation. The meaning of ﴿lam taghna﴾ (it did not flourish) is: it was not populated, that is, it was not populated with crops. One says: "ghaniya al-makan" when a place becomes populated. From this comes "al-maghna" for an inhabited place. The opposite of "aghna" is "aqfara," meaning the place became barren.

The ba' in "bil-amsi" is for the sense of time (zarfiyyah). Al-amsi (yesterday) is the day before your day. The lam in it is extra, for the sake of filling out the wording, like the one in the word "al-an" (now). What is meant by "al-amsi" in the verse is the general time that has passed, because "amsi" is used to mean what has gone of time, just as "ghad" is used to mean the future and "al-yawm" to mean the present. Zuhayr's verse gathers these:

"I know the knowledge of today and of yesterday before it, but I am blind to the knowledge of what lies in tomorrow."

His statement ﴿Thus do We detail the signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 32] up to its end is a comprehensive tadhyil (concluding statement that generalizes the lesson). That is: like this detailing, We detail, that is, We make clear, all the indications which point to the comprehensiveness of knowledge, power, and perfection of workmanship. So this is one of the clear signs, and it is one of the general signs. A parallel to it was mentioned in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Thus do We detail the signs, and that the way of the criminals may become evident﴾ [al-An'am: 55] in Surat al-An'am.

The lam in ﴿for a people who give thought﴾ is the lam of purpose (lam al-ajal).

Al-tafakkur (giving thought) means reflection and consideration. It is a form of tafa''ul derived from al-fikr, and it has been discussed at His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing alike? Will you not then give thought?﴾ [al-An'am: 50] in Surat al-An'am. In it there is an implicit reproach that those who did not benefit from the signs are not among the people of reflection, and the detailing of the signs was not for their sake. The word "qawm" (people) has been mentioned more than once earlier in this surah.

The sentence is conjoined to the sentence "Thus We detail the signs for a people who reflect" [Yunus: 24], meaning: We detail the signs, among which is the sign of the state of this world and its passing away, and We call to the Abode of Peace, the Abode of Eternity. Since the sentence "Thus We detail the signs" [Yunus: 24] serves as a concluding summary (tadhyil), and the nature of a concluding summary is that it be complete, comprehensive, and self-standing, the sentence conjoined to it was made equal to it in self-standing. Therefore the construction shifted from the pronoun to the explicit noun, since "Allah calls" (wallahu yad'u) was placed in the position of "We call" (nad'u). This is because a pronoun in the sentence would make it dependent on the sentence containing its antecedent.

The object of "yad'u" (calls) is omitted to generalize the meaning, that is, He calls everyone. Al-da'wa (the call) means solicitation and urging, and here it refers to the commands and prohibitions of the divine obligation (al-taklif).

Dar al-Salam (the Abode of Peace) is Paradise. He, may He be exalted, said: "For them is the Abode of Peace with their Lord" [al-An'am: 127]. The reason for its being so named has already been discussed in Surah al-An'am.

Al-hidaya (guidance) is indicating the beneficial goal. What is meant by it here is the creation of the attainment of the goal (khalq al-ihtida' ila al-maqsud), as indicated by His words "whomever He wills" following His words "Allah calls," which convey generality, since the call to Paradise is an indication toward it. Thus it is guidance in its original sense. It is therefore determined that "yahdi" (guides) here has the meaning of bringing about guidance in another sense, namely the actual attainment of being guided, that is, the creation of its occurrence through the command of creation (amr al-takwin), as in His words: "A group He guided, and a group upon whom misguidance was decreed" [al-A'raf: 30]. This creation occurs either in every particular of the particulars of being guided, according to the method of the Ash'ariyya (al-Ash'ariyya, the Ash'arite school), or by creating the capacity for it, such that one is able to be guided upon the arrival of the proofs, according to the method of the Mu'tazila (al-Mu'tazila, the Mu'tazilite school). The two are close in their present application, and the matters of the unseen are hidden. Something of this has already been discussed at His words, may He be exalted: "Guide us to the straight path" [al-Fatiha: 6].

Al-sirat al-mustaqim (the straight path) is the path that conveys (to the goal).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 26:

﴿For those who did good is the best (reward) and more. Neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces. Those are the companions of Paradise; therein they will abide forever.﴾

This sentence is a badal al-ishtimal (a substitute of inclusion) for the sentence ﴿And Allah calls to the Abode of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [Yunus: 25], because guidance "to whom He wills" implies both one who is guided and one who is not guided. So in this sentence there is mention of what includes both groups, and you may consider it a badal mufassal (a detailed substitute) from a mujmal (a summarized statement).

When the mention of "those who did good" came in the explanatory sentence, the listener understood that they are those whom Allah guided to a straight path, that the straight path is good action, and that "the best" (al-husna) is the Abode of Peace. The words of the Exalted in Surat al-An'am explain this verse: ﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam; and whomever He wills to leave astray, He makes his breast tight and constricted, as if he were climbing into the sky. Thus does Allah place defilement upon those who do not believe﴾ [al-An'am: 125]. ﴿And this is the path of your Lord, straight. We have detailed the verses for a people who remember﴾ [al-An'am: 126]. ﴿For them is the Abode of Peace with their Lord, and He is their Protector for what they used to do﴾ [al-An'am: 127].

Al-husna: originally it is the feminine elative adjective of "al-ahsan" (the best). Then it was treated as a noun of genus, so the particle of genus definition (al-) was attached to it, and it moved away from being an adjective and no longer follows its noun.

Its definiteness conveys comprehensiveness (al-istighraq), like "al-bushra" and like "al-salihah" whose plural is "al-salihat." The meaning is: for those who did good, the genus of the best conditions is theirs (with them), i.e., they have that in the Hereafter. By this it is established that what it refers to is Paradise, because it is the best reward to which those who did good will arrive. By this the Qur'an made it a proper name by dominance for Paradise and its bliss, from attaining great pleasures.

As for "and more" (ziyadah), it is necessarily an increase for them that is not included in the kind of "the best" in the meaning that became a proper name by dominance. So it should not be interpreted as a type of what is in Paradise, because then it would be included in what the word "al-husna" covers. It is therefore determined that it is a matter that returns to elevation of ranks. It has been said: it is the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted, as He said: ﴿And pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence, and approval from Allah is greater﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72]. It has also been said: it is their seeing Allah, the Exalted. This has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) in Sahih Muslim and Jami' al-Tirmidhi, from Suhayb, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿For those who did good is the best and more﴾, he said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, a caller will call out: Indeed for you there is a promise from Allah which He wishes to fulfill for you. They will say: Did He not whiten our faces, save us from the Fire, and admit us to Paradise? He said: Then the veil will be lifted. He said: By Allah, Allah has not given them anything more beloved to them than looking at Him." And this is the clearest of what has been related in its interpretation.

Al-rahaq: covering, overtaking. Its verb is from the pattern of "fariha."

Al-qatar: a color that is dust-colored tending toward blackness. It is also called qatarah. What has become clear to me from the words of the scholars and usage is that qatarah is a color that covers the surface of the face from intense misery, wretchedness, and fear. It is one of the effects of the agitation of the liver from the trembling of the heart out of fear and apprehension.

Al-dhillah: humiliation. What is meant is the trace of humiliation that appears on the face of the humiliated. The statement is used both literally and figuratively: i.e., their faces will not be disfigured by dust and the trace of humiliation, and there will not come to them what would produce dust or the form of humiliation.

The negation of dust and humiliation from them within the description of their attributes is not a praise of them, because that does not come to mind as an occurrence after the affirmation to them of "the best and more." Rather, the meaning is an allusion (ta'ridh) to those whom Allah did not guide to a straight path, and they are those who earned evil deeds, hastening the displeasure that will come to them by way of allusion before the explicit statement that comes in His saying: ﴿And humiliation will cover them﴾ [Yunus: 27], up to His saying: "dark."

The sentence ﴿Those are the companions of Paradise; therein they will abide forever﴾ is a conclusion (natijah) of the premise, so between it and the preceding one there is complete connection, and for this reason it is separated from it and not joined by a conjunction.

The demonstrative noun refers back to ﴿those who did good﴾ [al-Najm: 31]. In it is an indication that they deserved eternal abiding because of their goodness, similar to His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 27:

﴿And those who earned evil deeds – the recompense of an evil deed is one like it, and humiliation will cover them. They will have no protector from Allah; it is as if their faces were covered with pieces of the darkness of night. Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿For those who did good is the best reward﴾ [Yunus: 26]. In describing the wrongdoers, he used the verb ﴿earned (kasabū) evil deeds﴾ rather than the verb "did evil" (asāʾū), which he used in describing those who did good, to indicate that their evil is from their own action and effort. ﴿Allah does not wrong them, but they wrong themselves.﴾

Page 148
The relative clause is intended to refer specifically to the polytheists, as shown by His saying after it, ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾ For eternal abiding in the Fire applies only to disbelievers, as the abundant textual evidence indicates, contrary to the Mu'tazila and the Khawarij.

The clause ﴿the recompense of an evil deed is one like it﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of (those who earned evil deeds). The indefinite form "evil deed" (sayyiʾah) is for generality, meaning the recompense of every evil deed is one like it. Although it is in an affirmative context, the generality is derived from the situation, which is the situation of the generality of the subject, as in the saying of al-Hariri:

"O people of this abode, may harm be kept from you,"
meaning every harm. This generality dispenses with a pronominal link between the nominal clause and the subject, or a genitive may be supposed, meaning "the recompense of an evil deed from them," as was supposed in His saying, ﴿So whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head, then a ransom of fasting﴾ [al-Baqara: 196], meaning "then upon him."

He limited himself to humiliation for them without adding "and dust will cover them," because what is more severe will come, which is His saying: ﴿as if their faces were covered with pieces of the darkness of night.﴾

The clause ﴿They have no protector from Allah﴾ is a second predicate, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from (those who earned evil deeds), or a parenthetical clause (muʿtaridah). It is a threat and a removal of hope.

Al-ʿĀṣim means the preventer and the guardian. The meaning of ﴿from Allah﴾ is "from His vengeance and His recompense." This is from the attachment of the verb to the name of the Essence, and what is meant is some of the states of the Essence, which the context indicates, like ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3].

The clause ﴿as if their faces were covered﴾ etc. is an explanation of the clause ﴿humiliation will cover them﴾ [al-Qalam: 43], an explanation by way of illustration (bayān tamthīl), or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in His saying "will cover them."

﴿Ughshiyat﴾ is the causative of ghashiya, meaning to surround and cover; with the hamza it became transitive to two objects, of the pattern of kasā. It was discussed in His saying, ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾ [al-A'raf: 54] in al-A'raf, and His saying, ﴿when He caused slumber to overcome you﴾ [al-Anfal: 11] in al-Anfal.

Page 149
The word "qiṭaʿ" – with a fatha on the ṭāʾ – in the reading of the majority is the plural of qiṭʿah, which is a part of a thing. It was named qiṭʿah because it is generally cut off from a whole; it is a form (fiʿlah) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ūlah) that was transferred to the status of a noun. Ibn Kathir, al-Kisai and Ya'qub read "qiṭʿan" with a sukun on the ṭāʾ. It is a noun for a portion of the time of the dark night. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So travel with your family in a portion of the night﴾ [Hud: 81].

His saying "muẓliman" (dark) is a circumstantial clause from "al-layl" (the night). Describing the night, which is the time of darkness, as "dark" serves to convey that the description is firmly established in it, like the expressions "a very dark night" (laylun alyal), "a deep shade" (ẓillun ẓalīl), and "a poetic poem" (shiʿrun shāʿir). Thus what is meant by the night is the intensely dark night, with its stars concealed and its darkness firmly established. Their faces' dusk is likened to the darkness of night.

His saying ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾ is like His saying ﴿Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally﴾ [Yunus: 26].

This clause is conjoined to the clause ﴿But those who earned evil deeds﴾ [Yunus: 27], insofar as that clause is itself conjoined to the clause ﴿For those who did good is the best reward﴾ [Yunus: 26]. When the two preceding clauses mentioned the particular recompense of each of the two groups and its marks, this clause came with a general summary of a state encompassing both groups, and then with a detailed description of a state that distinguishes the polytheists. Thereby there is a dreadful mention of the condition of those who reached the extreme in earning evil deeds, namely the evil of polytheism (shirk), which is the greatest of the major sins. With this, the connection with the preceding clause, which requires its being conjoined to it, is achieved.

The intended purpose of the report is the mention of their being gathered all together, and then what takes place in that gathering of the exposure of those who associated partners with God. So the apparent form would have been to say, "and We gather them all." However, the word *yawm* (day) was added at the beginning of the clause because that day, being the time of the gathering and of great events, was intended to be mentioned as a means of awe and admonition.

The accusative of ﴿The day We gather them﴾ is either as an object, with the implied meaning "remember" (*udhkur*), or as an adverb of time (*zarf*) governing a verb that is implied and indicated by His saying ﴿Then We say to those who associated partners, "Stay in your place"﴾. The estimated meaning is: "And We say to those who associated partners, 'Stay in your place,' on the day We gather the people all together." The pronoun in ﴿We gather them﴾ refers to those previously spoken of, namely those who did good and those who earned evil deeds. His saying *jamīʿan* (all together) is a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*) from the explicit pronoun in ﴿We gather them﴾, to specify that the pronoun is intended in its full generality, since gathering encompasses all people. Among the subtle points of mentioning the gathering of all together here is an alert that the dreadful state of the polytheists and their exposure will take place in the sight and hearing of the believers. Thus, being safe from that condition becomes an additional blessing for the Muslims and a strengthening of the humiliation of the polytheists.

*Al-ḥashr* (gathering) is bringing together from various places to one place. It was previously discussed in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We gathered against them every thing﴾ [al-An'am: 111], in Surat al-An'am.

His saying ﴿makānakum﴾ (your place) is in the accusative as an object of an implied verb whose estimate is: *ilzamū makānakum* (keep to your place). Its use in this way is common in the speech of the Arabs for ordering someone to remain, with the obligatory omission of the governing verb, until it becomes like the demonstrative verb-nouns (*asmāʾ al-afʿāl*) that are formed for the imperative, such as *ṣah* (be quiet). It is joined with a pronoun suitable for the addressee, whether singular or otherwise. ʿAmr ibn al-Iṭnāba said:

*makānaki tuḥmadi aw tastarīḥī*
(Stay in your place, you will be praised, or you will rest.)

Their being ordered to remain in place is a form of confinement and detention. Since the addressees and their partners were gathered in that place, it is known that this detention is for a common crime between the two groups, which is that one of the two groups worshipped and the other was worshipped.

His saying ﴿antum﴾ (you) is an emphasis (*taʾkīd*) of the implied attached pronoun in the implied verb, and it is what permits the conjunction over it. By this conjunction the partners became those ordered to remain in the place.

*Al-shurakāʾ* (the partners) are the idols. They were described as "partners" because of the addressees' belief in that, and for this reason it was made a genitive construction with their pronoun, meaning "you and those whom you claimed to be partners." Therefore the genitive construction of *shurakāʾ* with the pronoun of the addressees is a mockery.

*Fa-zayyalnā* (then We separated) is conjoined with the particle *fāʾ* of sequence, to convey that this occurred immediately after the time of the order to remain. Since the *fāʾ* requires the temporal order of the conjoined element occurring right after the element it is conjoined to, and since the intention here is that the separation took place simultaneously with their being made to stay in place, the act of separation was expressed in the past tense to convey the certainty of its occurrence, like His saying, ﴿The command of God has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1].

*Zayyala* is the intensive form of *zāla*, which is transitive. It is said: *zālahu ʿan mawḍiʿihi yazīluhu*, meaning *azālahu* (he removed it from its place). They made its middle radical *yāʾ* to distinguish it from *zāla* (intransitive), whose middle radical is *wāw*. So *zayyala* is a verb for intensifying the separation, like *farraqa* is an intensification of *faraqa*. The meaning is that a strong separation occurred among them, such that all the bonds that were between them were severed. The separation here is figurative, so it includes the difference of speech.

The attribution of the separation to the idols is on account of the creation of its meaning in them when God made them speak in a way that contradicts the claim of their worshippers.

The clause ﴿And their partners said﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿So We separated﴾, so it falls within the scope of immediacy (*taʿqīb*). It is also permissible to make it a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*).

The partners say these words by God creating speech in them, a supernatural event, which people understand, to inform those worshippers that their idols have disowned them. This increases their regret. The words of the idols indicate the denial that they worshipped them, but rather that they worshipped others. There is a difficulty in the coherence of this, because the reality is that they did worship them and also worshipped others. So how could their speech deny their worship of them, when it is speech that God created in them? How could it be a lie? The commentators have interpreted this in various ways that do not satisfy the heart.

What appears to me is that the final part of the speech of the idols explains what its beginning had summarized: they denied that they had worshipped them with complete worship, which is the worship in which the worshipper intends to comply with the command of the one worshipped and to please him. This requires that the one worshipped be knowing and be one who commands that worship. Since the idols were neither knowing nor commanding, their denial that their worshippers had worshipped them with that worship was accurate. They had only worshipped others who commanded them to worship, namely the devils. For this reason they said, ﴿Indeed, we were unaware of your worship﴾, as the following verse explains, namely His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Did these people used to worship you?﴾ [Saba': 40] ﴿They will say, "Glory be to You! You are our Protector, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them believed in them"﴾ [Saba': 41].

Therefore, by "the partners" is meant only the idols and nothing else. It is also permissible that their speech denying the worship of the polytheists was that God created for them intellects, so their intellects were newly created on that day, and no knowledge had been established in them that the polytheists had worshipped them. This is explained by their saying afterwards, ﴿Indeed, we were unaware of your worship﴾.

The clause ﴿So God suffices as witness﴾ is emphasized by an oath, so that they would establish their disassociation from what was attributed to them. The answer to the oath is ﴿Indeed, we were unaware of your worship﴾. Their saying ﴿God suffices as witness﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43] is not an oath upon their preceding speech, because the nature of an oath is that it occurs at the beginning of a clause.

The clause of the oath is conjoined with the *fāʾ* to indicate that the oath is a consequence of the preceding speech. Their report that they did not worship them is a strange statement that contradicts what is observed, so it was appropriate that there follow from it what confirms and clarifies it, with the emphasis of an oath. The use of the *fāʾ* of consequence when a statement is followed by an oath-clause is from eloquent usage, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿As We sent down upon the dividers﴾ [al-Hijr: 90] ﴿who made the Qur'an into parts﴾ [al-Hijr: 91] ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 92]. Among its characteristics is that when it is conjoined with the *fāʾ* of consequence, it emphasizes what precedes it through the manner of the oath being a consequence of it, and it emphasizes what follows it through the manner of being the answer to the oath. This verse has not been explained as it deserves.

*Al-shahīd* (the witness) is the one who testifies, and he is the one who supports and confirms the claim of a claimant, as was previously mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So when you hand over their properties to them, then call witnesses against them, and God suffices as reckoner﴾ [al-Nisa': 6].

*Kafā* means "it suffices and is enough without another." It was previously discussed in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And God suffices as protector﴾ [al-Nisa': 45] in Surat al-Nisa'. It is in the form of a report used to express the making of an oath. The *bāʾ* is an addition for emphasis. Its original form is *kafā Allāhu shahīdan* (God suffices as witness).

*Shahīdan* is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyīz*) of the attribution of sufficiency to God, because of the generality it contains.

The clause ﴿Indeed, we were unaware of your worship﴾ is the answer to the oath. *In* is a lightened form of *inna*. Its subject is a pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-shaʾn*) that is obligatorily omitted.

The clause ﴿we were unaware of your worship﴾ explains the pronoun of the matter. The *lām* distinguishes between the emphatic lightened *in* and the negating *in*.

The fronting of ﴿of your worship﴾ before its governing element is for emphasis and for the sake of rhyme with the verse-ending.

This clause is conjoined to the clause ﴿But those who earned evil deeds﴾ [Yunus: 27], insofar as that clause is itself conjoined to the clause ﴿For those who did good is the best reward﴾ [Yunus: 26]. When the two preceding clauses mentioned the particular recompense of each of the two groups and its marks, this clause came with a general summary of a state encompassing both groups, and then with a detailed description of a state that distinguishes the polytheists. Thereby there is a dreadful mention of the condition of those who reached the extreme in earning evil deeds, namely the evil of polytheism (shirk), which is the greatest of the major sins. With this, the connection with the preceding clause, which requires its being conjoined to it, is achieved.

The intended purpose of the report is the mention of their being gathered all together, and then what takes place in that gathering of the exposure of those who associated partners with God. So the apparent form would have been to say, "and We gather them all." However, the word *yawm* (day) was added at the beginning of the clause because that day, being the time of the gathering and of great events, was intended to be mentioned as a means of awe and admonition.

The accusative of ﴿The day We gather them﴾ is either as an object, with the implied meaning "remember" (*udhkur*), or as an adverb of time (*zarf*) governing a verb that is implied and indicated by His saying ﴿Then We say to those who associated partners, "Stay in your place"﴾. The estimated meaning is: "And We say to those who associated partners, 'Stay in your place,' on the day We gather the people all together." The pronoun in ﴿We gather them﴾ refers to those previously spoken of, namely those who did good and those who earned evil deeds. His saying *jamīʿan* (all together) is a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*) from the explicit pronoun in ﴿We gather them﴾, to specify that the pronoun is intended in its full generality, since gathering encompasses all people. Among the subtle points of mentioning the gathering of all together here is an alert that the dreadful state of the polytheists and their exposure will take place in the sight and hearing of the believers. Thus, being safe from that condition becomes an additional blessing for the Muslims and a strengthening of the humiliation of the polytheists.

*Al-ḥashr* (gathering) is bringing together from various places to one place. It was previously discussed in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We gathered against them every thing﴾ [al-An'am: 111], in Surat al-An'am.

His saying ﴿makānakum﴾ (your place) is in the accusative as an object of an implied verb whose estimate is: *ilzamū makānakum* (keep to your place). Its use in this way is common in the speech of the Arabs for ordering someone to remain, with the obligatory omission of the governing verb, until it becomes like the demonstrative verb-nouns (*asmāʾ al-afʿāl*) that are formed for the imperative, such as *ṣah* (be quiet). It is joined with a pronoun suitable for the addressee, whether singular or otherwise. ʿAmr ibn al-Iṭnāba said:

*makānaki tuḥmadi aw tastarīḥī*
(Stay in your place, you will be praised, or you will rest.)

Their being ordered to remain in place is a form of confinement and detention. Since the addressees and their partners were gathered in that place, it is known that this detention is for a common crime between the two groups, which is that one of the two groups worshipped and the other was worshipped.

His saying ﴿antum﴾ (you) is an emphasis (*taʾkīd*) of the implied attached pronoun in the implied verb, and it is what permits the conjunction over it. By this conjunction the partners became those ordered to remain in the place.

*Al-shurakāʾ* (the partners) are the idols. They were described as "partners" because of the addressees' belief in that, and for this reason it was made a genitive construction with their pronoun, meaning "you and those whom you claimed to be partners." Therefore the genitive construction of *shurakāʾ* with the pronoun of the addressees is a mockery.

*Fa-zayyalnā* (then We separated) is conjoined with the particle *fāʾ* of sequence, to convey that this occurred immediately after the time of the order to remain. Since the *fāʾ* requires the temporal order of the conjoined element occurring right after the element it is conjoined to, and since the intention here is that the separation took place simultaneously with their being made to stay in place, the act of separation was expressed in the past tense to convey the certainty of its occurrence, like His saying, ﴿The command of God has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1].

*Zayyala* is the intensive form of *zāla*, which is transitive. It is said: *zālahu ʿan mawḍiʿihi yazīluhu*, meaning *azālahu* (he removed it from its place). They made its middle radical *yāʾ* to distinguish it from *zāla* (intransitive), whose middle radical is *wāw*. So *zayyala* is a verb for intensifying the separation, like *farraqa* is an intensification of *faraqa*. The meaning is that a strong separation occurred among them, such that all the bonds that were between them were severed. The separation here is figurative, so it includes the difference of speech.

The attribution of the separation to the idols is on account of the creation of its meaning in them when God made them speak in a way that contradicts the claim of their worshippers.

The clause ﴿And their partners said﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿So We separated﴾, so it falls within the scope of immediacy (*taʿqīb*). It is also permissible to make it a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*).

The partners say these words by God creating speech in them, a supernatural event, which people understand, to inform those worshippers that their idols have disowned them. This increases their regret. The words of the idols indicate the denial that they worshipped them, but rather that they worshipped others. There is a difficulty in the coherence of this, because the reality is that they did worship them and also worshipped others. So how could their speech deny their worship of them, when it is speech that God created in them? How could it be a lie? The commentators have interpreted this in various ways that do not satisfy the heart.

What appears to me is that the final part of the speech of the idols explains what its beginning had summarized: they denied that they had worshipped them with complete worship, which is the worship in which the worshipper intends to comply with the command of the one worshipped and to please him. This requires that the one worshipped be knowing and be one who commands that worship. Since the idols were neither knowing nor commanding, their denial that their worshippers had worshipped them with that worship was accurate. They had only worshipped others who commanded them to worship, namely the devils. For this reason they said, ﴿Indeed, we were unaware of your worship﴾, as the following verse explains, namely His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Did these people used to worship you?﴾ [Saba': 40] ﴿They will say, "Glory be to You! You are our Protector, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them believed in them"﴾ [Saba': 41].

Therefore, by "the partners" is meant only the idols and nothing else. It is also permissible that their speech denying the worship of the polytheists was that God created for them intellects, so their intellects were newly created on that day, and no knowledge had been established in them that the polytheists had worshipped them. This is explained by their saying afterwards, ﴿Indeed, we were unaware of your worship﴾.

The clause ﴿So God suffices as witness﴾ is emphasized by an oath, so that they would establish their disassociation from what was attributed to them. The answer to the oath is ﴿Indeed, we were unaware of your worship﴾. Their saying ﴿God suffices as witness﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43] is not an oath upon their preceding speech, because the nature of an oath is that it occurs at the beginning of a clause.
