Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 30:

﴿There, every soul will experience what it sent ahead.﴾

*Tadhyil* (a concluding phrase that restates a general truth after a passage) and *fadhlaka* (a summarizing recapitulation) of the preceding clauses, from his saying: ﴿And Allah invites to the Abode of Peace﴾ [Yunus: 25] up to here. It is an *i'tiraḍ* (an interjected clause placed between clauses joined by conjunction).

The demonstrative refers to the place indicated by his saying: ﴿We will gather them﴾ [Yunus: 28], meaning in that place where We will gather them. The demonstrative is in the accusative position as an adverb of place (*zarfiyya*). Its governing verb is *tablu*, and this adverbial phrase was placed first for emphasis, because the most important purpose of the speech is the greatness of what occurs in it.

*Tablu* means "tests," and here it is a *kinaya* (metonymy) for certainty and definitive knowledge. *Aslafat* means "sent ahead," i.e., a deed it sent ahead. The meaning is that it tests its state and its outcome, so it knows what is good and beneficial and what is ugly and harmful, since it has become clear to them what leads its owner to bliss and what leads to the opposite.

The majority of readers read *tablu* with a single *ba'* after the initial *ta'* (تَبْلُو). Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a *ta'* after the first *ta'* (تَتْلُو), on the basis that it derives from *talw*, which means "following," i.e., every soul follows what it sent ahead of deeds, and so it leads it to Paradise or to Hell.

* * *

Page 154
﴿And they will be returned to Allah, their true Master﴾

It is permissible that this clause be conjoined to the clause ﴿There, every soul will experience what it sent ahead﴾, in which case it is part of the *tadhyil*, and the pronoun in *ruddū* refers to ﴿every soul﴾. It is also permissible that it be conjoined to his saying ﴿And the day We gather them all﴾ [Yunus: 28] and so on, in which case it is not connected to the *tadhyil*, meaning: "And We return them to Us," and the pronoun in *ruddū* refers specifically to those who associated partners with Allah. The meaning is that the gathering they used to deny has become certain for them. The phrase ﴿their true Master﴾ fits this meaning, since it implies a rebuke of them by nullifying their false masters.

*Radd* means returning. Returning to Allah means being returned to His disposal, to be recompensed for what pleases Him and what does not, and previously, during the life of this world, they had been left unrequited.

*Mawla* means master, because between him and his servant there is a bond of ownership. It is also used for one who takes charge of the affairs of others and provides for their needs.

*Haqq* means what accords with reality and truth, i.e., "return to the true God, not to the false." The description with *haqq* is the description of a verbal noun in the sense of an active participle: "the one who makes the mastership real," i.e., rather than the false allies they imagined.

* * *

﴿And what they used to fabricate has vanished from them﴾
This clause is specific to the polytheists, as is clear.
*Dalal* means loss or disappearance.

﴿What they used to fabricate﴾ means what they used to lie about, namely their attribution of divinity to the idols. It is permissible that the referent of the relative *ma* be the idols, in which case the returning pronoun has been deleted along with its preposition without the relative being governed by the same preposition that governs the returning pronoun, which is a permissible option according to the sound view. The estimated sense then is: "what they used to lie about (against it or concerning it)." Its *dalal* is the non-existence of it in the claimed description.

Page 155
It is also permissible that the referent of the relative *ma* be the fabrication itself, i.e., the fabrication they used to invent. Its *dalal* is the manifestation of its falsehood and untruth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 31:

﴿Say: "Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? Or who controls hearing and sight? And who brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living? And who arranges the affair?" They will say, "Allah." So say, "Will you not then be mindful of Him?"﴾ This is a shift from one aim to another within the various methods of refuting polytheism (shirk) and affirming the Oneness of Allah, exalted is He, in divinity (uluhiyya). This sentence serves as evidence for His saying: ﴿their true Master﴾ [Yunus: 30], because it is proof that He is the one deserving of guardianship (wilaya).

He argues for this through the gifts of provision by which life is sustained, through the gift of the senses, through the system of reproduction and propagation by which the species survive, and through the arrangement of the world's order and the determination of what is decreed. All of these are gifts from Allah, and they knew that none of what was mentioned is done except by Allah, since they did not attribute these matters to their idols. Therefore, the one who exclusively possesses them is certainly the one deserving of guardianship and divinity.

The interrogation is taqriri (a question intended to elicit affirmation from the listener).

The argument was presented in the form of question and answer because that is in the form of a dialogue, so the proof obtained through it has a stronger impact on the souls of the listeners. For this reason, among the methods of teaching, when something's firm establishment is desired among scientific principles, it is presented in the form of question and answer.

His saying ﴿from the heaven and the earth﴾ is a reminder of the conditions of provision so that it may be more vividly present in the mind. Provision from the heaven is the rain, and provision from the earth is all vegetation: grains, fruits, and herbage.

The particle ʼam (or) in His saying ﴿Or who controls hearing and sight﴾ is for idrab intiqali (a transitional turning away), from one interrogation to another.

The meaning of ﴿controls hearing and sight﴾ is that He has disposal over them, and it is the control of bringing these two faculties into existence. This is an argument and a reminder of the most beneficial and most precise of creations.

He used the singular "hearing" (al-sam') because it is a verbal noun (masdar), so it indicates the genus that exists in all human senses. As for "sight" (al-absar), it was used in the plural because it is a noun (ism), and it is not explicit in indicating generality, since there is the possibility of supposing a particular sight. So the plural was more indicative of the intended generality and more effective in negating the possibility of a specific reference (al-'ahd) or the like. This contrasts with His saying: ﴿Indeed, the hearing and the sight and the heart, all of those will be questioned about﴾ [al-Isra: 36], because the intended meaning there is the singular for each addressee in His saying: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾ [al-Isra: 36]. This was already discussed under His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Have you considered: if Allah should take away your hearing and sight﴾ [al-An'am: 46] in Surat al-An'am.

The bringing forth of the living from the dead is the generation of animal offspring from sperm and from eggs. The sperm or egg has no life in it, then it develops into a form capable of life, and then life exists in it. The "min" (from) in His saying "from the dead" indicates the starting point. The bringing forth of the dead from the living is the bringing out of the sperm and eggs from the animal.

The definite article in "the living" (al-hayy) and "the dead" (al-mayyit) in both instances is the definite article of genus (ta'rif al-jins).

This argument concerning that wondrous creative act has been organized in the style of riddles and enigmas (al-ahaji wa al-alghaz), and it was made with the embellishment of antithesis (tadadd). All of this is to increase the sense of wonder at it. The discussion of its counterpart has already been presented in His saying: ﴿You bring the night into the day, and You bring the day into the night, and You bring the living out of the dead, and You bring the dead out of the living﴾ [Al 'Imran: 27] in Surat Al 'Imran. However, the "ma" here does not symbolize anything.

His saying ﴿And who arranges the affair﴾ has already been discussed in its counterpart at the beginning of this surah. Here it is a generalization after a specification, mentioning what contains greater lesson within themselves, like the lesson in His saying: ﴿And in yourselves. Will you not see?﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 21] ﴿And in the heaven is your provision and that which you are promised﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 22].

The fa' (then) in His saying ﴿so they will say, "Allah"﴾ is the fa' of causation (fa' al-sababiyya), which by its nature accompanies the response to a conditional when that response is not suitable to be directly preceded by the conditional particle. That is because it intended that their saying "Allah" be the consequence of the question that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was commanded to ask. So the verb "say" (qul) was treated as if it were a conditional, and it is as if it were said: "If you say, 'Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth?' they will say, 'Allah.'" Among this usage is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Be stones or iron﴾ [al-Isra: 50] ﴿or a creation of what is greater in your breasts." They will say, "Who will restore us?"﴾ [al-Isra: 51]. This usage is like the treatment of a command as a conditional in the apocopation of the verb that is spoken, treating it as the response to a conditional, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say to My servants who have believed that they should establish prayer﴾ [Ibrahim: 31], and His saying: ﴿And say to My servants that they should say that which is best﴾ [al-Isra: 53]. The implied meaning: "If you say to them, 'Establish prayer,' they will establish it; and if you say to them, 'Say that which is best,' they will say it." This is frequent in the Qur'an according to the view of the verifying grammarians (al-muhaqqiqun min al-nuhat), while the custom of the grammatical analysts (al-mu'rabun, those who analyze i'rab, grammatical case and syntax) is to interpret it as the omission of an implied conditional that the context indicates. The two views are close, except that what the verifying grammarians adopted is the estimation of meaning, and the estimation for them is a consideration, not an actual usage; while what the analysts adopted is the estimation of i'rab, and what is estimated for them is like what is stated.

Had the command not been treated as a conditional, the fa' would not have come, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it, if you should know?" They will say, "To Allah."﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 84] and the verses that follow.

The fa' in His saying "so say" (fa-qul) is the fa' of consequence (fa' al-fasiha), meaning: if they say that, then say, "Will you not then be mindful?" The fa' in His saying ﴿Will you not then be mindful?﴾ is the fa' of derivation (fa' al-tafri'), meaning: derived from your acknowledgment that He is the sole Doer is the denunciation of your failure to be mindful.

The object of ﴿be mindful﴾ (tattaqun) is omitted, and its estimated form is "tattaqunahu" (be mindful of Him), meaning: by exalting Him above any partner.

Allah informed about them that they would acknowledge that the Provider, the Creator, and the Arranger is Allah, because they did not believe otherwise, just as this information about them was repeated in many verses of the Qur'an. In this there is a challenge to them, for if they were able, they would have denied that what was attributed to them was correct. But their fear of the shame of lying prevented them from that, and therefore the proof was established against them by His saying: ﴿So say, "Will you not then be mindful?"﴾

Page 158

﴿So that is Allah, your true Lord. Then what is there after the truth except error? So how are you turned away?﴾

The fa' (فَ) here marks a consequence of the rebuke implied in His words: ﴿Will you not then fear Allah?﴾ [Yunus: 31]. Thus what is consequent is part of what was said.

The demonstrative (اسم الإشارة, ism al-ishara) refers back to the Name of Majesty (اسم الجلالة, ism al-jalala), to draw attention to the fact that the one indicated is worthy of the judgment that follows the demonstrative, on account of the attributes mentioned before it: that He is the Provider, the Giver of perception, the Creator, the Governor. The demonstrative has gathered these together, and it also signals that the judgment that comes after it is grounded in the totality of these attributes. The Name of Majesty serves as an appositive (بيان, bayan) to the demonstrative, for added clarity, with an implicit reproach to the strength of their error and misguidance regarding divinity. ﴿Your Lord﴾ is the predicate (خبر, khabar), and ﴿the true﴾ is its adjective (صفة, sifa). The description "the true" has already occurred just above in a verse like this one.

The fa' in His words ﴿Then what is there after the truth except error?﴾ is a consequence of the rhetorical interrogation of denial, following the conclusion drawn after the proof. So it is a consequence of a consequence, and a rebuke following a rebuke.

Mādhā (ماذا) is composed of the interrogative ma (ما) and dhā (ذا), which is a demonstrative. It frequently occurs after the interrogative ma. The best view is that after the interrogative it is an extra particle used merely for emphasis. Its extra status is expressed by calling it "nullified" (مُلْغًى, mulgha), to avoid the obligation that the noun be extra, as here. It may also convey the sense of a relative pronoun (موصولية, mawsuliyya), as previously explained in His words: ﴿What did Allah intend by this as a parable?﴾ [al-Baqara: 26] in Surat al-Baqara. Refer to what comes at His words: ﴿What is it that the criminals seek to hasten?﴾ [Yunus: 50] in this surah.

The interrogation here is a denial, meaning negation, and for this reason the exception follows it in His words: ﴿except error﴾.

Ba'd (بَعْدَ) here is used in the sense of ghayr (غَيْر, "other than"), on the basis that the different arises after a difference and when it is absent.

So the meaning is: what is it that comes about when the truth is absent?

Since the interrogation is not in its literal sense, because there is no uncertainty about what is being asked, it is determined to be a denial and nullification. Therefore the exception follows it in His words: ﴿except error﴾. The meaning is: nothing comes about when the truth is absent

Page 159

except error, since there is no intermediate state between the two. Since Allah is the true Lord, it is determined that anything else to which divinity is ascribed is false. He expressed falsehood by "error" because error is the most heinous kind of falsehood.

The fa' in ﴿So how are you turned away?﴾ is likewise a consequence, that is, a consequence of the explicit rebuke following the denial and nullification.

Anna (أنّى) is an interrogative about place, meaning: to what place do your minds turn you? This is a figurative place, meaning that you are in error and blindness, like one who has lost his way and finds none but someone who describes for him a path that does not lead to his destination, so he is turned from one error to another. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The Qur'anic expression in conveying these meanings surpasses every commentary in eloquence, conciseness and clarity.

These verses contain nine fa' particles, starting from His words: ﴿Then they will say, "Allah"﴾ [Yunus: 31]. The first is a response (جوابية, jawabiyya), the second is an explanatory one (فصيحة, fasiha), and the rest are consequential (تفريعية, tafriʿiyya).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 33:

﴿Thus has the word of your Lord come true against those who defied [Allah], that they will not believe.﴾

It is a tadhyil (a concluding sentence that reinforces and completes the preceding statement) expressing wonder at their persistence in disbelief after the proofs and signs had become manifest to them, and a declaration of despair regarding their faith, by conveying that the absence of belief from them is by a decree from Allah, Exalted is He, upon them. Thus, what He had decreed through His word from eternity has been shown to have come to pass. The kaf (ka) that precedes the demonstrative noun is the kaf of comparison (kaf al-tashbih).

The object of comparison (al-mushabbah bihi) is the thing pointed to, namely their state and their misguidance. That is: just as you have witnessed, the word of your Lord has come true, meaning that in what you have witnessed there is something that makes clear to you that the word of your Lord has indeed come true against them, that they will not believe.

His saying ﴿that they will not believe﴾ is a badal (substitute apposition) for kalimah or for kalimat. What is meant is the content of the clause ﴿that they will not believe﴾.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read (kalimat Rabbika) in the plural. The rest read it in the singular. The meaning is one, because the kalimah (word) is applied to the whole of a speech, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nay, it is but a word he is saying﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100], and because the plural may be taken in view of the multiplicity of words, or in view of the repetition of a single word with respect to many people.

Al-fisq (defiance, transgression): departing from the path which a thing is meant to follow. What is meant by it here is defiance in receiving the call of the Messengers and in exercising reflection. It has already been discussed in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He leads astray thereby none except the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26], in Surah al-Baqarah.

Then it is permissible that what is meant by ﴿those who defied﴾ is everyone who persists in his defiance and therefore does not believe, so the sentence would be a tadhyil for the generality it contains, encompassing those being spoken of, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus does Allah strike the truth and falsehood﴾ [al-Ra'd: 17]. It is also permissible that what is meant by ﴿those who defied﴾ is specifically those being spoken of, in which case it is an use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, to convey that they, together with their earlier attributes, have also been characterized by defiance, and to convey that their defiance is the cause of the word of Allah having come true against them. The object of comparison would then be the haqq (truth) derived from haqqat, meaning: thus has truth come true, the word of your Lord has come true against them, emphasizing its manifestness, to the extent that when it is desired to liken it and bring it close, it is compared only to itself, in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And thus We made you a community of moderation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], in Surah al-Baqarah.

Along with this, it is also a tadhyil for what it contains of summation (fadhlakah) and wonder.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 34:

﴿Say, "Is there any of your partners who originates creation and then repeats it?" Say, "It is Allah who originates creation and then repeats it. So how are you deluded away?"﴾

This is a resumption in the manner of repetition of his earlier words, ﴿Say, "Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth?"﴾ [Yunus: 31]. This is a context of affirming and enumerating the proofs, and it is among the motives for repetition. It is an argument against them, that the condition of their deities is the opposite of the attributes of Allah, the Exalted. So after he established against them the proof of Allah's exclusive possession of provision, His creation of the senses, His creation of the kinds, and His management of all affairs, and that He is the one deserving of divinity by reason of that exclusivity, he here makes clear that their deities are stripped of the attributes of perfection, and that Allah is characterized by them. It was not joined by a conjunction because it is a separate, independent purpose, and the placement of the repetition adds to its independence.

The interrogative is a denial and an affirmation by way of denying that, since the speaker is not seeking an answer, and they cannot but acknowledge it. It therefore carries the meaning of negating that any of their deities originates creation and then repeats it. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to ascend with them in the argument by saying: ﴿Allah originates creation and then repeats it﴾. The two sentences together thus became a restriction of the attribute of originating creation and its repetition to Allah, the Exalted, a restriction of exclusivity: that is, apart from your partners. That is, the idols do not deserve divinity, and Allah alone is singular in it.

The mention of the repetition of creation in both places, although they do not acknowledge it, is a kind of incorporation (idmaj) into the argument, and it is a wondrous art.

The attribution of the partners to the pronoun of the addressees has had its reason explained earlier, at His saying: ﴿Stay in your place, you and your partners﴾ [Yunus: 28].

His saying ﴿So how are you deluded away?﴾ is like His saying ﴿So how are you turned away?﴾ [Yunus: 32]. Afaka (أفك) means: he turned it over. The meaning: to what place are you turned over? The turning is figurative, and it is the corruption of judgment. Anna (أنّى) here is an interrogative about a figurative place, and the realities in which thinking is turned are likened to it. The metaphorical use of "place" for them is like the application of "subject" (mawdu') and "field" (majal) to them as well.

[Page 162]

This is another repetition, after His saying: ﴿Say: Is there any of your associates who originates creation and then repeats it?﴾ [Yunus: 34]. This is an argument from the deficiency of their gods in guiding to the perfection of the soul by spreading the truth, and from the fact that God, exalted is He, is the One who guides to perfection and truth.

[Page 163]

Taken together, the two clauses restrict the attribute of guidance to the truth to God, exalted is He, to the exclusion of their gods. This is *qasr* (restriction) of the type *qasr ifrad* (restriction that refutes a rival claim), as was previously explained with its counterpart. It is well known that the favour of guidance to the truth is the greatest of favours, because through it the community is made righteous and its members are safe from the aggression of the strong against the weak. Without guidance, the blessing of existence would be defective or would perish.

By "the truth" is meant the religion (*din*), which consists of righteous deeds, and its foundations, which are sound belief (*i'tiqad*).

He has followed the argument for the perfection of the Creator through the beginning and repetition of creation with an argument for His perfection through guidance, as in the words of Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿Who created me, and it is He who guides me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 78]; the words of Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation, then guided it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 50]; and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, and who determined and guided﴾ [al-A'la: 1–3]. This is because man, who is the most perfect being on earth, is composed of a body and a soul. Thus, the argument for the existence and perfection of the Creator through the bringing into being of bodies and what is in them is *khalq* (creation), and the argument for Him through the ordering of the states of souls and their rectitude is *hidaya* (guidance).

His saying ﴿Is one who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed...﴾ up to the end is a consequence, in the form of an interrogation of affirmation (*istifham taqriri*), of what the two preceding clauses have established: that the guidance to the truth is restricted to God, exalted is He, to the exclusion of their gods. No people of sound intellect should differ about this: whoever guides to the truth leads to the spiritual perfection, which is the lasting perfection for eternity, the existence protected from corruption. The creation of bodies is intended for the sake of souls, and the goal for souls is to be guided. Therefore the highest aim is guidance. Since minds are subject to confusion and error, souls need a guidance received from the source that is protected from error, which is the side of God, exalted is He. For this reason, the one who guides to the truth is more worthy to be followed, because he reforms souls and the order of the human world. Following him is obligatory by reason, while following anyone else has no justification, since there is no benefit to be expected from following him. The actions of rational beings are protected from being purposeless.

His saying ﴿Or one who does not find guidance unless he is guided﴾ means: one who is not guided himself, let alone guiding others. That is, he does not accept guidance, so how could he guide others? Therefore it is not right that he be followed.

[Page 163 continued]

By "the one who does not find guidance" (*man la yahiddi*) is meant the idols, for they are not guided to anything, as Abraham said: ﴿O my father, why do you worship what neither hears nor sees and cannot avail you in anything?﴾ [Maryam: 42].

The reciters have differed concerning His saying ﴿Or one who does not find guidance﴾ (*amman la yahiddi*). Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read it with a *fatha* on the *ya'* (with the prefix *ya'*, as the imperfect) and a *fatha* on the *ha'*, on the basis that its original form is *yahtadi* (finds guidance). The *ta'* was changed to *dal* because their points of articulation are close, it was assimilated into the *dal*, and the vowel of the *ta'* was transferred to the quiescent *ha'*. (There is no significance in the reading of Qalun from Nafi', or in the reading of Abu 'Amr with the *fatha* of the *ha'* made *mukhtalas* (intermediate, between *fatha* and quiescence), because this is among the modes of recitation and is therefore not considered a difference in the reading.)

Hafs from 'Asim and Ya'qub read it with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, a *kasra* on the *ha'*, and a shadda on the *dal*. This is on the basis of dropping the vowel of the assimilated *ta'*, and placing a *kasra* on the *ha'* to avoid the meeting of two quiescent letters (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*). Abu Bakr from 'Asim read it with a *kasra* on the *ya'* and a *kasra* on the *ha'*, making the vowel of the *ya'* follow the *kasra* of the *ha'*. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, a quiescent *ha'*, and a light *dal*. This is on the basis that it is the imperfect of the intransitive *hada* (to be guided), meaning *ihtada* (to find guidance), just as one says *shara* meaning *ishtara* (to buy).

The exception in His saying ﴿unless he is guided﴾ is a mockery, a form of emphasizing a matter by means of something resembling its opposite. By "guidance" (*hady*) is meant transport from one place to another; that is, he does not find his way to a place except when people carry him and place him where they want him to be. Thus, transport from one place to another is likened to walking, and the thing transported is likened to the walker by way of metaphor (*makniyya*). This is indicated by what belongs to walking, which is guidance, in ﴿does not find guidance unless he is guided﴾.

Some exegetes have permitted that the verb in ﴿unless he is guided﴾ means the conducting of the bride (*ihda' al-'arus*), that is, her transfer from her family's house to her husband's house. It is said: "She was guided (*hudiyat*) to her husband."

The clause ﴿So what is wrong with you? How do you judge?﴾ is an interrogation of wonder (*istifham ta'jibi*), a consequence of their following one who does not find guidance in any state. Their following is their worship of them.

*Ma* is an interrogative noun (*ism istifhamiyya*), the subject (*mubtada'*); *lakum* is the predicate (*khabar*); and the *lam* is the *lam* of specification (*lam al-ikhtisas*). The meaning is: what is it that is established for you, that you follow one who does not find guidance by himself, but is transported from place to place?

[Page 164]

The Arabic saying *ma laka?* ("what is the matter with you?") and similar expressions are an interrogation that is treated in the same way as an interrogation both in its literal and its figurative use. In a hadith, a man said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Direct me to a deed that will admit me to Paradise." The people said: "What is wrong with him! What is wrong with him!" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "He has a need... What is wrong with him?" Thus, when the matter asked about is an evident state, there is no need to mention anything after "what is wrong with him," as occurs in the hadith.

Al-Zajjaj took this verse as an example of this, saying: "*Ma lakum*" is a complete statement, meaning: what is there for you in worshipping idols?

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The reciters stop at *fa-ma lakum*, then begin with *kayfa ta'kumun*."

When it is otherwise, they follow the interrogation with a state (*hal*), which is the more common usage, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?﴾ [al-Saffat: 25]; and ﴿What is the matter with them, that they turn away from the reminder?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 49]. For this reason some grammarians said: "A statement like this is not complete without mention of a state after it." Therefore the difference between their view and the view of al-Zajjaj is verbal.

The clause ﴿How do you judge?﴾ is an interrogation that takes the place of an explanation of the generality contained in the clause "what is wrong with you." For this reason it is separated from it. It is likewise an interrogation of wonder at their erroneous judgment, since they judged the divinity of one who does not find guidance. Thus it is wonder upon wonder.

You may also take this clause as evidence for an omitted state.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 36:

﴿And most of them follow nothing but conjecture. Indeed, conjecture does not avail against the truth at all. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the sentence ﴿Say: Is there any of your partners who guides to the truth?﴾ [Yunus: 35], by way of conjoining that sentence to its two similar counterparts mentioned before it. So after Allah commanded His Messenger to dispute with them concerning what they had made into gods, which have no control, no governance, and no guidance, He followed this with the statement that their worship of them is the following of a false conjecture, meaning: if indeed they have in it no semblance of truth.

The pronoun in His saying "most of them" refers to the people referred to by the pronoun in "your partners" and by "What is the matter with you? How do you judge?" [Yunus: 35]. He generalized the address in the pronouns of "your partners" and "What is the matter with you? How do you judge?" [Yunus: 35], but He specified the judgment of following conjecture to "most of them," because all the polytheists agreed in following the worship of idols. Here He made clear that they are not equal in the belief that moved them to worship them, as an indication that among them are a few intelligent people whose understanding rose above believing that the idols have any control, but they openly worshipped them, following their desires and preserving leadership among their people. The aim of this is not to absolve those who worshipped idols without any conjecture regarding their divinity, for they are worse than those who worshipped them out of imagination. Rather, the aim is to increase the argument against the invalidity of their worship, to the point that among its worshippers there is a group who are not at peace regarding the certainty of their divinity. On reflection it becomes clear that these are the elite of the people and their men of understanding, since the context is one of correcting that conjecture. So in it there is an awakening for their masses, and in it is an increase of admonition for their elite, so that they may desist from continuing to worship that which their hearts are not at peace with. This is like His later saying: ﴿And among them are those who believe in it, and among them are those who do not believe in it﴾ [Yunus: 40].

Conjecture (ẓann): it is applied to degrees of perception. It is applied to firm belief that is not mixed with doubt, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed it is difficult, except for the humble﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45], ﴿who are certain that they will meet their Lord and that they will return to Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 46]. It is also applied to belief mixed with doubt. It appears that it is literal in this second sense and metaphorical in the first, but in the first it is widespread, so it has become like a homonym. This has been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah at the discussion of the aforementioned verse. From it is His saying: ﴿The chiefs of those who disbelieved among his people said: Indeed, we see you in foolishness, and indeed we think you are among the liars﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 66] in Surat al-Aʿraf, and His saying: ﴿And they thought that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 118] in Surat Bara'a (al-Tawbah).

It has also been used figuratively for a mistaken belief, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, some conjecture is sin﴾ [al-Hujurat: 12], and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Beware of conjecture, for conjecture is the most false of speech."

Conjecture has been frequently used in the Qur'an and the Sunnah for mistaken knowledge, compound ignorance, and false imaginings. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Beware of conjecture, for conjecture is the most false of speech." It is also sometimes applied to the conjecture of probability, as in His saying: ﴿The believing men and believing women thought well of themselves﴾ [al-Nur: 12], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, some conjecture is sin﴾ [al-Hujurat: 12]. This meaning is the technical term among the scholars of the principles of religion (uṣūl al-dīn) and the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh). It is knowledge based on a preponderant proof with a slight possibility of error. This conjecture is the basis of legal responsibility for the branches of the Shariʿa.

So the way to reconcile these conflicting usages is to apply each in its appropriate place according to the contexts and settings of the discourse. Thus the meaning of His saying here, ﴿Indeed, conjecture does not avail against the truth at all﴾, is that knowledge mixed with doubt does not avail anything in establishing the sought truth. That is what requires firmness and certainty from the knowledge gained through rational proof, because firmness is possible in them for one who applies his reason correctly, since certainty results from rational proofs. As for what is attained through apparent evidences by which certainty cannot be reached in all circumstances, it suffices in that case with preponderant conjecture after applying reflection, and this is what is called ijtihad.

"Ẓannan" is in the accusative as the object of "yattabiʿu" (follow). Since conjecture requires something conjectured, following conjecture is following the conjectured object, meaning they follow something for which there is no proof except conjecture, that is, a false belief.

The indefiniteness of "ẓannan" is for belittlement, meaning a feeble conjecture. The form of restriction (qasr) indicates that they, in their beliefs that contradict monotheism, possess nothing of the truth, in refutation of their belief that they are upon the truth.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, conjecture does not avail against the truth at all﴾ is a causal explanation (taʿlil) of what the restriction indicates, namely that they are not upon anything of the truth, so how can they claim that they are upon the truth?

"Al-Haqq" (the truth) is that which is established in reality. What is meant by it here is knowledge of Allah and His attributes, of what is indicated by rational proof, such as His existence and life, and what is indicated by the act of Allah, such as knowledge, power, and will.

"Shay'an" is an absolute object emphasizing its verb, meaning it avails nothing at all of availing.

"Min" is for substitution, meaning in place of the truth.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) serving as a threat of punishment.

[Page 167]

﴿And this Qur'an could not have been fabricated apart from God, but it is a confirmation of what lies between its hands and a detailed explanation of the Book, there is no doubt in it, from the Lord of the worlds﴾

Since the primary purpose of this surah is to refute the astonishment of the polytheists at the revelation of the Qur'an to the Prophet (ﷺ), and to show that they have not been guided to its clear signs, which indicate that it is from God, and how they did not consider the circumstances of the Messenger, which indicate that what he brought is revelation from God, and how, despite this, they asked him to bring a Qur'an other than it or to change its verses to suit their desires. Then he moved on to their request that another sign from God, other than the Qur'an, be sent down to him. All of this was interwoven with a description of their fabrication of lies in claiming partners for God, the establishment of proofs for God's sole divinity and for the resurrection, a warning to them of what befell the nations before them, a reminder of God's blessings upon them and His granting them respite, and an explanation of their error in holding polytheism as a belief based on faulty reasoning and corrupt analogy. Therefore, the discourse returns to their claims about the Qur'an, refuting their opinion, which is also of the vain conjecture, by their analogy of the circumstances of prophethood and revelation to the measure of their customs, just as they analogized the reality of divinity to something similar. So this verse confronted them by mentioning the attributes of the Qur'an itself, which indicate that it is truth from God, and challenged them to produce its like.

So the clause ﴿And this Qur'an could not have been fabricated apart from God﴾ may be coordinated with the clause ﴿And most of them follow nothing but conjecture﴾ [Yunus: 36], on account of their following conjecture in both matters: the affairs of divinity and the affairs of prophethood. It may also be coordinated with the whole of what preceded it, as the coordination of one aim upon another aim and one narrative upon another narrative, and it conveys a detailing of what the mention of the disjointed letters at the beginning of the surah and the three sentences that follow those letters had summarized. The clause may also be coordinated with the clause ﴿Say: It is not for me to change it on my own accord﴾ [Yunus: 15], as a completion of the answer to their words ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it﴾ [Yunus: 15]. This statement is directed toward the challenge of the Qur'an's inimitability, and it conveys the emphasis in negating that it could be fabricated by other than God, that is, attributed to God falsely while it comes from other than Him. Indeed, His saying ﴿And this Qur'an could not have been fabricated﴾ is more eloquent than saying "It is not fabricated," because of what the verb "to be" (kāna) indicates of existence, meaning: it was not such that it could be fabricated. Its very existence is incompatible with its being fabricated. Thus the evidence of its own essence is sufficient to show that it is not fabricated. That is, if the discerning person reflects sincerely upon the surahs of the Qur'an, he will know that it is from God and that it cannot be of human composition. The structure "mā kāna an yuftara" is therefore equivalent to "mā kāna li-yuftara" with the lam of negation (lām al-juḥūd), and the lam has been omitted in accordance with the habitual omission of the preposition with "an." Since "an" appears here, the lam of negation has been omitted. Although it is more common for the lam of negation to be mentioned and "an" to be presumed and not mentioned, when the verb "kāna," which normally accompanies the lam of negation, is mentioned, one dispenses with mentioning the lam of negation for the sake of brevity.

The reason for departing from the use of the lam of negation, by saying "mā kāna hādhā al-Qur'ānu li-yuftarā," is that the lam of negation most often occurs in the negation of an action from an agent rather than from an object, because of the meaning of ownership that the lam indicates.

Know that a statement with "an" and a verb is equivalent to a statement with a verbal noun (maṣdar), and this verbal noun has the sense of the passive participle (maf'ūl), because the relative clause of "an" here is a verb in the passive voice. The implied construction is "mā kāna hādhā al-Qur'ānu iftirā'a muftarin," so that the verbal noun formed from "an" becomes a verbal noun in the sense of the object, like "al-khalq" in the sense of "al-makhlūq" (the created). It is also more emphatic than saying "mā kāna muftarā," and so emphasis is achieved from two directions: the direction of the verb "kāna" and the direction of the causal "an."

The "min" in His saying ﴿min dūni Allāh﴾ ("apart from God") is for the figurative starting point, connected to "yuftarā," meaning: that it be fabricated against God by a fabricator. So His saying ﴿min dūni Allāh﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "yuftarā," and it is in the sense of a descriptive qualifier that clarifies.

"Al-iftirā'" means lying, and it has been mentioned before in His saying ﴿But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against God﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 103] in Surat al-'Uqūd.

When the fabrication was negated from the Qur'an, it was described as being a confirmation and a detailing. Accordingly, all its descriptions came in the form of verbal nouns, to signal that it has reached the utmost limit in these meanings, to the point that it has become one with their genera.

As for ﴿a confirmation of what lies between its hands﴾, its being a confirmer of the earlier Books means that it clarifies what is true in them, distinguishes it from what was added to them and what was distorted in their interpretation, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿confirming what is before it of the Book and a guardian over it﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 48], as has been mentioned in Surat al-'Uqūd. Also, it is "muṣaddaq" (with the dal vowelled with a fatḥa), that is, it is confirmed by the testimony of the earlier Books in what they took as a covenant from their people, that they should believe in the Messenger who would come as a confirmer and a seal. The description with the verbal noun is thus suitable for both matters, because the verbal noun requires an agent and an object.

As for "tafṣīl" (detailing), it is clarification in its various kinds. The apparent meaning is that the definiteness of "al-Kitāb" is the definiteness of the genus, so it encompasses all the Books. The meaning of the Qur'an being a detailing of them is that it clarifies what came in summary form in the earlier Books, abrogates what the people have no benefit in continuing to apply, and resolves the ambiguous matters through which the People of the Book went astray. All of this falls under the meaning of "tafṣīl," and this is the meaning of His saying ﴿and a guardian over it﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 48] in Surat al-'Uqūd. This is other than the meaning of His saying ﴿and a detailing of all things﴾ [Yūsuf: 111] in the other verse.

The clause ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ is a resumptive clause (mustaʼnafa) that refutes the allegations of those who claimed it is fabricated, by uprooting the claim of its fabrication, and by showing that such claims do not pass with people of insight and sound reason. The doubt negated from it is that there should be, in its essence or in what accompanies it, something that gives rise to doubt. For this reason, the doubt of those who doubt about it is an alleged and claimed doubt, and if they were to examine themselves, they would find that they are not in doubt. This has been discussed before with a parallel to this in the opening of Surat al-Baqara.

The placement of His saying ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾ admits of several possibilities, the most apparent of which is that it is a settled adverbial phrase (ẓarf mustaqirr) in the position of the predicate of an omitted subject, which is the pronoun referring to the Qur'an. The clause is then a second resumptive statement (istiʼnāf thānin), and "min" is for the starting point which indicates arrival, meaning: it has come from the Lord of the worlds, that is, from His revelation and His speech. This corresponds to His saying: "min dūni Allāh" (apart from God).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 38:

Page 170
﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say, "Then bring a surah like it, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful."﴾

Am (أم) here is for the transitional turning (al-idrab al-intiqali) from negation to the rhetorical interrogation of denunciation and wonder (al-istifham al-inkari al-ta'jibi), and it is an ascent in refuting their claim that the Qur'an is a fabrication (muftara) from Allah.

Since "am" is specifically used to conjoin interrogation, the interrogation is implied with it wherever it occurs. So the interrogation that "am" indicates is an interrogation of wonder and denunciation, and the meaning is: "Rather, do they say he invented it, after the proofs of its truthfulness and its freedom from fabrication have become clear to them?"

Among the eloquent features of this style is that the description of the Qur'an is placed first with what necessitates its distance from fabrication and with what it contains of the most noble attributes of books, and with the honouring of its attribution to Allah, may He be exalted. Then this is followed by the interrogation about the claim of the polytheists that it is a fabrication, so that the listener receives this claim with greater disgust and wonder at the folly of its proponents. Therefore their claim that it is a fabrication was placed within the scope of the interrogation of denunciation and wonder.

Allah commanded His Prophet to answer their claim of fabrication by challenging them (ta'jiz), and to cut off the argument against them. So He commanded them to bring a surah like it. The command is one of challenge (amr ta'jiz), and the challenge (tahaddi) by bringing forth a surah resembling the surahs of the Qur'an has occurred, meaning one that resembles it in eloquence and excellence of composition. This likeness has already been established when commenting on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then bring forth a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23] in Surat al-Baqarah.

His saying: ﴿and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful﴾ is like His saying in the verse of al-Baqarah: ﴿and call your witnesses besides Allah, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23]. The meaning of "truthful" here is: in your saying that he invented it. For if he is able to invent it, you are able to oppose it, for you are equal in this Arabic language.

The object of "istata'tum" is omitted because it is evident from the verb "ud'u": that is, "whomever you are able to call upon for support and assistance in composing a surah like the surahs of the Qur'an."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 39:

page 171
﴿Nay, they denied that which they did not encompass in knowledge, and its interpretation had not yet come to them. Likewise denied those before them. So see how was the end of the wrongdoers.﴾
"Bal" (nay) is a transitional idrab (change of subject), to explain the nature of their denial, and that their state in hastening to deny before reflecting is more astonishing than the very act of denial, since they rushed to deny it without considering the proofs of its authenticity, to which His saying indicated: ﴿And it was not [possible] for this Qur'an to be produced by other than Allah﴾ [Yunus: 37].

Al-takdhib (denial) is attributing falsehood to something, or describing it as false, whether this was from conviction or not.

The choice of expressing the Qur'an by way of the relative construction in His saying: ﴿that which they did not encompass in knowledge﴾ is because of what the relative clause implies of the strangeness of that state, which is incompatible with applying denial, for they denied before they tested, and this is of the nature of foolishness and ignorance.

Al-ihata (encompassing) of a thing is being around it like a wall, and it was previously mentioned just before in His saying: ﴿and they thought that they were encompassed by it﴾ [Yunus: 22]. It is used as a metaphor for being able to master a thing such that nothing of it escapes. From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they cannot encompass Him in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 110], and His saying: ﴿and He has encompassed what is with them﴾ [al-Jinn: 28], meaning He knew it. So His saying ﴿that which they did not encompass in its knowledge﴾ means: that which they did not perfect the knowledge of.

The ba' (bi) is for transitivity. Its usual function with the verb of encompassing is to enter upon the encompassed object, which is the known, and here that is the Qur'an. He turned away from saying "bima lam yuhituu bihi 'ilman" or "bima lam yuhit 'ilmuhum bihi" to "bima lam yuhituu bi'ilmihi" for emphasis, since knowledge has been made the object of knowing. The original phrasing before negation was "ahatu bi'ilmihi," meaning they perfected its knowledge to the utmost perfection. When it was negated it became "lam yuhituu bi'ilmihi," meaning it was required that they encompass its knowledge, because the abundance of the proofs of its truthfulness requires increased reflection and precise examination, such that the observer must know its proofs, then reconsider them, and apply knowledge upon knowledge and examination upon examination, until encompassing knowledge is attained. In this there is emphasis on how greatly it needs sincere reflection, and emphasis on declaring ignorant those who hastened to deny without reflecting on something truly worthy of reflection, after reflection.

page 172
The meaning is that they hastened to deny the Qur'an at the first hearing, before they understood it, knew the reality of its matter, and before they contemplated it. Such denial arises only from obstinacy and enmity, not from a conviction that it is falsehood. Furthermore, the non-encompassing of its knowledge varies: some of it is pure absence, which is the state of the common masses; and some of it is absence in a general sense, which is what happens with some kind of doubt and hesitation, or occurs while its truthfulness is preponderant but one does not encompass what denial leads to of severe punishment. A parallel to this verse is in Surat al-Naml: ﴿He said: Did you deny My signs while you did not encompass them in knowledge? Or what were you doing?﴾ [al-Naml: 84].

The clause ﴿and its interpretation had not yet come to them﴾ is conjoined to the relative clause, meaning: they denied that for which its interpretation had not yet come to them. This is an escalation in describing them with lack of deliberation and steadfastness, meaning: if they had waited until the interpretation of the Qur'an came to them, that is, what of it needs interpretation, rather they were determined to deny before the interpretation appeared.

Ta'wil (interpretation) is derived from "aala," meaning to return to a thing. It is used for the explanation of a word whose meaning is obscure, an explanation that reveals the meaning, so that it becomes clear after having been obscure. From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and none knows its interpretation except Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7], and so on. In this usage it is close to the meaning of tafsir (exegesis). It has been mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran and in the First Introduction of this commentary. Ta'wil is also used for the manifestation of what was hidden of the meaning of a word or a sign, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is the interpretation of my dream from before﴾ [Yusuf: 100], and His saying: ﴿Do they await anything but its interpretation?﴾ [al-A'raf: 53], meaning the manifestation of what He warned them of, of punishment. The ta'wil in this verse may bear both meanings, and perhaps both are intended: that the interpretation of what they claim they did not understand of the meanings of the Qur'an had not yet come to them, due to their not being accustomed to knowing its like, such as the wisdom of legislation, the occurrence of resurrection, the preference of weak believers over the chieftains of the disbelievers, the revelation of the Qur'an in installments, and similar matters. They used to judge matters by what they were accustomed to in perceptible things, and they used to measure the unseen by the seen, so they denied that and its like before its interpretation came to them. Had they believed and kept company with the Prophet ﷺ, they would have known them one by one. Also, what had not yet come to them is the interpretation of what they reckoned the non-hastening of as evidence of falsehood, as they said: ﴿If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], thinking that if they provoked Allah to anger, He would hasten punishment for them; so they supposed the delay in its occurrence to be evidence that the Qur'an was not truth from Him. Likewise they used to ask for signs of extraordinary events, such as their saying: ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush for us from the earth﴾ [al-Isra: 90], and so on. Had they submitted and kept company with the Prophet, peace be upon him, they would have known that Allah does not give weight to the proposals of misguidance.

page 173
On both interpretations, the particle "lamma" is set for negating the verb in the past while indicating that the negation continues up to the time of speaking. That implies the negated thing is expected to occur. So in its negation here there is an indication that the explanation of the meanings that were stated in summary will come later; thus it is a promise, and that what He threatened them with will befall them, like His saying: ﴿On the day its interpretation comes, those who had forgotten it before will say: The messengers of our Lord had indeed come with the truth. So are there any intercessors for us to intercede on our behalf?﴾ [al-A'raf: 53]. On this interpretation it is therefore a warning.

The clause ﴿Likewise denied those before them﴾ is a resumption (istinaf), and the address is to the Prophet ﷺ or to whoever is able to hear. The demonstrative "kadhalika" refers to their mentioned denial, meaning the denial of those before them was like their denial. What is meant by "those before them" are the nations that denied their messengers, as indicated by the thing compared to.

Among the purposes of this comparison are several matters: First, that this is the custom of obstinate disbelievers, so that the polytheists know they are alike to the nations that denied the messengers, and so they may take warning.

Second: an allusion to warning them that punishment will descend upon them as it descended upon those nations whose fate the listeners knew and whose dwellings they witnessed.

Third: consolation for the Prophet ﷺ, that he has met from his people only what the earlier messengers met from their peoples.

For this reason, the address to the Prophet ﷺ is made to follow the comparison with His saying: ﴿So see how was the end of the wrongdoers﴾, meaning the end of the nations who wronged themselves by denying the messengers as these people denied.

page 174
The command to look at the end of the wrongdoers is intended to make their like in denial be measured against them, expecting that calamities like those that befell those nations will befall them, so that you may know the magnitude of what they confront you with of denial, and so that you do not think they will escape punishment.

The seeing here is visual.

"Kayfa" may be free of interrogation, being a noun of state and manner, as in the common expression "be however you wish." From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He it is who forms you in the wombs however He wills﴾ [Al 'Imran: 6], in Surat Al 'Imran. In that case "kayfa" is the object of the verb "unzur," and the clause ﴿how was the end of the wrongdoers﴾ is a description of "kayfa." The meaning is: look with your eye at a state described as "how was the end of the wrongdoers," namely the state of the ruin of their dwellings, a ruin that arose from the vanishing of their inhabitants.

It is also possible that "kayfa" is an interrogative noun, and the meaning is: look into this question, that is, the answer to the question, meaning: reflect upon it and ponder it. Here "kayfa" is the predicate of "kana," and the verb of looking is suspended from acting upon its two objects by what "kayfa" carries of interrogative meaning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 40:

﴿And among them are those who believe in it, and among them are those who do not believe in it. And your Lord is most knowing of the corrupters.﴾

It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿Rather, they denied that which they did not encompass in knowledge of﴾ [Yunus: 39], because the report of their denial, that it occurs without comprehensive knowledge of what they denied, requires that their denial of it is not based on insight and reflection. Since the matter is of this standing, the state of those who deny it varies, to the point that it reaches a denial coupled with a belief in the negation of falsehood from it. For this reason, the placement of this verse after the other is in the position of specification (takhsis) of the general in its apparent sense, or clarification (bayan) of the unclear, regarding the lack of comprehensive knowledge of it, as its explanation has preceded in His saying: ﴿that which they did not encompass in knowledge of﴾ [Yunus: 39].

Thus their state regarding belief in the Qur'an was like their state in following the idols, when He said of them: ﴿And most of them follow not except assumption﴾ [Yunus: 36].

صفحة ١٧٥

The word "most of them" (aktharihim) indicates that among them are those who know the invalidity of idol-worship, but they follow it out of solidarity with their people and obstinate opposition to the truth. Likewise is their state in denying that the Qur'an is attributed to God: among them are those who believe in it yet conceal their belief out of obstinacy and hostility, and among them are those who do not believe in it and deny it through taqlid (blind imitation) of their elders.

The two groups are shared in denial outwardly, as the partitive "min" (some of them) indicates, and the plural pronoun refers back to what the pronouns of ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"﴾ [Yunus: 38] refer to. So the meaning of "believes in it" is that he affirms its truth in himself, but outwardly he displays its denial, combining the attribution of belief to them with making them part of those who say "he invented it."

The choice of the present tense (al-mudari') indicates the continuity of belief in it by some of them together with opposition, and the continuity of non-belief in it by some of them as well.

The clause ﴿And your Lord is most knowing of the corrupters﴾ is parenthetical (mu'taridah) at the end of the speech according to the view of the verifying scholars of the science of meanings (ʿulamaʾ al-maʿani), and it is an allusion to threat and warning, and that they are among the corrupters, since the mention of the corrupters here is only because these are among them; otherwise there would be no relevance in mentioning the corrupters. So the meaning is: "And your Lord is most knowing of them, because He is most knowing of the corrupters who are of their company."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 41:

﴿And if they deny you, say: "For me is my work, and for you is your work. You are free of what I do, and I am free of what you do."﴾

Since knowledge of their denial had already been established from the verses preceding it, it became clear that the denial supposed here by the conditional particle is denial in the future, that is, persistence in denial. This is because everything by which the truth of the Qur'an is shown also confirms the truth of the Messenger ﷺ who brought it. That is, if they insist on denial after you have confronted them with the proof, then know that proofs will not benefit them, and declare your disavowal of them, just as they have disavowed you.

The meaning of ﴿For me is my work, and for you is your work﴾ is disengagement (al-mutarakah). It is one of the expressions that have been treated as a proverb (mathal), and for this reason it was constructed with brevity and abundance of meaning. Exclusivity (al-hasr) is conveyed in it by fronting the object (taqdim al-ma'mul) and by expressing it through the genitive construction "my work" and "your work." It was not expressed as "for me is what I do and for you is what you do," as is expressed afterward.

Al-bari' (the one free) is one who is clear of being involved in something and of mixing with it. It is an intensive form (fa'il) derived from barra'a (the doubled form) contrary to the usual pattern (ala ghayr qiyas). The verb barra'a is derived from bari'a (with a kasra on the ra'), meaning: when he is free of a thing, its consequence and being held accountable for it have ceased.

This construction is not meant in its literal sense; rather, it is meant as a metonymy (kinayah) for distancing. This metonymically expressed meaning has come explicitly in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If they disobey you, then say: "I am free of what you do"﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:216]. For this reason, the clause ﴿You are free of what I do﴾ through its end is an explanation (bayan) of the clause ﴿For me is my work, and for you is your work﴾, and for this reason it was separated (fusilat) from it without a conjunction.

The expression did not use "work" as a verbal noun (masdar), as it was used in His saying ﴿For me is my work, and for you is your work﴾; instead it was expressed with a verb as the relative clause (silah) of "ma" (what), to indicate disengagement from every work that occurs in the present and future. As for past work, since it has ended, the purpose does not relate to mentioning disengagement from it. Had it been expressed with "work" (as a noun), it might have been wrongly assumed that a specific work is meant, since an annexed verbal noun does not generalize; and also to avoid repeating the same word within a single utterance, since the explanatory clause is part of what it explains; and also because this wording is more suited to the smoothness of the composition, for in the "ma" in His saying "mimma a'malu" there is an elongation (madd) that makes it more fitting for prolonging the breath at the end of the verse and preparing for a pause on His saying "mimma ta'maluna," and because of the elongation also in "ta'maluna," and because it observes the closing rhyme (fasilah).

This is among the subtleties of the eloquence of the Qur'an that lie beyond the eloquence commonly recognized among the eloquent.

[Page 177]

﴿Among them are those who listen to you. Can you make the deaf hear, even though they do not understand?﴾ ﴿Among them are those who look at you. Can you guide the blind, even though they do not see?﴾

When the division of the polytheists was previously made with respect to their belief in the idols, into those who follow conjecture (*ẓann*) and those who are certain that the idols are nothing, and when their division with respect to the confirmation of the Qur'an was made into two categories, those who believe in its truthfulness and those who do not, this verse completed their division with respect to receiving from the Prophet (ﷺ) into two categories. One category attends his gathering and listens to his speech. The other category does not attend his gathering but only observes him and looks at his bearing (*samt*). In both states there is a great path to guidance, had they been guided. For hearing the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his guidance illuminates the minds of those who are receptive to guidance. Therefore, the persistence of the polytheists in their disbelief, despite hearing the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ) or seeing his conduct, indicates that they have reached the utmost extent of misguidance, and that the truth has been despaired of reaching them. This is not because his speech is deficient in its power to convey to guidance. Just as observing his noble bearing and the clear proofs of his prophethood in all his circumstances is sufficient to turn the soul toward him wholeheartedly, so the benefit is not lacking for the disbelievers who see his noble person with their own eyes, except because of the intensity of their hatred and envy of him. The context of the speech indicates that they listen to him and look at him, and do not benefit from that, because those who listen to him and those who look at him here continued in disbelief, as shown by His saying ﴿Among them﴾ in both places. Thus the clause ﴿and do not benefit﴾, or something similar to it, has been omitted for brevity, by the indication of the division. The imperfect verb was used instead of the active participle to indicate the repetition of listening and looking. Being deprived of guidance despite that repetition is more astonishing.

The clause ﴿Can you make the deaf hear, even though they do not understand?﴾ is a consequence (*tafrī'*) of the clause ﴿who listen to you﴾, together with what has been omitted within it. In this consequence there is an explanation of the reason they do not benefit from hearing the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ), as well as consolation for him and instruction for the Muslims. This strange condition is brought close to them by saying that those listeners are like deaf people who do not understand, in that they have been deprived of being affected by the speech they hear.

[Page 178]

So they are equated with the deaf who do not understand in this respect. This is an explicit metaphor (*isti'āra muṣarraḥa*), since He made them the very essence of the deaf.

Based on this, a question is built about the ability to make these deaf people hear and to guide these blind people, although they have added to their deafness the lack of understanding and added to their blindness the lack of insight. These two interrogatives are used to express astonishment at their condition: they listen to the call of the Prophet (ﷺ) without understanding it, and they look at his acts and conduct without being guided by them. Therefore these two interrogatives do not carry the meaning of denial toward the Prophet's (ﷺ) effort to convey to them and guide them, because the context rejects that.

These figurative meanings vary according to the context and the indicators. Therefore the two interrogatives are not a denial, and for this reason there is no problem arising from the position of *law* (*lawa*) as a connective particle here after what has the meaning of negation, such that the emphasis for which *law* was brought would be undermined. Rather the meaning is the reverse.

In these two interrogatives there is an *tarshīḥ* (a sustaining of the metaphor) for the metaphor of the deaf and the blind for these disbelievers. That is, when God created their souls disposed to obstinacy, stubbornness, and hatred and envy of the one whom God has favored, these qualities became barriers between them and being affected by what is heard and seen. So the form of the astonished interrogative was used, containing an affirmation of the predicate by placing the subject before the verbal predicate, in His saying ﴿Can you make hear﴾ and His saying ﴿Can you guide﴾, instead of saying "Do you make the deaf hear, and do you guide the blind?" Thus this astonishment becomes emphatic and strengthened.

The *law* in His saying ﴿even though they do not understand﴾ and His saying ﴿even though they do not see﴾ is a connective *law*, indicating exaggeration in the states, and it is the kind in which what follows it is the furthest extent to which the purpose can be attached.

For this reason, they estimate, to explain its meaning, a clause before the clause of *law* whose content is the opposite of the clause that *law* entered upon. So it is said here: "Can you make the deaf hear, if they were to understand? Rather, even if they do not understand."

Since the purpose here is to express astonishment at their condition, in that they did not reach guidance, their lack of comprehension and their lack of insight is a metonymy (*kināya*) for their not understanding and their having no insight. So the meaning of "do not understand"

[Page 179]

is that they do not have the perception of minds. That is: even if their deafness were combined with the absence of their minds, a deaf person who is sensible may perhaps read the face of the one addressing him and infer from his features.

As for the meaning of ﴿do not see﴾, they have no insight by which they can see clearly. This is what al-Kashshāf (*al-Kashshāf*, Zamakhshari's commentary) explained, and it is the correct view, since without it the meaning of ﴿do not see﴾ would be equivalent to the meaning of blindness, and so the exaggeration conveyed by the connective *law* would not fall in its proper place, because it would become: "Can you guide the blind even though they are blind?" The implication of al-Kashshāf's statement is that one says *abṣara* when one uses one's insight, which is reflection and consideration of the realities of things. The words of *al-Asās* (*Asās al-Balāgha*, by Zamakhshari) revolve around this. Whatever the case, the intended meaning of His saying ﴿do not see﴾ is the sense of contemplation. That is: even if the blindness of the blind were combined with the absence of reflection, as is the condition of those who look at you, whether that is understood from the verb ﴿see﴾ in its literal or figurative usage. So with this wonderful arrangement, which includes a metaphor at its beginning, a metonymy at its end, and astonishment with its strengthening in the middle, it is established that they do not benefit with their hearing or their sight, and that they do not understand or reflect on the realities.

It is known that this condition with which they are characterized is one that God brought them to by His creation, and He made it a punishment for them for their rebellion in their disbelief, their stubbornness in their polytheism, and their turning away from the call of His Messenger. For this reason He made them deaf and blind. So the meaning is not that God is the One who makes them hear and guides them, rather than you, because this is a matter that is well known and does not need to be stated.

Ibn 'Arafa (*al-Shaykh Ibn 'Arafa*) raised a question about the difference between His saying ﴿who listen﴾ and His saying ﴿who look﴾, since the plural pronoun was used in the first and the singular pronoun in the second. He answered that hearing occurs from all directions, whereas looking occurs only from the facing direction. This answer is not clear, because the multiplicity of directions suitable for one of the two verbs has no effect when the listeners and the lookers are the same group, and because the plural and singular are equivalent here, since the meaning of the relative *man* in both is "those from whom the act proceeds," and they are a number, and the one who looks is not a single person.

The correct view is that both usages are equal in observing the wording and meaning of *man*. Perhaps the beginning with the plural in the relative clause of the first *man* indicates that the intended *man* is more than one specific person, and that the shift away from the plural in the relative clause of the second *man* is for variety and to avoid repeating the plural form because of its heaviness, especially after the meaning has been understood. Or perhaps the difference between the two forms is for suitability with the root of the two verbs *yastami'u* and *yanẓuru*. The verb *yanẓuru* does not suit the plural form, because its letters are heavier than the letters of *yastami'u*. So the shift is a thorough attention to the requirements of eloquence.
