The correct view is that both usages are equal in observing the wording and meaning of *man*. Perhaps the beginning with the plural in the relative clause of the first *man* indicates that the intended *man* is more than one specific person, and that the shift away from the plural in the relative clause of the second *man* is for variety and to avoid repeating the plural form because of its heaviness, especially after the meaning has been understood. Or perhaps the difference between the two forms is for suitability with the root of the two verbs *yastami'u* and *yanẓuru*. The verb *yanẓuru* does not suit the plural form, because its letters are heavier than the letters of *yastami'u*. So the shift is a thorough attention to the requirements of eloquence.

**Tadhyil** (a concluding statement that generalises the preceding point): ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people in anything, but it is the people who wrong themselves.﴾

The generality of "the people" includes the polytheists who listen but are not guided, and who look but do not take heed. The purpose of this concluding statement is an allusion (**ta'rid**) to a warning: that they will suffer what befell all those who wronged themselves by denying the messengers of Allah. The first occurrence of "the people" retains its general sense, while the second occurrence is intended in the specific sense of those people who wronged themselves, as indicated by the context of the statement. The use of the general form for these people was fitting, since it treats the great number as if it encompassed all, because that was the predominant state of people at that time.

This "but" (**istidrak**) implies an unstated statement following the negation of wrongdoing from Allah, namely: Allah does not wrong people by punishing those who did not deserve punishment, but people wrong themselves, so they deserve punishment. The meaning thus becomes: Allah does not wrong people by punishing them, but they wrong themselves by transgressing against what He willed from them, so He punishes them justly, because they did wrong and thereby incurred punishment.

The fronting of the object before its verb serves to emphasise the error of their thinking: that by their disbelief they only harmed themselves, and they did not wrong Allah or His messengers. Thus their deeds did no harm except to themselves.

Regarding the recitation: the majority (al-Jumhur) read **لَكِنَّ** with a doubled nun and **النَّاسَ** in the accusative (naṣb). Ḥamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a single (light) nun and **النَّاسُ** in the nominative (raf'). In the first reading, the accusative of **النَّاسَ** is the object of the verb, and the sentence is "but they wrong themselves." In the second reading, the nominative of **النَّاسُ** makes it the subject, with the particle lightened to a form that does not govern the noun in the accusative.

[Page 181]

﴿And on the Day We gather them﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*, conjunction) with ﴿And on the Day We gather them all, then We will say to those who associated partners [with Allah]: "Stay in your place"﴾ (Yunus: 28). This is a coordination of one narrative with another (*'atf al-qissa 'ala al-qissa*), a return to a theme of the discourse after its elaboration and its branching out, and after the censure and rebuke directed at those addressed. When the discussion previously mentioned the Day of Gathering, which is the time when the error of the polytheists is exposed through the disavowal of their associates from them, it followed this with a rebuke for their worship of idols, despite the clarity of the proofs of Allah's oneness (*tawhid*, the affirmation of God's unity). Since the Qur'an had already conveyed to them what would have protected them from that humiliating situation had they been guided by it, it followed this with an exaltation of the Qur'an and an affirmation that it lies beyond the capacity of humans, and with a denunciation of those who denied it and who varied in their turning away from it. When the theme had been fully addressed, the discourse returned to mention the Day of Gathering a second time, for it is the time of the disappointment of those who denied the resurrection, namely the very ones who associated partners [with Allah], and the exposure of their polytheism became manifest on the Day of Gathering. This is like the repetition of the final part upon the first part (*radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr*, a rhetorical device of echoing the end of a passage back to its beginning).

﴿Yawm﴾ ("Day") is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*zarf*, adverbial complement of time) governed by the verb *khasira* (﴿have lost﴾). The sense is: ﴿Those who denied the meeting with Allah have certainly lost, on the Day We gather them﴾. The context thus runs: ﴿And they were returned to Allah, their true Master, and what they used to fabricate has strayed away from them. And those who denied the meeting with Allah have certainly lost on the Day We gather them.﴾ The placing of the adverb of time before its governing verb is for emphasis, because the principal intent is to remind them of that Day, affirm its occurrence, and warn and threaten them with what will befall them therein.

For this reason, the discourse shifted from the pronominal form to the relative form in the words ﴿Those who denied the meeting with Allah have certainly lost﴾, rather than ﴿they have certainly lost﴾ (*qad khasiru*). This indicates that the cause of their loss is their denial of the meeting with Allah, and that this denial is one of the effects of polytheism. Thus it is linked to the first sentence, namely ﴿And on the Day We gather them all, then We will say to those who associated partners [with Allah]: "Stay in your place"﴾ (Yunus: 28), up to His words ﴿And what they used to fabricate has strayed away from them﴾ (Yunus: 30).

The majority of readers recite ﴿nahshuruhum﴾ ("We gather them") with the *nun* of majesty (first person plural, referring to Allah). Hafs, from 'Asim, recited it with the *ya'* of the third person (*ya' al-ghayba*), so the pronoun refers to the Name of Majesty, Allah, mentioned in the preceding words ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people in anything﴾ (Yunus: 44).

[Page 182]

The clause ﴿as if they had not remained except an hour of the day﴾ is either a parenthetical insertion between the clause ﴿nahshuruhum﴾ and the clause ﴿recognizing one another among themselves﴾, or a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the object pronoun in ﴿nahshuruhum﴾.

The *ka-'anna* here is the lightened (*mukhaffafa*) form of *ka-anna* with the doubled *nun*, one of the sisters of *inna*, and it is a particle of comparison. When it is lightened, its noun is usually omitted, and the implied form here is: ﴿as if they had not remained except an hour of the day﴾. The omitted noun is indicated by the pronouns preceding it.

The meaning is the comparison of those gathered, after periods of time that passed over them in the graves, to themselves as if they had remained in the graves only an hour of the day.

The *min* in ﴿min al-nahar﴾ ("of the day") is partitive (*tab'idiyya*), and it describes ﴿sa'a﴾ ("an hour"). This description is not intended as a restriction, since in a short span of time there is no difference whether it is of the day or of the night. Rather, it is a description that came out in the manner of what is usual, because the day is the time that comes to mind in ordinary speech, like the mention of the word "man" in reporting human conditions, as in His words: ﴿And on the Heights there will be men﴾ (al-A'raf: 46). Of this kind is what occurred in the hadith: "Indeed, it was made lawful for me only for an hour of a day," where the intended meaning is an hour of time, namely the hour in which the fighting with the people of Makkah took place, without regard to a restriction that it was in the daytime, although it happened to be in the daytime.

*Al-sa'a* ("hour") means a measure of time, and it is most commonly applied to a short period unless there is an indicator otherwise. It was discussed earlier at His words: ﴿They cannot delay an hour nor advance it﴾ (al-A'raf: 34), in the Surah al-A'raf.

The aspect of resemblance between the state of the time they spent in the graves and the staying for an hour of the day consists of several points: the certainty and occurrence (of the resurrection), such that the lapse of time did not prevent them from being gathered, and that they were gathered in the attributes by which they lived in this world, so that it is as if they had not perished. This is a consideration of the great power of Allah to return them.

The purpose of the comparison is an indirect allusion to the refutation of the claim of the polytheists, who considered the resurrection impossible on the pretext that the lapse of a long time and the change of bodies is incompatible with their revival: ﴿They say: "Shall we indeed be returned to our former state? Even when we have become decayed bones?"﴾ (al-Nazi'at: 10).

[Page 183]

The clause ﴿recognizing one another among themselves﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the object pronoun in ﴿nahshuruhum﴾.

*Al-ta'aruf* ("recognizing one another") is a reciprocal form (*tafa'ul*) from *'arafa* ("to know"). That is, each one of them on that day recognizes the one he knew in the world, and the other likewise recognizes him.

The purpose of mentioning this circumstance is the same as the purpose of mentioning the state ﴿as if they had not remained except an hour of the day﴾: to depict that they are gathered in the condition in which they were in the world, in their bodies and in their perception, as an additional clarification of the refutation of their claim that resurrection is impossible on the pretext that it contradicts the scattering of bodies in the graves and the extinguishing of minds through death.

Thus their loss became manifest on that day, in that they denied the resurrection and so did not prepare for its Day by accepting what the Messenger (ﷺ) had called them to.

[Page 184]

The mention of their denial, which appeared at the beginning of the surah in His words, (﴿The disbelievers said, "Indeed, this is clear magic."﴾ [Yunus: 2]), followed by the threat of a punishment that would befall them, and the indication that they denied the threat in His words, ﴿And if God hastened for people the evil [as they hasten for good]...﴾ [Yunus: 11], up to His words ﴿so that He may see how you act﴾ [Yunus: 14], was a warning of an expected punishment that would befall them in this world, as it had befallen the generations before them. It was well known of the character of the Prophet (ﷺ) that he was compassionate toward people and eager that this religion be completed and that all those invited to it be guided. Thus the Prophet may have feared that the punishment of total annihilation (ʿadhab al-istiʼsal) would descend upon them, so that their guidance would be lost. His words, ﴿And if God hastened for people the evil as they hasten for good, their term would have been decreed for them. But We leave those who do not expect Our meeting in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [Yunus: 11], were an explicit statement of the possibility of sparing them and an allusion to giving them respite. This verse came as an explanation of that and as a warning that, if they were given respite and were allowed to remain in this world, they would still not escape the final destination of the punishment of the Hereafter when they return to God's disposal, with no barrier.

[Page 185]

The speech was framed in the manner of leaving vague the outcome of the two conditions, so as to place people between fear and hope, even though it was addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ).

What is meant by ﴿some of what We promise them﴾ is the punishment of this world, for they were threatened with the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, for those who did wrong, there is a punishment besides that﴾ [al-Tur: 47]. The meaning, then, is: whether the punishment of this world befalls them, and you see it, or it does not befall them while God takes you (in death), their destination is to Us in every case.

So the content of "or We take you (in death)" is the counterpart of the content of "We show you some of what We promise them."

The two clauses together are two conditional clauses, and the answer of the condition is His words, ﴿then to Us is their return﴾.

Since the answer of both conditions was their return to God, expressed as a reference to the deferred punishment, it became necessary that the division in the condition be a disjunction between two states that have a relation to the realization of the return to God's punishment in both cases: the state of hastening the punishment for them in this world, and the state of deferring the punishment to the Hereafter. As for the Messenger's wish that they be punished and his death without seeing it, there is no relation between these two and the return to God in both of them, except by considering that one of them coincides with the state of hastening and the other corresponds to the state of deferral.

The hastening was expressed metaphorically as God showing the Messenger (the punishment), as an allusion to the fact that in the state of hastening the punishment, God wants from it only to grant justice to His Messenger by showing him the punishment of his opponents. Therefore, its opposite was built upon it: the opposite of hastening, which is expressed by His taking (the Prophet) in death, meaning not hastening the punishment, indeed deferring it, since the wisdom of hastening was to grant justice to the Messenger (ﷺ).

Since He made the content of the clause "We take you (in death)" the counterpart of the content of the clause "We show you," it became necessary that His showing him what they were threatened with of the punishment of this world was a recompense for their denial of him and their harm to him, in order to grant him victory, so that his affair would follow the custom of God regarding the messengers, as Noah said: ﴿My Lord, help me, for they have denied me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 26]. This was indicated by His words, exalted is He, immediately after it: ﴿For every nation there is a messenger﴾ [Yunus: 47], and His words: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ [Yunus: 48]. God, exalted is He, had indeed shown him some of what He had threatened them with: the famine that lasted seven years, through his supplication against them, and what befell them on the day of Badr of humiliation and the killing of their chieftains. This is indicated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿So watch for the day when the sky will bring a visible smoke, covering the people. This is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Dukhan: 10–11]; ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers﴾ [al-Dukhan: 12]; ﴿How can they have the reminder when a clear messenger had come to them?﴾ [al-Dukhan: 13]; ﴿Then they turned away from him and said, "A taught, possessed man"﴾ [al-Dukhan: 14]; ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little, but you will return [to disbelief]﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15]; ﴿On the day We strike with the greatest assault, indeed We will take retribution﴾ [al-Dukhan: 16].

The smoke (al-dukhan) is what they used to see in the years of famine, a resemblance of smoke in the land. The greatest assault (al-batshah al-kubra) is the assault of the day of Badr.

Consider His words, ﴿Then they turned away from him﴾ [al-Dukhan: 14] and His words, ﴿Indeed We will take retribution﴾ [al-Dukhan: 16].

Then God withheld from them the punishment of this world, also to please him, since he wished to preserve the remnant of them and would say: "Perhaps God will bring forth from their loins one who worships Him."

As for disbelief in God, its recompense is the punishment of the Hereafter.

Thus, in the speech, sentences were omitted, indicated by the sentences that are mentioned, with a firm conciseness, and the force of the speech became as follows: "And if We hasten for them some of the punishment, We will show you its descent upon them; or We take you in death, then We will defer the punishment from them after your death, that is, because the wisdom in hastening it no longer applies. Then their return is to Us, that is, their return is constantly and firmly to Us. We are most knowing of the wisdom that requires the execution of the threat against them at the appropriate time in this world, if We wish, during your life or after you, or in the Hereafter."

The word ﴿ʾimmā﴾ is (in) the conditional particle and (mā) the reinforcing particle for the conditional attachment. It is written in the Mushaf without a nun and with a doubled mīm, imitating the way it is pronounced. The conditional verb has been emphasized with the emphatic nun (nūn al-tawkīd), for when the verb of the condition is to be emphasized with the nun, the addition of (mā) after in (the conditional particle) becomes obligatory. The two are interdependent according to al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjaj and the author of al-Kashshaf, in their interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿So whether We show you﴾ [Ghafir: 77] in Surat Ghafir. Therefore, they do not say "in tukrimnī ukrimka" with the emphatic nun, but they say "in tukrimnī" without the emphatic nun, just as one does not say "immā tukrimnī" without the emphatic nun, but one says "in tukrimnī." The verse of al-A'sha is anomalous:

"So whether you see me, and I have a lock of hair, for calamities have worn it away."

Then he emphasized the conditional attachment a second time with the emphatic nun, and by placing the prepositional phrase before its governing element, which is "marjiʿuhum" ("their return"), for the sake of importance. The nominal sentence "ilaynā marjiʿuhum" ("to Us is their return") indicates permanence and stability, that is, this is a matter that is constantly in Our disposal.

The sentence ﴿then God is a witness over what they do﴾ is conjoined to the sentence ﴿then to Us is their return﴾. The particle "thumma" (then) here indicates rank-based sequence, as is the case with "thumma" when it conjoins sentences. Rank-based sequence means that the conjoined sentence is higher in rank than the one it follows. The sentence ﴿then God is a witness over what they do﴾, because it contains an allusion to requital for the evil of their deeds, was of greater importance in the purpose, which is the purpose of informing that their return is to God. For their return to God is general, and His knowledge of their deeds, expressed as a reference to calling them to account for them, is a detailed explanation of the general threat, and detail is more important than generality. The complete establishment of the purpose toward which the speech is directed, and the confirmation of the threat, were achieved by the generality and then by its detail. As for the matter of the punishment of the Hereafter occurring after their return to God with an interval, with all the strain involved in establishing that interval, it is of such a kind that it does not suit a eloquent speech to take up its mention.

His words, ﴿God is a witness over what they do﴾, are a statement used in its figurative meaning, since it is a metaphor for the threat of requital for everything they did in this world, such that He leaves nothing out.

Al-shahīd (the witness) is the one who testifies. Its real meaning is one who informs about a matter in which there is confirmation of the informant. It is used here for one who knows with certainty.

He used the present tense in His words "yafʿalūn" (they do) to indicate that He is knowing of what their deeds are occurring, and as for what has passed, it is more fitting for His knowledge.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 47:

Page 187
﴿And for every nation there is a messenger. So when their messenger comes, judgment is made between them with justice, and they are not wronged.﴾

It is an conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿And whether We show you some of what We promise them﴾ [Yunus: 46], and it stands in the position of the cause for the content of the clause before it. This clause makes clear that the coming of the Messenger to a nation is the end of the respite, and that if the nation denies its messenger, it deserves punishment for that. This is an announcement that their denial of the Messenger is what brings upon them the threat of punishment. It thus looks to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the cities until He sends into their mother [city] a messenger reciting to them Our verses﴾ [al-Qasas: 59], and His saying: ﴿And We would never punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra': 15].

The clause ﴿For every nation there is a messenger﴾ is not the intended object of the information; rather it is a preparation (tamhid) for the consequence derived from it by His saying: ﴿So when their messenger comes,﴾ etc. Therefore, it is not to be understood from the first clause that a messenger must be sent to every nation, because specifying the nation by time, lineage or place cannot be fixed, and a tribe, people, era or land may be without a messenger coming to it, even if that absence lasted a long time. Allah, Exalted is He, has said: ﴿So that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you﴾ [al-Qasas: 46]. The meaning, then: for every nation among the nations possessing laws there is a known messenger who came to it, such as ʿAd, Thamud, Madyan, the Jews, and the Chaldeans. The purpose of this speech is what is derived from it in His saying: ﴿So when their messenger comes, judgment is made between them with justice.﴾

The fa' (fa) is for consequence, and "idha" (when) is for temporal adverbiality, stripped of futurity. The meaning: at the time of the Messenger's coming, judgment between them takes place with justice. Placing the adverbial phrase before its governing verb, "quḍiya," serves to create suspense (tashwif) toward receiving the information.

The word "bayn" (between) indicates intermediacy between two things or among things, so it is determined that the pronoun to which it is attached here refers to the whole of the nation and its messenger; i.e., judgment is made between the nation and its messenger with justice, that is, God judges between them according to their conduct with their messenger.

Page 188
The meaning: God grants the nation respite in what it is in of error; then, when He sends a messenger to it, his sending is a sign that God, Exalted is He, intends their turning away from error. The term of respite ends with the messenger's conveying to them God's purpose regarding them. If they obey him, God is pleased with them and they profit; if they disobey him and oppose him, God judges between all of them with the recompense of each, a judgment of truth in which there is no injustice, and this is a judgment in this world.

The words ﴿judgment is made between them﴾ have indicated the occurrence of opposition between the disbelievers and the believers, among whom is the Messenger ﷺ.

This is a warning against opposing the Prophet ﷺ and a warning to the people of Makkah of what befell others. It was among the blessing and the compassion of the Prophet ﷺ that God preserved the Arabs and did not uproot them; but He showed them His might and destroyed their leaders on the day of Badr, then led them gradually into the fold of Islam until it embraced them, and they became its callers to the nations and bearers of its law to the world.

Since the words ﴿judgment is made between them﴾ indicated that the judgment is a judgment of deterrence for them for opposing their messenger, and that it is a severe punishment, such that whoever sees it or hears of it may suspect it is exaggerated, the clause ﴿and they are not wronged﴾ was brought, as a circumstantial clause (hal) emphasizing its governing element, which is ﴿judgment is made between them with justice,﴾ to indicate that the sin for which they were judged is a grave sin.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verses 48–49:

﴿They say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿Say, "I possess not for myself any harm or benefit, except what Allah wills. For every nation is a term. When their term comes, they will not remain behind it an hour, nor will they precede it."﴾

This is an conjunction with the clause ﴿And whether We show you some of what We promise them﴾ [Yunus: 46]. The connection is that when the preceding verse explained that hastening the threat for them in this world and delaying it are equal in the sight of Allah, since the complete threat is the threat of the Hereafter, this verse was attached to relate their mocking of the delay of the threat.

Their saying is related in the present tense to evoke the state, as in His saying, ﴿And he was constructing the ship﴾ [Hud: 38], to indicate the repetition of its occurrence from them. The promise is used to refer to what is promised, so the question about it with the adverb of time is interpreted with a supposition indicated by the context: "When is its manifestation?"

The question is used for expressing impatience, and it is a metonymy for their lack of concern for it and that they pay it no heed, so that it moves from that to their denying its occurrence by way of allusion, by the indication of their saying ﴿if you are truthful﴾, meaning: if you are truthful that it is going to happen, then specify for us its time. They mean: "We will not believe you until we see what you promised us," a metonymy for their belief that it will not befall and that they do not believe in it. The promise mentioned here is the punishment of this world with which they were threatened.

The address in their saying "if you are truthful" is to the Messenger, and the pronoun of respect is used for mockery, as in His saying: ﴿And they said, "O you to whom the Reminder has been revealed, indeed you are mad"﴾ [al-Hijr: 6], and His saying: ﴿And they said, "What is wrong with this messenger that he eats food"﴾ [al-Furqan: 7], and the saying of Abu Bakr ibn al-Aswad al-Kinani:

"The Messenger tells us that we will live, but how can the life of echoes and skulls be?"

This interpretation is the one suited to their answer with His saying: ﴿Say, "I possess not"﴾. It is also possible that the address is to the Prophet and to the Muslims, who are addressed together because the Prophet informed them of it and the Muslims believed in it, so they were addressed all together to deny the Prophet and to introduce doubt into the hearts of the believers in it. The command to answer them was specifically addressed to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, because he is the one who informed them of the threat, while the believers follow him in that.

The meaning of ﴿I possess not for myself any harm or benefit﴾ is: I am not able, as was previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿Say, "Do you worship besides Allah that which possesses not for you any harm or benefit"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 76] in Surat al-'Uqud.

Harm is mentioned before benefit because it is more appropriate to the purpose, since they displayed impatience at what would bring them harm, namely the threat, and because the ability to cause harm is easier than the ability to bring benefit, so mentioning benefit after it is an ascent.

The purpose of combining the two matters is to encompass both kinds of states. The reason for placing benefit before harm in a parallel verse was discussed in Surat al-A'raf.

His saying ﴿except what Allah wills﴾ is a disjunctive exception meaning "but," i.e., but my benefit and harm are what Allah wills for me. This answer entails refuting their speech by the method termed in the science of rhetoric the "theological method" (al-madhhab al-kalami), i.e., by a demonstrative path; for if he cannot possess for himself any harm or benefit, then his inability to possess what harms others by this promise is more so, since the nearest of things to a person's capacity is what is specifically related to his own self. For Allah deposited in man the capacity to use his powers and limbs; so if Allah had empowered him to bring about some of the benefits and harms in the states of existence, the nearest of things to his empowerment would be what relates to the states of his own self, since some of its causes lie within his capacity. Thus man is necessarily directed in his affairs by the power of Allah, because most causes of benefits and harms among events are interlinked, so that their agreements and disagreements lie outside human capacity; therefore harm may befall him while he is unable to repel it. So the meaning of the answer is: the promise is from Allah, not from me, and I am not able to bring it down upon you, because it has a term with Allah.

The clause ﴿For every nation is a term﴾ is part of what is said and commanded, and its position relative to the clause ﴿I possess not for myself any harm or benefit﴾ is that of a cause, because the clause ﴿I possess not for myself﴾ entailed the absence of the ability to bring the promise about.

The clause ﴿For every nation is a term﴾ implies that the reason for the lack of ability in this matter is that Allah has decreed the terms of the states of nations. Among these, He set the term for the descent of punishment upon them by a wisdom that required those terms, so punishment does not descend upon them except when its appointed term comes; no one can change what Allah has determined.

The form of the demonstrative argument is that the proposition ﴿For every nation is a term﴾ is a universal proposition that encompasses every nation. Since those addressed are among the nations, they are included under the ruling of this proposition, so it is as if it were said to them: "You are a nation among the nations, and every nation has a term; therefore you have a term, so await its arrival."

The clause ﴿When their term comes, they will not remain behind it an hour, nor will they precede it﴾ is a qualifier of "term," meaning: a specified term that does not accept change. The discussion of its parallel has already preceded in Surat al-A'raf.

The "idha" in this verse carries the meaning of a condition, and therefore the clause of its verb is joined with the fa' that links the answer, treating the verb governing "idha" as the answer of a condition.

﴿They say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿Say, "I possess not for myself any harm or benefit, except what Allah wills. For every nation is a term. When their term comes, they will not remain behind it an hour, nor will they precede it."﴾

Their saying is related in the present tense to evoke the state, as in His saying, ﴿And he was constructing the ship﴾ [Hud: 38], to indicate the repetition of its occurrence from them. The promise is used to refer to what is promised, so the question about it with the adverb of time is interpreted with a supposition indicated by the context: "When is its manifestation?"

The question is used for expressing impatience, and it is a metonymy for their lack of concern for it and that they pay it no heed, so that it moves from that to their denying its occurrence by way of allusion, by the indication of their saying ﴿if you are truthful﴾, meaning: if you are truthful that it is going to happen, then specify for us its time. They mean: "We will not believe you until we see what you promised us," a metonymy for their belief that it will not befall and that they do not believe in it. The promise mentioned here is the punishment of this world with which they were threatened.

The address in their saying "if you are truthful" is to the Messenger, and the pronoun of respect is used for mockery, as in His saying: ﴿And they said, "O you to whom the Reminder has been revealed, indeed you are mad"﴾ [al-Hijr: 6], and His saying: ﴿And they said, "What is wrong with this messenger that he eats food"﴾ [al-Furqan: 7], and the saying of Abu Bakr ibn al-Aswad al-Kinani:

"The Messenger tells us that we will live, but how can the life of echoes and skulls be?"

This interpretation is the one suited to their answer with His saying: ﴿Say, "I possess not"﴾. It is also possible that the address is to the Prophet and to the Muslims, who are addressed together because the Prophet informed them of it and the Muslims believed in it, so they were addressed all together to deny the Prophet and to introduce doubt into the hearts of the believers in it. The command to answer them was specifically addressed to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, because he is the one who informed them of the threat, while the believers follow him in that.

The meaning of ﴿I possess not for myself any harm or benefit﴾ is: I am not able, as was previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿Say, "Do you worship besides Allah that which possesses not for you any harm or benefit"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 76] in Surat al-'Uqud.

Harm is mentioned before benefit because it is more appropriate to the purpose, since they displayed impatience at what would bring them harm, namely the threat, and because the ability to cause harm is easier than the ability to bring benefit, so mentioning benefit after it is an ascent.

The purpose of combining the two matters is to encompass both kinds of states. The reason for placing benefit before harm in a parallel verse was discussed in Surat al-A'raf.

His saying ﴿except what Allah wills﴾ is a disjunctive exception meaning "but," i.e., but my benefit and harm are what Allah wills for me. This answer entails refuting their speech by the method termed in the science of rhetoric the "theological method" (al-madhhab al-kalami), i.e., by a demonstrative path; for if he cannot possess for himself any harm or benefit, then his inability to possess what harms others by this promise is more so, since the nearest of things to a person's capacity is what is specifically related to his own self. For Allah deposited in man the capacity to use his powers and limbs; so if Allah had empowered him to bring about some of the benefits and harms in the states of existence, the nearest of things to his empowerment would be what relates to the states of his own self, since some of its causes lie within his capacity. Thus man is necessarily directed in his affairs by the power of Allah, because most causes of benefits and harms among events are interlinked, so that their agreements and disagreements lie outside human capacity; therefore harm may befall him while he is unable to repel it. So the meaning of the answer is: the promise is from Allah, not from me, and I am not able to bring it down upon you, because it has a term with Allah.

The clause ﴿For every nation is a term﴾ is part of what is said and commanded, and its position relative to the clause ﴿I possess not for myself any harm or benefit﴾ is that of a cause, because the clause ﴿I possess not for myself﴾ entailed the absence of the ability to bring the promise about.

The clause ﴿For every nation is a term﴾ implies that the reason for the lack of ability in this matter is that Allah has decreed the terms of the states of nations. Among these, He set the term for the descent of punishment upon them by a wisdom that required those terms, so punishment does not descend upon them except when its appointed term comes; no one can change what Allah has determined.

The form of the demonstrative argument is that the proposition ﴿For every nation is a term﴾ is a universal proposition that encompasses every nation. Since those addressed are among the nations, they are included under the ruling of this proposition, so it is as if it were said to them: "You are a nation among the nations, and every nation has a term; therefore you have a term, so await its arrival."

The clause ﴿When their term comes, they will not remain behind it an hour, nor will they precede it﴾ is a qualifier of "term," meaning: a specified term that does not accept change. The discussion of its parallel has already preceded in Surat al-A'raf.

The "idha" in this verse carries the meaning of a condition, and therefore the clause of its verb is joined with the fa' that links the answer, treating the verb governing "idha" as the answer of a condition.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verses 50–51:

﴿Say: "Tell me, if His punishment comes upon you by night or by day, what is it that the criminals would hasten to?"﴾ ﴿Then, when it has occurred, will you believe in it? Now? And you had been [before] seeking to hasten it.﴾

This is a second answer to their saying, ﴿When is this promise, if you are truthful?﴾ [Yunus: 48], in consideration of what their statement implies of a promise that they will believe when the threat with which he threatens them comes to pass, as is related of them in the other verse, ﴿And they said, "We will not believe you until you cause to gush forth for us from the earth a spring," ... or you cause the sky to fall upon us in fragments, as you have claimed﴾ [al-Isra: 90–92]. This answer exposes the defect in their speech and the inconsistency of their mockery. It occurred in this manner: after he was commanded to answer them with His saying, ﴿Say, "I possess not for myself any harm or benefit except what Allah wills"﴾ [Yunus: 49], he was then made to answer them with this answer. This answer stands in the position of dialectical concession, after the one in error has been refuted. The sum of this answer is: supposing that what you asked for occurs, namely the specifying of its time and the descent upon you of a fragment from the sky or the like, what benefit would you gain in seeking to hasten its occurrence? For you cannot avoid claiming that you will believe at that time; but that is false, because the punishment will overtake you with destruction, and then your faith will not be realized. This is as one of the preachers said: "We want not to die until we repent, and we do not repent until we die."

Within this answer there is an artful use of imagery to magnify this promised punishment, by His saying, ﴿if His punishment comes upon you by night or by day﴾, an imagery suited to the certainty of its occurrence, for these two times are not free of the occurrence of events in one of them. Moreover, it is a disjunction regarding the meaning of a punishment that comes swiftly, either near or less near, that is: it comes upon you during the night of this day you asked for, or in its early morning. Moreover, in mentioning these two times there is a certain imagery of the form of the punishment's occurrence, evoking it before them in a manner by which they are reminded, taking advantage of the opportunity for admonition, like the reminder of it in His saying, ﴿Say, "Tell me, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you suddenly or openly, will any be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?"﴾ [al-An'am: 47].

Al-bayat (البياتُ) is the verbal noun of tabyit (التبييت), meaning at night, like salam for taslim. It means a surprise attack. "Bayatan" is in the accusative of time, with an elided noun, i.e., "at a time of bayat."

The response to the conditional "if His punishment comes upon you" is elided, indicated by His saying, ﴿what is it that the criminals would hasten to?﴾, which serves as a substitute for the two objects of "Tell me" (ara'aytum), since the interrogative "what" (madha) suspends its governance.

"Madha" consists of two words: the interrogative "ma" and "dha." Originally, "dha" is a demonstrative pointing to something taken from the speech following it. "Dha" is used together with the interrogative "ma" in the sense of "alladhi" (which), because they regard the word "alladhi" as elided. It may appear, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Who is it that intercedes with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]. This interrogation is used for reproach against them, and for expressing wonder at their hastening of the punishment, on the assumption that they would believe in it when it descends.

"Min" here is partitive. The meaning is: what is it, of the punishment, that the criminals would hasten to? That is, none of the punishment is suitable for their hastening it, because every part of it is destructive and stands between them and the ability to believe at the time of its arrival.

The purpose of pointing to it is to magnify it, to give it grandeur, or to express wonder at it, like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿What did Allah intend by this as an example?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26]. So the meaning is: what is this great punishment, given that the criminals hasten to it? Thus the clause ﴿they hasten to it﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the demonstrative noun; that is, its like is not hastened, rather its proper course is to be delayed.

"Min" is explanatory (bayaniyyah), and the meaning with it is what is called in the science of rhetoric (badi') "tajarrud" (abstraction).

Know that the grammarians mention the use of "madha" in the sense of "alladhi," but they mean by this only some of its usages, and it is not a consistent usage. Ibn Malik, in al-Khulasa, clarified it when he added a condition to this usage, saying:

"Like 'ma' is 'dha' after an interrogative, or 'man' if it is not made void in the speech."

He means: if it is not superfluous. He expressed it by "made void" only to avoid the objection that nouns are not made superfluous. The truth is that what is meant by superfluity is that the demonstrative noun neither conveys its meaning as originally posited, nor does it establish a new meaning in the speech; rather, it serves to strengthen and emphasize the pointing to what the speech contains. The author of Mughni al-Labib has referred to its usages in a section he devoted to "madha," and he enumerated many meanings, but did not clarify how some of them derive from others. See what preceded at His saying, ﴿So what is there after the truth but error?﴾ [Yunus: 32], mentioned just before, and His saying, ﴿What did Allah intend by this as an example?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26] in Surat al-Baqarah.

"Al-mujrimun" are those possessed of crime (jurm), which is the crime of polytheism. What is meant by them are those who say "When is this promise," and they are the polytheists of Makkah. The explicit noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, instead of saying "what do they hasten to," for the purpose of marking them with criminality, and to draw attention to their error in hastening the threat, because it comes upon them with destruction, and they then proceed to the Hereafter where they arrive at the everlasting punishment. Their proper course is therefore to delay the promise, not to hasten it. This indicates that the meaning is: they hasten to it only in evil.

The clause "then, when it has occurred" is conjoined with the particle "thumma," indicating a delay in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), as is the case with "thumma" in conjoining clauses, because their believing in the punishment, which they used to deny would occur, at the moment it befalls them, is more remarkable and more important than their hastening toward it. The interrogative hamza is placed before the conjunction, by a deferment, as is its usage with conjunctive particles that convey coordination. The estimated form is: "thumma a-idha ma waqa'a," and the intent is not to ask about the delay.

What is asked about is the occurrence of faith at the time the punishment befalls, and this interrogation is used for denial, in the sense of confuting them and corrupting their opinion, for they had promised to believe at the descent of the punishment in mockery. So the reply came by matching their apparent state and explaining their errors, that is: "Will you believe in the promise when it has occurred?" in the manner of the wise style (al-uslub al-hakim), like His saying, ﴿They ask you about the crescent moons. Say: they are times for the people and for the pilgrimage﴾ [al-Baqarah: 189].

The word "al-an" (الآنَ) is an interrogative of denial concerning the occurrence of their faith at the arrival of what He threatened them with. He expressed the time of its occurrence by the name of the present time, "al-an" (now), as a representation of the tongue of the state of one denying against them at that time, who evokes the state of the arrival of the promise as if it were present at the time of speaking. This evocation is from imagining the future state as occurring. For this reason, it is fitting to take "al-an" as a metaphor by implicit comparison (isti'arah makniyyah), likening the future time to the time of the present, with the aspect of comparison being evocation. He indicated the comparandum by mentioning a term from its attributes, namely the name of the present time.

The clause ﴿and you had been [before] seeking to hasten it﴾ is an elaboration (tarshih), and it may also be an implied saying (taqdir qawl) in the speech, that is: it will be said to them, when they believe after the descent of the punishment, "Now? You believed!" as most of the exegetes have held. That is an estimation of meaning, not an estimation of structure and grammatical parsing, because the composition of this speech is more refined than that.

The meaning of "tasta'jilun" is "you deny." He expressed denial by hastening, representing their statement "When is this promise," which takes the form of hastening, and what is meant by it is denial.

The placement of the prepositional phrase first serves to give importance to the promise they denied, and for the sake of the rhyme of the verse-ending.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 52:

﴿Then it will be said to those who did wrong, "Taste the punishment of eternity. Are you being recompensed except according to what you used to earn?"﴾

This is coordinated (ma'tufah) upon the statement ﴿Say: "Have you considered: if His punishment comes to you by night or by day..."﴾ [Yunus: 50] and so on. "Thumma" (then) here indicates sequence in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), since this punishment is greater than the punishment mentioned in His words ﴿Say: "Have you considered: if His punishment comes to you by night or by day..."﴾ [Yunus: 50].

Page 195

For that is the punishment of this world, whereas the punishment of eternity is the punishment of the Hereafter, and this is greater than the punishment of this world. Hence the placement of its clause coordinated with the particle "thumma."

The past tense in His words ﴿It will be said to those who did wrong﴾ is used in the sense of the future, to emphasize the certainty of its occurrence, like ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1].

And those who did wrong are the ones who were saying, "When will this promise be fulfilled?" The expression "those who did wrong" is used in a place where a pronoun could have been used, in order to record the attribute of wrongdoing upon them, which is the wronging of the self through association (ishrak). The meaning of "zalamu" (did wrong) is: they associated partners (with Allah).

Al-dhawq (tasting) is used in the sense of perception (ihsas), and this is a well-known metaphor based on the relation of generality (ʿalaqat al-itlaq).

The interrogative in ﴿Are you being recompensed...﴾ is denial-bearing (inkari), meaning negation, and for this reason it is followed by the exception ﴿except according to what you used to earn﴾.

The clause ﴿Are you being recompensed except according to what you used to earn﴾ is an explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani), because the clause ﴿Taste the punishment of eternity﴾ provokes a question in their minds about the magnitude of that punishment, so the answer is that it is in proportion to the enormity of the deeds they earned, together with conveying the reason for the imposition of the punishment upon them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 53:

﴿They ask you, "Is it true?" Say, "Yes, by my Lord, it is certainly true, and you cannot escape it."﴾

This is a report of one of the varied forms of their denial: at times they feign impatience with the promise, belittling it, and at other times they approach the Messenger in the guise of one seeking information, asking him: "Is this everlasting punishment, that is, the punishment of the Hereafter, true?"

The sentence is coordinated with the sentence ﴿They say, "When will this promise be fulfilled?"﴾ [Yunus: 48]. The plural pronoun refers back to them, so it is they who are asking, and no one else. The pronoun in ﴿huwa﴾ ("it") refers to ﴿the everlasting punishment﴾ [Yunus: 52].

Al-haqq (the true) means that which is firmly established and certain to occur; it carries the sense of ḥāqq, that is, established. The meaning is that its occurrence is established. Thus the establishment is attributed to the punishment itself, with an omitted modifier (taqdir muḍaf) indicated by the context, since an essence is not described as being "established."

The sentence ﴿Is it true?﴾ (ʾa-ḥaqqun huwa) is an interrogative clause that suspends the verb yastanbi'ūnaka (they ask you) from acting on the second object, and the clause serves as an explanation (bayan) of the clause yastanbi'ūnaka, since its content is the matter asked about.

The pronoun may be the subject (mubtada'), with ʾaḥaqqun as the predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam).

They used the interrogative in mockery, and therefore the command to answer took into account both states. First, it considered the outward state of their question, and they were answered by way of the wise method (al-uslub al-ḥakim), by taking their words in a sense contrary to their intent, as an alert that the more fitting course for them would be to ask in earnest seeking guidance. This was to confound them and to seize the opportunity for guidance, based on the outward appearance of their question. For this reason the answer was emphasized with verbal emphasis, since it combined the particle ʾi, which is an answering particle that confirms what is asked about, with the sentence that conveys what that particle implies, and with an oath, with inna, and with the lam of commencement. All of these are emphatic devices.

The second consideration is that of their intent in asking, so they were answered with His words: ﴿and you cannot escape it.﴾ The sentence ﴿and you cannot escape it﴾ is coordinated with the sentence that answers the oath, so its content is part of what is sworn to. Since what is sworn to is an answer to their question, the content of ﴿and you cannot escape it﴾ is also an answer to the question, taking into account what they concealed of denial. That is, it is certain to occur, and you will be struck by it, not escaping from it.

The verb yastanbi'ūnaka is not used in the sense of feigning, in the way that His words ﴿The hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down about them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 64] are used, as was mentioned earlier at "Bara'ah," because the reality of asking is present here, since they have explicitly adopted the form of a question.

ʾIy, with a kasra on the hamza, is an answering particle used to confirm what the questioner's question implies. It is synonymous with na'am (yes), but a distinctive feature of this particle is that it is never used except when followed by an oath.

al-Mu'jizun (those who escape) means those who prevail, that is, you are not prevailing over Him who seeks you, that is, you will not escape. This was discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿What you are promised is surely coming, and you cannot escape it﴾ [al-An'am: 134], in Surah al-An'am.

[Page 197]

﴿Had every soul that did wrong possessed whatever is on the earth, it would surely offer it as ransom.﴾

The more apparent view is that this clause is part of the same speech, and it is coordinated (*'atf*, conjunction) with the clause ﴿Yes, by my Lord, it is indeed true﴾ [Yunus: 53]. It informs them of the terror of that punishment, so that they may perhaps beware of it. For this reason the second complement of the verb *iftada* (to ransom oneself) has been omitted, because the verb requires both something by which one ransoms and something from which one is ransomed. The meaning is: it would ransom itself with it from the punishment.

The meaning is that no soul can bear this punishment, despite the differences among souls in their tolerance of pain. For this reason it says *kulli nafs* (every soul) and does not say "had there been for you whatever is on the earth, you would have ransomed yourselves with it."

The clause ﴿that for every soul that did wrong is whatever is on the earth﴾ stands in the position of the protasis (*shart*) of *law* (if/had). *Ma fi al-ard* is the subject (*ism*) of *anna* (indeed), and *li-kulli nafs* is its predicate (*khabar*). The predicate has been placed before the subject for the sake of emphasis on the universality it contains, so that it makes clear that no soul is safe from this. The clause *zalamat* (did wrong) is a qualifier (*sifa*) of *nafs* (soul). The clause ﴿would ransom itself with it﴾ is the apodosis (*jawab*) of *law*.

Thus the generality of *kull nafs* includes the souls of those addressed together with others.

The meaning of *zalamat* (did wrong) is "associated partners with God" (*ashrakat*), and this is the wronging of the self: ﴿Indeed, associating partners with God is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13].

*Ma fi al-ard* (whatever is on the earth) encompasses everything on the surface of the earth and within it, because the locative sense here is a locative of gathering and containment (*zarfiyya jam' wa-ihtiwa'*).

*Iftada* is a synonym of *fada* (to ransom). In it there is the addition of the *ta'* of *ifti'al* (the reflexive augment), to indicate an increase in meaning, that is, that it would exert itself to pay its ransom with it.

* * *

﴿And they will conceal their regret when they see the punishment, and judgment will be passed between them with justice, and they will not be wronged.﴾

This is a resumptive new sentence (*jumla mustaʼnafa*), coordinated as a conjunction of one speech with another. The pronoun in *asarru* (they concealed) refers to *kull nafs* (every soul) according to its meaning, with the masculine given precedence over the feminine (*taghlib al-mudhakkar*). The verb is expressed in the past tense for future concealment, as an admonition to the certainty of its occurrence, so that it is as though it has already happened; the meaning is: they will surely conceal their regret. Likewise is His saying ﴿and judgment has been passed between them﴾.

*Al-nadama* means regret (*al-nadam*), which is a grief arising in the soul over the loss of something whose doing was possible in the past. Regret is among the inner promptings of the soul, so it is a matter that is not apparent but is nonetheless frequent, meaning that from its bearer there issues a word or deed that indicates it. When the one who regrets restrains himself and shows neither word nor deed, he has concealed his regret, that is, he has kept it to himself and not revealed it by displaying some of its signs. This happens only from the intensity of terror; they concealed their regret because they were astonished at the sight of what they had not expected, so they were unable to bear crying out or wailing.

The clause ﴿and judgment has been passed between them﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with the resumptive clause *wa-asarru* (and they concealed).

The meaning of *qudiya baynahum* (judgment was passed between them) is *qudiya fihim* (judgment was passed upon them), that is, judgment was passed upon each one of them according to what he deserves in justice. So the judgment in justice took place among them. The meaning is not that judgment was passed between each one and another, because the judgment here is not a judgment of dispute but a judgment of rebuke and reproach, since the discourse here concerns only the polytheists, who are one category. This is unlike His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when their messenger comes, judgment will be passed between them with justice﴾ [Yunus: 47], for that is judgment between those to whom messengers were sent and the messengers, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ [al-A'raf: 6] ﴿Then We will surely relate to them with knowledge, and We were not absent﴾ [al-A'raf: 7].

The clause ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verses 55–56:

﴿Surely to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Surely the promise of God is true, but most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿He gives life and causes death, and to Him you will be returned.﴾

This is a concluding appendage (tadhyil) ending the discourse concerning the truthfulness of the Messenger and the Qur'an, and what they brought of threat, and the anticipation of the Day of Resurrection and the Day when punishment descends upon the polytheists. This appendage comprises a summary of the detailed purpose of that discourse, and gives its rationale: that One whose affairs are such cannot fail to bring about what He has informed of its occurrence.

Its opening is that God is the one who alone possesses the dominion of whatever is in the heavens and the earth; so He disposes of people and their conditions in this world and the Hereafter with a disposal in which no other shares with Him. His disposal of the affairs of the heavens encompasses all the unseen matters, among them the manifestation of recompense in the abode of reward and the abode of punishment; and His disposal of the affairs of the earth encompasses His disposal of people. Then it follows with the fulfilment of His promise, follows with the ignorance ascribed to those who deny it, and follows with the explicit mention of what is most important of that, namely giving life, causing death, and resurrection.

This appendage opens with the particle of alerting (harf al-tanbih), and the particle of alerting is repeated in it to draw attention to hearing it, and to signal that it is a comprehensive statement, the essence (hawsalah) of the purpose whose details they heard just before.

The emphasis of the predicate with the particle "inna" is a response to the polytheists, because when they ascribed partners to God, they made them not owned by God. Their saying ﴿We only worship them so that they bring us near to God in closeness﴾ [al-Zumar: 3] does not avert this from them, because that is confusion and incoherence.

The predicate of "inna" is placed before its subject (ism) to give importance to the name of Him, exalted is He, and to convey restriction (qasr), in order to refute their belief in partnership, as you have known.

It is emphasized with the particle of emphasis after the particle of alerting in both places, for the sake of giving it importance, and to refute the denial of those who deny part of it, and of those who are in the position of deniers of its other part.

The "li" in "li-Allah" denotes possession, and "ma" is a relative pronoun indicating the generality of everything to which the relative clause applies among existing things, the apparent and the hidden.

The "promise of God" is His promise of punishment for the polytheists, and it is a threat; it is also permissible that His promise be intended as resurrection, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿As We began the first creation, We shall repeat it — a promise upon Us; indeed We are ever doing it﴾ [al-Anbiya': 104], calling the re-creation of creation a promise.

The Name of Majesty (ism al-jalalah) is made explicit in the second clause rather than replaced by a pronoun, so that the clause stands independently and functions like a proverb and a comprehensive statement.

A contrast occurs with His saying: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, because the two clauses preceding it were intended as a refutation of those who hold the opposite of them, so they came to have the force of negating doubt about their content. It is as if it were said: there is no doubt at all in that, but most of them do not know, and therefore they doubt.

Restricting the negation of knowledge to "most" indicates that among them are those who know it but deny it out of arrogance, as He said in the previous verse: ﴿And among them are those who believe in it, and among them are those who do not believe in it﴾ [Yunus: 40]. So the pronoun in "aktharuhum" refers to those spoken of earlier.
