[Page 201]

Resumption or parenthetical insertion (*istina'*, *i'tira4*). It may be that it introduces a new theme, which is addressing all of mankind by informing them of the status of the Qur'an and its guidance. This follows a discussion in which the subject was the polytheists' disputation and the argument against them from the inimitability (*i'jaz*) of the Qur'an, showing that it is from God and that the one who brought it is truthful in what he brought, including his threat and warning to them of the consequence of the nations' denial of their messengers, and the threat that was appended to that and the realization of what they were threatened with. So the discourse now turns to the theme opened with His saying, ﴿And it is not [conceivable] that this Qur'an be fabricated apart from God﴾ [Yunus: 37], up to His saying, ﴿Even if they do not see﴾ [Yunus: 43]. The discourse therefore returns to addressing all of mankind, because of the beneficial things in the Qur'an that are good for them, and the indication of their differing in the extent of benefit they take from it. For this reason the address here is general to all people, and nothing has come in it that requires directing it specifically to the polytheists, such as pronouns referring to them, descriptions of them, or relative clauses. On this understanding, the address with *ya ayyuha al-nas* ("O mankind") is not a shift (*iltifat*) from third person to second person. The meaning is that the Qur'an is an admonition for all people, but only the believers have benefited from its admonition, so they were guided and it became a mercy for them.

It is also possible that it is an address to the polytheists, based on the predominant usage in the Qur'an of *ya ayyuha al-nas*. In that case, the praise of the Qur'an as guidance and mercy for the believers is an interweaving (*idmaj*) and a recording against the polytheists, that they deprived themselves of benefiting from the Qur'an's admonition and its healing of what is in the breasts, while the believers benefited from that.

The opening of the speech with *qad* (قَدْ) is for emphasis, because among the addressees there are many who deny these attributes of the Qur'an.

The verb *al-maji'* (المَجِيءُ, "coming") is used figuratively to mean informing about something, as it is also used to mean reaching. However, "reaching" (*al-bulugh*) is more well known and more common in this sense, one says: "The news of such-and-such reached me," and one also says: "The news of such-and-such came to me or came upon me." The use of *al-maji'* for it in this verse is more eloquent.

What is meant by what came to them and reached them is what was sent down of the Qur'an and recited to them. It is described with four attributes, which are the foundations of its perfection and its distinctive features: that it is an admonition (*maw'iza*), that it is a healing for what is in the breasts, that it is guidance (*huda*), and that it is a mercy for the believers.

*Al-maw'iza* (المَوْعِظَةُ, "admonition") is *al-wa'z*, which is speech containing advice and warning against what is harmful. Its discussion has already passed at His saying, ﴿So turn away from them and admonish them﴾ [al-Nisa': 63], in Surat al-Nisa', and at His saying, ﴿an admonition and an explanation of all things﴾ [al-A'raf: 145], in Surat al-A'raf. He described it with *min rabbikum* ("from your Lord") to draw attention to its reaching the utmost degree of perfection of its kind.

*Al-shifa'* (الشِّفاءُ, "healing") was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿and heal the breasts of a believing people﴾ [al-Tawba: 14], in Surat Bara'a [al-Tawba]. Its literal sense is the removal of illness and pain, and its figurative sense is the removal of deficiencies and misguidance and whatever causes hardship to the self. This is what is meant here.

What is meant by *al-suduur* (الصُّدُورِ, "breasts") is the souls (*nufus*), as is common in usage.

*Al-huda* (الهُدى, "guidance"): its discussion has already passed at His saying, ﴿a guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Baqara: 2], at the beginning of Surat al-Baqara. Its root meaning is indicating the path that leads to the intended goal. Its figurative sense is the explanation of the means of attaining true benefits.

*Al-rahma* (الرَّحْمَةُ, "mercy") has already been discussed in the explanation of the basmala.

The description of the Qur'an with healing alludes to a representation (*tamthil*) of the condition of souls in relation to the Qur'an and what it brought, by the condition of a sick, ailing person whose temperament's order has changed from the state of soundness, so that he has become disturbed in his conditions and weak in his powers. He awaits a physician who prescribes healing for him. The physician must give the patient admonition, warning him against what causes the arising and persistence of his illness. Then he specifies the medicine by which he is cured of the disease, and then prescribes for him the regimen he should follow so that health and well-being endure for him and the disease does not relapse. If he accepts the physician's advice, he becomes healthy and sound and lives a good life, with no pain afflicting him and no complaint of fatigue. This representation, by its perfection, was capable of dividing the comparison into parts: the Qur'an's restraints and admonitions are likened to the physician's advice by way of the metaphor implied (*makniyya*); its refutation of misguided beliefs is likened to prescribing medicine for healing from harms by way of the explicit metaphor (*tasriHiyya*); its religious teachings and manners are likened to the rules of preserving health by way of the implied metaphor, and these are expressed by guidance (*huda*); and its mercy to the worlds is likened to living in safety by way of the implied metaphor. It is known that the words of the implied metaphor may be used in their literal meanings, as here, and may also be made into an imaginative depiction (*takhyil*), like the claws of the *manniyya* (the figure of the death-wish in poetry). Moreover, this includes a comparison of the standing of the one who sent the Qur'an to a physician knowledgeable about diseases and their remedies. From this arises a comparison of the manner in which people receive the Qur'an, benefit from it, and how the Messenger ﷺ treats them by repeating advice and guidance, to the condition of the sick before a physician who prescribes for them what will cure them and improve their temperaments. Among them is the one who accepts and benefits, and among them is the one who is obstinate and refuses.

The first three attributes are established for the Qur'an in its own essence, equally for the one who accepted and acted upon them and for the one who turned away from them and rejected them. However, since describing it as guidance (*huda*), being a verbal noun (*masdar*) that implies intensification (*mubalagha*) to the point that it is as if it were the very essence of guidance, it is more fitting that what is meant by it is the actual attainment of guidance through it. Thus it is in conjunction with the fourth attribute. The fourth attribute, which is mercy, is specific to the one who acted in accordance with the requirements of the first three attributes, so he benefited from them, and the Qur'an became a mercy for him in this world and the Hereafter. This refers to His saying, ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, and it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss﴾ [al-Isra': 82]. So the qualifier *li'l-mu'minin* ("for the believers") is without doubt connected to *rahma* ("mercy"), and the majority of the exegetes have restricted it to this.

Some of the verifying scholars (*muhaqqiqin*) have made it a qualifier for both *huda* and *rahma*, referring to His saying, ﴿a guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Baqara: 2], since He did not make it a guidance for other than the God-conscious, who are the believers.

The view is that its being an admonition is an inherent attribute of it, because admonition is speech that warns against harm. For this reason it is followed by *min rabbikum*, so it is general to all those addressed by *ya ayyuha al-nas*. As for its being a healing, it is in itself suitable for healing, but healing through medicine only occurs for the one who uses it.

As for its being guidance and mercy, the complete description of the Qur'an with them applies to the one in whom their reality has been realized. As for the one in whom their effects have not been realized, describing the Qur'an with them means its suitability for that, which is the description by potentiality (*al-wasf bi'l-quwwa*) in the terminology of the logicians (*ahl al-mantiq*). The other verse explicitly states that it is ﴿a healing and a mercy for the believers﴾ [al-Isra': 82], and the verse of al-Baqara explicitly states that it is ﴿a guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Baqara: 2]. So the more apparent view is that the qualifier *li'l-mu'minin* refers to both *huda* and *rahma* together, according to the rule of a qualifier that follows a list of singular nouns. As for its referring to *shifa'*, it is possible, because the attribute *shifa'* has been followed by the qualifier ﴿for what is in the breasts﴾, so it is cut off from the two attributes after it. Also, the definition of *al-suduur* with the article *al-* implies generality, so *shifa'* should be understood in the sense of medicine, which is suitable for healing whoever takes it. This usage is common, and the lexicographers *al-Lisan* and *al-Qamus* begin with it, and they cite as an example His saying, concerning honey, ﴿In it is healing for people﴾ [al-Nahl: 69].

As for the connection of the verb of coming (*al-maji'*) with the pronoun of the people in His saying, ﴿There has certainly come to you﴾, it is on account of their being, in general, the intended audience for the sending down of the Qur'an. Then the detail occurred regarding what their reception and benefit differed in, as indicated by His following saying, ﴿Say: "By the grace of God and His mercy, so let them rejoice in that"﴾ [Yunus: 58], meaning the believers. He expressed guidance by grace (*fadl*) in His saying: ﴿O mankind, there has come to you a proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a clear light﴾ [al-Nisa': 174], and ﴿As for those who believed in God and held fast to Him, He will admit them into mercy from Him and grace and guide them to Himself on a straight path﴾ [al-Nisa': 175]. So He generalized to all people in the coming of the proof and the sending down of the light, and He specified the mercy, grace and guidance for the believers. This is the pinnacle of eloquence and correctness of division.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 58:

﴿Say: "In the grace of Allah and in His mercy—in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they accumulate."﴾

It follows from the Qur'an being guidance and mercy for the believers that it draws their attention to the fact that this is a grace from Allah upon them and a mercy toward them, so it is fitting for them to rejoice in both, to appreciate the measure of these two blessings, and to know that it is a blessing that surpasses the blessing of wealth, of which most believers are deprived and most polytheists are granted. Therefore the sentence was fittingly introduced with the conjunctive fa' (fa' al-tafri', the fa' of consequence).

The command "Say" is placed as an interjection between the consequent sentence and the sentence it follows, to give prominence to the consequent sentence, such that the Messenger is specifically commanded to say it, although everything revealed to him of the Qur'an is something he is commanded to say.

The estimated structure of the discourse is: "Say to them: let them rejoice in the grace of Allah and in His mercy—by that, let them rejoice."

Thus the fa' in His words "fa-l-yafrahu" (then let them rejoice) is the fa' of consequence. "Bi-fadl Allah wa bi-rahmatihi" (in the grace of Allah and in His mercy) is a prepositional phrase governed by the verb "fa-l-yafrahu," placed before its complement for the sake of emphasis on it, for the benefit of the Muslims, and to convey restriction (qasr). That is: in the grace of Allah and His mercy, and not in anything else, which is indicated by His words "it is better than what they accumulate." This is a restriction of correction (qasr qalb), alluding to a rebuttal of the polytheists who rejoiced in the display of wealth and said: "We have more wealth and children."

The demonstrative in His words "bi-dhalika" (in that) refers to what was mentioned, namely the combination of grace and mercy. The demonstrative was chosen to express it because it conveys glorification and exaltation along with precision and brevity. Since he intended to emphasize the entire sentence together with the restrictive form contained in it, he joined the demonstrative with the fa', as an emphasis on the fa' of consequence in "fa-l-yafrahu." Since it was placed before its complement, it was joined with the fa' to make the consequence manifest at the beginning of the sentence. The verb of "li-yafrahu" has been omitted, so it conveys the meaning of two similar sentences with a wondrous brevity. The estimated meaning of the speech is: "Say: let them rejoice in the grace of Allah and His mercy, and not in anything else; so let them rejoice in that, and not in anything else."

Al-faraḥ (rejoicing) is intense joy.

You may also take the speech as a fresh resumption arising from what preceded concerning the blessing upon the believers through the Qur'an. Since the prepositional phrase "bi-fadl Allah wa bi-rahmatihi" was placed first, the meaning of a condition (shart) arose from its placement, so the sentence following it was joined with the fa' that links the response, for the purpose of conveying the meaning of a condition. This is common in usage, like His words, exalted is He: "And for that let those who compete compete" (al-Mutaffifin: 26), and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "fa-fihima fa-jahid" (then in them, strive), and his saying: "As you are, so shall you be ruled" (kama takunu yuwalla alaykum), with the jussive on both "takunu" and "yuwalla." The fa' in "fa-bi-dhalika" is the linking particle for the response, and the fa' in "fa-l-yafrahu" reinforces the linkage.

The exegetes do not differ that the Qur'an is intended by Allah's grace and mercy. A hadith has been related from Anas ibn Malik, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The grace of Allah is the Qur'an, and His mercy is that He made you among its people" (meaning: that He guided you to follow it). Similar has been related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and al-Bara', as a mawquf report. This is what the wording requires, for the grace is the guidance of Allah contained in the Qur'an, and the mercy is the success in following the Sharia, which is mercy in this world and the next.

The sentence "huwa khayrun mimma yajma'un" (it is better than what they accumulate) clarifies the intended meaning of the restriction derived from the fronting of the two prepositional phrases. He used the singular pronoun in view of the referent being "what was mentioned," just as the demonstrative was used in the singular. The pronoun refers to the demonstrative, that is: "that is better than what they accumulate."

"Mā yajma'ūn" (what they accumulate) refers to wealth and gains, because the verb "jama'a" (to accumulate) is predominantly used for accumulating wealth. He said, exalted is He: "Who has accumulated wealth and counted it" (al-Humazah: 2). It is customary that one who accumulates wealth rejoices in his accumulation.

The pronoun in "yajma'ūn" refers to the people in His words: "O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord" (Yunus: 57), by contextual indication, and it does not refer to what the pronoun in "yafrahu" refers to, for context directs similar pronouns to their proper referents, as in the saying of 'Abbas ibn Mirdas:

"We returned, and had it not been for us, their multitude would have surrounded the Muslims, and they would have secured what they had gathered."

The pronoun in "aḥrazū" (they secured) refers to the polytheists, to whom the pronoun in "jam'uhum" (their multitude) referred. The pronoun in "jama'ū" (they gathered) refers to the Muslims, that is: had it not been for us, the polytheists would have seized what the Muslims had gathered of the spoils. From this is His saying, exalted is He: "And they cultivated it more than they cultivated it" (al-Rum: 9) in the chapter of al-Rum.

On this reading, the sense of restriction becomes most fully manifest, and it is also appropriate to the state of the Muslims and the state of the polytheists at that time, for the Muslims were in weakness, since most of them were of the weak among their people, or because their relatives among the polytheists had seized their wealth and withheld their rights from them, compelling them to return to disbelief. Allah described the polytheists with wealth in many verses, such as His saying: "And leave Me with the deniers, possessors of luxury" (al-Muzzammil: 11), and He said: "Because he possesses wealth and children. When Our verses are recited to him, he says: 'Legends of the ancients'" (al-Qalam: 14), and He said: "Let not the movement of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you; it is brief enjoyment" (Ali 'Imran: 196). Perhaps the polytheists used to belittle the Muslims, as related of the people of Noah, their saying: "And we do not see you followed except by those who are the lowest of us" (Hud: 27). Allah said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening" (al-An'am: 52), through His saying: "Is not Allah most knowing of those who are grateful?" (al-An'am: 53), when the polytheists said to him: "If you drove these slaves away from your gathering, we would sit with you." So Allah rebuked them by stating that the Muslims are better than them, because their intellects were perfected through sound beliefs and sublime manners. This reading is the one that fits the use of the present tense in His words "yajma'ūn," which implies the renewal and repetition of accumulation, and that requires their concern with gathering wealth, whereas the Muslims were not in that condition. The meaning is that this is better than what the polytheists accumulate, together with their being characterized by polytheism, for even if they obtain what brings some comfort in this world, they are base souls and lowly of perception.

Al-Jumhur read "yajma'ūn" with the ya' of the third person, so the pronoun refers to something understood from the speech, that is: what the polytheists accumulate of wealth. Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far, and Ruways from Ya'qub read "mimma tajma'ūn" with the ta' of address, so it is addressed to the polytheists who were included in the address at the beginning of the verse with His words: "O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord" (Yunus: 57), for after generalizing the address, it singled out the believers by mention and by their worthiness of rejoicing, so the address remained for those other than the Muslims, namely the polytheists, since there were no other groups of people there besides these two groups. It is not fitting to make the address to the Muslims, since that is not their characteristic as already mentioned, and because the sense of preference appears from it only by consideration, since the Muslims have attained the grace and mercy, and if they attain wealth along with them, that does not diminish their perfection through grace and mercy.

The verse has summarily stated the aspect of preferring this grace and mercy over what they accumulate, in order to direct reflection toward the aspects of its preference, for these are many, some clear and some hidden. The indication of the aspect of preference in the sentence is in the attribution of grace and mercy to Allah and the attribution of the verb "yajma'ūn" to the pronoun of the people. This grace is both otherworldly and worldly. As for the otherworldly, it is evident; as for the worldly, the perfection of the soul, soundness of belief, the soul's aspiration toward perfections, and its devotion to righteous deeds produce comfort in this world and a pleasant life. He said, exalted is He: "O reassured soul" (al-Fajr: 27), "Return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing" (al-Fajr: 28), so He made its being pleased a state for it at the time of its return to its Lord. Fakhr al-Din said: The purpose of the verse is to indicate that spiritual felicities are better than corporeal felicities, so a person should not rejoice in any of the corporeal states, because corporeal pleasures are nothing but the removal of pains according to a group of philosophers, and a negative meaning does not deserve to be rejoiced in. And even supposing these pleasures are positive attributes, they are never pure, but are mixed with kinds of displeasures, and they do not remain; so the more one delights in them, the greater and more intense are the regrets arising from fear of their loss.
Moreover, their non-permanence entails the brevity of the period of enjoying them, unlike spiritual pleasures.

[Page 208]

This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), in which the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to say this to the polytheists. It opens with "Say" (qul) to draw the attention of the listeners to what follows. Its placement after what came before is explained as follows: the preceding discourse related their denial of the Qur'an and their claim that it is a fabrication and not the truth. It then refuted the idea that the Qur'an is a fabrication against God, because it contains a detailed explanation of the Law (shari'ah) and confirms the earlier scriptures, and because it left those who denied it unable to produce a equal to it. When this had been fully established with the clearest proof, and the path was made clear to whoever seeks guidance, it was inevitable that the discourse turn to exposing the folly of their minds and the disorder of their denial. Having denied something whose knowledge they did not encompass, they became entangled in their own religion, since it necessarily entails the same condition they had rejected. They had devised a religion by making some of their provisions lawful for themselves and others unlawful for them.

[Page 209 continues the argument]

If that was true according to their claim, then who conveyed those laws to them from God, and why did they accept them from the one who legislated them for them without denying him, when they could not bind themselves to such things? And if it came from their own selves, then they have fabricated against God, and what they attributed to the Prophet ﷺ falls back upon them, while God cleared His Messenger of it. This line of reasoning is of the type called "reversal" (qalb) in the science of disputation ('ilm al-jadal).

Furthermore, choosing to argue against them with some of their own legislation concerning their provisions adds to the appropriateness of this argument with the final part of the preceding discourse, so that the fine transition to it becomes evident. The last clause of the preceding discourse is the statement ﴿He is better than what they gather﴾ [Yunus: 58], meaning from their wealth. That wealth is what God provided for them, and they made some of it lawful and some of it unlawful, and they were ungrateful for God's blessing when they prohibited for themselves some of the good things their Lord had given them. This is sufficient to make their disgrace clear, and the doors of goodness closed in their faces.

The interrogative in "Have you considered" (ara'aytum) and in ﴿Did God permit you, or do you fabricate against God?﴾ is an interrogative of affirmation (taqriri), in that it compels them to accept one of two matters: either God permitted them, or they are fabricators against God. Affirmation is here mixed with censure of both options.

The seeing (ru'yah) is cognitive ('ilmiyyah), and ﴿what God has sent down to you of provision﴾ is the first object of "you have considered". The clause ﴿so you made of it﴾ and what follows is coordinated with the relative clause by the connecting "fa" (fa' of sequence), meaning: that which God sent down to you, so you made of it. The interrogative in ﴿Did God permit you, or do you fabricate against God?﴾ is the second object of "you have considered", and the connective between the clause and the object is omitted; its estimated form is: "Did He permit you that?" This is indicated by His saying ﴿so you made of it unlawful and lawful﴾.

The second "Say" is an emphasis of the first "Say". It is inserted between the first interrogative clause and the second interrogative clause to increase the attention of the listeners to it. It is an equalizing construction (mu'adalah) with the interrogative hamza, because it stands between the two clauses that are the objects of the verb "you have considered". The verb of seeing is suspended (ta'liq) from acting upon the second object, because the more correct view is that suspension from the second object is permissible. Al-Radi claimed that the seeing is visual (basariyyah). I have expanded on this point at his saying ﴿Have you considered what you emit?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 58] ﴿Is it you who create it?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 59] in Surah al-Waqi'ah.

The "am" (or) is connective, and it is equalizing the interrogative hamza, because the question concerns one of the two matters.

[Page 210]

Provision (rizq) is that which is benefited from. It was discussed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and from what We have provided for them they spend﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3] in Surah al-Baqarah, and in His saying ﴿or from what God has provided you﴾ [al-A'raf: 50] in al-A'raf.

The giving of provision is expressed by "sending down" (inzal) because most of their wealth consisted of fruits, grapes and grains, all of which are effects of rain, which descends from the clouds by God's creation. Thus the sending down is attributed to God on this basis. Most of their wealth was livestock, and their life depends on pasture and herbage, which are also from the effect of rain. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Let man look at his food﴾ [Abasa: 24] ﴿that We poured down water in abundance﴾ [Abasa: 25] ﴿then We split the earth in splitting﴾ [Abasa: 26] ﴿and caused grain to grow therein﴾ [Abasa: 27] ﴿and grapes and herbage﴾ [Abasa: 28] ﴿and olives and palms﴾ [Abasa: 29] ﴿and gardens of dense trees﴾ [Abasa: 30] ﴿and fruit and pasture﴾ [Abasa: 31] ﴿as a provision for you and your cattle﴾ [Abasa: 32]. And He said: ﴿and in heaven is your provision﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 22], meaning the cause of your provision, which is rain. The Arabs were known as "sons of the water of the sky", and this is a metaphorical use in the word "sons", because "son" is used figuratively for one who is constant with a thing. He also expressed the giving of livestock by sending down in His saying ﴿and He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar: 6], on this basis.

What was made unlawful is partly related by God from them in His saying: ﴿And they say: these are cattle and tilled land, forbidden; none may eat of them except whom we will, by their claim; and cattle whose backs are forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 138], and His saying: ﴿And they say: what is in the wombs of these cattle is exclusively for our males, and forbidden to our females﴾ [al-An'am: 139], in Surah al-An'am.

The primary locus of denunciation is their making some of what God provided for them unlawful for themselves. As for coordinating "lawful" (halal) with "unlawful" (haram), it is a denunciation by implication, because when they targeted some of what God had made lawful for them and made it unlawful, separating it from the whole of provision, they also made the lawful lawful by a new decree, when they said it was lawful. They thus placed themselves as overseers over God's rulings, when they targeted the lawful part of them and turned it into unlawful, while leaving some of the lawful as lawful. Had they not left it lawful, it would not have remained lawful for them, and its benefit would have been suspended. Therefore He denounced their making some provision unlawful and some lawful. Otherwise, they did not make what was unlawful lawful, since there was no prohibition in the pre-Islamic period (jahiliyyah).

The phrase "lawful" (halalan) is coordinated with "unlawful" (haraman), and the estimated meaning is "and from it lawful", because all that God provided for them does not go beyond these two categories among them. The meaning is not "you made some of it unlawful and lawful, and some of it neither unlawful nor lawful", because that does not hold.

[Page 210 continues]

The placing of the divine name (Allah), which is the subject, before its predicate, the verb, in ﴿Did God permit you﴾ is for reinforcing the judgment together with emphasis. The placing of the prepositional phrase before its governing verb in ﴿or do you fabricate against God﴾ is for emphasis on this complement, to censure the attribution of fabrication to it. The divine name is made explicit to magnify the gravity of fabrication against Him.

The complement of "permitted" (adhina) is omitted because it is evident. The estimated meaning is: "Did God permit you by that making?"

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 60:

﴿And what will be the opinion of those who fabricate lies against Allah on the Day of Resurrection? Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind, but most of them do not give thanks.﴾

It is a conjunction with the sentence ﴿Say: Have you considered...﴾ [Yunus: 59]. It is therefore speech not included within the saying that was commanded, but it is the beginning of an address to all of mankind. The "mā" (what) is interrogative. The interrogation is used to express wonder at their condition, and its intended purpose is an indirect rebuke of the polytheists, so that they may awaken from their heedlessness and take account of themselves.

For this reason, the apparent form would have been to bring the pronoun "hum" (them) as a genitive complement of "ẓann" (opinion), either a pronoun of address or of the third person, so that one would say: "wa mā ẓannukum" (and what is your opinion) or "wa mā ẓannuhum" (and what is their opinion). Instead, he departed from the apparent form and used the relative pronoun with the clause specific to them, to alert that the disjunction between Allah having permitted them in what they forbade and their being fabricators against Him has been confined to the second part, namely that they are fabricators, since there is no justification for them in claiming that He permitted them. Once it is established that they are fabricators, fabrication has become their particular condition. In the relative construction there is also an indication of the reason for the wonder at their opinion of themselves on the Day of Resurrection.

The two objects of "ẓann" are omitted in order to generalize what it may refer to, that is: what is their opinion of their state, of their recompense, and of themselves. "Al-kadhib" (the lie) is in the accusative as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq), and the "al" in it is for the definition of the genus, as if it were said "kadhiban" (a lie), but it was made definite to magnify its matter, meaning: it is the lie that is well known among people and abhorred by minds.

"Yawm al-qiyāmah" (the Day of Resurrection) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and its governing word is "ẓann", meaning: what is their opinion on that day, that is, when they see the wrath upon them on that day, what will their opinion be that they will encounter it? This is a means of instilling awe.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) for the speech that opened with His saying: ﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord and a cure for what is in the breasts﴾ [Yunus: 57]. In it there is a cutting off of the excuse of the polytheists and a recording against them of rebelliousness, in that Allah has bestowed upon them provision, admonition and guidance, yet they met that with disbelief instead of thanks, and made their provision into [the act of] denying. Whereas the believers met it with joy and gratitude, and so they benefited from it in this world and the Hereafter.

[Page 212 begins within this passage at "necessarily"; the page markers are retained below.]

This verse is coordinated (*ma'tuf*) with the clause ﴿And what will those think who fabricate lies against Allah on the Day of Resurrection?﴾ [Yunus: 60], as a coordination of one purpose with another purpose (*'atf gharad 'ala gharad*). The separation of the first purpose by a concluding statement (*tadhyil*, a summarising sentence that closes a point with a general principle) is evidence that the speech has moved to another purpose. That purpose is a promise of reward to the Messenger for what he undertakes of conveying the command of Allah, managing the affairs of the Muslims, and supporting the religion of Islam, and a promise of reward to the Muslims for following the Messenger in what he has called them to. This promise comes by way of allusion (*ta'rid*) to Allah the Exalted's approval of them in His words ﴿except that We are witnesses over you﴾, because they know that their deeds and the deeds of the Prophet were nothing but for the pleasure of Allah. It is thus like His words, ﴿Who sees you when you stand [for prayer], and your movements among those who prostrate﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 218]. This contains also an honouring of the Prophet ﷺ for his noble deeds, and a consolation for what he encounters from the polytheists of denial and harm, because Allah's observation of that, and His knowledge that it is for His pleasure, is sufficient consolation, as in His words, ﴿So be patient for the judgement of your Lord, for indeed you are under Our eyes﴾ [al-Tur: 48]. For this reason the address was first directed to the Prophet ﷺ, then it was directed to him and to those with him among the Muslims.

The first *ma* and the second *ma* are both negating particles.

[Page 213]

*Al-sha'n* (the matter) means an important deed and an important state. The *fi* (in) here is for figurative containment (*al-zarfiyya al-majaziyya*), which carries the meaning of intensity of involvement. The pronoun in *minhu* (from it) either refers back to *sha'n*, meaning: "and you do not recite from the matter any Qur'an," in which case *min* explains the relative *ma*, or *min* carries the meaning of the causal *li* (for), meaning: "you do not recite, for the sake of the matter, any Qur'an." The coordination of ﴿and you do not recite﴾ is coordination of the specific upon the general, for the sake of giving it importance, since recitation is the most important of the affairs of the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace.

Or it refers back to *qur'an*, meaning: "and you do not recite from the Qur'an any Qur'an," in which case *min* is partitive (*lil-tab'id*), and the pronoun refers forward to what comes later, in order to create anticipation for it so that it settles in the listener's mind. The *waw* in *tatlu* is a radical letter of the verb (*lam al-kalima*), and the verb bears a singular pronoun addressing the Prophet ﷺ.

So the speech begins with the affairs of the Prophet ﷺ, among which are things that are specific to him, such as the night prayer. It then mentions a second category, what concerns him in relation to people, which is the recitation of the Qur'an to them. It then mentions a third category, what concerns the community, in His words ﴿nor do you do any deed﴾. Although the address in this is inclusive of the Prophet ﷺ, the prior mention of *sha'n* at the beginning of the verse specifies the generality of the address in *ta'malun* (you do), so that what is intended is only what the rest of the Muslims do.

Negation occurred twice with the particle *ma* and once with the particle *la*, because the particle *ma* is originally meant to restrict the present tense to the present time. He first intended to bring to mind the great state of the affairs of the Prophet ﷺ and of his recitation of the Qur'an. When the deeds of the community were negated, the particle that originally restricts the present tense to the future was used, to vary the negation from the start of the speech, indicating the continuation of that in all times.

From the contextual indication of generality in the three verbs, through the three indefinite nouns connected to those verbs and occurring in the context of negation, it is known that what occurs in the present and what occurs in the future of those actions is the same. This is from the wonderful brevity and inimitability (*al-i'jaz*). Likewise is the combination of the present-tense forms in the generalised verbs (*takunu, tatlu, ta'malun*) with the past-tense form in the verb that occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from them, ﴿except that We were﴾, to draw attention to the fact that what has occurred, what occurs, and what will occur are the same in the knowledge of

[Page 214]

Allah the Exalted, by way of *al-ihtibak* (a rhetorical device in which one term is omitted from each of two parallel elements because the other covers it). It is as if it were said: "You were not and are not, and so on, except that We were and are witnesses over you."

*Min 'amal* is the object of *ta'malun*. It is a verbal noun with the meaning of the passive object, and *min* was introduced to it to specify generality, so that it includes the great and the small, the good and the evil deed.

The exception in His words ﴿except that We were witnesses over you﴾ is an exception from the general states that the generality of the affair, the generality of the recitation, and the generality of the deed require. That is, "except in a state in which We know of that." So the clause ﴿We were over you﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause. The presence of the exceptive particle made unnecessary the linking of the circumstantial clause with the particle *qad*, because the connection is clear by means of the exception.

*Al-shuhud* is the plural of *shahid*. The plural form is used to refer to one, namely Allah the Exalted, following the plural pronoun used for magnification. A similar example is His words, ﴿Indeed We were doers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 104]. A parallel to this in the use of the plural of addressing for a single addressee is the verse of Ja'far ibn 'Ulba al-Harithi:

*Fa-la tahsabi annī takhashsha'tu ba'dakum*
*Li-shay'in wa-la annī mina al-mawti afraqu*

Do not think, [my beloved], that after you I have become humble to anything, nor that I fear death.

This is a metaphor (*isti'ara*), by likening the one to the group in strength, because a group does not lack many qualities spread among its members.

*Al-shahid* means the present one, and it is applied to the knower by way of metonymy (*al-majaz al-mursal*, figurative use with a non-metaphorical link). For this reason it takes the preposition *'ala* (over).

*Idh* is an adverb of time, meaning: "at the time when you engage in it."

*Al-ifada* in a deed means plunging into it, that is, beginning the deed with strength and concern. This root indicates that what is intended is their deeds in pursuit of Allah's pleasure and their perseverance in bearing the harm of the polytheists. This state and this time were singled out for mention after the generalisation of deeds, for the sake of giving attention to this type, and it is like the mention of the specific after the general. It is as if it were said: "nor do you do any deed, of any kind, or any great deed in which you plunge, except that We were witnesses over you when you do it and when you plunge into it."

[Page 215]

The clause ﴿And there is not hidden from your Lord﴾ and so on is coordinated with the clause ﴿And you are not engaged in any matter﴾. It serves as a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) for what it contains of additional generality in the connection of Allah the Exalted's knowledge to all existing things, after the discussion of its connection to the deed of the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims.

*Al-'uzub* means distance, and it is used here metaphorically for concealment and the escaping of knowledge, because concealment is a necessary feature of a distant thing. For this reason it is linked to the name of the essence rather than to the attribute of knowledge, so He said ﴿from your Lord﴾.

The majority read *ya'zubu* with a *damma* on the *zay*. al-Kisa'i read it with a *kasra* on the *zay*. These are two valid forms of the present tense of *'azaba*.

The *min* in His words ﴿of an atom's weight﴾ is extra (*mazida*), to emphasise the generality of the negation that is in *ma ya'zubu* (is not hidden).

*Al-mithqal* is a noun of instrument for that by which the weight of a thing is known. It is the pattern *mif'al* from *thaqula* (to be heavy), and it is the name of a standard weight determined by a specific measure, by which heaviness is weighed.

*Al-dharra* is the small ant. It is also applied to the mote that is seen in sunlight, like very fine dust. The apparent meaning in the verse is the first. The atom is mentioned as an exaggeration of smallness and fineness, as a metonymy for the encompassing of knowledge over everything, since what is greater than the atom is more deserving of the judgement.

What is meant by *al-ard* and *al-sama'* here is the lower world and the upper world. The intention is to generalise directions and dimensions in the briefest expression. The earth is mentioned first here because what is in it is more closely related to the purpose of the speech, which is the deeds of people, since they are of the people of the earth. This is unlike what is in Surat Saba': ﴿Knower of the unseen; not hidden from Him is an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth﴾ [Saba': 3]. There, since the context was the mention of knowledge of the unseen, and the unseen is what is hidden from people and most of it is in the heavens, it was fitting that the heavens be mentioned before the earth.

﴿And not smaller than that, nor greater﴾ is coordinated with *dharra* (atom), to state explicitly what was alluded to by *mithqal dharra* from all bodies.

[Page 216 would follow; the text continues on the next page of the commentary.]

*Asghar* with a *fatha* in the reading of the majority is not declined, because it is coordinated with *dharra*, which is in the genitive case, on the basis that *la* is extra for the emphasis of negation. It is also permitted that the coordination be of a clause, with *la* being a negating particle of the genus, and *asghar* its noun, built on the *fatha*, so that it begins a new speech.

Hamza, Khalaf and Ya'qub read *wa-la asghru wa-la akbaru* with a *damma* on both, on the basis that *asghar* is coordinated with the position (*mahall*) of *mithqal*, since it is the grammatical subject (*fa'il*) of *ya'zubu* in meaning. Its vowel is the vowel of the genitive of the extra particle, and this is one of the eloquent usages. Or it is on the basis of coordinating a clause with a clause, with *la* being a negating particle functioning like *laysa* (is not), and *asghar* being its noun.

The exception, on the first two readings, from the reading with *fatha* or *damma* on *asghar*, is a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*), meaning *lakinna* (but). That is: "that is not hidden, but it is present in a Book." It is also permitted that it be a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*) from the general states of the hiddenness of an atom's weight, or what is smaller or greater than it. Its interpretation is that it is of the kind of emphasising a thing by what resembles its opposite. The meaning is: "nothing on the earth or in the heavens is hidden from Him, except in a state in which it is in a clear Book," that is, "except as something known and written down." The hearer knows that what is written in a clear Book cannot be hidden, so the absence of its concealment is established by a demonstrative method (*tariq burhani*).

The prepositional phrase on all of this is in the position of a circumstantial clause. On the last two readings, the exception is connected, and the prepositional phrase is an independent adverbial in the position of the predicate of the negating *la*. It is then in the position of nominative or accusative, meaning: "nothing smaller than an atom or greater exists, except in a clear Book," as in His words, ﴿and no moist or dry thing, but it is in a clear Book﴾ [al-An'am: 59].

*Al-kitab* is the knowledge of Allah. The word "Book" is borrowed for it because it is established and does not deviate from the truth by addition or subtraction. *Mubin* is an active participle from *abana*, with the meaning of *bana* (to be clear), meaning: clear, manifest, with no possibility of ambiguity in it.

[p. 216]

This is a resumption that makes explicit the promise to the believers that was alluded to in His words ﴿And We are witnesses over you when you are engaged in it. And not absent from your Lord is any [part] of an atom's weight...﴾ [Yunus: 61], and it consoles the Prophet (ﷺ) for the harm and threats he suffers from the disbelievers. God announced to the Prophet and the believers security from the fear of their enemies and from the grief that results from it, and He hinted to them at the outcome of victory. He promised them good tidings in the Hereafter, a promise that admits no change or failure, to reassure their souls, as indicated by His words that follow it: ﴿There is no alteration to the words of Allah﴾.

Opening the statement with the particle of alerting (ألا, "Unquestionably") signals the importance of the matter, as was mentioned in His words ﴿Unquestionably, they are the corrupters﴾ [al-Baqarah: 12] in Surat al-Baqarah. For this reason the sentence is emphasized with "inna" after the particle of alerting.

In the expression ﴿the friends of Allah﴾, instead of using a pronoun of address, as the context following His words "and whatever deed you do" would require, there is an indication that the addressees have earned the right to be among the friends of Allah, while also conveying a general ruling that encompasses them and includes whoever follows their path.

The clause ﴿there is no fear for them, nor do they grieve﴾ is the predicate of "inna".

Fear (al-khawf) is the anticipation of the occurrence of something disliked to the one anticipating it, and it takes its object directly: one says "khafa al-shay'" (he feared the thing), as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me﴾ [Al 'Imran: 175]. If the anticipation of the occurrence of something disliked concerns someone other than the one anticipating, one says of the anticipated person: "khafa 'alayhi" (he feared for him), as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾ [al-A'raf: 59].

The structure of the sentence requires the negation of the genus of fear, because "la" (no) when it enters upon an indefinite noun indicates negation of the genus. If the noun after it is built on the fatha, the negation of the genus is explicit; if it is not built on the fatha, the negation of the genus is apparent, with the possibility that it means the negation of one individual of that genus, provided the context allows this possibility. This applies to genera that have individual members, such as "rajul" (a man). As for genera of abstract meanings, this possibility does not arise, so the raising of the noun of "la" and its being built on the fatha are equivalent in them, as in the saying of one of the women in the narration of Umm Zar': "My husband is like the night of Tihama: neither hot nor cold, neither fear nor weariness" [a line from the narration]. These nouns have been transmitted both with the nominative case and with the fatha as the final vowel.

[p. 217]

The meaning of ﴿there is no fear for them﴾ is that they are in a state in which no one fearing would fear for them, that is, they are in security from anything disliked befalling them that one might fear the like of. Although fear may stir in their souls toward the enemies, a passing stirring arising from the natural disposition of souls when they witness the signs of danger, others who know their condition do not fear for them, because they look at circumstances with the gaze of certainty, unaffected by appearances. Their condition is the condition of one who should not fear, and therefore their friends do not fear for them, because they feel secure for them from the outcome of what they apprehend with dread. So the fear, which is a verbal noun in the verse, is to be understood as annexed to its agent, who is necessarily someone other than them; that is, no fear that a fearful person would feel for them. As for themselves, when fear overtakes them, it does not remain long before it is dispelled from them and tranquility settles in its place, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the earth was constricted for you despite its vastness, then you turned back in retreat﴾ [al-Tawbah: 25], ﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 26], and He said to Musa: ﴿Do not fear being overtaken, and do not be apprehensive﴾ [Ta-Ha: 77], and He said: ﴿Indeed, those who fear Allah, when a touch of Satan afflicts them, remember [Him], and at once they have insight﴾ [al-A'raf: 201].

On the day of Badr, the Prophet (ﷺ) would call upon Allah for victory and would invoke Him much, saying: "O Allah, if You destroy this band, You will not be worshipped on the earth." Then he went out while saying: ﴿The multitude will be routed and they will turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 45].

Because of this meaning to which the verse points, the style changes in His words ﴿nor do they grieve﴾. Here the negated grief is attributed to the pronoun of "the friends of Allah," with the subject placed first, and the verb after it is given as a predicate, which strengthens the ruling. Grief is the breaking of the soul following the occurrence of something disliked to it, so its reality does not exist except after its occurrence, whereas fear occurs before it.
