"The man of keen insight who suspects of you what seems as though he has seen and heard [it]."

His words ﴿and they were mindful of Allah﴾ indicate that God-consciousness is a constant attribute of theirs, taken from the form "kanu" (they were), and that it is a renewed act on their part, taken from the present form in His words "yattaqun" (they are mindful). I used to say in discussions many years ago, during the days of study, that this verse is the strongest basis for defining the reality of the "walī" (friend of Allah) in the Sharia, and that the meaning of His words in the sacred hadith narrated by al-Tirmidhi from the Prophet (ﷺ) is to be understood in accordance with this reality: "Allah, Exalted is He, said: Whoever shows enmity to a friend of Mine, I have declared war against him."

The indication of the verse concerns Allah's allying with them in honor, by His words ﴿For them are good tidings in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾.

The definite article in "al-bushra" (the good tidings) is the definite article of the genus, so it is true of many glad tidings.

[p. 219]

"Fi al-hayat al-dunya wa fi al-akhirah" (in the life of this world and in the Hereafter) is a circumstantial clause describing "al-bushra." The meaning is that they are given good tidings of benefits before they occur: in this world, through the repeated glad tidings found in the speech of Allah, Exalted is He, and the speech of His Messenger (ﷺ); and in the Hereafter, through what they receive from the angels and what they hear of Allah's command concerning them, leading to lasting bliss, as in His words: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds that they will have gardens﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25].

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu al-Darda' that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about His words, Exalted is He: ﴿For them are good tidings in the life of this world﴾. He said: "No one has asked me about it besides you since it was revealed. It is the good dream that a Muslim sees, or that is seen for him." Al-Tirmidhi said: "In it is not 'Ata' ibn Yasar," meaning that the hadith does not state that Abu Salih narrated it from 'Ata' ibn Yasar, as is well known in the transmission of Abu Salih from Abu al-Darda'. Accordingly, the hadith is disconnected and its chain is not continuous. Al-Tirmidhi narrated it through two other chains in which 'Ata' ibn Yasar narrates from a man of the people of Egypt, from Abu al-Darda', and that chain includes an unknown narrator. Therefore the condition of the chain of this report is unstable, since it is evident that 'Ata' did not hear it from Abu al-Darda'.

The interpretation of this report is that the good dream is among the glad tidings in this world, because it informs its seer of good that will come about in this world or in the Hereafter. Or it may be that the questioner asked about the glad tidings of this life, while the glad tidings of the Hereafter were already known from His words: ﴿Their Lord gives them good tidings of mercy from Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 21] and similar verses.

In the Muwatta' [of Malik], from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, that he used to say concerning this verse ﴿For them are good tidings in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾: "It is the good dream that a man sees, or that is seen for him." Among the glad tidings is the promise that they will have the outcome of victory over the enemies, and that they will be empowered with authority in this world, and that they will have everlasting bliss in the Hereafter.

The juxtaposition of grief with good tidings is among the embellishments of antithesis (tibaq).

The clause ﴿There is no alteration to the words of Allah﴾ explains the meaning of the emphasis of the promise contained in His words ﴿For them are good tidings in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾, reminding them that what Allah has promised them of glad tidings, such as victory

[p. 220]

and a good outcome, is a fixed matter that does not fail, because it is one of the words of Allah. The alteration is negated by the form of exoneration, which indicates the negation of the genus of alteration.

"Al-tabdil" means change and nullification, because nullifying a thing entails establishing its opposite.

"Kalimat Allah" (the words of Allah) refers to the sayings that He revealed to the Messenger concerning the promise referred to. It is understood from the generality of "the words of Allah" and the generality of the negation of alteration that everything that is an alteration is negated from its very root.

It is narrated that al-Hajjaj gave a sermon in which he mentioned 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr and said: "He has altered the Book of Allah." Ibn 'Umar was present, and he said to him: "Neither you nor Ibn al-Zubayr are able to do that. There is no alteration to the words of Allah."

The clause ﴿That is the great success﴾ reinforces the clause ﴿For them are good tidings﴾ and establishes its content, and for this reason it is separated [without a conjunction].

The demonstrative "dhalika" (that) refers to what has been mentioned in the content of the three preceding clauses. The choice of the demonstrative noun is because it is the most comprehensive of what has been mentioned, and in it there is complete distinction of it, for the sake of further establishing its meaning. The pronoun of separation (huwa) is mentioned after the demonstrative to add emphasis and to convey restriction, that is: it is the great success and nothing else, unlike the other things in which the polytheists move about in the life of this world, such as provision, protection, and strength; because such things are not considered success when they are followed by humiliation and disgrace in this world, and after them by everlasting punishment in the Hereafter, as indicated by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve throughout the land deceive you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 196], ﴿A brief enjoyment; then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾ [Al 'Imran: 197].

[Page 221]

﴿And do not let their speech grieve you. Indeed, all honor belongs to Allah; He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ This clause is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the clause ﴿Unquestionably, the allies of Allah have no fear, nor will they grieve﴾ [Yunus: 62]. It is a conjunction of the particular to the general (ʿaṭf al-juzʾī ʿalā al-kullī), because the grief mentioned here is a type of the grief negated in His words ﴿nor will they grieve﴾ [Yunus: 62]. It is also because the Messenger (ﷺ) is one of the allies of Allah of whom ﴿there is no fear, nor will they grieve﴾.

So the apparent form would have been to conjoin it with the consequential fa' (fāʾ al-tafrīʿ, "therefore"), since the removal of this grief follows from that negation. However, it was changed to conjunction with waw so that the content of the conjoined clause would be stated as an independent matter, intended in itself, and thus would be the start of a new statement, without losing the sense of consequence, which is evident from the context.

The grief whose onset is forbidden is the grief arising from the harm the polytheists inflicted on Muhammad (ﷺ) through their vile words and threats. The reason for restricting the response to this is that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not encounter from the polytheists any cause of grief except the harm of vile speech.

The form ﴿do not let their speech grieve you﴾ is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ). The apparent meaning of its form is a prohibition against the speech of the polytheists grieving the Prophet (ﷺ). Yet the norm for a prohibition is that the address be directed to the one who commits the forbidden act. The intended purpose of such a construction is a prohibition of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) from being affected by what is naturally grief-causing to people from their words. When the address is directed to him with a prohibition concerning an act that is in fact the act of others, it becomes determined that this is a metonymy (kināya) for forbidding him from the occurrence of that grief within himself, by his turning away from its causes and necessary consequences. It thus comes to the meaning: "Do not leave their speech to grieve you." This is like how people say: "Let me not see you doing such-and-such," or "Let me not find you doing such-and-such." The speaker forbids the addressee from being seen by the speaker doing such-and-such. What is meant is the prohibition of doing it, so that the speaker does not see it; this is the use of the necessitating for what is necessitated (iṭlāq al-malzūm wa-irādat al-lāzim). The meaning is: "Do not do such-and-such, lest I see you doing it." The meaning of ﴿do not let their speech grieve you﴾ is: "Do not grieve at their speech, lest it grieve you."

It is well known that the speech of the polytheists which grieved the Prophet (ﷺ) was speech of denial and mockery. Therefore the object of the verb "speech" is omitted, because the verbal noun here has been treated as the verbal noun of an intransitive verb.

The clause ﴿Indeed, all honor belongs to Allah﴾ gives the reason for removing grief from him. For this reason it is separated from the clause of prohibition, as if the Prophet (ﷺ) were saying: "How should I not grieve, when the polytheists boast over us and threaten us, and they are people of might and power?" So it is answered: their might is as nothing, because it is limited and transient, while true might belongs to Allah, who sent you.

It is also in the position of an explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī). Every clause whose content is a cause of the clause before it is likewise an explanatory resumption, so the explanatory resumption is more general than causation (taʿlīl).

[Page 222]

It is introduced with the emphatic particle for the sake of emphasis on it, and because it conveys the function of the particle of causation (lām al-taʿlīl) and the consequential fāʾ in such a context, in which the purpose is not to refute a denial from the addressee.

It is good to pause on the word "their speech" (qawluhum), so that a listener does not suppose that the clause ﴿Indeed, all honor belongs to Allah﴾ is a quotation of their speech, and then ask why this speech should be a cause of the Messenger's (ﷺ) grief. And how would the Messenger (ﷺ) grieve at their words ﴿Indeed, all honor belongs to Allah﴾, even though the context already guides the hearer quickly to the intended meaning?

A parallel to this misunderstanding is what is related: Ibn Qutayba, namely ʿAbdullah ibn Muslim ibn Qutayba, mentioned the recitation of Abu Haywa, "*ʾanna al-ʿizzata lillāh*" with the hamza of "*ʾanna*" opened, and parsed it as a substitution (badal) for "qawluhum," and he ruled that this recitation was disbelief. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reported this from him. He also pointed to this in al-Kashshaf, saying: "Whoever makes it a substitution for 'qawluhum,' then denies it, the denied thing is his parsing of it."

Perhaps Ibn Qutayba meant that although breaking the hamza (kasr) is possible, so that the clause after it is governed by "qawluhum," because the norm of "*ʾinna*" after a verb of saying is that it not be opened, that is only a possibility not decisively fixed, since it also allows the clause to be a resumption, and the context determines the correct possibility.

As for when the hamza is opened, as Abu Haywa recited, it becomes determined that it is governed by what was mentioned before it, namely the word "qawluhum." It has no other interpretation in his view except that it (i.e., the verbal noun formed from it) is a substitution for the word "qawluhum." The meaning then becomes: "Allah forbade His Prophet from grieving at the speech of the polytheists that 'all honor belongs to Allah,' and how could it be so, when he was calling them to that?" Since the prohibition of something requires permitting that the one prohibited might be engaged in the thing prohibited, this implies permitting the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) to be afflicted with grief at one who says this statement. This permission leads to the disbelief of whoever permits it, by the method of excommunication through a necessary implication (takfīr bi-l-lāzim), and its aim is to vilify the holder of this recitation.

[Page 223]

Ibn Qutayba built his statement upon the apparent wording of the Qur'an, without positing a particle before "*ʾanna*." Perhaps he considered that positing one departs from the basic principle, or that it is insufficient to remove the misunderstanding. The fact is that Ibn Qutayba exaggerated what has an acceptable interpretation, and the scholars rejected his view with a sound rejection.

The definiteness of "al-ʿizza" (might, honor) is the definiteness of the genus (taʿrīf al-jins), which conveys comprehensiveness (istighrāq) by the indication of the context.

The "lām" in His words "lillāh" indicates ownership (al-milk). By making the genus of might a possession of Allah, it conveys that all its types belong to Allah, so it indicates that He has its strongest and most supreme types. Thereby it indicates that others possess from it only a few types. Thus no type of might found in the possession of another is such that the greater of its kind is not a possession of Allah, the Exalted. Therefore what others possess of might has no effect when it opposes the might of Allah, the Exalted, and it has no effect except when Allah grants it respite. So every might that its holder uses to oppose one whom Allah wills to help is refuted and defeated, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail." Indeed, Allah is Strong, Mighty﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21]. And since the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) knew that Allah had sent him and commanded him to restrain the polytheists from what they were in, he was such that he believed in victory when Allah informed him that this was His will, and he knew that whatever might the polytheists had was, beside the might of Allah, the Exalted, as nothing.

"Jamīʿan" (all, altogether) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from "al-ʿizza," emphasizing the content of the clause before it, which conveys that Allah, the Exalted, is exclusively the possessor of the entire genus of might, in order to remove the possibility that what is meant is exaggeration in possessing that genus.

The clause ﴿He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ is a resumed clause (mustaʾnafa). Applying this predicate to the Name of Majesty (Allah), which occurs as a pillar of the causal clause, carries the sense of causation over to this clause, so the clause conveys another causation, or a completion of the first causation. For when the addressee recalls that the Lord of might knows their words and their conditions, that increases the strength in removing grief from their words from his own self. For He who forbade him from grieving at their words and their deeds is far stronger than them, and His knowledge encompasses what they say and their conditions. So when He forbids you from grieving at their words, He has forbidden it only because He has guaranteed you safety from them despite your weakness and their strength, since He supports you with His strength, and He knows best how to bring about the causes of your victory over them.

[Page 224]

By "al-Samīʿ" (the All-Hearing) is meant the One who knows their words which are of the kind that can be heard, and by "al-ʿAlīm" (the All-Knowing) is meant what is more general than their conditions, which are not things heard; so the name "All-Hearing" is not applied to the knowledge of these.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 66:

﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth. And those who invoke other than Allah as partners do not follow [in reality] except assumption, and they are not but guessing.﴾

The purpose of directing this statement is the polytheists, to make them despair of every possibility of victory over the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims. For when many of them understand, from the five preceding verses, from His saying ﴿and you are not in any matter﴾ [Yunus: 61] up to here, the explicit statement of the lowliness of their station before Allah and before His Messenger, and the allusion to the imminence of the overthrow that will befall them, some doubt creeps into them concerning the truthfulness of the Messenger and whether what he threatened them with is true. Then they deceive themselves and console their hearts that if that should come about, they will find intercession from their gods in averting harm from them, and they say to themselves: "For such a thing we worshipped them, and for intercession with Allah we prepared them." So this statement is brought to cut off their hope in them, by demonstrating that they are far below what is supposed of them.

The sentence is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i, a fresh beginning), and the reason for its occurrence after the sentence ﴿let not their saying grieve you﴾ [Yunus: 65] is that their sayings are refuted by the content of this sentence. As for its occurrence after the sentence ﴿Indeed, all might belongs to Allah﴾ [Yunus: 65], it is because it serves as proof that might belongs to Allah, since the One to whom belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth is the One to whom true might belongs.

The opening of the sentence with the particle of alerting (harf al-tanbih, "alā") is intended to show the importance of knowing its content and establishing it; for this reason it is followed by the particle of emphasis (harf al-ta'kid, "inna"). This emphasis is increased by the fronting of the predicate in His saying ﴿to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾ and by bringing in the lam of ownership.

The relative pronoun "man" (من) is ordinarily used for rational beings, and it is used here although the primary aim is to establish that their deities are the property of Allah, and they are inanimate stones that lack reason. This is by way of giving precedence to rational beings (taghlib) and because of their belief that those deities are rational. This is one of the ways of accommodating the opponent in debate, in order to bind him by the cogency of the argument even according to the necessary implication of his own belief. The ruling that the rational existents in the heavens and the earth are the property of Allah, Exalted is He, implies all the more that those stones are the property of Allah, because whoever owns the stronger is more capable of owning the weaker. Among the Arabs there were those who worshipped the angels, and among them were those who worshipped the Messiah, namely the Christians of the Arabs.

The mention of the heavens and the earth is for encompassing the places of existent things, so it is as if it were said: "Indeed, to Allah belongs all existent things."

The clause ﴿and those who invoke other than Allah as partners do not follow﴾ etc. is conjoined (ma'tufah) to the clause ﴿to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾. It serves as a conclusion (natijah) to the first clause, since the meaning is that all existent things belong to Allah, and the polytheists' following of their idols is a mistaken and false following.

"Ma" is necessarily negative, by the evidence of its being emphasized by "in" (إنْ), the negative particle, and by the exception introduced after them.

"Shuraka'" (شُرَكاءَ) is the object of "yad'una" (يَدْعُونَ), which is the relative clause (silah) of "alladhina" (الَّذِينَ).

The clause ﴿they do not follow except﴾ — "in yattabi'un" (إنْ يَتَّبِعُونَ) — is a verbal emphasis (ta'kid lafzi) of the clause "ma yattabi' alladhina yad'un." Its content is repeated to fulfil the requirement of eloquence, since the long relative clause creates a separation between the exception and the excepted element, producing something resembling verbal complexity, and this is not befitting of the most eloquent speech. Moreover, this repetition serves the function of emphasis, because the context calls for thoroughness in establishing the purpose.

"Al-zann" (الظَّنَّ) is the object of both verbs "yattabi'" (يَتَّبِعُ) and "yattabi'un" (يَتَّبِعُونَ), since they are like a single verb.

This is not a case of tanazu' (competition between two verbs for one object), because the verb of a verbal emphasis does not require an object, since its purpose is the repetition of the word without the function of governing. The estimated sense is: "And the polytheists do not follow except assumption, and they are not but guessing."

Here "al-zann" is a noun treated as if it were intransitive, not intended to be linked to a specific object of assumption; that is, their practice is to follow assumptions. By "al-zann" is meant here mistaken knowledge.

The following clause has clarified that their assumption has no proof, by His saying ﴿and they are not but guessing﴾.

"Al-kharsh" (الخَرْص) is speaking by conjecture and estimation. A parallel to this verse has preceded in Surat al-An'am, namely His saying: ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you from the way of Allah. They follow not but assumption, and they are not but guessing﴾ [al-An'am: 116].

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 67:**

﴿It is He who made the night for you that you may rest therein, and the day giving sight. Indeed in that are signs for a people who listen.﴾

This is a parenthetical sentence (*jumla mu'tarida*) placed between the sentence ﴿they follow nothing but conjecture﴾ [Yunus: 66] and the sentence ﴿They say: God has taken a son﴾ [Yunus: 68]. It comes in the manner of an argument (*istidlal*) against the falsity of their conjecture and guesswork, by means of the evident signs of the creation of night and day, which are witnessed twice every day of one's life, while they are heedless of their indication, namely the establishment of the order of day and night.

How the day was made a time in which light spreads, so that it suits seeing, since people in the movements of their work need the sense of sight, by which the essences of things and their states are distinguished, so that they may take what is good from them for action and discard what is not good for action.

How the night was made a time when darkness covers it, so that it suits rest, since people in it need repose from the fatigue of the labours which they toil at during the day. Thus darkness moves people to rest and sets its time for them, such that the discerning and the heedless alike share in this.

Since he contrasted rest on the side of the night with sight on the side of the day, and since night and day are opposites, this indicates that the cause of rest is the absence of sight, and that sight requires movement. Thus there is *ihtibak* (a rhetorical device in which each of two contrasting elements is left implicit where the other is mentioned) in the speech.

The description of the day as ﴿giving sight﴾ is a rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*, attributing to a thing an act that properly belongs to its agents) for the sake of emphasis on the occurrence of seeing within it, to the point that the day itself is made the one who sees. The intended meaning is: giving sight in which people see.

Among the subtle points of this correspondence is that the light, which is the condition of the time of day, is an existent thing, so its time is fitting to be described with the attributes of rational beings. By contrast, the night's darkness is a privation, so in considering it as a lesson he confined himself to mentioning the benefit obtained in it, which is that they rest in it.

In his words ﴿It is He who made the night for you﴾ there is one of the ways of restriction (*qasr*), which is the definiteness of the predicate and the subject. Here it is a true restriction and not a relative one, contrary to what some writers have imagined when they took it to be a restriction of specification (*qasr ta'yin*). They acknowledge it and cannot repel this argument. So the aim is to argue for His being singled out, exalted is He, with the attributes of divinity, among which is creation and determination, and that their deities are devoid of the attributes of divinity. Along with the argument there occurs a reminder of favour (*imtinan*) to people by the making of night and day in this order. This reminder of favour is derived from His words ﴿made for you﴾, and from the stated reason for the creation of night, which is people's rest in it, and of the creation of day, which is people's seeing. Every person knows the blessing in the rest of the night and the blessing in their seeing by day likewise. For in working by day there are many blessings: the attainment of desires, the sight of beloved things, and the acquisition of wealth and sustenance. And in resting at night there are many blessings: the restoration of exhausted powers and the turning to conversation with family and children. Moreover, the variety of circumstances removes from a person weariness.

In the integration (*idmaj*) of the argument with the reminder of favour there is an allusion (*ta'ridh*) that those who ascribed partners to God have combined two blemishes: the blemish of opposing the truth, and the blemish of ingratitude for the blessing.

The sentence ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*mustanfa'a*). The "signs" are the proofs that indicate the oneness of God in divinity, exalted is He, for the order that gives rise to night and day contains many subtleties of knowledge, wisdom, power and perfection of craftsmanship.

[Page 228]

Among those signs: the creation of the sun, the creation of the earth, the creation of light in the sun and the creation of darkness in the earth, the arrival of the sun's ray at the earth, the earth's rotation every day such that half of its sphere faces the ray while its other half is screened from the ray, the creation of the human being, and the arrangement of his nervous temperament to be affected by the ray with activity, and by darkness with lassitude, the creation of the sense of sight and its being linked to the impression of light, the arrangement of the working system to be tied to the sense of sight, and the creation of the human temperament containing powers capable of strength and weakness, then driven to use its powers, both intentionally and unintentionally, by reason of its nervous activity, then losing through work a portion of its powers and needing to be replenished with powers that are restored by rest and by the lassitude which compels him to seek repose. What signs are greater than these, and what favour to the human being is greater than that God has deposited in him incentives that drive him to his own good and the good of his kind, by an impulse from within himself?

The word "a people" is described as ﴿who listen﴾, indicating that those signs and proofs have a force of indication for the intellects through reflection upon them, and that turning thought toward their indications needs nothing but being alerted to them and having attention drawn to them. Since hearing God's reminder of them is the principal root in drawing out their indication, or in deriving their implications, given the varying degrees of intelligence among minds and the arrangement of proofs, he made the signs of their indication available to those who listen.

It is also permissible that what is meant is: those who listen to the details of those indications within the chapters of the Qur'an. In either case, the description with hearing is an allusion that those who were not guided by them and did not perceive their indication are like the deaf, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Can you make the deaf hear, or guide the blind?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 40].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 68:

[Page 229]
﴿They said: "God has taken a son." Glory be to Him! He is the Self-Sufficient. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. You have no authority for this. Do you say about God what you do not know?﴾

This is an elaboration of the statement "Surely to God belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth," and so on to its end. In this elaboration there is an incorporation (idmaj) that recounts a further kind of their disbelief, distinct from their claim of partners with God, because this is a hidden kind of disbelief within their religion, and because the argument for refuting it is distinct from the argument for refuting the partners.

The pronoun in "they said" refers to those who call upon partners besides God, meaning: the polytheists said, "God has taken a son." The pronoun is not meant to include others, such as the Christians, because the surah is Meccan, and the Meccan Qur'an did not take up refuting the deviation of the beliefs of the People of the Book. This is because many of them (the polytheists) claimed that God had daughters, namely the angels, who are His daughters from the noblest of the women of the jinn. For this reason, some groups of the Arabs worshipped the jinn. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿On the Day We gather them all together and say to the angels, "Did these used to worship you?"﴾ [Yunus: 28] ﴿They will say, "Glory be to You! You are our Protector, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them believed in them."﴾ [Saba': 41]

Ittikhadh (taking) means making something for the benefit of the maker. It is derived from akhdh (taking), because the one who takes (muttakhidh) takes the thing he chooses. It has been mentioned in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do you take idols as gods?﴾ [al-An'am: 74], in Surat al-An'am, and in His saying: ﴿And if they see the way of right guidance, they do not take it as a way﴾ [al-A'raf: 146], in al-A'raf. Thus ittikhadh applies both to taking an existing thing for exclusive possession, and to producing a thing for benefit from it. Here it is suitable for both meanings, because some of them believe that a child is born from God, the Exalted, and some of them believe that God adopted some of His creatures.

Walad (son/child): a noun patterned on the form fa'al, like 'amad and 'arab. It is derived from wilada (birth), i.e., offspring. One says: the woman and the she-camel gave birth (walidat). Perhaps the origin of walad is a verbal noun (masdar) of the form fa'al, like farah (joy).

[Page 230]
Because of this it is applied to the singular and the plural, as it is described by a verbal noun. One says: "These are the offspring (walad) of so-and-so." In the hadith: "I am the master of the children (walad) of Adam." Here the intended meaning is the plural, because they said: the angels are the daughters of God, whom He begot from the noblest of the jinn. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they attribute daughters to God, glory be to Him﴾ [al-Nahl: 57].

The phrase "Glory be to Him" (subhanahu) is an utterance of declaring Him transcendent, serving as a response to them. Therefore the sentence is an answer to that statement, and for this reason it is separated from the one before it. Subhan is a verbal noun (ism masdar) of sabbaha, when one declares Him free of imperfection; it stands in place of the verb, meaning: we glorify Him. It was mentioned at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They said, "Glory be to You! We have no knowledge"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 32], in Surat al-Baqarah, meaning: exalted is God above this, because what they said entails a deficiency in God, the Exalted. For this reason the sentence of transcendence is clarified by the sentence "﴿He is the Self-Sufficient﴾," as an explanation of the aspect of transcendence, meaning: He is the Self-Sufficient, free of taking a son. Because divinity requires absolute self-sufficiency, free of any need for something that completes a deficiency in essence or actions. Taking a son either arises from a natural impulse to satisfy desire without intending procreation, which is a manifest deficiency; or it arises from intention and reflection on producing a son, and this happens only to fill a gap of need, for meaning in life or a successor after death. All of this contradicts divinity, which requires the attribute of perfect completeness in essence, attributes, and actions.

Al-Ghaniyy (the Self-Sufficient): one characterized by ghina (self-sufficiency). It is of the pattern fa'il for intensification, from the verb "ghaniya" (to be free of need) with "'an" when one is not in need. The self-sufficiency of God is absolute self-sufficiency. In the principles of religion (usul al-din), absolute self-sufficiency has been defined as the absence of need for a specifier (mukhassis) and for a substrate (mahall). The specifier is that which determines for the contingent (mumkin) one of the two states, existence or non-existence, in place of the other. By this, necessary existence (al-wujud al-wajib) is established for the Deity, meaning existence whose non-existence cannot be conceived. For this reason composition from parts and portions is negated of Him, and because of this it is impossible that anything should separate from Him. A son arises from a part separated from the father. Therefore, the Self-Sufficient is necessarily transcendent of a son in terms of separation. Furthermore, it is also impermissible that He should take one of His creatures as a son by adoption, because He is self-sufficient of the needs that move one to take a son, such as seeking help, companionship, or a successor. He, the Exalted, said:

[Page 231]
﴿And they said, "God has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honored servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 26], and He said: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth; how could He have a son?﴾ [al-An'am: 101].

The sentence "﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾" confirms the attribute of self-sufficiency, that whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth is His dominion. He subjects every existent to what He created it for, so He has no need of the help of a son, nor of elevating anyone's rank in order to make him a helper, as kings do with the commanders of their armies and the governors of their provinces and domains, to win their affection and sincerity. This is equivalent to the argument for negating a partner in His saying just before: ﴿Surely to God belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth. And those who call upon other than God as partners do not follow them; they follow only assumption﴾ [Yunus: 66]. His saying, "﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾," indicates that the attribute of servitude (ubudiyyah) contradicts the attribute of sonship (bunuwwah), as in His saying: ﴿And they said, "The Most Merciful has taken a son. Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honored servants"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 26].

From this it is derived that a son is not enslaved to his father or mother, and for this reason a child is freed by whoever owns him, whether father or mother, and their ascendants.

The sentence "﴿You have no authority for this﴾" is a second answer to their saying "﴿God has taken a son﴾." Therefore it is separated just as the sentence "Glory be to Him" was separated. After He argued against their statement, He recorded against them that they have no proof for their saying that.

"In" is a particle of negation.

"Min" is redundant, for emphasizing the negation by comprehensiveness, meaning comprehensive negation of all kinds of proof, strong and weak, rational and legal.

"Indakum" (with you) is used here figuratively. He likened the existence of proof for the one who argues to being in a place, and the meaning is: you have no proof.

"Sultan" (authority) is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "indakum," and the final consonant of the subject was preceded by the kasra of the redundant preposition, instead of the damma.

[Page 232]
Sultan means proof and argument, because it grants the one who argues by it an authority over his opponent and disputant. It was mentioned at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿God has sent down no authority for it﴾ [al-A'raf: 71], in Surat al-A'raf.

The "ba'" (bi-) is for accompaniment, and it is in the position of an adjective to "sultan," meaning: an authority accompanying this. The demonstrative refers to the said statement.

The meaning is: you have no proof accompanying your statement that God has taken a son.

The sentence "﴿Do you say about God what you do not know?﴾" is a third answer, arising from the first two, because when He refuted their claim by proof, and negated that they have any proof for their statement, they deserved rebuke and condemnation for being bold against the sacred presence of God, describing God with what they do not know, meaning what they do not hold certain. Because it is an answer, it was separated.

The interrogative is used for rebuke, because what follows it is a blameworthy thing, a great audacity, and a compound great ignorance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verses 69–70:

﴿Say: Indeed, those who fabricate lies against Allah will not prosper.﴾ ﴿(They have) enjoyment in this world; then to Us is their return; then We will make them taste the severe punishment because they used to disbelieve.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), opened with the command to the Prophet ﷺ to say it, in order to alert the listeners to pay heed to what follows the command to speak, indicating that it is an important matter that must be conveyed. This is because what is said is a general proposition from which a threat arises for those who said: ﴿Allah has taken a son﴾ [Yunus: 68], for that statement of theirs, and for similar things, such as their saying: ﴿What is in the bellies of these cattle is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives﴾ [al-An'am: 139], and their saying that what belongs to their deities of the tilth and cattle does not reach Allah, while what belongs to Allah of that reaches their deities, and their saying: ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾ [al-Isra': 90], and the like. All of that is fabrication against Allah, because they say it as if it were religion, and the essence of religion is that it is a divine legislation, so it is attributed to Him. From that proposition there arises a threat for the likes of the polytheists, and for everyone who fabricates against Allah what He has not said. Thus, those primarily addressed by the saying are the polytheists.

Al-falah (success): the attainment of what the doer intended by his action, without reversal or evil outcome. This was discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah. Thus the negation of success here is a negation of the attainment of their aim from lying and from denying Muhammad ﷺ.

The clause ﴿(They have) enjoyment in this world﴾ is an explanatory resumptive sentence (isti'naf bayani), because the judgment that they do not prosper prompts a questioner to ask: how do we see them in power and might, capable of harming the Muslims and turning people away from following the Messenger ﷺ? The questioner is answered that this is a brief enjoyment in the world that is not regarded, and that the failure to prosper manifests in the Hereafter. So "matā'un" (enjoyment) is the predicate of an omitted subject known from the preceding sentence, i.e., their affair is enjoyment.

Al-matā' is the small benefit in this world, since by their lies they maintain their lordship and honour among their people, then that passes away.

The root of "matā'un" indicates that it is not lasting, as mentioned in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place and enjoyment for a time﴾ [al-A'raf: 24], at the beginning of Surat al-A'raf.

Its indefiniteness indicates its diminution, and restricting it by "in this world" emphasizes both its passing and its smallness. The "thumma" in His statement ﴿then to Us is their return﴾ is for graduated sequence (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because its content is the certainty that they will not prosper, so it is more important in rank than the content of "they will not prosper."

Al-marji' (the return) is a mimi verbal noun meaning the return. The meaning of returning to Allah is returning to the time when His direct judgment takes effect upon them.

The fronting of ﴿ilayna﴾ over its complement, which is "al-marji'", is for emphasis, to draw attention to the reminder of it and to make it present in the mind, like His statement: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain﴾ [al-Nur: 39], up to His statement: ﴿and found Allah with him, and He paid him in full his account﴾ [al-Nur: 39]. It is also permissible that "al-marji'" be a metaphor for death.

The clause ﴿then We will make them taste the severe punishment﴾ explains the clause "then to Us is their return." The "thumma" in this place emphasizes its counterpart in the explained clause, indicating that by "al-marji'" is meant arrival at the execution of Allah's judgment.

The four clauses are all part of what was said, which the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to convey from Allah, exalted is He.

Idhaqat al-'adhab (making punishment taste) is making it reach the sensation, and it is called "tasting" as a comparison with the sense of taste in its penetration of the most sensitive organ of touch in the body, which is the tongue.

The "ba'" in ﴿bima kanu yakfurun﴾ is causal.

His statement ﴿kanu yakfurun﴾ indicates the repetition and renewal of that from them, in various kinds of disbelief.
