Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 71 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And recite to them the news of Noah, when he said to his people: "O my people, if my standing (among you) and my reminding you of the signs of Allah has become burdensome to you, then in Allah I have placed my trust. So resolve upon your affair, along with your partners, then let not your affair be obscure to you; then carry out your decision against me and give me no respite."﴾

This is a transition from disputing with the polytheists, with clear proofs of the falsehood of their religion and with evident evidences refuting their lies and their denial, and what was interspersed within that of admonition and warning of the swift and deferred punishment and intimidation, to alluding to them through mention of what befell the nations whose circumstances resemble theirs, in order to exhaust the methods of argument against the people of obstinacy. For Noah (peace be upon him) with his people is a parallel to the situation of Muhammad (ﷺ) with the polytheists of his people at the beginning of the matter and its development. So in mentioning the outcome of the people of Noah (peace be upon him) there is an allusion to the polytheists that their outcome will be like theirs, or that they are only being given enjoyment for a little while and then will be seized with a severe seizing,
Page 235
just as the people of Noah were given enjoyment for a long time and then did not escape punishment in this world. Thus the mention of the story of Noah with his people is an admonition to the polytheists and a cause of fear and terror in their hearts. In that there is also consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) and for the Muslims, that they are a model (uswah) like the prophets and the righteous of their peoples. Likewise the story of Moses (peace be upon him) follows it, as his saying at the end of these stories indicates: "﴿Will you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ [Yunus: 99]" and so on. And his saying: "﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, then ask those who read the Book before you﴾ [Yunus: 94]" and so on.

With this, the appropriateness of the placement of "idh" (when) in His saying "﴿when he said to his people, O my people﴾" to its end becomes clear. For restricting the news to the time of his saying "to his people" is a hint that his dialogue with his people and their persistence in turning away is the place of lesson, because it is the point of resemblance between the polytheists and the people of Noah (peace be upon him) in deafening their ears to the call of their messenger. And his saying that to them came only after he had repeated his call to them for a long time, so that was the last argument between him and them. The Prophet (ﷺ) had called the people of Mecca for years at the time of the revelation of this surah, then he debated and argued with them. And because that period was the greatest position Noah (peace be upon him) took with his people, and it was the decisive stance after which the punishment by drowning followed.

"Idh" is a noun denoting past time, and here it is a badal al-ishtimal (inclusive substitute) from "naba'" or from "Noah." In the mention of the story of Noah (peace be upon him) and what follows it there is a detailing of what was previously stated in summary in His saying, may He be exalted: "﴿And We destroyed the generations before you when they did wrong, and their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾ [Yunus: 13]."

The pronoun in "ʿalayhim" refers to "﴿those who fabricate lies against Allah﴾ [Yunus: 60]."

Tilawa (recitation) is reading. It has preceded in Surat al-Anfal.

Naba' is news. It has preceded in His saying: "﴿And there has certainly come to you from the news of the messengers﴾ [al-An'am: 34]" in Surat al-An'am.
Page 236

The introduction of Noah (peace be upon him) and his history has passed at the beginning of Al 'Imran.

The definiteness of the people of Noah by way of idafa (construct) to Noah's pronoun in His saying "﴿when he said to his people﴾" — since there is no other way to define them, as that nation had no name by which it was known; for they were one nation on the earth, so there was no call to name them by the name of an ancestor or a land, since there was nothing that would call for distinguishing them, as there was no other people. Do you not see Allah's narration about Hud in his saying to his people: "﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah﴾ [al-A'raf: 69], and when He related about Salih when he said to his people: "﴿And remember when He made you successors after 'Ad﴾ [al-A'raf: 74]."

The adverbial phrase "idh" and what is attached to it is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) relating to "naba'" of Noah.

The opening of Noah's address to his people with "O my people" is a notice of the importance of what he will convey to them; for the call (nida') is a request for attention. Since here it is not for the purpose of requesting their attention to him, because he did not begin his address to them except in their assembly, it is determined that the call is used figuratively to mean requesting a figurative attention, which is directing their minds to understanding what he is about to say.

The choice of expressing them by the description of being his people is an endearment to them in his own self, so that they take his speech as the speech of a counselor seeking good for them; for a person does not want for his people except good. The ya' of the speaker is omitted from the vocative noun attached to it, according to the well-known usage in addressing a noun attached to the ya' of the speaker.

The meaning of "﴿if my standing has become burdensome to you﴾" is that it was hard for you and distressed you.

Kibar (greatness) is the abundance of the bulk of a body in comparison with its similar bodies of its kind. Kibar is figuratively used for a quality of essences or meanings being stronger in it than in its counterparts of its kind. It may be praise, as in His saying, may He be exalted: "﴿And indeed it is heavy except for the humble﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45]," and it may be blame, as in His saying: "﴿Great is the word that comes out of their mouths﴾ [al-Kahf: 5]." Kibar is also figuratively used for hardship and distress, as in His saying, may He be exalted: "﴿Hard upon the polytheists is that to which you call them﴾ [al-Shura: 13]" and His saying: "﴿And if their aversion is burdensome to you﴾ [al-An'am: 35]," and likewise here.
Page 237

Maqam is a mimi verbal noun synonymous with qiyam (standing). It is used here in the meaning of a person's affair and condition, as in His saying: "﴿And for one who fears the standing of his Lord, there are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46]" and His saying: "﴿Those who disbelieved said to those who believed: which of the two groups is better in station (maqaman)﴾ [Maryam: 73]," meaning better in condition and affair. This usage is of the type of kinayah (metonymy), because a person's place and standing are among the necessary attributes of his essence, and in them are the manifestations of his conditions.

Among his conditions with them, what was singled out for mention is his reminding them of the signs of Allah, because that is among the most important of his affairs with his people; so its mention after the general is an instance of mentioning the specific after the general. Thus the meaning of "﴿my standing and my reminding has become burdensome to you﴾" is: you have become weary of my conditions with you, especially by my reminding you of the signs of Allah.

The rejection of the truth by people like them is the habit of those who immerse themselves in corruption and are enslaved by desire; for when the call to abandon it and the urging toward rectitude comes to them, it has a bitter taste in their souls and a painful severity on their hearts, because of the struggle of the truth against their souls, a dominance over them that they cannot dismiss and that their desires do not obey them in submitting to. So they fall into confusion and an inner conflict that weighs on them, and their souls recoil from it, and it disturbs for them the purity of their following their desires.

The attribution of the reminding to his pronoun is an idafa of the verbal noun to its agent.

The "ba'" in "bi-ayat Allah" is for emphasizing the transitivity of the verbal noun to its second object, and the first object is omitted, the estimate being: my reminding you (iyyakum).

"Ayat Allah" is the second object of "tadhkir." It is said: "I reminded him of a matter he had forgotten," so its transitivity by "ba'" is for emphasizing transitivity, as in His saying, may He be exalted: "﴿And remind them of the days of Allah﴾ [Ibrahim: 5]," and the saying of Miswar ibn Ziyadah al-Harithi:

I remind (him) by the pledge concerning whoever struck me, and my pledge is that I am striving, not negligent.

For this reason they said concerning His saying, may He be exalted: "﴿and wipe over your heads﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]" that the "ba'" is for emphasizing adherence, i.e., the adherence of the act to its object.
Page 238

"Ayat Allah" means: the indications of His favor upon them, and the indications of His oneness; for when they associated others with Allah, they forgot those indications, so he would remind them of them, and that would distress and embarrass them.

The clause "﴿then upon Allah I have placed my trust﴾" is the answer to the condition "﴿if my standing has become burdensome to you﴾," on the basis that that condition implied that his rejection of them had reached their souls to a degree they could not bear, and that they were prepared to repel it. So he informed them that the possibility of their repelling it, while they are in multitude and strength and he is in few and weakness, does not divert him from continuing the call, and that even if he is alone among them, that does not weaken him, because he relies upon Allah.

For this reason the prepositional phrase was placed before its governing verb in "﴿then upon Allah I have placed my trust﴾," meaning: not upon anyone else.

Tawakkul is relying upon the one who manages one's affair. It has passed at His saying: "﴿So when you have resolved, then rely upon Allah﴾" [Al 'Imran: 159] in Surat Al 'Imran.

The "fa" in "﴿So resolve upon your affair﴾" is for sequencing upon the clause "﴿upon Allah I have placed my trust﴾," so the sequenced clause has the status of the answer to the condition, since it is sequenced upon the clause of the answer. Do you not see that, had he not intended to hasten to inform them that he is unconcerned with their opposition to him, the apparent sense of the speech would have required him to say: "if my standing has become burdensome to you, etc., then resolve upon your affair, for I have placed my trust upon Allah," as Hud said to his people: "﴿So scheme against me all together, then give me no respite﴾" [Hud: 55] "﴿Indeed I have placed my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord﴾" [Hud: 56].

Ijma' al-amr (resolving the matter) is determining to act after hesitation between doing it and its opposite. It is derived from jam' (gathering), which is the opposite of tafriq (dispersal); for the one who hesitates over what to do has scattered matters in his mind, so he deliberates and reflects, and when his opinion settles on one of them, he has gathered what was scattered. So the hamza in it is for making, i.e., he made his affair a gathered whole after it had been scattered.

They say: "they came and their affair was jami'," meaning gathered, not scattered by divergent aspects.

The amr (affair) is their matter of intending to repel him and to harm him, and their hesitation over the ways and means of that.
Page 239

"Shurakaʾakum" is in the reading of the majority in the accusative as a maf'ul ma'ahu (object of accompaniment). The waw is in the sense of "ma'a" (with), meaning: resolve upon your affair, with your partners along with you, whom you seek help from.

Ya'qub read "wa-shurakaʾukum" in the nominative, as a conjunction upon the pronoun of "fa-ajmiʿu," and the separation between the pronoun and what is conjoined to it by the object justified it. The meaning: let your partners also gather their affair.

The imperative form in His saying "fa-ajmiʿu" is used in the sense of equalizing (taswiyah), meaning: their resolve does not harm him, in that he incites them to take up complete readiness to oppose him. The mention of their partners adds to indicate that he does not fear them, because in their belief they are more severe in seizing than the people, and that is mockery of them, as in His saying, may He be exalted: "﴿Say: Call upon your partners, then scheme against me, and give me no respite﴾" [al-A'raf: 195].

The conjunction of the clause "﴿then let not your affair be obscure to you﴾" with "thumma," which indicates delay in rank, because the second clause includes an escalation in his lack of concern for what they prepare against him of harm, to the point that he confronts them like one who advises, facilitating for them the attainment of harming him, which they intend, and removing the obstacles that stand between them and their aim. He brought what outwardly is a prohibition against their affair becoming an obscurity upon them, as an exaggeration in forbidding them from hesitating in ascertaining the attainment of their aim, to the extent that their affair itself seems to be what is forbidden from becoming a confusion for them; that is, strive so that this does not happen.

Al-ghummah is a noun of the verbal noun of ghamm, which is covering. Its meaning in such a construction is the figurative covering, namely the vagueness of a state and the non-clarity of its rightness. Perhaps this construction became like a proverb, for Tarafah had said earlier:

By your life, my affair is not an obscurity upon me, neither my day nor my night is upon me perpetual.

The manifestation of the word "amr" in "﴿then let not your affair be obscure to you﴾," although it is the very same as in "﴿So resolve upon your affair﴾," is because this construction is among what has become like a proverb, which requires that its wording not be changed.
Page 240

"Thumma" in His saying "﴿then carry out (uqdu) to me﴾" is for delay in rank, for the rank of executing the opinion with what they resolve upon of harming him is stronger than planning that, and higher than the rank of unifying opinion upon it. So it is an ascent from one thing to something higher than it, and therefore "thumma," which indicates delay in rank, is used to conjoin the clauses.

"Uqdu" is an imperative from qada', which may be from qada' in the sense of completing and deciding, meaning: carry out what you see of harm to me.

Ibn ʿAshur, al-Taḥrir wa al-Tanwir, on Surah 10, verse 71 (part 2 of 2):

It is also permissible that it be from qaḍāʾ (decision, judgment) in the sense of ḥukm (ruling), which is close to the first aspect; that is, "Carry out your decision."

It is transitive with "ilā" (to) rather than "ʿalā" (against) because it has been made to imply the meaning of conveying and delivering, explicitly indicating the meaning of execution by the act. For qaḍāʾ may be by speech, which is followed by execution, deferral, or pardon, and it may be by act, so it is a judgment of execution, and it is called by the jurists "al-qaḍāʾ al-fiʿlī" (judgment by action).

His saying: "﴿And do not give me respite﴾" is an emphasis on the implication of the implied sense conveyed by the preposition "ilā." Al-inẓār means delay (al-taʾkhīr), and the yāʾ of the first person was dropped from "tunẓirūna" for lightness, and this deletion is common in eloquent speech; the retention of the nūn al-wiqāyah indicates it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 72:

﴿And if you turn away, then I have not asked you for any wage. My wage is only from Allah, and I have been commanded to be among the Muslims.﴾

The fa' (فَ) here serves to make the speech follow from the preceding speech, so the conditional clause and its response are both derived from the two previous clauses. Since their turning away from his call had already occurred and continued, it is determined that the turning away in the conditional clause is meant to refer to what had already taken place, so that the response to the condition, which is also something that has already occurred, is consequently built upon it. What was intended was to have them acknowledge it, to cut off their excuses and to exhaust their pretexts. The meaning is:

Page 241

"If you have indeed turned away, then you know that I have not asked you for any wage, so that you might accuse me of desiring a benefit that would accrue to me from your call, and thus turn away from it out of stinginess with your wealth or out of accusing me of lying." This is a binding argument against them: that their turning away did not admit the possibility of their accusation against him of seeking a benefit for himself. With this he cleared himself of being a cause of their turning away. By this it is determined that what is dependent upon this condition is the realization of the connection between the content of the conditional clause and the content of the response clause, not the occurrence of the response clause at the occurrence of the conditional clause. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إنْ كُنْتُ قُلْتُهُ فَقَدْ عَلِمْتَهُ﴾ ["If I had said it, You would have known it" – Al-Ma'idah: 116] at the end of Surat al-'Uqud. It has already been explained at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وإنْ كانَ طائِفَةٌ مِنكم آمَنُوا بِالَّذِي أُرْسِلْتُ بِهِ وطائِفَةٌ لَمْ يُؤْمِنُوا فاصْبِرُوا حَتّى يَحْكُمَ اللَّهُ بَيْنَنا﴾ ["And if there is a group among you who believed in that with which I have been sent and a group who did not believe, then be patient until Allah judges between us" – Al-A'raf: 87] in Surat al-A'raf.

The clause ﴿إنْ أجْرِيَ إلّا عَلى اللَّهِ﴾ ["My wage is only from Allah"] is a generalization of the negation of his seeking a wage for his call, whether from them or from others. The restriction is real, and through it the emphasis of the clause ﴿فَما سَألْتُكم مِن أجْرٍ﴾ ["I have not asked you for any wage"] is achieved, along with the added generality. The means by which he was certain that Allah would reward him for this is Allah's promise to him, through what was revealed to him.

He used the particle "عَلى" (upon), which indicates that it is a right due to him with Allah, based on Allah's promise to him; and He informed him that Allah does not break His promise. Thus, by the promise, it became a right upon Allah, which Allah has committed Himself to.

Al-ajr (الأجر, wage): the compensation given in return for a work done by the one who takes the compensation.

The clause ﴿وأُمِرْتُ أنْ أكُونَ مِنَ المُسْلِمِينَ﴾ ["and I have been commanded to be among the Muslims"] is conjoined to the response clause, and the implied sense is: "If you turn away, then I have been commanded to be among the Muslims," that is, Allah has commanded me to follow the true religion even if I am alone. This is a discouragement to them, that their unanimity in turning away from him does not blunt his resolve nor prevent him from opposing their misguided religion.

The verb "أُمِرْتُ" (I have been commanded) is formed in the passive in wording, because the one who commands is known, since it is evident from the context of the speech that the one who commanded him is Allah, exalted is He.

His saying: ﴿أنْ أكُونَ مِنَ المُسْلِمِينَ﴾ means: from the group to which this description applies, which is Islam, that is, the affirmation of Allah's oneness without worshipping a partner, because it is derived from submitting worship and devoting it to Allah, exalted is He, to the exclusion of others. As in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿فَقُلْ أسْلَمْتُ وجْهِيَ لِلَّهِ ومَنِ اتَّبَعَنِ﴾ ["Say, 'I have submitted myself entirely to Allah, and so have those who follow me'" – Al 'Imran: 20].

Tawhid and the pure true religion have been called Islam in various eras, and Allah named the paths of the Messengers by it. He related it from Noah, peace be upon him, here, and from Abraham with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إذْ قالَ لَهُ رَبُّهُ أسْلِمْ قالَ أسْلَمْتُ لِرَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾ ["When his Lord said to him, 'Submit,' he said, 'I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds'" – Al-Baqarah: 131], and from Isma'il: ﴿رَبَّنا واجْعَلْنا مُسْلِمَيْنِ لَكَ﴾ ["Our Lord, and make us Muslims [in submission] to You" – Al-Baqarah: 128], and from Ya'qub and his sons when He related of them: "and we are to Him Muslims," and from Yusuf: ﴿تَوَفَّنِي مُسْلِمًا﴾ ["Cause me to die as a Muslim" – Yusuf: 101], and from Musa, who said: ﴿وقالَ مُوسى يا قَوْمِ إنْ كُنْتُمْ آمَنتُمْ بِاللَّهِ فَعَلَيْهِ تَوَكَّلُوا إنْ كُنْتُمْ مُسْلِمِينَ﴾ ["And Musa said, 'O my people, if you have believed in Allah, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims'" – Yunus: 84], and from Sulayman: ﴿ألّا تَعْلُوا عَلَيَّ وأْتُونِي مُسْلِمِينَ﴾ ["Do not be haughty toward me, and come to me in submission" – An-Naml: 31], and from Jesus and the disciples: ﴿قالُوا آمَنّا واشْهَدْ بِأنَّنا مُسْلِمُونَ﴾ ["They said, 'We have believed, so bear witness that we are Muslims'" – Al-Ma'idah: 111]. The explanation of this has already been detailed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿رَبَّنا واجْعَلْنا مُسْلِمَيْنِ لَكَ﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 128] in Surat al-Baqarah.

His saying: ﴿أنْ أكُونَ مِنَ المُسْلِمِينَ﴾ is stronger in indicating attributes of Islam than "an akūna musliman" (that I be a Muslim), as has already been mentioned at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وارْكَعُوا مَعَ الرّاكِعِينَ﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 43] in Surat al-Baqarah, and at His saying: ﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وكُونُوا مَعَ الصّادِقِينَ﴾ ["O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful" – At-Tawbah: 119] in Surat "Bara'ah."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 73:**

﴿So they denied him, and We saved him and those with him in the ship, and We made them successors, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. So see how was the end of those who were warned.﴾

The fa' (فاء) here is *al-tafri' al-dhikri* (the "fa'" of resumptive mention), meaning that the mention of these preceding sentences is being followed up. The norm is that what comes after the fa' has a connection to what precedes it, which calls for it to be mentioned next; so the fa' is used to indicate that connection, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Enter the gates of Hell, abiding therein; and wretched is the abode of the arrogant﴾ [al-Zumar: 72]. Otherwise, the denial of Noah's people occurred before he said to them ﴿If my standing [among you] and my reminding you of the signs of Allah is burdensome to you﴾ [Yunus: 71], etc., because he did not say that to them except after he had seen from them a frowning at his call.

You may also take the meaning of the verb *kadhdhabuhu* (they denied him) to be continuance in denying him, like the verb *amanu* (they believed) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 136]. Then the fa' indicates that what follows occurred after what precedes it.

As for the fa' in the clause *fa-najjaynahu* (so We saved him), it indicates sequence and immediacy, because the denial of his people continued until the time of their drowning and the saving of Noah, peace be upon him, and those who followed him. This is a wonderful arrangement and an inimitable concision, as the discourse returns to explicitly stating the denial of his people, which was not mentioned before but was only alluded to implicitly in His saying: ﴿When he said to his people: "O my people, if my standing [among you] is burdensome to you..."﴾ [Yunus: 71] and so on, making it like the return of the last part to the first (*radd al-ajuz 'ala al-sadr*). Then its continuance through all times was alluded to until it ended with their drowning; so He mentioned the saving of Noah and the drowning of those who denied him. Thereby the discourse returns to what followed Noah's final dispute with his people, which ended with His saying: ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾ [Yunus: 72]. Thus it was a wonderful variation in the arrangement together with a delightful concision.

The mention of his being saved was placed before the mention of the drowning, from which the saving occurred, to indicate that his being saved is more important to Allah, exalted is He, than the drowning of his deniers, and to hasten joy for the Muslims who hear this story.

*Al-fulk* (الفُلْك): the ship. It was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the ship that runs in the sea﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164], in Surat al-Baqarah.

*Al-khala'if* (الخَلائِف): the plural of *khalifah* (خَلِيفَة), which is a noun for one who succeeds another. It was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a successive authority﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], in Surat al-Baqarah. The plural form here is in view of those who were with him in the ship, from each pair of whom a community (*umma*) descended.

The definition of Noah's people by way of the relative clause (*al-mawsuliyya*) in His saying: ﴿and We drowned those who denied Our signs﴾ indicates the cause of their punishment by drowning, namely that it was denial of the signs of Allah, as a warning to the polytheists among the Arabs. Therefore it is followed by His saying: ﴿So see how was the end of those who were warned﴾, i.e., those warned of the punishment who denied the warning.

*Al-nazar* (النَّظَر) here is the seeing of the eye; their news has been treated, because of its clarity and the certainty regarding it, as if it were witnessed.

The address with *unzur* (انْظُرْ) may be to everyone who hears, so no specific addressee is intended; or it may be an address to Muhammad ﷺ, singled out with the address to magnify his status, namely that those who denied him are about to be struck by a punishment similar to what befell the people of Noah, peace be upon him. In this there is consolation for him regarding the harm he encounters from them, and a display of Allah's care for him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 74:

﴿Then after him We sent messengers to their peoples, and they came to them with clear proofs, but they were not going to believe in what they had denied before. Thus do We seal the hearts of the transgressors.﴾

"Thumma" (then) here indicates gradation in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi, i.e., a sequence of increasing rank and remoteness), because the sending of many messengers to many nations, whom their peoples received in the same manner in which Noah's people received him, is more remarkable as a matter than the case of Noah's people, since those nations agreed upon one single path of disbelief. "Thumma" here is not for expressing temporal delay, which is dispensed with by his saying: "min ba'dihim" (after them).

The messengers are left unspecified in this verse. It is stated in other verses that they were Hud and Salih, Abraham, Lot and Shu'ayb. There may be other messengers, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and messengers We have not related to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 164]. The intended meaning here must be those who came before Moses, due to His saying: ﴿Then after them We sent Moses﴾ [Yunus: 75].

The verse contains an indication that Noah was the first of the messengers. "Al-bayyinat" (the clear proofs) are the evident arguments indicating truthfulness. The "fa" (so) in "faja'uhum" denotes sequence, meaning they showed them the miracles immediately after sending them. The "ba" in "bil-bayyinat" denotes accompaniment, meaning they came to their peoples, conveying the message, accompanied by the clear proofs.

Page 245

The plural of "messengers" has been paired with the plural of "clear proofs," so it is true of many clear proofs distributed among many messengers; each prophet may have many signs, and some prophets may have a single sign, such as the sign of Salih, which was the she-camel.

The "fa" in His saying: ﴿fa-ma kanu li-yu'minu﴾ is for consequence, meaning that as a result of that, they did not believe.

The negation is expressed with the form of the emphatic negative lam (lam al-juhud), intensifying the absence of faith from them in the strongest degree of negation, as if they had not come into existence to believe in what they had denied. That is, they did not budge from it. The form of the emphatic negation indicates that the messengers attempted to bring them to faith repeatedly.

His saying: ﴿bima kadhdhabu bihi min qablu﴾ indicates that there was a denial which they hastened to direct at their messengers, and that they did not desist from their denial with which they confronted the messengers. This is because denial occurs only in response to a report from a reporter. So His saying: ﴿faja'uhum bil-bayyinat﴾ implies that denial had occurred; when they denied them, they came to them with the clear proofs of their truthfulness, but they persisted in denial, so they were not going to believe in what they had denied before. This is an instance of concise omission of many sentences. This requires repeated calls and repeated proofs; otherwise, His saying: ﴿fa-ma kanu li-yu'minu bima kadhdhabu bihi min qablu﴾ would have no impact, since the denial that occurred the first time, if it was not followed by what would normally cause its cessation, would be a single, forgotten denial.

This is from the eloquence of the meanings of the Qur'an.

By this, the impact of His saying after it becomes clear: ﴿Thus do We seal the hearts of the transgressors﴾, for sealing indicates that upon their hearts had come what, if their hearts were free of sealing at its arrival, would normally have led them to faith; but the sealing upon their hearts prevented the clear proofs from affecting their hearts.

The sealing that befell these people has been made an example of the manners of sealing upon the hearts of the transgressors. So His saying: ﴿Thus do We seal the hearts of the transgressors﴾ means: like this wondrous sealing, We seal the hearts of the transgressors, so reflect upon it and take lesson from it.

Page 246

"Al-tab'" (sealing) is stamping. It is a metaphor for faith not entering their hearts. It was previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿God has sealed upon their hearts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7] in Surat al-Baqarah.

"I'tida'" (transgression) is an iftial form from "ada 'alayhi," meaning he wronged him. So "al-mu'tadin" is synonymous with "al-zalimin" (the wrongdoers), and what is meant by it is the polytheists, because polytheism is transgression, for they denied the messengers and thus transgressed against the truthful by accusing them of lying. A parallel to this verse in Surat al-A'raf has: ﴿Thus does God seal upon the hearts of the disbelievers﴾ [al-A'raf: 101]; this variation is for the sake of diversifying the expression of this lesson in the two places.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 75:

﴿Then after them We sent Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh and his chieftains with Our signs, but they were arrogant, and they were a guilty people.﴾

Thumma (ثُمَّ) is for the sequence of rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because the mission of Moses and Aaron - peace be upon them both - was greater than the missions of those prophets who came before them. The mission of Moses and Aaron is singled out for mention because it was a great transformation and a new development in the history of the divine laws (shara'i') and in the order of intellectual and legislative civilization. The messengers who came before Moses were sent to independent peoples, and their religions were limited to calling to the reform of belief, the refinement of souls, and the abolition of grave corruptions in dealings. They were not comprehensive laws covering everything the nation needs in terms of its social order and the arrangement of its present and future.

As for the mission of Moses, it brought about the formation of a nation and its liberation from the enslavement of another nation over it, the establishment of an independent homeland for it, the laying of the foundations of its independence, the founding of a complete community (jami'ah) for it, the establishment of a system of government for the nation, a policy by which its affairs are managed, and a system of defence that repels aggressors among the nations and enables it to enter the lands of other nations, and the giving of a Book that contains the laws of its social life in many of its aspects. Thus the mission of Moses was the first general manifestation of the divine laws, for which no parallel had preceded it in the history of the divine laws or in the history of the order of nations.

And it, despite its superiority over all the laws that preceded it, was distinguished by being an instruction from God, who is aware of the realities of affairs, and who wills the establishment of the good and the removal of the corrupt.

Moses and Aaron were both sent, insofar as God answered Moses' request that He make his brother Aaron with him as a supporter and one who expresses his intentions. Thus he was, by this, commanded by God to participate in the works of the messengership, as Surat al-Qasas has explained. So the one sent in essence is Moses, while Aaron was sent as his helper and supporter, because that mission was the first mission to be accompanied by the formation of a nation.

Pharaoh (Fir'awn) is the king of Egypt. The discussion about him has already passed at the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿Then after them We sent Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh and his chieftains﴾ in Surat al-A'raf, and on the manner of the sending of Moses to Pharaoh and his chieftains. This Pharaoh is Merneptah II (Minifatah al-Thani), one of the pharaohs of the nineteenth dynasty, which ruled the land of the Copts.

The chieftains (al-mala') means the notables of the people and their leaders, because Moses was sent to the Children of Israel and was sent to Pharaoh and the people of his realm, so that they would release the Children of Israel.

The sin and the ta in "istakbarū" (اسْتَكْبَرُوا) are for intensification in pride, and the meaning is that they were arrogant toward receiving the call from Moses, because they despised him and deemed it impossible that he be a messenger from God, while he was from a people enslaved whom Pharaoh and his people had enslaved. This is the reason for choosing the expression of their turning away from his call by arrogance, as God related of them when they said: ﴿Shall we believe two humans like us, when their people are servants to us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 47].

The linking of "istakbarū" to the clause "We sent" indicates that every turning away and denial from them during the period of the call and the mission is arrogance.

The clause ﴿and they were a guilty people﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: while guilt had become their habit and their character, so their arrogance toward Moses was part of their guilt.

Ijram (الإجْرامُ) is the act of crime (al-jurm), which is a offence and a great sin. It has already been discussed at the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿And thus do We recompense the guilty﴾ [al-A'raf: 40] in Surat al-A'raf.

The Pharaohs were tyrants and oppressors; they regarded themselves as gods to the Copts, they had laid down laws that were not free of injustice, and they enslaved the strangers. They enslaved the Children of Israel and humiliated them for centuries; when they asked for their rights, they uprooted them, mutilated them, and killed them, as God related of them: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and made its people into factions, oppressing a group among them, slaughtering their sons and keeping their women alive. Indeed, he was among the corrupters﴾ [al-Qasas: 4]. The Copts believed in misguided illusions and superstitions. Therefore God, the Exalted, said: ﴿they were a guilty people﴾, meaning that their arrogance toward the truth and right guidance is not to be wondered at. Do you not see their saying about Moses and Aaron: ﴿These two are indeed sorcerers who want to drive you out of your land with their sorcery and to abolish your most excellent way﴾ [Ta-Ha: 63]? Delusion overcame them so that they named their error and their weakness "the most excellent way".

He expressed it as "qawman mujrimin" rather than "kanu mujrimin" for the reason that has been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah and in several places of this surah.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 10, verses 76–77:

﴿So when the Truth came to them from Us, they said, "Indeed, this is evident magic."﴾ ﴿Musa said, "Do you say this of the Truth when it has come to you? Is this magic? But magicians do not succeed."﴾

That is: when they saw the miracles, which are a firmly established truth and not illusions and deceptions, and they knew that Musa was truthful in what he claimed, they progressed from mere refusal rooted in arrogance to slander rooted in the sense of being defeated.

Al-haqq (the truth): it is used as a noun for that which is the opposite of falsehood, namely the just and right, and it is used as an adjective for what is firmly established with no doubt about it, as one says: "You are the truly sincere friend" (al-siddiq al-haqq). It is always in the singular because it is a verbal noun (masdar) described by it. The thing to which arrival is attributed here is the signs which Musa displayed as a miracle to them, based on His saying before it: ﴿Then after them We sent Musa with Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 103]. So making the Truth come with those signs is suitable for both meanings of al-haqq; because those signs, being firmly established with no doubt about them, were in themselves truth, so their coming is their occurrence and manifestation, and the purpose of it is to establish the truthfulness of Musa in his mission, so the Truth came with them. Its coming is its establishment, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And say, "The truth has come and falsehood has vanished"﴾ [al-Isra': 81]. By this it becomes clear that the word al-haqq here has a precision in indicating the complete intended meaning, and the phrase "from Us" has a conciseness that no other word has, and this is among the limits of inimitability (i'jaz).

By this it is clear that the verse indicates that the signs of truthfulness appeared, and that those who were refuted were certain of the truthfulness of Musa and that he had come with the Truth.

Their excuse for the appearance of the signs, by calling them magic, is the excuse of the defeated who has no proof, whom proof has overpowered and whom the authority of the Truth has dazzled, so he has no grip left on acceptable opposition, and so he hastens to adopt objections with excuses that do not stand up to scrutiny and do not hold under the test of criticism.

For the defeated there must be some cold excuse (bārid al-'udhr).

And since it is well known among the common people with delusions that magic shows a thing in the form of its opposite, they claimed that what appeared of the proofs of Musa's truthfulness is magic, by which falsehood appeared in the form of truth through the imagining of magic.

The meaning of claiming the Truth to be magic is that its proofs belong to the category of imaginings and deceptions, so its signified content is the content of magic, which is the production of false imagining in the souls of the bewitched. Their sense of the weakness of their excuse led them to present their claim in the form of an assertion whose speaker is firm, so they emphasized the statement with the particle of emphasis inna and the lam of initiation: "Indeed, this is magic." They added to this promotion by describing the magic as "evident" (mubin), that is, extremely clear. Mubin is an active participle of abana (intransitive), synonymous with bana: "became manifest."

The reference in His saying "Indeed, this" is to what was witnessed among them when the miracle was displayed, such as the staff turning into a serpent and the hand emerging white; that is, "this action you are witnessing is evident magic."

The clause "Musa said" is a reply from him to their statement, so it is disjoined from the conjunction according to the method we derived in narrating statements, as previously mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will place upon the earth a successive authority." They said, "Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], and its many parallels. Musa alone, without Harun, took up the debate with them, because he was the one primarily charged with the call, and because the miracles appeared at his hands.

The interrogative in "Do you say" is one of denunciation (istifham inkari).

The lam in "for the Truth" is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil). Some call it the lam of explanation (lam al-bayan), and some call it the lam of transgression in the sense of 'an (lam al-mujawazah bi-ma'na 'an).

The clause "Is this magic?" is a resumptive clause (mustanafah) for rebuke and denunciation: Musa denounced their describing the true signs as magic. The demonstrative indicates a rebuke of their ignorance and the corruption of their statement, that pointing to those signs is sufficient to show their reality and that they have nothing to do with magic. For this reason the object of "Do you say" is omitted, the context indicating it, namely ﴿Indeed, this is evident magic﴾. The estimated sense is: "Do you say this statement about the Truth when it has come to you?" A close parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "There have certainly come to you messengers before me with clear proofs and with what you have said"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 183], and His saying: ﴿A group of them spent the night devising other than what you say﴾ [al-Nisa': 81].

When Musa negated, regarding the signs of Allah, that they were magic, he went further and explained to them the corruption of magic and the evil end of its practitioners, belittling them, because they used to exalt the affair of magic. So the clause ﴿But magicians do not succeed﴾ is conjoined to the clause "Is this magic?"

The meaning is: this is not magic; rather, I know that the magician does not succeed. That is, if it were magic, he would not have disparaged the state of magicians, since a practitioner of a craft does not belittle his craft, for if he saw it as belittled he would not have committed himself to it.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 10, verses 76–77:

﴿So when the Truth came to them from Us, they said, "Indeed, this is evident magic."﴾ ﴿Musa said, "Do you say this of the Truth when it has come to you? Is this magic? But magicians do not succeed."﴾

That is: when they saw the miracles, which are a firmly established truth and not illusions and deceptions, and they knew that Musa was truthful in what he claimed, they progressed from mere refusal rooted in arrogance to slander rooted in the sense of being defeated.

Al-haqq (the truth): it is used as a noun for that which is the opposite of falsehood, namely the just and right, and it is used as an adjective for what is firmly established with no doubt about it, as one says: "You are the truly sincere friend" (al-siddiq al-haqq). It is always in the singular because it is a verbal noun (masdar) described by it. The thing to which arrival is attributed here is the signs which Musa displayed as a miracle to them, based on His saying before it: ﴿Then after them We sent Musa with Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 103]. So making the Truth come with those signs is suitable for both meanings of al-haqq; because those signs, being firmly established with no doubt about them, were in themselves truth, so their coming is their occurrence and manifestation, and the purpose of it is to establish the truthfulness of Musa in his mission, so the Truth came with them. Its coming is its establishment, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And say, "The truth has come and falsehood has vanished"﴾ [al-Isra': 81]. By this it becomes clear that the word al-haqq here has a precision in indicating the complete intended meaning, and the phrase "from Us" has a conciseness that no other word has, and this is among the limits of inimitability (i'jaz).

By this it is clear that the verse indicates that the signs of truthfulness appeared, and that those who were refuted were certain of the truthfulness of Musa and that he had come with the Truth.

Their excuse for the appearance of the signs, by calling them magic, is the excuse of the defeated who has no proof, whom proof has overpowered and whom the authority of the Truth has dazzled, so he has no grip left on acceptable opposition, and so he hastens to adopt objections with excuses that do not stand up to scrutiny and do not hold under the test of criticism.

For the defeated there must be some cold excuse (bārid al-'udhr).

And since it is well known among the common people with delusions that magic shows a thing in the form of its opposite, they claimed that what appeared of the proofs of Musa's truthfulness is magic, by which falsehood appeared in the form of truth through the imagining of magic.

The meaning of claiming the Truth to be magic is that its proofs belong to the category of imaginings and deceptions, so its signified content is the content of magic, which is the production of false imagining in the souls of the bewitched. Their sense of the weakness of their excuse led them to present their claim in the form of an assertion whose speaker is firm, so they emphasized the statement with the particle of emphasis inna and the lam of initiation: "Indeed, this is magic." They added to this promotion by describing the magic as "evident" (mubin), that is, extremely clear. Mubin is an active participle of abana (intransitive), synonymous with bana: "became manifest."

The reference in His saying "Indeed, this" is to what was witnessed among them when the miracle was displayed, such as the staff turning into a serpent and the hand emerging white; that is, "this action you are witnessing is evident magic."

The clause "Musa said" is a reply from him to their statement, so it is disjoined from the conjunction according to the method we derived in narrating statements, as previously mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will place upon the earth a successive authority." They said, "Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], and its many parallels. Musa alone, without Harun, took up the debate with them, because he was the one primarily charged with the call, and because the miracles appeared at his hands.

The interrogative in "Do you say" is one of denunciation (istifham inkari).

The lam in "for the Truth" is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil). Some call it the lam of explanation (lam al-bayan), and some call it the lam of transgression in the sense of 'an (lam al-mujawazah bi-ma'na 'an).

The clause "Is this magic?" is a resumptive clause (mustanafah) for rebuke and denunciation: Musa denounced their describing the true signs as magic. The demonstrative indicates a rebuke of their ignorance and the corruption of their statement, that pointing to those signs is sufficient to show their reality and that they have nothing to do with magic. For this reason the object of "Do you say" is omitted, the context indicating it, namely ﴿Indeed, this is evident magic﴾. The estimated sense is: "Do you say this statement about the Truth when it has come to you?" A close parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "There have certainly come to you messengers before me with clear proofs and with what you have said"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 183], and His saying: ﴿A group of them spent the night devising other than what you say﴾ [al-Nisa': 81].

When Musa negated, regarding the signs of Allah, that they were magic, he went further and explained to them the corruption of magic and the evil end of its practitioners, belittling them, because they used to exalt the affair of magic. So the clause ﴿But magicians do not succeed﴾ is conjoined to the clause "Is this magic?"

The meaning is: this is not magic; rather, I know that the magician does not succeed. That is, if it were magic, he would not have disparaged the state of magicians, since a practitioner of a craft does not belittle his craft, for if he saw it as belittled he would not have committed himself to it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 78:

Page 251
﴿They said: "Have you come to us to turn us away from that upon which we found our fathers, and so that greatness in the land may belong to you two? We will not believe you two."﴾

The discussion of the clause "قالوا أجئتنا" (They said: "Have you come to us") is similar to the discussion of the clause "قال موسى أتقولون" (Moses said: "Do you say..."). The interrogative in "أجئتنا" expresses their denial, directed at Moses' error regarding what he brought, and at their bad opinion of him and of Harun concerning the aim that the two of them were seeking through what Moses brought. They addressed Moses directly because he was the one who undertook the call and displayed the miracle; then they associated his brother Harun with him in their bad opinion of both of them regarding the purpose of their work.

"وتلفتنا" is the present form (muda'ari') of "لفت" from the pattern "ضرب", used transitively: it means to turn someone's face away from looking at something facing his face. The intransitive form of it is only for the reflexive sense; one says "التفت" (he turned). Here it is used metaphorically for diverting from an action or a belief to something else, a diversion after which no looking back at what one used to look at remains. Its origin is an allegorical (tamthiliyyah) metaphor, which then became so common that it became equal to the literal meaning.

The relative clause "ما وجدنا عليه آباءنا" (that upon which we found our fathers) comprises all the conditions in which their fathers were engaged.

The expression "وجدنا" (we found) was chosen because it indicates that they grew up upon these things and understood them, which gives them an attachment to them; and that these were the states of their fathers, which increases their attachment to them, following the love of their fathers, because love of a thing requires love of its conditions and circumstances.

In this there is an indication that these things are, in their view, correct and true, because they had followed their fathers, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And thus We did not send before you a warner into a city but its affluent ones said: "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps."﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 23]. And He said about the people of Ibrahim, peace be upon him: ﴿They said: "We found our fathers worshipping them."﴾ [al-Anbiya': 53] ﴿He said: "You and your fathers have certainly been in manifest error."﴾ [al-Anbiya': 54]. Moses had come to them with the aim of turning them away from what their fathers had been upon, so that was the object of their denial, because they reckoned changing that to be corruption: ﴿And the chiefs of Pharaoh's people said: "Will you leave Moses and his people to cause corruption in the land?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 127].

The use of the particle "على" (upon) indicates the firm establishment of their fathers in those states and their constant attachment to them.

The conjunction of ﴿وتكون لكما الكبرياء﴾ (and that greatness may belong to you two) is upon the verb that is given as the cause, and the conjoined clause is the cause in meaning, because they meant that they had perceived the purpose of Moses and Harun in their coming to them with what they brought, i.e., that the two of them are seeking a benefit for themselves, not the welfare of those being called; and that benefit is seizing the sovereignty of Egypt by stratagem.

"الكبرياء" (greatness): magnificence and the display of superiority over people.

"الأرض" (the land): it is the one known among them, namely the land of Egypt, as in His saying: ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land﴾ [al-A'raf: 110]. Since they had thought that the two were seeking sovereignty, they used in addressing Moses the dual pronoun of the second person, because Harun was present; so they turned from addressing one person to addressing two.

They associated Harun in this suspicion only inasmuch as he came with Moses but did not undertake the call himself; so they thought he had come with him in order to obtain a share of his brother's sovereignty for himself.

The clause ﴿وما نحن لكما بمؤمنين﴾ (We will not believe you two) is conjoined to the clause "أجئتنا". It is in effect the result of that clause together with the cause it carries, i.e., since your intention has become clear, we will not believe you two.

The placing of "لكما" before its complement is because the two addressees are the more important element of the negative clause, since the negation of their belief was on account of Moses and Harun, for they imagined that the two of them were seeking benefit for themselves.

Thus the intended referent of the dual pronoun is the two persons themselves, in view of what they harbored of intent to nullify the religion of the fathers of the Copts and to seize the sovereignty of their land.

The clause ﴿وما نحن لكما بمؤمنين﴾ was phrased as a nominal sentence rather than "وما نؤمن لكما", to convey permanence and constancy, and that their disbelief in the two is firmly established and fixed, with no hope for anyone of its opposite.

[Page 253]

The clause ﴿And Pharaoh said﴾ is coordinated ('atf, coordination) with the clause ﴿They said, "Indeed, this is clear magic"﴾ [Yunus: 76]. This clause therefore stands in the position of a second answer to the conditional particle *lamma* (when). First, it reports how Pharaoh and his chiefs (malaʾ) received Moses' call and his miracle, namely by denying that what he brought could be a confirmation from Allah. Then it reports, secondly, how Pharaoh in particular received that call, namely by trying to support their claim ﴿Indeed, this is clear magic﴾ [Yunus: 76], so as to show that they were able to produce its like. The means to that (its causes and preparations) were among the special privileges of Pharaoh. This also contains a command to the elite of the nation to prepare to nullify what was feared from it.

The addressees of his words ﴿Bring me﴾ are the chiefs of Pharaoh and his inner circle, those who held the execution of his command in their hands.

He ordered the bringing of all the magicians who were established in the knowledge of magic, because they were the most perceptive of its subtleties and the most capable of displaying what would surpass, in his supposition, the extraordinary acts of Moses. Their presence therefore made the presence of weaker practitioners of magic unnecessary, since their work was likely not to match what Moses had shown. If they produced something inferior to the miracle of Moses, that would promote the call of Moses among the common people of the nation.

The generality in his words ﴿every magician who is learned﴾ is customary generality (ʿumum ʿurfi), meaning: every magician whom you know and can reach. Or it may mean that "every" is intended to express abundance, as was mentioned earlier in his words ﴿Even if you brought to those who were given the Book every sign﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿So when the magicians came﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿And Pharaoh said﴾. It links the arrival of the magicians and Moses' words to them to the clause "Pharaoh said" by the *fa'* of sequence (fa' al-taʿqib), to indicate immediacy in their being brought. This sequence is in accordance with the customary haste in carrying out a commanded matter.

[Page 254]

The implied object of the coordination is omitted, because what naturally follows his words ﴿Bring me every magician﴾ is their being brought. But since that adds little to the purpose for which the story is told, it is omitted, relying on what is required and indicated by it, both by rational and verbal indication, from his words ﴿the magicians came﴾, by way of conciseness (ijaz). The estimated sense is: "So they brought them to him. And when they came, Moses said to them."

The definiteness in ﴿the magicians﴾ is definiteness of prior mention (ʿahd dhikri).

Moses commanded them to begin by throwing their magic, in order to display the strength of his proof. The one who begins a contest in an activity is normally in a better position to excel in it over his rival, especially in activities whose essence is deception and intimidation, and in which the one seeking victory aims at being first to impress and move the onlookers. The Qur'an mentions in other verses that the magicians gave Moses the choice between his beginning by displaying his miracle and their beginning, and that Moses chose that they be the ones to begin.

The imperative verb in his words ﴿Throw what you are going to throw﴾ is used for equalization (taswiya), whose purpose is choice and to show indifference to either of the two options.

*Al-ilqa'* (throwing) is casting something from the hand to the ground. The term *ilqa'* is applied to the act of magic because most of the magicians' manipulations in their magical works consist of throwing things to the ground. It is reported in many verses that they threw their ropes and staffs, and that by their magic it was imagined that these were moving. The ultimate aim of the magician's work was to make inanimate things seem alive.

The phrase ﴿what you are going to throw﴾ is intended as a substitutive generalization (taʿmim badali), meaning: whatever you throw. This adds to the display of indifference to the extent of their magic, and prepares the assembled chiefs to know that Allah would nullify their magic through His messenger.

It is not problematic that Moses commanded them to cast magic, as though he commanded an act of disobedience. The people were unbelievers, and an unbeliever is not addressed by the divine laws. Also, the purpose of commanding them to throw it was to show its falsity. That is like presenting the doubt of a heretic in order to refute it after stating it, as in the method of ʿAḍud al-Din al-Iji in his book *al-Mawaqif*.

[Page 255]

The description of the form of their magic has been omitted in this verse, because the purpose of the lesson in this verse is to describe the persistence of Pharaoh and his chiefs in turning away from the call, what the oppressed believers who followed Moses (peace be upon him) suffered from Pharaoh's domination over them, and how Allah gave victory to His messenger and to the oppressed along with him, and how the good end was theirs, while the unbelievers had the evil end. This serves as an example for those who deny Muhammad (ﷺ). For this reason, it did not dwell on anything except the statement of Moses (peace be upon him) when he saw their magic, which indicates his certainty about his Lord and His promise, and that the final outcome belongs to the truth. That is more important in this context than mentioning the collapse of their magic before the miracle of Moses (peace be upon him). For this reason, the object of *alqaw* (they threw) was not mentioned, by treating the verb *alqu* (throw) as intransitive, since the purpose does not depend on stating its object.

The meaning of ﴿what you have brought﴾ is "what you have displayed to us." The verb *ji'tum* (you brought) is used metaphorically for displaying, because the one who brings something displays it in the place where he came. The connection is customary. It does not mean that they came from other regions accompanied by magic. Although many or all of the magicians had come from numerous cities, that supposition does not hold in every case where expressions like "he brought such-and-such" are used. For it holds in a verse like ﴿And they came upon his shirt with false blood﴾ [Yusuf: 18], but does not hold in a verse like ﴿Indeed, those who came with the falsehood﴾ [al-Nur: 11].

The composition of the speech in this style, by making *ma ji'tum* the subject rather than making it the object of the verb *sayubtiluhu* (He will nullify it), and by making it a vague noun, then explaining it by the clause *ji'tum bihi*, then clarifying it by an appositive (ʿatf al-bayan) for the purpose of emphasizing its mention and creating anticipation for knowing the predicate, which is the clause ﴿Indeed Allah will nullify it﴾, and then the pronoun of magic appearing as the object of *sayubtiluhu*: all of this is elaboration (itnab) and deviation from what the apparent situation requires, in order to establish the report of a reality about magic for him, to settle it firmly in the minds of the listeners, and to cast terror into their souls.

[Page 256]

His words ﴿the magic﴾: the majority of readers read it with a hamzat wasl at its beginning, which is the hamza of *al*, so *ma* in ﴿what you have brought﴾ is a relative pronoun, and *al-sihr* is an appositive to the relative pronoun. Abu ʿAmr and Abu Jaʿfar read *ālsiḥra* with a hamzat al-istifham (interrogative hamza) at its beginning and with lengthening to ease the second hamza (tashil), so *ma* in ﴿what you have brought﴾ is interrogative, and *ālsiḥra* is an interrogative clarifying the interrogative *ma*. It is used for belittlement (tahqir). The meaning is: it is a trivial matter that many people can accomplish.

The clause ﴿Indeed Allah will nullify it﴾ is the predicate of the relative *ma* according to the reading of the majority, and a resumptive explanatory clause (istinaf bayani) according to the reading of Abu ʿAmr and those who agree with him. The emphasis of the predicate by *inna* is an increase in instilling fear into their souls.

*Ibtal* (nullification) of it means showing that it is imagination and not reality, because showing that is a nullification of what was intended by it. That is, Allah will nullify its effect on people by exposing its secret. The sign of the future tense indicates the nearness of its nullification. This knowledge was granted to Moses (peace be upon him) either through a specific revelation in that matter, or through a general one by its falling under a universal rule, which is the meaning of ﴿Indeed Allah does not allow the work of corrupters to prosper﴾.

The clause ﴿Indeed Allah does not allow the work of corrupters to prosper﴾ is parenthetical (iʿtiraḍiyya), serving as the cause (taʿlil) of the content of the clause ﴿Indeed Allah will nullify it﴾, and as a concluding statement (tadhyil) for the speech with what includes the negation of rectification. The definition of ﴿the corrupters﴾ by the generic *lam* (lam al-jins) implies generality in the negated genus of rectification and in the genus of corrupters, so that it is known that their magic belongs to the category of the work of corrupters. The attribution of ﴿work﴾ to ﴿the corrupters﴾ indicates that it is corrupt work, because it is the act of those whose nature is corruption, so it is a pattern modeled on them and a course following their customary practice. What is meant by the rectification of the work of corrupters which He negated is that He does not support it. It does not mean negating making it righteous, because the reality of corruption cannot become righteousness, so that its transformation into that would be negated from Allah. Its rectification is rather to give it righteousness. So when Allah negates its rectification, that is by leaving it to itself. It is in the nature of corruption to diminish over time until it vanishes.

[Page 257]

Since the words ﴿Indeed Allah will nullify it﴾ were placed first, it is understood that what is meant by negating its rectification is that Allah sends the causes of its nullification against it, until its effect is nullified. And the non-rectification of the work of such people means the nullification of their aims from it, as in His words ﴿and [that] He might nullify falsehood﴾ [al-Anfal: 8], meaning: that He might show its falsehood.

The magicians were corrupters only because their intention was to mislead people's minds so that they would be subjugated to them and would not know the causes of things, so that they would remain instruments in what the magicians command them, and would not find a way to rectify their own souls. As for the magicians whom Moses (peace be upon him) addressed, their corruption is more evident, because they were trying to nullify the call to the truth and the upright religion, and to promote polytheism and misguidance.

The clause ﴿And Allah establishes the truth﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿Indeed Allah will nullify it﴾, meaning: He will nullify it, and He will establish the truth, that is, He will confirm the miracle.

*Ihqaq* (establishing) means confirmation. From it the truth (*haqq*) is so named because it is what is firm.

The apparent use of the divine name (Allah) in this clause, although the apparent requirement would have been a pronoun, is intended to cultivate awe in their souls.

The *ba'* in ﴿by His words﴾ indicates causation (sababiyya).

The word *kalimat* (words) is used metaphorically for the connection of His power, exalted is He, to bringing things into existence. This is the connection expressed by "bringing into being" (takwin), which proceeds in accordance with His will and in accordance with His knowledge. This is an elegant metaphor, because that connection resembles speech in that it gives rise to the comprehension of a meaning, and indicates the will of the speaker and his knowledge.

The clause ﴿even if the criminals dislike it﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). *Law* here is concessive (wasliyya), and it implies that the situation following it is an extreme case of what might be supposed to contradict the preceding judgment, as was mentioned earlier in His words ﴿even if he offered it as ransom﴾ [Al ʿImran: 91] in Surat Al ʿImran. Thus any other circumstances are more fitting and more deserving for the realization of the preceding judgment alongside them. The dislike of the criminals for the establishing of the truth is an extreme case of what might be supposed to contradict the establishing, because such dislike is likely to move them to [Page 258] oppose the truth that displeases them, and to try to refute it, and they were a powerful group for whom hardship would be easy. So He informed them that Allah is their forsaker.

By "the criminals" he means Pharaoh and his chiefs. He turned away from the pronoun of address to the explicit noun, because it includes describing them with criminality, as an indirect reproach to them. He did not address them with the description of criminality by saying, "Even if you dislike it, O criminals," avoiding confronting them with blame, standing by the command of Allah, exalted is He, when He said to him, ﴿So speak to him gently﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44]. He presented the matter in the form of a universal proposition, while meaning that they are among its particulars, without stating that explicitly. This is different from the situation of the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), when Allah said to him, ﴿Say, "Is it other than Allah that you order me to worship, O ignorant ones?"﴾ [al-Zumar: 64], because that was after the repeated call to them, while Moses (peace be upon him) was at the beginning of the call. Also, the polytheists were trying to get the Prophet (ﷺ) to worship their gods, so he was in a position of denial requiring the most forceful rejection of them, while Moses (peace be upon him) was trying to persuade Pharaoh and his chiefs to believe, so he was in a position of encouragement through gentleness.
