Abu ʿAmr and Abu Jaʿfar read *ālsiḥra* with a hamzat al-istifham (interrogative hamza) at its beginning and with lengthening to ease the second hamza (tashil), so *ma* in ﴿what you have brought﴾ is interrogative, and *ālsiḥra* is an interrogative clarifying the interrogative *ma*. It is used for belittlement (tahqir). The meaning is: it is a trivial matter that many people can accomplish.

The clause ﴿Indeed Allah will nullify it﴾ is the predicate of the relative *ma* according to the reading of the majority, and a resumptive explanatory clause (istinaf bayani) according to the reading of Abu ʿAmr and those who agree with him. The emphasis of the predicate by *inna* is an increase in instilling fear into their souls.

*Ibtal* (nullification) of it means showing that it is imagination and not reality, because showing that is a nullification of what was intended by it. That is, Allah will nullify its effect on people by exposing its secret. The sign of the future tense indicates the nearness of its nullification. This knowledge was granted to Moses (peace be upon him) either through a specific revelation in that matter, or through a general one by its falling under a universal rule, which is the meaning of ﴿Indeed Allah does not allow the work of corrupters to prosper﴾.

The clause ﴿Indeed Allah does not allow the work of corrupters to prosper﴾ is parenthetical (iʿtiraḍiyya), serving as the cause (taʿlil) of the content of the clause ﴿Indeed Allah will nullify it﴾, and as a concluding statement (tadhyil) for the speech with what includes the negation of rectification. The definition of ﴿the corrupters﴾ by the generic *lam* (lam al-jins) implies generality in the negated genus of rectification and in the genus of corrupters, so that it is known that their magic belongs to the category of the work of corrupters. The attribution of ﴿work﴾ to ﴿the corrupters﴾ indicates that it is corrupt work, because it is the act of those whose nature is corruption, so it is a pattern modeled on them and a course following their customary practice. What is meant by the rectification of the work of corrupters which He negated is that He does not support it. It does not mean negating making it righteous, because the reality of corruption cannot become righteousness, so that its transformation into that would be negated from Allah. Its rectification is rather to give it righteousness. So when Allah negates its rectification, that is by leaving it to itself. It is in the nature of corruption to diminish over time until it vanishes.

[Page 257]

Since the words ﴿Indeed Allah will nullify it﴾ were placed first, it is understood that what is meant by negating its rectification is that Allah sends the causes of its nullification against it, until its effect is nullified. And the non-rectification of the work of such people means the nullification of their aims from it, as in His words ﴿and [that] He might nullify falsehood﴾ [al-Anfal: 8], meaning: that He might show its falsehood.

The magicians were corrupters only because their intention was to mislead people's minds so that they would be subjugated to them and would not know the causes of things, so that they would remain instruments in what the magicians command them, and would not find a way to rectify their own souls. As for the magicians whom Moses (peace be upon him) addressed, their corruption is more evident, because they were trying to nullify the call to the truth and the upright religion, and to promote polytheism and misguidance.

The clause ﴿And Allah establishes the truth﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿Indeed Allah will nullify it﴾, meaning: He will nullify it, and He will establish the truth, that is, He will confirm the miracle.

*Ihqaq* (establishing) means confirmation. From it the truth (*haqq*) is so named because it is what is firm.

The apparent use of the divine name (Allah) in this clause, although the apparent requirement would have been a pronoun, is intended to cultivate awe in their souls.

The *ba'* in ﴿by His words﴾ indicates causation (sababiyya).

The word *kalimat* (words) is used metaphorically for the connection of His power, exalted is He, to bringing things into existence. This is the connection expressed by "bringing into being" (takwin), which proceeds in accordance with His will and in accordance with His knowledge. This is an elegant metaphor, because that connection resembles speech in that it gives rise to the comprehension of a meaning, and indicates the will of the speaker and his knowledge.

The clause ﴿even if the criminals dislike it﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). *Law* here is concessive (wasliyya), and it implies that the situation following it is an extreme case of what might be supposed to contradict the preceding judgment, as was mentioned earlier in His words ﴿even if he offered it as ransom﴾ [Al ʿImran: 91] in Surat Al ʿImran. Thus any other circumstances are more fitting and more deserving for the realization of the preceding judgment alongside them. The dislike of the criminals for the establishing of the truth is an extreme case of what might be supposed to contradict the establishing, because such dislike is likely to move them to [Page 258] oppose the truth that displeases them, and to try to refute it, and they were a powerful group for whom hardship would be easy. So He informed them that Allah is their forsaker.

By "the criminals" he means Pharaoh and his chiefs. He turned away from the pronoun of address to the explicit noun, because it includes describing them with criminality, as an indirect reproach to them. He did not address them with the description of criminality by saying, "Even if you dislike it, O criminals," avoiding confronting them with blame, standing by the command of Allah, exalted is He, when He said to him, ﴿So speak to him gently﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44]. He presented the matter in the form of a universal proposition, while meaning that they are among its particulars, without stating that explicitly. This is different from the situation of the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), when Allah said to him, ﴿Say, "Is it other than Allah that you order me to worship, O ignorant ones?"﴾ [al-Zumar: 64], because that was after the repeated call to them, while Moses (peace be upon him) was at the beginning of the call. Also, the polytheists were trying to get the Prophet (ﷺ) to worship their gods, so he was in a position of denial requiring the most forceful rejection of them, while Moses (peace be upon him) was trying to persuade Pharaoh and his chiefs to believe, so he was in a position of encouragement through gentleness.

[Page 253]

The clause ﴿And Pharaoh said﴾ is coordinated ('atf, coordination) with the clause ﴿They said, "Indeed, this is clear magic"﴾ [Yunus: 76]. This clause therefore stands in the position of a second answer to the conditional particle *lamma* (when). First, it reports how Pharaoh and his chiefs (malaʾ) received Moses' call and his miracle, namely by denying that what he brought could be a confirmation from Allah. Then it reports, secondly, how Pharaoh in particular received that call, namely by trying to support their claim ﴿Indeed, this is clear magic﴾ [Yunus: 76], so as to show that they were able to produce its like. The means to that (its causes and preparations) were among the special privileges of Pharaoh. This also contains a command to the elite of the nation to prepare to nullify what was feared from it.

The addressees of his words ﴿Bring me﴾ are the chiefs of Pharaoh and his inner circle, those who held the execution of his command in their hands.

He ordered the bringing of all the magicians who were established in the knowledge of magic, because they were the most perceptive of its subtleties and the most capable of displaying what would surpass, in his supposition, the extraordinary acts of Moses. Their presence therefore made the presence of weaker practitioners of magic unnecessary, since their work was likely not to match what Moses had shown. If they produced something inferior to the miracle of Moses, that would promote the call of Moses among the common people of the nation.

The generality in his words ﴿every magician who is learned﴾ is customary generality (ʿumum ʿurfi), meaning: every magician whom you know and can reach. Or it may mean that "every" is intended to express abundance, as was mentioned earlier in his words ﴿Even if you brought to those who were given the Book every sign﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿So when the magicians came﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿And Pharaoh said﴾. It links the arrival of the magicians and Moses' words to them to the clause "Pharaoh said" by the *fa'* of sequence (fa' al-taʿqib), to indicate immediacy in their being brought. This sequence is in accordance with the customary haste in carrying out a commanded matter.

[Page 254]

The implied object of the coordination is omitted, because what naturally follows his words ﴿Bring me every magician﴾ is their being brought. But since that adds little to the purpose for which the story is told, it is omitted, relying on what is required and indicated by it, both by rational and verbal indication, from his words ﴿the magicians came﴾, by way of conciseness (ijaz). The estimated sense is: "So they brought them to him. And when they came, Moses said to them."

The definiteness in ﴿the magicians﴾ is definiteness of prior mention (ʿahd dhikri).

Moses commanded them to begin by throwing their magic, in order to display the strength of his proof. The one who begins a contest in an activity is normally in a better position to excel in it over his rival, especially in activities whose essence is deception and intimidation, and in which the one seeking victory aims at being first to impress and move the onlookers. The Qur'an mentions in other verses that the magicians gave Moses the choice between his beginning by displaying his miracle and their beginning, and that Moses chose that they be the ones to begin.

The imperative verb in his words ﴿Throw what you are going to throw﴾ is used for equalization (taswiya), whose purpose is choice and to show indifference to either of the two options.

*Al-ilqa'* (throwing) is casting something from the hand to the ground. The term *ilqa'* is applied to the act of magic because most of the magicians' manipulations in their magical works consist of throwing things to the ground. It is reported in many verses that they threw their ropes and staffs, and that by their magic it was imagined that these were moving. The ultimate aim of the magician's work was to make inanimate things seem alive.

The phrase ﴿what you are going to throw﴾ is intended as a substitutive generalization (taʿmim badali), meaning: whatever you throw. This adds to the display of indifference to the extent of their magic, and prepares the assembled chiefs to know that Allah would nullify their magic through His messenger.

It is not problematic that Moses commanded them to cast magic, as though he commanded an act of disobedience. The people were unbelievers, and an unbeliever is not addressed by the divine laws. Also, the purpose of commanding them to throw it was to show its falsity. That is like presenting the doubt of a heretic in order to refute it after stating it, as in the method of ʿAḍud al-Din al-Iji in his book *al-Mawaqif*.

[Page 255]

The description of the form of their magic has been omitted in this verse, because the purpose of the lesson in this verse is to describe the persistence of Pharaoh and his chiefs in turning away from the call, what the oppressed believers who followed Moses (peace be upon him) suffered from Pharaoh's domination over them, and how Allah gave victory to His messenger and to the oppressed along with him, and how the good end was theirs, while the unbelievers had the evil end. This serves as an example for those who deny Muhammad (ﷺ). For this reason, it did not dwell on anything except the statement of Moses (peace be upon him) when he saw their magic, which indicates his certainty about his Lord and His promise, and that the final outcome belongs to the truth. That is more important in this context than mentioning the collapse of their magic before the miracle of Moses (peace be upon him). For this reason, the object of *alqaw* (they threw) was not mentioned, by treating the verb *alqu* (throw) as intransitive, since the purpose does not depend on stating its object.

The meaning of ﴿what you have brought﴾ is "what you have displayed to us." The verb *ji'tum* (you brought) is used metaphorically for displaying, because the one who brings something displays it in the place where he came. The connection is customary. It does not mean that they came from other regions accompanied by magic. Although many or all of the magicians had come from numerous cities, that supposition does not hold in every case where expressions like "he brought such-and-such" are used. For it holds in a verse like ﴿And they came upon his shirt with false blood﴾ [Yusuf: 18], but does not hold in a verse like ﴿Indeed, those who came with the falsehood﴾ [al-Nur: 11].

The composition of the speech in this style, by making *ma ji'tum* the subject rather than making it the object of the verb *sayubtiluhu* (He will nullify it), and by making it a vague noun, then explaining it by the clause *ji'tum bihi*, then clarifying it by an appositive (ʿatf al-bayan) for the purpose of emphasizing its mention and creating anticipation for knowing the predicate, which is the clause ﴿Indeed Allah will nullify it﴾, and then the pronoun of magic appearing as the object of *sayubtiluhu*: all of this is elaboration (itnab) and deviation from what the apparent situation requires, in order to establish the report of a reality about magic for him, to settle it firmly in the minds of the listeners, and to cast terror into their souls.

The clause ﴿And Allah establishes the truth﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿Indeed Allah will nullify it﴾, meaning: He will nullify it, and He will establish the truth, that is, He will confirm the miracle.

*Ihqaq* (establishing) means confirmation. From it the truth (*haqq*) is so named because it is what is firm.

The apparent use of the divine name (Allah) in this clause, although the apparent requirement would have been a pronoun, is intended to cultivate awe in their souls.

The *ba'* in ﴿by His words﴾ indicates causation (sababiyya).

The word *kalimat* (words) is used metaphorically for the connection of His power, exalted is He, to bringing things into existence. This is the connection expressed by "bringing into being" (takwin), which proceeds in accordance with His will and in accordance with His knowledge. This is an elegant metaphor, because that connection resembles speech in that it gives rise to the comprehension of a meaning, and indicates the will of the speaker and his knowledge.

The clause ﴿even if the criminals dislike it﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). *Law* here is concessive (wasliyya), and it implies that the situation following it is an extreme case of what might be supposed to contradict the preceding judgment, as was mentioned earlier in His words ﴿even if he offered it as ransom﴾ [Al ʿImran: 91] in Surat Al ʿImran. Thus any other circumstances are more fitting and more deserving for the realization of the preceding judgment alongside them. The dislike of the criminals for the establishing of the truth is an extreme case of what might be supposed to contradict the establishing, because such dislike is likely to move them to [Page 258] oppose the truth that displeases them, and to try to refute it, and they were a powerful group for whom hardship would be easy. So He informed them that Allah is their forsaker.

By "the criminals" he means Pharaoh and his chiefs. He turned away from the pronoun of address to the explicit noun, because it includes describing them with criminality, as an indirect reproach to them. He did not address them with the description of criminality by saying, "Even if you dislike it, O criminals," avoiding confronting them with blame, standing by the command of Allah, exalted is He, when He said to him, ﴿So speak to him gently﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44]. He presented the matter in the form of a universal proposition, while meaning that they are among its particulars, without stating that explicitly. This is different from the situation of the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), when Allah said to him, ﴿Say, "Is it other than Allah that you order me to worship, O ignorant ones?"﴾ [al-Zumar: 64], because that was after the repeated call to them, while Moses (peace be upon him) was at the beginning of the call. Also, the polytheists were trying to get the Prophet (ﷺ) to worship their gods, so he was in a position of denial requiring the most forceful rejection of them, while Moses (peace be upon him) was trying to persuade Pharaoh and his chiefs to believe, so he was in a position of encouragement through gentleness.

﴿So none believed in Musa except some offspring of his people, out of fear of Fir'awn and their chiefs, that he would persecute them. Indeed Fir'awn was haughty in the land, and indeed he was among the transgressors.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of the preceding dialogue. That is, it follows from it that Fir'awn and his chiefs did not believe in Musa, because restricting the believers to some offspring of Musa's people implies that others did not believe, which is the intended meaning. The restrictive form (qasr) in this context is therefore a form of concision (ijaz). The implied sense is: "Following from this, they were resolved to turn away."

The events that took place between the dialogue and their resolve to turn away have been omitted: Musa casting his staff and its swallowing what they had cast of their magic. This is because the purpose is not served by describing it. The aim is to arrive at the point that they resolved to turn away, since this is the setting for drawing a parallel between their conduct and that of the polytheists of Makkah.

The verb āmana (to believe) originally was *aʾmana* with two hamzas. The first is original to the root, since the word derives from *amanah* (trustworthiness). The second is an added hamza for transitivity, meaning "made him one who is trustworthy," i.e., not a liar. Thus *āmana* comes to mean "to affirm/confirm as true" (saddaqa). Its basic construction would take the object directly, but it is transitive with the preposition *li-* (to), to distinguish *āmana* meaning "to affirm as true" from *āmana* meaning "to make him secure," i.e., free from fear of him.

Ibn Malik called this *lam al-tabyin* (the lam of specification), and Ibn Hisham followed him. It enters upon the object to strengthen the sense of objecthood, and in cases like *āmana* meaning "to affirm," it confirms the intent of strengthening and prevents confusion with the verb *āmana* meaning "to make him secure." Its occurrence is also found in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "We will never believe you"﴾ (al-Isra 17:90) in Surat al-Isra.

It may also be transitive with *bi-* since it is implicitly meaning *saddaqa*, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "I believe that there is no deity except the One in whom the Children of Israel believed"﴾ (Yunus 10:90).

*Dhurriyyah* means offspring or children, and it was discussed earlier in His statement: ﴿offspring, some of whom are from others﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:34) in Surat Al 'Imran.

That is: none believed in what Musa brought except the sons of the Children of Israel, and his call did not reach the rest of his people, or he had not been commanded to deliver it to them at that time.

The *ʿala* in His statement, ﴿out of fear of Fir'awn﴾, is in the sense of *maʿa* (with), like His statement: ﴿and gave wealth despite love for it﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:177). That is: they believed while they were fearful. It is a stative adverbial phrase in a position of circumstance (hal) relative to *dhurriyyah*, meaning in a state of their firmly established fear.

This is praise of them, that they believed and the fear of Fir'awn did not prevent them from faith.

The meaning is that they believed when his miracle appeared, that is, they publicly declared their faith in him on that occasion, because faith is not recognized except through its display, and there is no benefit in it except that display, namely from among those present at that scene of the Children of Israel. The custom of such gatherings is that young people and adolescents attend them, so He referred to them as *dhurriyyah*, meaning children, just as one says *al-ghilman* (the boys). They would then have believed of their own accord. None of this implies that the rest of his people disbelieved in him, since it is possible that they believed in him afterward when his call reached them. For he would have begun with the call to Fir'awn, hastening to comply with the command from God: ﴿Go, you two, to Fir'awn; indeed he has transgressed﴾ (Taha 20:43). Thus the primary command would have been the call to Fir'awn and the liberation of the Children of Israel from captivity.

*Al-mala'* was mentioned just previously in this narrative. *Al-mala'* is attributed to a plural pronoun referring to *dhurriyyah*, meaning: out of fear of Fir'awn and out of fear of their people, who are the rest of the people who did not attend that scene, fearing that they would be angry with them and harm them for their faith in Musa, because they anticipate that Fir'awn would hold the entire tribe accountable for an act of some of its men, following the custom of tyrants of seizing a tribe for the deed of some of its men.

*Al-fatn* is bringing dread and turmoil upon the mind through the imposition of what the soul cannot bear. It was discussed in His statement: ﴿and persecution is worse than killing﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:191) in Surat al-Baqarah. This is the explanation of the verse.

The sentence ﴿Indeed Fir'awn was haughty in the land, and indeed he was among the transgressors﴾ is in a position of circumstance (hal). It is coordinated with His statement, ﴿out of fear of Fir'awn﴾, and it conveys the sense of giving a reason for their fear of Fir'awn, that is, they are justified in their intense fear. Having praised them for believing in a state of intense fear, it then goes further to explain that they are deserving of fear. In this there is additional praise for the strength of their faith, since they believed while fearing the king despite his power to harm them, and despite their chiefs, that is, their people, which is a severe fear. For its effects reach a person in all his states, even in his solitude and privacy, because of the intensity of his people's involvement with him in all his affairs, such that he finds no escape from them. Then it follows this with an explanation of the extent of Fir'awn's power and his excess in tyranny. One whose condition is such will not be restrained from inflicting harm on his opponents by any restraint.

[p. 261]

The emphasis of the predicate with *inna* is for the sake of attention to the certainty of Fir'awn's oppression.

*Al-'uluww* (haughtiness) is used metaphorically for domination and tyranny, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed Fir'awn exalted himself in the land﴾ (al-Qasas 28:4), and His statement: ﴿Do not exalt yourselves over me, but come to me in submission﴾ (al-Naml 27:31).

*Al-israf* (excess) is going beyond the known limit of moderation in an action. It is therefore a blameworthy transgression, and its most common usage is in spending. The object of the excess is not mentioned, so it is specified as excess in what was known of the kings of their time in terms of disliked qualities that are commonly associated with kings.

His statement *min al-musrifin* (among the transgressors) is more eloquent in describing him with excess than saying *wa innahu lamusrif* (indeed he is a transgressor), for the reason already discussed at His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Then I would have strayed, and I would not be among the guided﴾ (al-An'am 6:56) in Surat al-An'am.

[p. 262]

He links the rest of the story to its beginning, so this is conjoined (*'atf*) to the clause ﴿Pharaoh said﴾ [Yunus: 79]. This is Moses addressing all of his people, the Children of Israel who were in Egypt. It indicates that he addressed them this way after he had called them and they had believed in him, as his words ﴿If you have believed in God﴾ suggest. The purpose is to strengthen those who believed in him in the presence of Pharaoh in their reliance on God (*tawakkul*, trust in God), and to command those other than them, whose offspring they feared would be harmed, not to reproach them for openly displaying faith, and not to let their sons be cowardly and not to fear Pharaoh. For this reason he said, ﴿If you have believed in God, then put your trust in Him﴾. The meaning is: if you have truly believed in God, as your statements have shown, then rely on Him for your victory and for the removal of harm from you, and do not rely on yourselves by currying favour with Pharaoh, nor on Pharaoh by displaying loyalty to him.

[p. 263]

He intended to stir up the sincerity of their faith and to inspire their hearts by making their faith dependent on a condition that may or may not occur, since they feared that Pharaoh would test them, so they wished to conceal their faith out of dissimulation (*taqiyya*, precautionary concealment of belief under threat) before Pharaoh and his chiefs. He made their indifference to Pharaoh's brutality a sign of their faith, because in the early stage of a call, the call is not established except by its followers openly showing themselves as a community, so dissimulation is not excused at that time. On this basis the early Muslims acted, such as Bilal, Ammar and Abu Bakr: they declared their faith and bore the harm. Dissimulation was permitted to individual believers only after the community of faith had become established. That is the context of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in God after his belief, except one who is compelled while his heart remains firm in faith﴾ [al-Nahl: 106].

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before its governed verb in His words ﴿upon Him put your trust﴾ serves to convey restriction (*qasr*, exclusivity), and it is a restriction relative to a specific context (*qasr idafi*), which His words explain: ﴿out of fear of Pharaoh and his chiefs that he would test them﴾ [Yunus: 83]. So the meaning returns to forbidding them from fearing Pharaoh.

*Tawakkul* has already been discussed earlier in the story of Noah.

The clause ﴿if you are Muslims﴾ is a second condition that reinforces the condition ﴿if you have believed in God﴾. From the two clauses together it follows that the realization of this trust depends on the realization of their faith and submission, to give greater emphasis to trust and to show that it is inseparable from faith and Islam, and it also clarifies the first condition. That is, if your faith is the faith of one who submits to God, that is, one who is sincere toward Him, not mixing it with doubt about God's power or about whether His promise is true. Thus the two conditions together require that each condition be made dependent on the other.

This is an instance of the question of making one condition dependent on another. Faith (*iman*) is affirmation of what the Messenger brought, and it is an inward act of the heart, which is not legally recognized except together with Islam. Islam is the uttering of what indicates faith, and it is not legally recognized except together with faith. So faith is an inner emotional state of the heart, and Islam is a bodily act, and they are mutually entailed in being counted as valid for following the religion, since the affirmation of the heart is not known to be present except through speech and obedience, and speech is not true except when it agrees with what is in the soul. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say: "You have not believed, but say, 'We have submitted,' for faith has not yet entered your hearts"﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14]. This is explicitly stated in the hadith of Gabriel's questioning in the two Sahihs (the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari and *Sahih* of Muslim).

It is not meant that if they did not place their trust they would be believers but not Muslims, nor that if they did place their trust they would be Muslims but not believers, because the practice of religion does not support that. For this reason His words ﴿upon Him put your trust﴾ serve as the answer to both conditions. That is, a response similar to the answer of the first condition is to be supposed for the second condition. This is the proper understanding of the verse, and what many exegetes attempted goes beyond the open path of the discourse.

The sincerity of their faith, together with the force of the prophetic command that their prophet confronted them with, quickly led them to strip away fear and currying favour, and to resolve firmly on trust in God. For this reason they hastened to answer him with the words ﴿upon God we have put our trust﴾, containing the particular exclusivity that requires their being free from trust in anyone other than God, exalted is He.

Their hastening is indicated by the conjunction of their statement to Moses's speech with the particle *fa'* of immediate sequence, contrary to the usual style in recounting the speeches in dialogues, which is that they are not conjoined. The apparent requirement is thus set aside for this subtle purpose.

Then they concluded their statement by turning to God and asking Him to protect them from the harm of Pharaoh, considering in this the benefit of the religion before their own benefit, because if the disbelievers were able to destroy them or torture them, the strength of the supporters of disbelief would grow, and they would say to themselves: "If these people were upon the truth, what befell them would not have happened to them," and thereby the common disbelievers would be tempted and would think that their religion is the truth.

[p. 264]

*Fitna* (trial, temptation, discord) has already been explained earlier. They called it *fitna* because it increases people's deep immersion in disbelief, and disbelief is a *fitna*.

*Fitna* is a verbal noun (*masdar*). So the meaning of their request that God not make them *fitna* is that He not make them a cause of *fitna*. The transitive use of the verb ﴿make us﴾ to their pronoun, described by "*fitna*", is a transitivity according to the figure of speech of attributing an act to something other than its real agent (*al-majaz al-'aqli*, rational metaphor). The predicate "*fitna*" is not a report of the verbal noun in the sense of asserting the act itself, since they do not posit that they would be tempters, and the context does not permit that they meant "do not make us those tempted by the wrongdoing people."

They described the disbelievers as ﴿the wrongdoing people﴾ because polytheism is wrongdoing, and because it indicates that they are afflicted with various kinds of wrongdoing: wronging themselves and wronging creatures. Then they asked for what is good for them, so they sought deliverance from ﴿the disbelieving people﴾, that is, from their brutality and harm.

The addition of ﴿by Your mercy﴾ serves to disavow self-conceit regarding their faith, because the favour belongs to God over them, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: "Do not count your Islam as a favour upon me. Rather God confers favour upon you that He has guided you to faith, if you are truthful"﴾ [al-Hujurat: 17].

The mention of the word "people" in His words ﴿for the wrongdoing people﴾ and His words ﴿from the disbelieving people﴾ is for the reason we pointed out in the middle of al-Baqara and several times in this surah.

The transitive use of the verb ﴿make us﴾ to their pronoun, described by "*fitna*", is a transitivity according to the figure of speech of attributing an act to something other than its real agent (*al-majaz al-'aqli*, rational metaphor). The predicate "*fitna*" is not a report of the verbal noun in the sense of asserting the act itself, since they do not posit that they would be tempters, and the context does not permit that they meant "do not make us those tempted by the wrongdoing people."

They described the disbelievers as ﴿the wrongdoing people﴾ because polytheism is wrongdoing, and because it indicates that they are afflicted with various kinds of wrongdoing: wronging themselves and wronging creatures. Then they asked for what is good for them, so they sought deliverance from ﴿the disbelieving people﴾, that is, from their brutality and harm.

The addition of ﴿by Your mercy﴾ serves to disavow self-conceit regarding their faith, because the favour belongs to God over them, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: "Do not count your Islam as a favour upon me. Rather God confers favour upon you that He has guided you to faith, if you are truthful"﴾ [al-Hujurat: 17].

The mention of the word "people" in His words ﴿for the wrongdoing people﴾ and His words ﴿from the disbelieving people﴾ is for the reason we pointed out in the middle of al-Baqara and several times in this surah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 87:

﴿And We revealed to Moses and his brother: "Settle your people in Egypt in houses, and make your houses into a qiblah (direction of prayer), and establish the prayer, and give good tidings to the believers."﴾

It is permissible that this be a conjunction (ʿatf) with the sentence ﴿And Moses said, "O my people..."﴾ [Yunus: 84]. It is also permissible that it be the conjunction of one narrative (qissa) onto another narrative, that is, onto the whole of the preceding discourse, because the whole of his narratives is a relating of the stages of the story of Moses and his people.

The revelation of this command came to Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both, because it is among the matters that concern the management of the community's affairs, so it is possible for the messenger and his supporter to share in it.

Al-tabawwu' (settling) means taking a place to dwell in. It is a form (tafaʿʿul) from al-bawʾ, meaning return, as if the owner of the dwelling burdens himself with returning to his place of residence, even if he has gone far from it in the affairs of his livelihood, by going to the market, hunting, gathering firewood, picking fruit, or the like. This was already mentioned at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You settle the believers in positions for battle﴾ [Al 'Imran: 121] in Surat Al 'Imran. So the meaning of ﴿Settle your people﴾ is: make your people those who settle into houses.

The doer of this verb is, originally, the one who dwells in the dwelling place. It is attributed here to the pronoun of Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both, by way of what is called al-majaz al-ʿaqli (figurative attribution, a metaphor of the intellect), since they were the cause of their people's settling into houses. The indicator is His saying ﴿for your people﴾, since it made the settling for the sake of the people.

The meaning of settling into houses for their people is that they command their people to take houses in the form that they order them. Since the Children of Israel already had dwellings in Egypt before this, for they would not be residing in Egypt without dwellings, and they were living in the land of (Goshen, Jasan) near the city of (Memphis, Manfis), the capital of the kingdom at that time, in the south of the Egyptian lands, as we explained in Surat al-Baqarah, it is certainly the case that the houses commanded to be settled are other than the houses in which they had been living.

The exegetes (mufassirun) differed over what was intended by these houses, and they mentioned reports that are not suitable to the condition of the people at that time. It was said: the houses are houses of worship, that is, mosques in which they pray. Perhaps those who interpreted it this way were moved by the placement of His saying ﴿and establish the prayer﴾ right after it. But this is far-fetched, because God knew that the Children of Israel would soon depart Egypt by His permission. It was also said: the houses are houses for dwelling, and they refrained from speaking of the purpose of these houses. This view is the most fitting to the word "settling," since settling means dwelling, and it is also the most fitting to the unqualified word "houses" and to their being in Egypt.

On the basis of this, what appears is that these houses were tents or huts (akhsas) which God commanded them to take, in preparation for departure. They were other than their homes which they had been living in at (Goshen, Jasan) near the city of Pharaoh. The Torah has what bears witness to this interpretation, in the fourth chapter of the Book of Exodus (Sifr al-Khuruj): God commanded Moses to go out with the Children of Israel into the desert to keep the feast of Passover for three days, and that this was the first thing Moses requested from Pharaoh, and that Pharaoh prevented them from it, and that Moses repeated the request to Pharaoh, and he kept refusing, as in the seventh and eighth chapters of the Book of Exodus. This became a feast for them after their departure.

[Page 266]

His saying ﴿and make your houses into a qiblah﴾ means: these tents or huts which you take, make them open toward the qiblah. Ibn ʿAtiyya said this, from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The qiblah is a term in Arabic for the direction of the Kaʿba. That direction is what lies between east and west, because the qiblah of the lands of Egypt, like the qiblah of Medina, is between east and west, and it is the south. So it is permissible that the expression of that direction as "qiblah" in the verse be a rendering of Moses' expression of it with something that indicates the sense of facing the direction toward which they pray, which is the qiblah of Abraham. Then the command to the Children of Israel on that day would be proceeding according to the upright religion (al-milla al-hanifiyya) before it was abrogated (naskh, cancellation) by facing the Rock of Jerusalem (Sakhrat al-Quds). It is also permissible that Moses expressed it with something that conveys the meaning of the south, so his expression was related in the Qur'an with the synonymous word that is common among the Arabs for expressing the south, which is the word qiblah.

The wisdom in making the houses face the qiblah is that the sun enters them through their doorways during most hours of the day in all seasons, and in that there are many benefits.

Those who explained the houses as houses for dwelling explained qiblah either as meaning "facing" (mutaqabila), or as meaning "make your houses the place of your prayer." Both explanations are far from customary usage.

As for those who interpreted the houses as mosques, they explained qiblah as the qiblah of prayer, that is, the direction of the Kaʿba.

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: the Kaʿba was the qiblah of Moses.

It is reported from al-Hasan: the Kaʿba was the qiblah of all the prophets. This explanation fits the structure of ﴿and make your houses into a qiblah﴾, because the structure requires that what is made a qiblah is the houses themselves, not that the prayer be made in them facing the direction of the qiblah. When we consider all these interpretations, we find them nothing but disjointed and forced, except for the explanation on which we relied, though they differed over it, and God guided us to it.

The verb "make" (ijʿalu) is attributed to the plural pronoun because that making is the work of Moses, his brother, and their people, since each person is responsible for making his own house a qiblah.

[Page 267]

He commanded them to establish the prayer, that is, the one God prescribed for them through Moses, and which they used to pray before Moses came, following Abraham, peace be upon him, and his sons. The apparent reason for commanding them to establish the prayer is that the taking of houses was during a state of journeying, so their condition was liable to distract them from establishing the prayers, and therefore they were commanded to maintain the establishment of the prayer during the period of their journey.

The conjunction of the sentence ﴿and give good tidings to the believers﴾ to what precedes it indicates that what they were commanded to do, namely taking houses, was a command in a state that suggests anticipating dangers and fear. They said ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial﴾ [Yunus: 85], so Moses was commanded to give them good tidings of a good outcome, and that they would be victorious over their enemy and saved from him. The believers are the people of Moses mentioned in His saying ﴿None believed in Moses except some offspring of his people﴾ [Yunus: 83], and in His saying ﴿If you have believed in God, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims﴾ [Yunus: 84], and ﴿They said, "In God we have put our trust"﴾ [Yunus: 85].

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 88:**

﴿And Moses said, "Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the life of this world. Our Lord, that they may lead astray from Your way. Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment."﴾

He connects the remainder of what occurred in the story, which contains lessons and admonition. This is an introduction to the account of Moses and those with him leaving the land of Egypt. This introduction defines the honour that Moses, peace be upon him, had with his Lord, in that He answered his supplication and carried out, through his mission, the purpose of God, exalted is He, of rescuing the Children of Israel from enslavement. Moses prepared for his supplication with a preparation that indicates that what he asked of God to restrain Pharaoh and his chiefs was only for the benefit of the religion, not for taking revenge on them for his people or for himself. So he asked God to strip Pharaoh and his chiefs of blessing and to bring punishment upon them, in order to break their power and humble their tyranny, so that they would return from their misguidance and accepting faith would become easier for them.

[p. 268]

Since blessing is an incitement to rebellion for people of ignorance and wickedness, Moses made the provision of blessing to Pharaoh an incitement for Pharaoh to persist in turning away from the religion. Therefore Moses' supplication against them was a means of their reform and a seeking of their faith through means of severity against them. But God knew from their hearts what Moses did not know, and He decreed their annihilation.

The supplication was opened with the call (al-nida') because it suits the station of supplication. God was addressed with the attribute of Lordship (al-rububiyyah), in humble submission to show servanthood.

His saying, ﴿You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth﴾, is a preparation for the supplication against them. Its purpose is not the literal sense of informing, since Moses is certain that God knows this. Therefore it is established that the statement is used as a preparation for requesting the removal of blessing from them, in His saying, ﴿that they may lead astray from Your way﴾, and then the transition to the supplication for the removal of what they had been given.

The conjunction of the statement with the particle inna in His saying, ﴿You have given Pharaoh﴾ and so on, is intended to emphasise this meaning for which the statement is used, since the situation is not one of removing doubt or removing denial.

The exegetes differed concerning the grammatical position of the lam in His saying, ﴿that they may lead astray from Your way﴾. What the people of precision among them adopted is that the lam is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah) — that is, the lam whose outcome is the result rather than the intended purpose. This is transmitted from the grammarians of Basra: al-Khalil, Sibawayh, al-Akhfash, and their companions, in the same manner as the lam in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. Thus the lam, which is originally for causation (al-ta'lil), is borrowed for the meaning of sequence and consequence, which is the purpose of the fa' of succession (fa' al-ta'qib), by way of subsidiary metaphor (al-isti'arah al-tab'iyyah) in the related meaning of the particle. He likened the consequence of a thing upon another thing which is not its cause to the consequence of an effect upon its cause, for the sake of emphasising the strength of the consequence, until it became as if it were intended by the one in whom its effect appears. So the meaning is: You gave Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth, and by that they went astray and led others astray.

There are five other aspects (wujuh) that the exegetes give:

[p. 269]

The first: that it is for causation (lam al-ta'lil), and the meaning is: You did that as a gradual leading-on (istidraj) for them. This is attributed to al-Farra', and al-Tabari explained it in this way.

The second: that the speech is with the omission of a particle, and the estimate is: "lest they go astray from Your way," meaning "so they went astray." This is related by al-Fakhr (al-Razi).

The third: that the lam is the lam of supplication (lam al-du'a'). This was reported from al-Hasan. It is restricted to it in al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari), and Ibn al-Anbari said it. It is the most remote and the heaviest of the aspects.

The fourth: that it is with the omission of the interrogative hamzah. The estimate is: "Is it that they may lead astray from Your way? We gave them adornment and wealth," as a confirmation of the shamefulness upon them. Ibn 'Atiyyah said this. The interrogation is used in the sense of wonder (al-ta'ajjub), as al-Fakhr said.

The fifth: interpreting the meaning of misguidance (al-dalal) as ruin (al-halak), as al-Fakhr said. These are weak aspects with varying degrees of weakness, so we will not lengthen by explaining them.

Adornment (al-zinah) is that with which people adorn themselves, and what is pleasing in their eyes of the attractive things of this world, such as jewellery, gems, and imposing buildings. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14], and He said: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world﴾ [al-Kahf: 46], and He said: ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home at evening and when you send them forth to pasture﴾ [al-Nahl: 6].

Wealth (al-amwal) is that by which livelihood is sustained. So adornment distracts them from following admonitions and magnifies their status in the eyes of their people, and wealth enables them to subjugate the subjects to their obedience. The pharaohs had such abundance of provision and ease of living that its mention travelled throughout the horizons, and examples of it appear in their pyramids and their tombs.

The call (al-nida') is repeated between the clause that is caused (al-jumlah al-mu'allalah) and the clause that gives cause (al-jumlah al-mu'allilah), to confirm humble submission, to seek a response, and to show disavowal of any intent of objection.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far, and Ya'qub read liyadillu with a fatha on the ya' (﴿liyaḍillū﴾). 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma on the ya' (﴿liyuḍillū﴾), in the sense of their striving to mislead people.

[p. 270]

The meaning arising from the two readings is one, because when they went astray themselves while they were the leaders of their people, their misguidance became misguidance for others. Likewise, when they led people astray, they only led them astray while they themselves were astray like them. You have already learned that adornment is the cause of their misguidance and wealth is the cause of leading the people astray.

The call is repeated a third time to increase the emphasis on turning to God and supplicating humbly.

The clause ﴿obliterate their wealth﴾ is the intended purpose of this speech, and the call takes the place of connecting the clause with what precedes it, in the manner of a conjunction particle.

Al-tamṣ (obliteration) is erasure and removal. It was discussed earlier in His saying, ﴿before We obliterate faces﴾ [al-Nisa': 47], in Surat al-Nisa'. Its verb is transitive by itself, as in the verse of Surat al-Nisa', and it is transitive by the particle 'ala', as here, and in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾ [Ya Sin: 66], in Surat Ya Sin.

Perhaps its transitivity with 'ala' is to indicate the complete reach of the act upon the object, or because the verb tamṣ is construed with the meaning of being raised over, by means of the instrument of erasure and removal. So obliterating wealth means destroying and annihilating it.

As for His saying, wa-ushdud (and harden), I think it is derived from shadd, which is hardship. From it comes shiddah (severity) for a calamity and for distress. If something other than this were intended, it would have said wa-ṭba' (and seal) or wa-khtim (and set a seal) or something similar. So shadda would mean "he caused the tightening to enter," or he used it as jadda in his speech, i.e., he used earnestness (al-jidd).

The particle 'ala' is used metaphorically in the sense of the adverbial meaning (al-zarfiyyah), by subsidiary metaphor, to convey the firm establishment of the severity.

The meaning is: cause severity to enter into their hearts.

The hearts (al-qulub) are the souls and the minds.

The meaning is: He supplicates against them with grief and sorrows that make their hearts constricted and distressed, that is, put them in hardship and turmoil of mind as long as they are in disbelief. This is Moses' eagerness, peace be upon him, for the means of their guidance, in the hope that when blessings are removed from them and their breasts become constricted by the afflictions of life, they will reflect on the cause of that, and so they will hasten to repentance to God, as is the habit of heedless souls. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when harm touches a human being, he calls upon his Lord, turning back to Him in repentance﴾ [al-Zumar: 8].

[p. 271]

It is also possible that ushdud is from shadd, which is assault. It is said: "shadda 'alayhi" when he attacked him. That is because their hearts, in a state of blessing and ease, are secure and calm, so he supplicated God that He might assault them with His punishment, as a metaphor for the affliction of their souls with distress and sorrows, by the image of one who attacks his enemy to kill him. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And incite against them with your horses and your foot soldiers﴾ [al-Isra': 64], that is, subdue them to Your judgement and subject them.

By this it becomes clear that the position of the fa' in His saying, ﴿so they will not believe until they see the painful punishment﴾ is that it is the fa' of causation (fa' al-sababiyyah) in the response to the supplication, that is: do this to them so that they will believe. The verb is in the subjunctive by an implied "an" (an mudmarah), an obligatory implication after the fa' of causation.

So His saying, ﴿so they will not believe until they see the punishment﴾, is in the sense of saying: "so that they will believe when they see the punishment, not before that."

The answer to the supplication was turned away from being expressed in the form of affirming belief, to being expressed in the form of a negation limited by an end point, which is seeing the punishment. This is a wondrous method in the arrangement of speech, because he intended to combine the ordering of the response to the supplication with what had become clear to him of the nature of their souls: that arguments do not benefit them, and that the hardness of their hearts and the fierceness of their souls cannot be subdued except by physical and psychological pain. All of this is a remedy by what is likely to bring them through means of pressure and severity, since the means of argument did not avail with them. So He said: ﴿so they will not believe until they see the painful punishment﴾, that is: their condition is that. This is a wondrous concision, since it combined in this structure the response to the supplication and the explanation of the reason for the supplication against them in that manner. The original sense of the speech is: "so that they will believe, for they will not believe except when they see the painful punishment."

The intended purpose of the response to the verb of supplication is the end point of the response that comes after "until" (hatta). That is the destination of the response. This aspect in explaining the verse is one that is not burdened by a cloud of difficulty, and with it attaining the meaning is not hard.

[p. 272]

It is also possible that His saying, ﴿so they will not believe﴾ and so on, is coordinated (ataf) upon His saying, ﴿that they may lead astray from Your way﴾, and the clause of supplication lies between them as a parenthetical insertion (mu'taridah).

The meaning is: "that they may lead astray from Your way, so that their misguidance continues until they see the painful punishment." This is the interpretation of al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj.

By the painful punishment is meant the punishment of poverty and hunger, and the punishment of distress in the soul.

Seeing (al-ru'yah) is used for perception in the manner of a figurative metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal), or it is used as a metaphor (kinayah) for the descent of punishment upon them, because witnessing is inseparable from the descent of the thing witnessed.

[Page 273]

He said: ﴿Your supplication has indeed been answered, so go straight and do not follow the way of those who do not know.﴾

This is God's reply to the words of Musa (Moses), following the manner of narrating dialogues, in which its sentences are not joined by conjunctions, as has been mentioned more than once.

The opening of the sentence with *qad* (indeed) and the past-tense verb indicates the certain occurrence of the event in the future, so it is treated as if it had already happened.

The supplication is attributed to the dual pronoun, addressed to Musa and Harun (Aaron), although the supplication is only reported as coming from Musa, peace be upon him alone. This is because Musa, peace be upon him, supplicated while Harun was in agreement with him and was saying the same, since their supplication was one. It has also been said that Musa, peace be upon him, would supplicate while Harun, peace be upon him, said *amin* (Amen).

The meaning of the answering of the supplication is the granting of what Musa asked his Lord, namely that He deprive Pharaoh and his chiefs of blessings and send continuous calamities upon them, until they tire of resisting the call of Musa and their arrogance is brought low. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And We seized the people of Pharaoh with years of drought and a shortage of fruits, that they might take heed﴾ [al-A'raf: 130], and He said: ﴿So We sent upon them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood, as distinct signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 133].

Having made the command to go straight follow the answering of their supplication, it is known that going straight is a thanks for the honour bestowed, for God's answering the supplication of His servant is a kindness to the servant and an honouring of him, and this is a great blessing that deserves thanks; and the greatest thanks is obedience to the Bestower of the blessing.

Since Musa and Harun were upright, and what an uprightness that of prophethood is, the command to go straight was used to mean a command to persist in it. The exhortation to go straight was followed by a prohibition against following the way of those who do not know, although this is already included in going straight, as a warning to seek safety from deviating from the path of truth, with concern for warning against corruption.

*Al-istiqamah* (going straight): its real meaning is moderation, and it is the opposite of crookedness. It is frequently used to mean adherence to truth and right guidance, because it became common to liken error and corruption to crookedness and deviation. The truth has also been called "a straight path". This has already been discussed in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6]. Thus their command to go straight encompassed all the qualities of goodness and righteousness.

In the hadith of Abu 'Amra al-Thaqafi, he said: "I said: O Messenger of God, tell me a statement about Islam about which I need not ask anyone other than you. He said: Say: I have believed in God, then go straight."

Among going straight is that they continue calling to the religion and do not grow weary.

*Al-sabil* (the way): the path, and here it is used for conduct and the predominant course of action.

As for His saying ﴿wa la tattabi'anni﴾ (and do not follow), the majority read it with the *nun* doubled and vowelled with a kasra. There are two *nuns* here: one is the *nun* of the dual, and the other is the *nun al-tawkid* (the emphatic nun). Ibn Dhakwan, on the authority of Ibn 'Amir, read *wa la tattabi'an* with a single light *nun* vowelled with a kasra. This is the *nun* of the dual's nominative ending, not the emphatic nun. Therefore, on this reading, *la* must be a negation and not a prohibition, and the clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), with the *waw* being the *waw al-hal* (the waw of circumstance); because a present-tense circumstantial clause beginning with a negative particle may be connected with the *waw* or without it.

[p. 274]

﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea, and Pharaoh and his soldiers pursued them in insolence and enmity, until, when drowning overtook him, he said, "I believe that there is no deity except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of the Muslims."﴾

It is conjoined to the sentence ﴿And We revealed to Moses and his brother: "Settle your people in Egypt, in houses"﴾ [Yunus: 87]. It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) of the purpose onto the preliminary (tamhīd), meaning: We commanded them both to build those houses in preparation for the journey and for crossing the sea.

"Wa-jāwaznā" means: We caused them to cross the sea. The bāʾ is for transitivity (taʿdiya, making the verb transitive), meaning: We made them cross the sea, that is, We made them crossers of the sea. Its parallel occurred in Surat al-Aʿrāf. Their crossing of the sea necessarily implies their wading into it, because God made for them paths through the sea by which they passed.

"Atbaʿahum" means: overtook them. It is said: "tabiʿahu, fa-atbaʿahu," when one travels behind someone and catches up with him. From this is the verse ﴿then a piercing flame pursued him﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 10]. It has also been said that atbaʿa is a synonym of tabiʿa.

"Al-baghy" means injustice, the verbal noun of baghā. It occurred earlier at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and sin and injustice without right﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 33], in al-Aʿrāf.

"Al-ʿadw" is the verbal noun of ʿadā. It is transgression of limits in wrongdoing, and it is brought here to emphasise the injustice. It is conjoined because of the additional meaning it carries in wrongdoing, by way of the derivation of the verb ʿadā.

The meaning is: Pharaoh entered the sea seeking their traces, and he proceeded along those paths, wanting to encircle them and prevent them from travelling. His pursuit of them was an act of injustice and aggression, since he had no right whatsoever in it. The Children of Israel wished to leave the land of Pharaoh, and departing from one's country is not forbidden to anyone who has no right over him to remain there. The person of a homeland has a right to dwell in his homeland, so when he wishes to leave his homeland he has relinquished a right of his own, and a person may relinquish his own right.

[p. 275]

For this reason, in the pre-Islamic period, expulsion (al-khalʿ) was a punishment. In Islam, exile and banishment (al-nafy wa-l-taghrīb) are a penalty that may be imposed only on a legal ground (mūjib sharʿī). Confinement to a place was a punishment, and prison is one form of it. Therefore leaving one's homeland voluntarily is not aggression. When Pharaoh sought to prevent the Children of Israel from leaving, and he set out to overtake them in order to bring them back by force, he was in that act a wrongdoer and an aggressor, because he intended to compel them to remain, and because his purpose in this was to subjugate them.

"Ḥattā" here is inceptive (ibtidāʾiyya, introducing a new clause), because it is followed by the sudden "idhā" (fujāʾiyya, "when suddenly"). It marks the end point of the pursuit, meaning: his pursuit of them continued until the time when drowning overtook him. All the while he did not cease striving to catch them, until God delivered the Children of Israel, who crossed the sea, and God turned the surge of the water back upon Pharaoh and his soldiers, so they drowned, and Pharaoh perished by drowning. Thus the endpoint of the limit is the time indicated by "idhā," and the clause annexed to it is what follows it. In this there is an elliptical brevity (ījāz ḥadhf). The estimated sense is: "until drowning overtook him; so when drowning overtook him, he said, 'I believe.'" This is because the discourse is directed to the fact that the limit, namely the overtaking of him by drowning, is what stopped the pursuit. The limit is not his saying "I believe," although the two events were concurrent.

"Al-idrāk" means catching up and reaching the end of a journey. It indicates that drowning approached him gradually, through the terror of the sea and his struggle with the waves, while he still hoped for escape from it, and that he did not manifest belief until he despaired of salvation and became certain of death. That was because of his obstinacy in disbelief.

The construction of the sentence is concise, because it stands in place of five clauses:

A clause indicating that Pharaoh tried to catch up with the Children of Israel to the utmost extent possible and with hope of overtaking them.

And a clause indicating that he did not overtake them.

These two are derived from "ḥattā," and these two are a favour upon the Children of Israel.

And a clause indicating that the water covered him and he drowned. This is derived from his saying "idrākahu al-gharaq" (drowning overtook him), and it is a punishment for him and an honour for Moses, peace be upon him.

[p. 276]

And a clause indicating that nothing remained for him but belief in God, because the proofs of faith overpowered him. This is derived from the linking of the clause of his belief to the temporal adverb in His saying "idhā adrakahu al-gharaq" (when drowning overtook him). This is a virtue of faith, and that truth overcomes falsehood in the end.

And a clause indicating that he did not believe until he despaired of salvation, because of his obstinacy in disbelief; and despite that, God overpowered him. This is an admonition to the disbelievers and a manifestation of God's might, exalted is He.

The structure of the discourse has been built upon the clause "idhā adrakahu al-gharaq," and what accompanies it has been made as a means leading to it. Thus "ḥattā" was used to express the endpoint of the pursuit, and the endpoint was made his saying "I believe," because his pursuit of the Children of Israel was impelled by his rage against them for the sake of the religion their messenger brought, which was to bring them out of his land. Therefore his ultimate goal became his belief in their truth. For this reason he said "the One in whom the Children of Israel believe," to convey, together with his acknowledgement of God, his approval of the Children of Israel in what they had been guided to. He made the relative clause a path to his knowledge of God, and because he did not know the attributes specific to God except what the relative clause included, since he had not fully perceived Moses's call. For this reason he needed to add "and I am of the Muslims," because he used to hear from Moses the call to become a Muslim, so he uttered what he had heard and placed himself among the group to whom that description applies. For this reason he did not say "I have submitted" (aslamtu), but said "I am of the Muslims," meaning: what they are committed to is binding upon me. He expressed his faith in summary, because of the narrowness of the time for detail and because he did not know its details.

Later, in the commentary on the verse that follows this one, there will come a verification of the nature of Pharaoh's drowning and of what happened to the preservation of his body after his drowning.

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read "āmantu annahu" with the hamza of "annahu" open (fatḥ), on the assumption that the preposition bāʾ is omitted. Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read it with the hamza of "innahu" kasra, considering "inna" to occur at the beginning of a clause, and its clause to be a substitute (badal) for the clause "āmantu," with the object of the verb "āmantu" omitted, because the clause of the substitute indicates it.

[Page 277]

﴿Now? And you had rebelled before and were among the corrupters.﴾ ﴿So today We will save you in your body, that you may be a sign to those who come after you. And indeed, many of the people are heedless of Our signs.﴾

This is a continuation of a speech whose beginning has been omitted because the context indicates it; its implied form is: "Allah said." It is a response to his saying "I believe," because by that statement he intended to seek deliverance from drowning, acknowledging Allah's lordship, as though he were addressing Him with words. So Allah answered him with speech.

Allah said this speech to him through the tongue of the angel assigned to punish him, to despair him of deliverance in this world and in the Hereafter. That is the deliverance he had hoped for when he said "I believe," and so on to the end. For he did not believe except after he had truly accepted everything Moses had said, and he knew that what had befallen him was due to the wrath of Allah. He hoped that by his acknowledgment of Allah's oneness He would pardon him and save him from drowning. This is shown by Allah's words following his speech: ﴿So today We will save you in your body﴾, as will come.

The interrogative in ﴿الآنَ﴾ (al-Ān, "now") is one of denial (inkārī).

Al-Ān is an adverb of time governing a deleted verb indicated by his saying "I believe." The estimated form is: "Now you believe," i.e., "at this time." The verb is estimated to come after, because the adverb indicates it, and because the focus of the denial is the adverb.

The denial indicates that the time in which the denial is attached is not a time in which faith benefits, because the denying interrogative has the force of a negation. So the meaning is: "No faith now."

What is negated is faith that saves the one who possesses it in this world and in the Hereafter. It did not benefit him because he brought it at the time of the onset of death. That is a time in which the faith of an unbeliever is not accepted, nor is the repentance of a sinner, as was already explained at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now," nor for those who die while they are disbelievers﴾ [an-Nisā' 4:18].

Page 278

Al-Ān is a noun of time for the present period. It was already discussed at His words, exalted is He: ﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you﴾ [al-Anfāl 8:66], in Surat al-Anfal.

The clause ﴿And you had rebelled before and were among the corrupters﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the deleted object of tu'minu ("you believe"). It emphasizes what is in the interrogative of denial, for his belief at that moment is rejected. What adds to the denial is that its bearer had been disobedient to Allah and a corrupter of the religion that Allah sent to him, and a corrupter on earth through injustice, oppression, and the deception of sorcery.

The form ﴿وكُنْتَ مِنَ المُفْسِدِينَ﴾ ("and you were among the corrupters") is more eloquent in describing him with corruption than "and you were a corrupter" (mufsidan), as was mentioned just before. In proportion to the sins and corruption he had committed, the punishment upon him is made more severe.

The fa' in His words "fa-al-yawma" (so today) is the fa' of faṣīḥa (the eloquent fa', fā' al-faṣīḥa), which reveals a deleted condition implied in the speech by the context. The meaning is: "If you wish, by your faith after the passing of its time, that I save you from drowning, then today We will save you in your body." The speech runs in the manner of sarcasm (tahakkum). So the application of "saving" to bringing him out of the sea is a sarcastic metaphor (isti'āra tahakkumiyya).

Its justification is not pure sarcasm, as is usually the case with this type, but there is a relation of resemblance in it: his being brought to dry land complete with his armor resembles saving, yet it is the opposite of saving. So by resemblance it is a metaphor, and by oppositeness it is sarcasm.

The prepositional phrase in His words ﴿بِبَدَنِكَ﴾ (bi-badanika, "in your body") is a circumstantial element (ḥāl).

The more apparent view is that the bā' in His words ﴿بِبَدَنِكَ﴾ is extra (zā'ida), for emphasis, meaning to emphasize the sign of saving the body. So His words "badanika" have the sense of an appositive substitute (badal muṭābiq) of the kāf in nunajjīka (We save you). This is like the extra bā' in al-Ḥarīrī's words: "Then behold, he is Abū Zayd in his very person and his very [inner] essence" (fa-idhā huwa Abū Zayd bi-'aynihi wa-maynihi).

Al-Badan ("the body") is the physical form without a soul. This is a precaution against the supposition that the intended meaning is saving from drowning. The meaning is: "We save you while you are a body," as one says: "I entered upon him and behold, he was a corpse (juththa)." For if the intended meaning were not to restrict the matter to that state, there would be no reason for the eloquent speaker to add that qualifier.

Page 279

For every addition in eloquent speech is intended to convey an additional meaning; otherwise it would be superfluous in speech, and eloquent speech is measured, and the language of the Arabs is founded on the principle of concision (ījāz).

﴿وَلِمَن خَلْفَكَ﴾ (liman khalfaka) means "to those who come after you." Al-Warā' ("what is behind") is used here in the sense of what comes later and what remains, i.e., those who are not with you. By them are meant those of the Pharaohs who succeed him, and those with them of the priests and viziers. That is, "that his very self may be a sign that Allah is the victor over those who associated others with Him, and that Allah is greater and more dominant than Pharaoh and his gods in the belief of the Copts." For they would see Pharaoh, whom they regarded as a god, lying prostrate on the seashore, drowned. That is a death by which they cannot resort to deceit, claiming he was raised to heaven, or that he kept following the Children of Israel, or other such lies. For they used to claim that Pharaoh cannot be defeated, and that the Pharaohs, when they die, are only transported to the abode of eternity. For this reason they used to deceive the people, building tombs for him in the pyramids and depositing in them his clothing, food, furnishings, and the most precious of his possessions. So his death by drowning while pursuing his enemies is a death that cannot be interpreted away by any of that. Therefore his being a sign for those after him was made the reason for bringing him out of the depths of the water as a complete corpse, so that they are compelled to acknowledge that he drowned when they consider that sign.

Pharaoh did not lose all benefit from his faith, for Allah, in His wisdom, decreed for him that he come out of the depths of the water. So he did not remain in the water as food for the fish, but the waves cast him up. That is a state less disgraceful than the states of the rest of his army, and by it the benefit of what he had of faith was manifested through what he attained of belief at the end of his affairs.

The word ﴿فاليَوْمَ﴾ (al-yawm, "today") is used in the sense of ﴿الآنَ﴾ (al-Ān, "now"), because the name "yawm" is applied, metaphorically, to a portion of the time of the present, by a relation of whole and part ('alāqat al-kulliyya wa-l-juz'iyya).

The clause ﴿وإنَّ كَثِيرًا مِنَ النّاسِ عَنْ آياتِنا لَغافِلُونَ﴾ ("And indeed, many of the people are heedless of Our signs") is a concluding appendage (tadhyīl) to the admonition of the polytheists. The waw is parenthetical (wāw i'tirāḍiyya), or the waw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl).

Page 280

What is meant by it is: to repel the suspicion of deficiency in the signs of Allah, when many people are deprived of being guided by them. For they are in themselves indications of guidance, whether or not some people benefit from them. So the shortcoming is on their part.

Know that this verse is the clearest verse in the Qur'an in indicating that Pharaoh, to whom Moses was sent and who pursued the Children of Israel after their departure from Egypt, was afflicted by drowning. The verse in Surat al-A'raf and the verse in Surat al-Baqara also point to it.

This Pharaoh is Merneptah II (Minfitāh al-Thānī), who is called (Mayrnbtā), with a Persian bā', or (Minfitāḥ), or (Minīftā). He was the son of Ramesses II, known to the Greeks by the name (Sesostris), one of the kings of the nineteenth dynasty of the Pharaonic dynasties, and they were around the year 1491 BC.

Ibn Jurayj said: "This Pharaoh was short and reddish." There is no doubt that Minephtah II died drowned in the sea, and that his body was recovered after drowning and buried in the Valley of the Kings in Upper Egypt. The archaeologists reported that his tomb was found there, and that points to His words, exalted is He: ﴿So today We will save you in your body, that you may be a sign to those who come after you.﴾ The existence of a tomb for him, if it is established on a firm basis, does not contradict his having died drowned, although the historians of the Copts did not address the manner of his death. That is only because the priests agreed on concealing it, lest doubt enter the nation about what the priests glorify every Pharaoh with, of the attributes of descent from the gods.

His daughter named (Tawsiyar) succeeded him in the kingdom of Egypt, because he left her and a young son.

The mention of Pharaoh's drowning has come in the Torah in chapter fourteen of the Book of Exodus, in phrases varying in clarity and obscurity.

Among the subtleties of the Qur'an is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So today We will save you in your body, that you may be a sign to those who come after you﴾, which is an expression that has not come with its like in what has been written of the reports about Pharaoh. Indeed it is among the scientific miracles of the Qur'an, Page 281 since the sign applied exactly to the historical reality. The apparent view is that the waves cast his body onto the western shore of the Red Sea, where those who went out tracing his traces found him, from among those who remained after him in the city of Egypt, when they were slow to see his return and the return of his army. So they lifted him up to the city, and he became a lesson for them.
