Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 93:

﴿We had certainly settled the Children of Israel in a secure abode, and provided them with good things. They did not differ until knowledge had come to them. Indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that about which they used to differ.﴾

This is a continuation (ʿaṭf) of the preceding sentences, since the purpose of all those sentences is to admonish the disbelievers among the Arabs by means of the circumstances of the nations before them, in that their disbelief resembles theirs, and by means of the kinds of punishment that befell those nations as recompense for their disbelief. As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Are your disbelievers better than those? [Al-Qamar: 43]﴾

When God struck the example of evil, He followed it with the example of righteousness, namely the state of those who affirmed the Messenger and followed him, and how their final outcome was good, so that the difference between the destinies of the two groups would become clear: a Messenger came to them, one group believed in him and another group disbelieved in him. This was meant as an encouragement to the polytheists to believe, and as good news for the believers among the people of Mecca.

The Children of Israel here refers to the people spoken of in His words: ﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea [Yunus: 90]﴾, and the order of the report requires that God settled them in a secure abode immediately after their crossing of the sea and the drowning of Pharaoh and his armies. After that they entered the wilderness of al-Tih, felt secure for themselves, and devoted themselves to purifying their souls and setting their affairs in order. They were provided with manna and quails, and were given victory over the nations that confronted them, seeking to prevent them from possessing the good land. So they continued to ascend the stages of goodness and blessing, and this is the meaning of "a secure abode" (mubawwa' sidq).

And the provision (al-rizq) is "of the good things."

The meaning of ﴿They did not differ﴾ is: those (the first generation) did not differ, nor did those who came after them from their sons and descendants.

Al-tabawwu' (settling) has been mentioned just above, and al-mubawwa' is the place of settling, i.e., al-baw' (return), and what is meant is the dwelling, as has been mentioned. Its being annexed to ṣidq is an annexation of the qualified noun to the qualifier (idafat al-mawsuf ila al-sifa), and it is permissible for al-mubawwa' to be a mīmī verbal noun. Ṣidq here means "pure of its kind." It was mentioned earlier at His words: ﴿that they have a sure footing (qadam ṣidq) with their Lord [Yunus: 2]﴾. What is meant by mubawwa' al-ṣidq is what God opened for them of the lands of Palestine and what is in them of fertility and abundance. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We made the people who had been oppressed inheritors of the eastern and western parts of the earth, which We had blessed. And the fair word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel because of their patience [Al-A'raf: 137]﴾.

The clause ﴿They did not differ﴾ as a consequence (tafri') of "We settled" and what is conjoined to it is a consequence of praise for them, in that they were thankful for that blessing and did not disbelieve in it, as the polytheists disbelieved, those whom God settled in a sacred, secure sanctuary to which the fruits of every thing are brought, yet they made partners with God and then disbelieved in the Messenger sent to them. So there occurred in the speech an ellipsis by omission (ijaz hadhf). Its estimated meaning is: they were thankful for the blessing, followed the commands of the prophets, and did not oppose that except after knowledge had come to them.

Al-ikhtilaf is an ifti'al form, by which is intended the intensity of mutual opposition (shiddat al-takhalluf), and no bare verb is known for the root of this meaning. It is derived from the solid noun khalf, meaning "behind," so it is determined that the addition of the taʾ is for intensification (li-l-mubalagha), like iktasaba being an intensification of kasaba. Thus it is taken to mean opposition (khilaf) of an intensified kind, which is the contradiction of what the religion brought and what the Messenger ﷺ called to. This is the fitting interpretation for the context, for the speech is praise followed by a limit that indicates that what comes after the limit is the end of the praise and an affirmation of blame, since He negated disagreement from them up to a limit that indicates that disagreement occurred from them at that limit. So those who did not differ are those whom God settled in the secure abode. Then others came after them until there came those who differed concerning the prophets. These are the ones to whom the pronoun of the nominative in His words ﴿knowledge had come to them﴾ refers.

[Page 283]

And the knowledge that came to them may be what the prophets brought to them of God's law, and they did not act upon what they had brought, and the greatest of that is their denial of Muhammad, may the prayers and peace of God be upon him.

From Ibn 'Abbas: they are the Jews who were in the time of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Before his mission they used to affirm a prophet who would come. When knowledge came to them, which is the Qur'an, they differed about affirming Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are Qurayza, al-Nadir and Banu Qaynuqa'.

It is also permissible for knowledge to be the Qur'an, and on this view the meaning of the verse is like the meaning of His words: ﴿Indeed the religion with God is Islam. And those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after knowledge had come to them, out of envy among themselves [Al 'Imran: 19]﴾, and His words: ﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not separate except after the clear evidence had come to them [Al-Bayyinah: 4]﴾. For the clear evidence is Muhammad ﷺ, because before this is His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not going to desist until the clear evidence came to them [Al-Bayyinah: 1]﴾, ﴿a Messenger from God, reciting purified pages [Al-Bayyinah: 2]﴾, and the verse. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it [Al-Baqarah: 89]﴾.

This interpretation is the one fitting the particle ḥattā (until) in His words: ﴿They did not differ until knowledge came to them﴾.

The placement of "they did not differ" followed by the limit (al-ghaya) indicates that what comes after the limit is the end of the state of gratitude, meaning: they remained in that abode and in that blessing until they differed, and so their blessing was taken away, for God deprived them of their homelands.

The clause ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) and a warning (tawaʿud), and what is intended by it is that those people were a folk who passed away with what they had done, and their affair is with their Lord, like His saying: ﴿That is a nation that has passed away; for them is what they earned, and for you is what you earned [Al-Baqarah: 134]﴾. In it is an allusion that those present today should consider the means of deliverance from error and from falling into accountability on the Day of Resurrection.

Bayna (between) is a adverb of place for the judgment derived from the verb yaqḍī, so the act of judgment is as if it runs between them, because it is connected with clarifying the true from the false.

[Page 284]

The pronoun in baynahum refers to what is understood from His words "they did not differ": the existence of an opponent (bi-kasr al-lam, one who differs) and an opposed party (bi-fath al-lam, one who is differed with).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verses 94–95:

﴿So if you, [O Muhammad], are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, then ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you. The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord, so never be among the doubters.﴾ ﴿And never be among those who deny the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of the context of the stories that Allah made an example for the people of Makkah and a admonition through what befell their like. By this consequence the discourse moves from one mode to another, and both are an allusion (ta'rid) directed at the deniers. The previous mode is an allusion warning them lest what befell the similar nations befall them. This following mode is an allusion directed at them through the testimony of the People of the Book concerning those events, and what the earlier scriptures contain of the announcement of the message of Muhammad ﷺ. Thus what is meant by "what We have sent down" (ma anzalna) is the revelation from which this discourse branches, namely what was sent down in this surah of stories.

The verse admits of two meanings, and no others are sound. The first is that the particle "in" (fi), which indicates it, remains in its literal sense of containment (zarfiyyah), and "doubt" is used figuratively to mean its people. The meaning is: "If you are among a people of doubt concerning what We have sent down to you," that is, they doubt the occurrence of these stories, just as one says "he entered into the strife," meaning among its people. The meaning of "then ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you" is: ask the People of the Book a question of confirmation and of calling to witness about the nature of those reports, that they would tell the same as what you have told them. Thus the doubt will depart from the souls of the doubters, since it is not conceivable that you colluded with the People of the Book to agree on one description of those reports. So the purpose of the verse is to establish proof against the polytheists through the testimony of the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, to cut off their excuse.

The second meaning is that "in" (fi) is used in a figurative sense of containment, like the one in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So be not in doubt concerning what these worship﴾ [Hud: 109]. The address in this discourse is directed to the Prophet ﷺ in the manner of allusion, with the aim that the polytheists would hear it, so that the import of the discourse would settle in their souls more firmly than if it had been delivered to them directly. This is a method of indirect address that wise people and men of good character follow when the one meant by the speech is likely to be averse to it, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If you should associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely be nullified, and you will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. Or when there is in that address a fitting consideration for the one toward whom the speech is intended, as in the story of the two litigants who came to Dawud, mentioned in Surah Sad.

Both possibilities correspond with His saying: ﴿ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you﴾, for it requires that the matter asked about is something the People of the Book do not conceal, and that they bear witness to it. This is only fitting for the stories that agree with what is in their books, for they do not scruple to make them known and to bear witness to them. Any possibility other than these two creates difficulty with some part of the verse and implies that the addressee is the Prophet ﷺ because of His saying "before you."

The address pronouns do not refer to everyone who could be addressed, because His saying "what We have sent down to you" would contradict that except through forced interpretation.

The clause ﴿ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you﴾ is a response to the condition by reference to what the root of the word "ask" implies, namely that they answer with what removes doubt. Thereby the necessary connection between the condition and the response is completed, as indicated by the clause ﴿The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord﴾.

Ḥafṣ and others read fa-s'al (فاسألْ) with a hamzat al-wasl, a sukun on the sin, and a hamza after the sin. Ibn Kathir and al-Kisa'i read fa-sal (فَسَلْ) with a fatha on the sin, without the hamzat al-wasl, and with the hamza after the sin omitted, as the lightened form of sa'ala.

The clause ﴿The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord﴾ is a resumed statement (isti'naf bayani), answering a question arising from the condition and its response, as if the hearer says: "If you ask them, what will be the result?" So it is said: ﴿The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord﴾.

[Page 286]

Since the aim of this is that the hearers know it by way of allusion, not that the Messenger, peace be upon him, know it, because he has no need to be informed that he is upon the truth, the clause is joined with two emphatic particles: the lam of oath and qad, to repel the denial of those alluded to.

By this, the consequence ﴿so never be among the doubters﴾ is also an allusion to the polytheists, that they are in a state from which one must beware of becoming like them.

Imtira' (امتراء) means doubt concerning what has no basis for doubt. It is therefore more specific than shakk (doubt).

Likewise He joined ﴿And never be among those who deny the signs of Allah﴾, which is more explicit in alluding to them, ﴿lest you be among the losers﴾. This implies that they are losers. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿If you should associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely be nullified, and you will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. The sum of the meaning is: If you are doubting the truth of what We have sent down to Muhammad concerning what befell the deniers before you, then ask the People of the Book, and they will inform you that this is true. The truth has certainly come to you from the Lord of Muhammad ﷺ, so do not be doubters, and do not deny the signs of Allah, lest you be losers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 96–97:

﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has come into effect will not believe﴾ ﴿Even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment﴾

The connection of this verse with the one before it is shown by what we explained of the previous verse. When there had been an allusion to the polytheists who doubted the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ), and testimony was invoked against them regarding his truthfulness through the testimony of the People of the Book, this was followed by the statement that they belong to the group of those upon whom the word of Allah has come into effect, that they would not believe. Thus the argument does not benefit them, because they are people of obstinate denial, and they are not seekers of the truth, since the natural disposition (fitrah) upon which their minds were created is not receptive to the realities of faith. Those who do not believe in the signs that come are among those whom Allah knows will not believe; these are their indicators. This is presented in the manner of despairing of their faith.

Page 287
The meaning of ḥaqqat (حَقَّتْ) is "became established" (thabatat).
ʿAlā (عَلى) is for elevation in the figurative sense, which is the firm establishment of the act to which it is attached. What is meant by "the words of Allah" is the command of creation (amr al-takwin). The word "words" (kalimāt) is plural with regard to the fact that those to whom it applies are many people, so that each one of them has a word that becomes binding upon him.

Those other than Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read "kalimat rabbika" (كَلِمَةُ رَبِّكَ) in the singular, with regard to the generic sense, since a word becomes binding upon every nation. This statement is an admonition to the polytheists. Others have said: it is also a warning against their becoming a manifestation of those upon whom the word of wretchedness (kalimat al-shiqwah) has come into effect, and a warning that the punishment is about to descend upon them.

Thus, according to this interpretation, the relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) refers to a known group, and the whole sentence is resumptive (mustaʾnafah). The particle inna is for emphasis, its intended purpose being confirmation, meaning: there is no doubt that these are among those, their matter has become clear, and there is despair of their faith.

It is also possible to make the sentence serve as a justification (taʿlīl) for the preceding narratives, in which case it has the status of a concluding remark (tadhyīl). The relative pronoun then carries a general sense encompassing all the nations that are like the nations spoken of. In this case inna is merely for drawing attention to the report, and it conveys causation and connection, and it dispenses with the resumptive fāʾ, like the one in the verse of Bashshār:

"Indeed, that success lies in early rising"
As has been mentioned more than once. In the verse there would also be another allusion to the polytheists.

"Law" (even if) is a particle of emphasis (waṣliyyah lil-mubālaghah), meaning: they will not believe even if every sign comes to them, so how much more so if only some of the signs come to them.

"Kull" (every) is used in the sense of abundance, a usage that is frequent in the Qur'an, as will come at His words—exalted is He—﴿and upon every lean camel﴾ [al-Hajj: 27] in Surat al-Hajj, and His words: ﴿and He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31] in Surat al-Baqarah. That is, even if many signs came to them, resembling in their multitude the totality of all signs whose occurrence is possible. A similar usage has been mentioned just before.

Page 288
"Seeing the punishment" is a metonymy for its descent upon them.

The meaning is: they will not believe except at a time when faith will not benefit them, because the descent of the punishment is the beginning of their requital for their disbelief, and after requital has begun there is no pardon.

Among the blessings of this religion is that those who disbelieved in it, Allah has guided them before a punishment descended upon them.

[Page 288]

The *fa'* in ﴿Then why was there not a town that believed, so that its faith benefited it?﴾ is for deriving a rebuke from the fact that the people of the towns refused to believe in the messengers before the punishment came upon them. It is an information that those upon whom the word of God was justified, that they would not believe, will not believe until they see the punishment. The people of the towns are among those upon whom the word was justified, that they would not believe. The purpose of mentioning the people of the towns is an indirect reference (*ta'rid*) to the intended addressees, who are the people of Makkah, since they are a people of a town. This was like a transition by indirect allusion (*takhallus bi-l-ta'rid*) to those specifically meant, and it leads to the mention of the people of Yunus, since they too were a people of a town.

*Lawla* is a particle that comes with several meanings, among them reproach. Here it is used in its implication of reproach as a metonymy (*kinaya*) for rebuke, because the people of the towns have already passed away. The original meaning of *lawla* is *tahdid* (urging), which is the demand for an action with insistence. When it enters upon a verb whose occurrence has already become impossible, it is used for rebuke, blame and reproach for missing it. What follows it in this usage is a past-tense verb, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And why, when you heard it, did you not say, "It is not for us to speak of this"?﴾ (al-Nur: 16). When the speech containing *lawla* is directed to someone other than the doer of the action that it enters upon, it is used to express wonder at the state of the one being spoken about, like His saying: ﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses against him?﴾ (al-Nur: 13).

[Page 289]

And His saying: ﴿So why, when Our punishment came upon them, did they not humble themselves?﴾ (al-An'am: 43). This verse is even clearer in that regard because of the presence of *kana*, which indicates past tense and completion. The intended meaning is an indirect reference that the polytheists of Makkah are about to be on the same ways as the people of the towns. He, exalted is He, says: ﴿Not one town that We destroyed before them believed. Will they then believe?﴾ (al-Anbiya': 6). The parallel of this verse in usage and meaning is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Why were there not, among the generations before you, people of remnant who forbade corruption on earth, except a few of those whom We saved from among them?﴾ (Hud: 116). This is an indirect reference urging the people of Makkah to believe before the punishment descends.

What is derived from the reports concerning the people of Yunus is that they hastened to believe after Yunus had left them, anticipating the descent of the punishment and before it came down upon them. This is evidence that God's dealing with them is not contrary to how He dealt with others from among the people of the towns, and that they were not specially privileged. For this reason, their exclusion is not a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*).

Since the speech is a rebuke to the people of the towns who turned away from the call of the messengers, and an indirect warning against what they fell into, the speech is an affirmative statement. The occurrence of "a town" (*qarya*), which is indefinite, in the context of affirmation, conveys generality by the indication of the context, like the saying of al-Hariri: "O people of this abode, may you be protected from harm," meaning every harm, not a specific harm. It also conveys generality by the indication of the exception, for it is the criterion of generality. This exception is from an affirmative statement, and for this reason ﴿except the people of Yunus﴾ is in the accusative case. This is the way of explaining the verse. This was the view of al-'Ukbari in his *I'rab al-Qur'an* and of al-Kawashi in *al-Takhlis*. The majority of the commentators, however, treated the clause ﴿Then why was there not a town that believed﴾ as having the force of a negation, and treated the exception as disjunctive and in the accusative, with no need for that.

The clause ﴿when they believed﴾ (*lamma amanu*) is a resumptive clause (*mustani'a*) explaining the general meaning of the exception. The verse hints that the people of Makkah are treated by God in the same way as the people of Yunus, since they believed when they saw the punishment. This was their state when they heard of the coming of the army of the conquest, against which they had no power in number or equipment, so that an annihilating punishment was about to befall them, had they not hastened to believe on the day of the conquest. Then the Prophet ﷺ said to them: "You are the freed ones."

[Page 290]

The people of Yunus are the people of the town of Nineveh in the lands of Iraq. They were a mixture of Assyrians and Jews who had been in captivity under the kings of Babylon after Nebuchadnezzar. Yunus was sent to them at the beginning of the eighth century BCE. The mention and biography of Yunus has already been given in Surah al-An'am.

When the people of Nineveh denied him, he threatened them that their city would be overthrown after forty days, and he went out of the city angry at them. When he went out, they feared the descent of the punishment upon them, so they repented, believed in God, and God accepted their faith and did not punish them. It is reported that they saw a black cloud after thirty-five days from the time Yunus, peace be upon him, had threatened them with the arrival of the punishment, and they knew that it was the forerunner of the punishment. So they believed and submitted to God, exalted is He, and He withheld the punishment from them. What befell Yunus, peace be upon him, in his departure from that town, namely his being swallowed by the fish, will come in Surah al-Anbiya'.

*Al-kashf* is the removal of what covers something, and it is here a metaphor for lifting. The intended meaning is the decree of lifting and the annulment of the punishment before it occurred, so it is expressed by "removal" (*kashf*), treating the nearness of occurrence as occurrence itself.

*Al-khizy* is humiliation and disgrace. The attribution of the punishment to disgrace (*idafat al-'adhab ila al-khizy*) may be explanatory, since all punishment is disgrace, for it is a state of destruction that is not customary. When God decrees it for a people, He intends to humiliate them. It may also be a real attribution for specification, and the meaning of disgrace would be the state imagined from its descent, namely the atrocity of the condition for those who witness it, such as being swallowed by the earth, burning, or drowning. The most atrocious disgrace is what comes at the hands of men like them, namely the punishment of the sword that befell the leaders of Quraysh on the day of Badr, and which nearly befell all of Quraysh on the day of the conquest of Makkah, from which God saved them as He saved the people of Yunus.

[Page 291]

The phrase ﴿in the life of this world﴾ is a qualifier of ﴿the punishment of disgrace﴾, to indicate that the punishment that descends upon disbelieving nations is a retribution in this world, and after it there is a requital in the Hereafter, and that the nations that were not punished in this world have had the punishment of the Hereafter stored up for them.

*Al-tamti'* is granting respite.

The indefiniteness of *hin* (a period) is because it differs according to the differing terms of each of them. What is meant by it is enjoyment of life, not the removal of the punishment, because after their death they are safe from the punishment, since they had believed and were sincere.

Perhaps the wisdom in the salvation of the people of Yunus is represented in two matters:

The first: God knew that their denial of Yunus, peace be upon him, at the beginning of his call was not born of determination in disbelief or contempt for God's greatness, but was doubt about the truthfulness of Yunus, peace be upon him. Perhaps that is because they were still holding some remnant of the law of Musa, peace be upon him, and they had only altered and deviated from the path of faith in ways that God knows. For in Nineveh there were many of the captives of the Children of Israel who had been in captivity to the Assyrians, as you have just learned. When Yunus, peace be upon him, threatened them with punishment after forty days and they saw its signs after thirty-five days, they were guided and believed with sincere faith.

The second: when Yunus, peace be upon him, had committed the lapse of anger, he had mixed into his call something of self-interest, even if it was for the benefit of the religion. So God decreed the faith of his people because He knew the perfection of faith, patience and submission to God. This is a rebuke and discipline between him and his Lord. For this reason the Messenger of God ﷺ warned the community against the thought that what happened to Yunus, peace be upon him, of anger and punishment diminishes his rank. He ﷺ said: "No one should say, 'I am better than Yunus ibn Matta,'" meaning in the validity of the messengership, not in preference within it.

The situation of the people of Makkah was like the situation of the people of Yunus, in that they hastened to believe merely upon the entry of the army of the conquest into Makkah, and before they fell into the grip of captivity. For this reason, 'Abd Allah ibn Khatal was not saved from among them, because he did not come believing before the Muslims could overpower him, and clinging to the curtains of the Ka'ba did not benefit him, because that clinging is not faith, but is rather a practice of seeking protection (*'awadh*) from the pre-Islamic period, which Islam nullified when the Prophet ﷺ said: "The sanctuary does not protect a disobedient person." We have clarified this at the end of Surah Ghafir, at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they saw Our punishment, they said, "We believe in God alone"﴾ (Ghafir: 84), to the end of the surah, so refer to it.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 10, Verse 99:**

﴿Had your Lord willed, all those on earth would have believed, all of them together. Would you then compel people until they become believers?﴾

This is an conjunction (*'atf*) on the sentence ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has come into effect will not believe﴾ [Yunus: 96], serving to console the Prophet (ﷺ) for what he encountered from his people. It is also a concluding generalization (*tadhyil*, a summarizing appendix) to what preceded it, namely the comparison of the situation of the Quraysh with the Prophet (ﷺ) to the situation of the people of Noah, the people of Moses, and the people of Yunus. This sentence is like a general premise for the sentence that follows it, which is ﴿Would you then compel people...﴾, a consequence (*mufarra'a*) of the first sentence, and it is the intended purpose of the consolation.

"Al-nas" (the people) means the Arabs, or the people of Makkah among them. This is an indication that they are the intended audience of the narration of the past stories, as we explained at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And recite to them the news of Noah﴾ [Yunus: 71].

The emphasis with *kulluhum* (all of them) is to make explicit the generality already implied by *man* (whoever), the relative pronoun, since it denotes generality. The emphasis with *jami'an* (together) is for the added removal of the possibility of a customary (*'urfi*) generality rather than a literal (*haqiqi*) one.

The meaning is: Had God willed, He would have made the perceptive faculties of the people equal, inclined toward goodness, so that they would be equal in accepting guidance and in sound reflection.

*Law* (had) indicates the negation of its consequent because of the negation of its condition. So the meaning is: but He did not will that, and so His wisdom required that He create the minds of people affected and moved by the influences of differing in the perception of realities, so they did not agree upon belief. And it was not for any soul to believe except when the constitution of its intellect had been completed in what prepares it for sound reflection, for good awareness of the call to goodness, and for overcoming misguidance in acknowledging the truth.

The sentence ﴿Would you then compel people﴾ and so on is a consequence of the one before it, because when it was established that God's will was not connected with the agreement of people upon belief in God, there followed a denial of what is almost an attempt to bring about the belief of all of them.

The interrogation in ﴿Would you then compel people﴾ is denunciatory (*inkari*). It places the Prophet (ﷺ), because of his eagerness for the belief of the people of Makkah and his urgent striving for that by every suitable means, in the position of one who attempts to compel them to believe, so that this placement results in his being denounced for it.

Because this intense eagerness is the locus of the placement and the target of the denunciation, the subject was placed before the predicate verb, so it says ﴿Would you then compel people﴾ rather than saying "Would you compel people" or "Are you a compeller of people." This is because placing the subject before such a predicate indicates the strengthening of the judgment, and thus it indicates the strengthening of the occurrence of compulsion from the Prophet (ﷺ), so that this strengthening becomes the locus of denunciation. This is an allusive (*ta'rid*) praise of the Prophet (ﷺ) and an excuse for him for their not responding to him, and one who has exerted his utmost is entitled to be excused.

The placing of the subject here does not indicate restriction (*takhsis*, i.e., *qasr*), because the context is not suitable for considering restriction, since merely placing the Prophet (ﷺ) in the position of one who could compel people to believe is sufficient to indicate the comparison of his eagerness for their belief to the eagerness of one who could compel them to it. What occurred in *al-Kashshaf* regarding an indication of the meaning of exclusivity is not convincing, because the indicator of strengthening is clear, as al-Sakkaki indicated.

*Al-ikrah* (compulsion) means coercion and forcing.

[Page 293]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 100:

[Page 294]
﴿And it is not for any soul to believe except by the permission of Allah, and He places defilement upon those who do not reason.﴾
It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿Then will you compel the people [to become] believers?﴾ [Yunus: 99], to confirm its content, because its content is a denial that the Prophet ﷺ could compel people to faith, since it is Allah who has the power to do that.

It is also permissible for the waw to be a circumstantial (ḥāl) waw referring to the pronoun of the addressee, meaning: how can you compel people to faith, when the situation is that no soul can believe except by Allah's permission for it to believe?

The "permission" (idhn) here is the permission of creative decree (idhn takwīn wa taqdīr). He created the soul prepared to accept the truth, distinguishing between truth and falsehood, between what is right and what is corrupt, able through sound reflection to reach knowledge of what should be followed and what should not, empowered through the soundness of its will to restrain the call of desire and fleeting interests, and to follow the call of truth and lasting consequence. So when guidance is directed to it, guidance takes effect within it.

This meaning of permission is alluded to by His words in contrast to it: ﴿and He places defilement upon those who do not reason﴾. He thus set this state against the state of those who do not reason, and so it is known that the state of faith is the state of those who reason. The verse ﴿Had your Lord willed, all who are on earth would have believed﴾ [Yunus: 99] clarifies that the non-belief of those who do not believe is due to Allah not willing their faith. And this verse clarifies that the faith of those who believe is by Allah's willing their faith. Both point back to the decree of creation (taqdīr al-takwīn) in souls and minds.

The word rijs (defilement): its essential meaning is filth and corruption. Here it is applied to disbelief, because it is a filth of the soul. The indicator (qarīna) is that it is set in opposition to faith, like the opposition in His words: ﴿As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith﴾ [al-Tawba: 124], up to His words ﴿and it has increased them in defilement upon their defilement﴾ [al-Tawba: 125]. The meaning is: and He inflicts
[Page 295]
disbelief upon those who do not reason. What is intended is the negation of sound reason, that is, those whose minds do not guide them to perceiving the truth and who do not use their minds to reflect on the evidences.
The particle ʿalā here is for figurative elevation (al-istiʿlāʾ al-majāzī), used to denote control (al-tamakkun).

Al-Jumhur read ﴿wa-yajʿalu al-rijs﴾ with the third-person yāʾ, the pronoun referring back to the name of Majesty (Allah) preceding it. Abu Bakr, on the authority of ʿĀṣim, read it as najʿalu with the first-person plural nūn of majesty.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 101:

﴿Say: Look at what is in the heavens and the earth. But signs and warnings do not avail a people who do not believe.﴾

This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) arising from His words: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them together. Would you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ [Yunus: 99], and so on. He divided the people into two groups: believers and disbelievers. That is, call them to look into the proofs of divine unity and to guide them toward acquiring the causes of faith and dispelling the veils of disbelief. This is done by guiding them to reflect upon and draw inferences from the conditions of existing things around man and their changing states that point to divine unity, such as the bodies of the stars, the measures of their courses, the conditions of light and darkness, the winds, the clouds and the rain, and likewise the seas and the mountains.

The sentence is opened with "Say" (qul) to draw attention to its content.

He generalized "what is in the heavens and the earth" so that every soul may turn to what is closest to it and easiest for it to infer from.

The word "look" (nazar) here is used in a sense that suits both mental contemplation (nazar qalbi) and visual observation (nazar basari). For this reason it was diverted from operating as one of the two verbs (governing two objects), so that it would not be restricted to one of them. Thus an interrogative that suspends (mu'allaq) both verbs was placed after it, such that the verb "look" applies to both equally, and it became suitable for both the literal and the figurative meanings. This is among the purposes of the Qur'an.

"Wa-madha" (and what) here means "alladhi" (which), and "ma" is interrogative. "Dha" originally is a demonstrative noun, and when it comes after "ma" it takes the place of a relative pronoun (ism mawsul). The phrase ﴿fi al-samawati wa al-ard﴾ ("in the heavens and the earth") stands in place of the relative clause. The original structure of the expression was: "What is this in the heavens and the earth?", meaning: what is pointed to while being in the heavens and the earth. Its use became frequent until it came to mean "what is it that". The intended meaning is: look at what guides you to the answer to this question. Every thing that has a state is intended by the rational contemplation, when it is construed in the form of two objects, as in: "Look at the sun rising," and "Look at the cloud raining," and so on. And every thing that is itself a sign is intended by visual observation, as in: "Look at the earth's growth after its barrenness," which is a sign of the occurrence of resurrection. So "dha," when it takes the place of the relative noun, becomes one of the forms of generality, encompassing all bodies and their accidents that indicate the unity of God and His wisdom. Especially included is reflection upon the character of the Prophet ﷺ, the beginnings of his call, and contemplation of what he brought. All of that is evidence of his perfection and truthfulness.

The answer to the imperative has been omitted in the speech, since the command follows the causes of faith. The estimate is: "Look, and you will see signs leading to faith."

The clause ﴿And signs do not avail﴾ is a parenthetical (mu'taridah) sentence, appended to the sentence ﴿Look at what is in the heavens and the earth.﴾ It may be that it completes the saying of the speech (maqul al-qawl) of what the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to say to them, and it may be a resumptive statement of speech from God, Exalted. The meaning: convey to them what you were commanded to convey, and that signs do not avail a people who do not believe, that is, those whose souls God has made unable to believe. Since His saying ﴿Look at what is in the heavens and the earth﴾ indicates that these are signs, as was mentioned earlier, the expression "signs" fits well here. So the meaning of ﴿And signs do not avail﴾ is: and what is in the heavens and the earth does not avail a people who do not believe. The use of "signs" is like explicit mention in the place of a pronoun. "Warnings" (nudhur) was added and coordinated with "signs" for increased generality in this sentence, so that it has a broader indication than the preceding one, serving as a concluding remark (tadhyil) for it. This is because the Qur'an came to people with argument and with warning; then it recorded against this group that neither signs and proofs take effect in them, nor warnings and admonitions.

The phrase ﴿a people who do not believe﴾ indicates that the absence of faith from them is a description by which they are known, and that it is firmly settled in their souls. For the bringing in of the word "people" here, though it could be replaced by another word, indicates that the attribute mentioned after it is among the constituents of their peoplehood, since it has become one of their characteristics. This differs from saying "those who do not believe." Do you not see the saying of al-'Anbari:

"A people, when evil shows its molars against them, they rush to it in groups and individually."

That is: a people whose disposition is this. This was discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164], up to His saying: ﴿are signs for a people who reason﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164], in Surat al-Baqarah. It was also mentioned in this surah more than once just before. It is more eloquent here, because the expression was diverted from the pronoun. This is among the marvels of inimitability here.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verses 102–103:

﴿Are they waiting for anything but the like of the days of those who passed away before them? Say: "Wait, then; I am with you among those who wait."﴾ ﴿Then We shall save Our messengers and those who believed. Thus it is incumbent upon Us: We shall save the believers.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of the statement ﴿And signs and warnings avail not﴾ [Yunus: 101], in view of what it contains of the mention of warnings. It is an address from Allah, exalted is He, to His Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: it follows from their failure to benefit from the signs and warnings, and from their persistence, that he should be asked about them: "What are they waiting for?" And the answer is that they are only waiting for the like of what befell those before them, whose stories were related in the preceding verses. The interrogative with hal (هَلْ) is used because it conveys the affirmation of the question, and this is in view of the affirmation of what is asked about, and that it is deserving of an answer with affirmation.

The interrogative is a figurative (majaz) usage of mockery and denial (tahakkumi inkari). They are treated as those who wait for something to come to them so that they may believe, and there is nothing fit for them to wait for except the descent of the like of the days of those who passed away before them, in which they perished.

The interrogative has been given the meaning of negation by the evidence of the exceptive construction (al-istithna' al-mufarragh). The implied sense is: "Are they waiting for anything? They are not waiting except for the like of the days of those who passed away before them."

The word "days" (ayyam) is applied to the great events that occur within them. From this is the usage "the days of the Arabs" (ayyam al-'Arab) for battles. The clause ﴿Say: "Wait, then"﴾ is a consequence of the clause ﴿Are they waiting﴾. "Say" (qul) is inserted between the consequent and what it follows in order to increase emphasis, and in order to shift from the address of Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) to the address of the Messenger (ﷺ) to his people. By this, the consequence occurs between two statements of differing speakers, resembling the connective of instruction (ʿatf al-talqin) found in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: "And from my offspring?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. Moreover, the difference between the speech of Allah and the speech of the Messenger (ﷺ) in the context of revelation and conveyance is a weak difference, since both return to one speech. This is a rare placement for the consequential fa'.

By this arrangement a wonderful brevity (ijaz) is achieved, for by the consequence it is regarded as arising from the speech of Allah, exalted is He. It is as if Allah conveyed it to the Prophet (ﷺ), and then commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) to convey it to his people; so he has nothing but conveyance. It also contains Allah's promise to His Prophet that he will see what punishment awaits them, so it is a threat, and it also contains victory over them. He will make this explicit in His saying: ﴿Then We shall save Our messengers﴾.

The clause ﴿I am with you among those who wait﴾ is a explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) arising from the clause "wait", because it provokes the question of one who asks: "Here we are waiting, and what are you doing?" This is used as a metonymy (kinaya) for his expectation of victory, since it is not thought of him that he waits for evil; so it is determined that he waits for the opposite of what befalls them. The "with" (ma'iyya) is in the root of waiting, not in what results from the waiting.

Ma'a (مَعَ) is an emphatic circumstantial (hal mu'akkida). "Among those who wait" (min al-muntaziriin) is the predicate of inna, and its meaning is the meaning of ma'a in the sense of the referent: "the waiters" are the addressees who are waiting.

﴿Then We shall save Our messengers﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿Are they waiting for anything but the like of the days of those who passed away﴾, because the like of those days is a day of punishment. Since they were threatened with a punishment that would descend upon a place in which the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers were, Allah hastened the glad tidings to the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers that He would save them from that punishment by His power, as He saved the messengers before him.

The clause ﴿Thus it is incumbent upon Us: We shall save the believers﴾ is a concluding appendage (tadhyil). The demonstrative "thus" (kadhalika) refers to the saving derived from ﴿Then We shall save﴾.

"Incumbent upon Us" (haqqan 'alayna) is a parenthetical clause, since the infinitive has been substituted for the verb, meaning: "That has become incumbent upon Us as an obligation."

Allah made it incumbent upon Himself as a confirmation of His bounty and honour, until it became as if it were a right owed by Him.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿nunajji al-mu'minin﴾ with a fatha on the second nun and shadda on the jim, in the pattern of ﴿nunajji rusulana﴾. Al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim read ﴿nunji al-mu'minin﴾ with a sukun on the second nun and a light jim, from al-injа'. The variation between it and its counterpart before it is for stylistic variety (tafannun), and the meaning is one.

In the Mushaf it is written "nunaj al-mu'minin" without a yā' after the jim, in accordance with its pronunciation, because of the meeting of two sukuns.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 104:

﴿Say: O mankind, if you are in doubt about my religion, then I do not worship those whom you worship besides Allah, but I worship Allah, who causes you to die. And I have been commanded to be among the believers.﴾

This sentence is connected in meaning to the sentence ﴿Say: Look at what is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [Yunus: 101], since the purpose of the looking commanded there is reflection (istidlal) to establish the Oneness (al-wahdaniyyah) of God. Their denial of it is what led them to reject the Messenger ﷺ in his saying that Allah sent him to affirm it and to nullify association (al-shirk). So when He commanded them to the reflection that leads to the establishment of His being alone—exalted is He—in divinity, He followed it by informing them that if they persist in doubt concerning what the Messenger ﷺ brought, then the Messenger ﷺ is steadfast in what he brought, and the proofs of the soundness of his religion are clear to those who reflect. The word "people" (al-nas) in this address refers to the polytheists of Makkah, or to all the community of the call (ummat al-da'wah) who have not yet responded to the call.

The "fi" in His saying "in doubt" (fi shakk) is the metaphorical "fi" of container-ness (zarfiyyah majaziyyah), used for firmness, likening the firmness of an attribute to the firmness of a container around what it contains in terms of encompassment.

He attached the container to the religion itself, and the meaning is doubt in one of its states, namely the state that pertains to them, that is, the state of its being true.

The "min" in His saying "concerning my religion" (min dini) is for the metaphorical beginning (ibtida' majazi), meaning a doubt that comes from my religion. This beginning returns to the meaning of causation: that is, if you are doubting with a doubt whose cause is my religion, that is, it relates to its truth; because doubt is understood in every context according to what suits it, like His saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾ [Yunus: 94], and it has been mentioned just above, and His saying: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23].

Doubt about the religion is doubt about its being true and its being from Allah. This doubt arises only when the reality of this religion is not conceived in its essence and its truth is not established by reasoning; so doubt in its veracity entails doubt in its quiddity, for if they had grasped its essence they would not have doubted its truth.

The sentence ﴿so I do not worship those whom you worship besides Allah﴾ stands in the place of the answer to the condition and indicates it in meaning. So the estimated answer is: "then I am certain of the corruption of your religion, so I do not follow it, so I do not worship those whom you worship, but I worship Allah."

Since the content of this sentence is the essence of the religion of Islam, it is permissible that there be a second meaning in the verse, namely: if you are in doubt about knowing this religion, its summary is that I do not worship those whom you worship besides Allah, but I worship Allah alone. This is then in the sense of His saying—exalted is He: ﴿Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship﴾ [al-Kafirun: 1], then His saying: ﴿To you is your religion, and to me is my religion﴾ [al-Kafirun: 6]. Thus two purposes are achieved in this verse. The "people" in His saying ﴿Say: O people﴾ then refers to all the community of the call who have not embraced Islam.

Those whom they worship are the idols. The idols are treated as rational beings, so the relative pronoun used for groups of rational beings (alladhina) is applied to them, in conformity with what they believe about them of reason and governance. Similar instances in the Qur'an are numerous.

The choice of the relative clause of causing death (silat al-tawaffi) here, as a description of the Name of Majesty (ism al-jalalah), is for what it indicates of perfect control over the created; for the polytheists did not go so far in their association as to claim that the idols give life and cause death. Choosing this from among the attributes specific to Allah—exalted is He—is an allusion (ta'rid) to reminding them that they are exposed to death, so that they might restrain their transgression.

Combining the negation of worshipping the idols with the affirmation that he worships Allah stands in the place of the form of restriction (sigha al-qasr) that would say: "So I do not worship except Allah." The reason for departing from the form of restriction is that its nature is that the negated side is omitted in it, being dispensed with by the affirmed side, which is the intended purpose. That is when the primary aim is the affirmed side. But when the negated side is the more important, as here—namely the nullification of idol-worship first—one departs from the form of restriction to the mention of both a negation and an affirmation. This is an elaboration (itnab) required by the situation, like the saying of 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Abd al-Rahim al-Harithi or al-Samaw'al:

Our souls flow along the edges of swords,
and they flow only over the edges of swords.

"And I have been commanded" (wa-umirtu) is a conjunction with the sentence ﴿so I do not worship those whom you worship besides Allah﴾.

"That I should be" (an akuna) is connected to "umirtu" with the omission of the preposition, which is the "bi" that makes the verb "umirtu" transitive; and "an" is verbal (masdariyyah), because the subjunctive form of the imperfect verb after it specifies that it is verbal and prevents the possibility that it is explanatory (tafsiriyyah).

"The believers" (al-mu'minin) is intended to mean the ones who bear this title (aqa'ib hadha al-laqab), those who believed in Allah, His Messenger ﷺ, the Qur'an, and the Resurrection. When the word "believers" is used without qualification, it refers to the people characterized by Islam, and for this reason no complement is supposed for "the believers." In making the Prophet ﷺ one of the believers there is an honoring of this group and an exalting of it.

﴿And that you set your face upright toward the religion, as a ḥanīf﴾

The position of this clause is problematic, because the wāw here is certainly a coordinating conjunction (ʿaṭf), and it is followed by an. The most apparent reading is that an is a verbal particle (maṣdariyya, "that"-particle forming a verbal noun), but then a command-form verb comes after it, which is unusual, since the relative clause (ṣila) of an should normally be a declarative sentence. Al-Kashshaf says: "Sībawayh permitted that an be connected to an imperative and a prohibitive, because the purpose is to connect an to what, together with it, has the sense of a verbal noun (maṣdar), and the two verbs of command and prohibition indicate the verbal noun, since they are other than the rest of the verbs." End of quotation. It refers to what is in Sībawayh's book, in the chapter "a chapter in which (an) has the status of (ay)." So the meaning is: "I was commanded to set my face upright toward the religion, as a ḥanīf," and the coordination is coordination of single item to single item.

[Page 303]

It has also been said that the wāw coordinates a supposed verb indicated by the verb "I was commanded." The supposed verb is "and it was revealed to me," and an is then explanatory (tafsīriyya, "that"-particle of explanation) of the supposed verb, because it contains the sense of saying without its letters.

In my view, the composition of the verse in this way did not occur except for a rhetorical purpose, so there must be a special feature of the form aqim wajhaka in this context. Let us set aside what is in al-Kashshaf, and the making of the verse an example of what Sībawayh permitted, and let us take the wāw as an extended usage, in that it is used in the place of the verb that it coordinates, namely the verb "I was commanded," without intending to make it share with what it coordinates the same status as the coordinated item, but used merely to repeat it. The meaning is: "I was commanded that I set your face upright," so that an is an explanation of what is implied in the wāw by the supposed wording of "I was commanded," with the aim of quoting the wording that God commanded him with, in its exact form, and so that the coordination of ﴿and do not be among the polytheists﴾ on it may be possible. This is coordination of sentences, not coordination of single words. A similar case was mentioned earlier at His words: ﴿and that you judge between them by what God has sent down﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 49] in the surah of al-ʿUqūd (Al-Mā'idah), and this case here is more comprehensive.

Iqāmah (establishing) is making a thing upright. Here it is used metaphorically for devoting the face exclusively to turning toward a specific thing, so that it does not let its face turn aside to anything else. The lām is for cause, that is, for the sake of the religion, so the meaning becomes: "Make your face sincere for the religion; do not make anything other than the religion a partner in your turning." This representation is a metonymy (kināyah) for directing his whole self toward what God commanded him with, namely conveying the message, guiding the community, and reforming it. Close to it is His words: ﴿I have submitted my face to God﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 20] in the surah of Āl ʿImrān.

Ḥanīfan is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from "the religion," which is the religion of monotheism, because it "ḥanafa," meaning it inclined away from the gods and became purely devoted to God. It has been mentioned earlier at His words: ﴿Say: Rather, the religion of Abraham, as a ḥanīf﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135] in the surah of al-Baqarah.

* * *

[Page 304]

﴿and do not be among the polytheists﴾ is a prohibition that emphasizes the meaning of the command before it, by explicitly stating the meaning of ḥanīf. The emphasis of the forbidden verb with the emphatic nūn (nūn al-tawkīd) is for intensifying the prohibition against it, out of concern for disavowing polytheism.

It has been mentioned more than once that His words "among the polytheists" and similar expressions are more eloquent in describing the attribute than something like "do not be a polytheist," because of what it contains of disavowal of the group that holds the creed of association (ishrāk).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 106:

﴿And do not call upon, besides Allah, that which can neither benefit you nor harm you. For if you do, then you would be among the wrongdoers.﴾

It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon ﴿And never be among the polytheists﴾ [Yunus: 105].

The verb was not emphasized with the energetic nūn (nūn al-tawkīd), so that its presence would not prevent the deletion of the letter of weakness (ḥarf al-ʿillah). Its deletion is lightness and eloquence. Also, since the prohibition is accompanied by something that points to the cause, there is sufficiency in it without emphasis, because the relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) in His words ﴿that which can neither benefit you nor harm you﴾ points to the reason for the prohibition against calling upon it, since a rational person does not intend to call upon such things.

The phrase "besides Allah" is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) between the verb "call upon" and its object, and it is an embedding (idmāj) that urges calling upon Allah.

The consequential clause (tafrīʿ) "For if you do" follows on the two prohibitions, to indicate that there is no excuse for the one who commits what he has been forbidden after his prohibition has been emphasized and its cause has been explained. Whoever does it has wronged himself and transgressed against the right of his Lord.

He emphasized being "among the wrongdoers" under that supposition with ʾinna, to increase the warning, and ʾidhan was used to indicate an implied question, as if a questioner asked: "If you do, then what will happen?"

[p. 305]

In His words "among the wrongdoers" there is emphasis similar to what preceded in His words "among the polytheists" and its counterparts.

The purpose of this supposition is to alert people to the gravity of the enormity of this act, such that even if the noblest of creatures did it, he would be among the wrongdoers, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it has already been revealed to you and to those before you: If you should associate others with Allah, your work will surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar: 65].

This is connected to the preceding clause, "and do not call upon other than God that which neither benefits you nor harms you," by way of an allusive refutation of the belief of the polytheists that the idols are intercessors with God. When the previous verse negated that the idols could benefit or harm, and the attribution of benefit or harm usually refers to its being issued by its agent directly, without suggesting any intermediary in bringing it about, the clause ﴿and do not call upon other than God that which neither benefits you nor harms you﴾ [Yunus: 106] was followed by this clause to inform that God's will to benefit or harm anyone cannot be averted or interfered with by anyone else, except one whom God has empowered to do so through supplication or intercession.

The reason it is conjoined with the preceding clause is the difference in meaning between them, in detail and addition, and the generality of the two expressions in His saying ﴿there is no remover of it except Him﴾ and His saying ﴿there is no repeller of His bounty﴾, which include their idols, and these are the intended target, as stated explicitly in His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Zumar: ﴿Have you considered what you call upon other than God? If God intended some harm for me, could they remove His harm? Or if He intended mercy for me, could they withhold His mercy?﴾ [al-Zumar: 38].

[Page 306]

The address is directed to the Prophet (ﷺ) because he is the most deserving of people of good and of the negation of harm, so it is known that others are more deserving of this ruling, and this is the intended meaning.

Al-mass (touching): its literal meaning is placing the hand upon a body to test its touch, and it may be used figuratively, by metonymy of the effect, for affliction (al-isabah). This was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, those who fear God, when a touch from Satan afflicts them﴾ [al-A'raf: 201], at the end of Surat al-A'raf.

The will to good (al-irada bil-khayr) means its decreeing and intending it. Since the One whom nothing can overpower and whose knowledge is never uncertain, when He wills something He does it, the use of "will" here is a kinaya (metonymy) for affliction, as is indicated by His saying after it, ﴿He afflicts with it whom He wills of His servants﴾. He used "touch" in place of "will" in a parallel passage in Surat al-An'am: ﴿And if God touches you with good, then He is over all things competent﴾ [al-An'am: 17]. But here He expressed it with "will" for emphasis in negating power from anyone who might wish to oppose His will, exalted is He, whoever that may be, so that he is incapable of obstructing Him regarding His good, even if it were merely by His will before the act occurs, since obstruction at that stage is easier, because repelling is easier than removing. As for the verse of Surat al-An'am, its context is the explanation of God's power, exalted is He, not the declaration of His transcendence above any opponent or adversary.

Al-fadl (bounty) is good itself, and for this reason placing it in the position of a pronoun indicates that the good that reaches people is a bounty from God, for which they have no entitlement, because they are His servants, and He afflicts them with whatever He wills.

The indefiniteness of "harm" (darr) and "good" (khayr) is for generic type, which applies to both few and many.

Each of the clause ﴿there is no remover of it except Him﴾ and the clause ﴿there is no repeller of His bounty﴾ is a response to the condition stated with them, and the response is not omitted.

The clause ﴿He afflicts with it whom He wills of His servants﴾ stands in the position of an explanation of what precedes it and a conclusion for it, which is why it is separated from it.

The pronoun governed by the preposition "bi" (with it) refers to the good, so it is a favour and an incitement to seek the pleasure of God, so that one may be among those whom the will of God has decreed to afflict with good. Or it may refer to the harm mentioned earlier, and the pronoun, considering that it has been mentioned, serves as a warning, a glad tiding, an admonition, and an encouragement.

[Page 307]

The will here has been stated in general terms, and its causes have not been specified, so that people may pursue every path by which they hope to attain it in giving, and every path they fear may cause them to fall into deprivation.

Al-isabah (affliction) is the contact of one thing with another and its arrival upon it, and it has the same meaning as the earlier mass (touch). So His saying ﴿He afflicts with it whom He wills﴾ has the same meaning as His saying in Surat al-An'am: ﴿And if God touches you with good, then He is over all things competent﴾ [al-An'am: 17].

The concluding clause ﴿and He is the Most Forgiving, the Most Merciful﴾ points to the fact that the granting of good is a bounty from God and a mercy, and a pardon from Him, exalted is He, for the sins of His righteous servants, their shortcomings and their heedlessness. Had He willed, He would not have pardoned them for any of that, and they would all have been ruined.

And were it not for His forgiveness, they would not have been worthy of being afflicted with good, because they, despite their varying degrees of perfection, are never free from deficiency in regard to the everlasting bounty, which is perfection in the sight of God, as the Prophet (ﷺ) indicated by his saying: "Indeed, my heart is veiled over, so I seek forgiveness from God seventy times a day."

It also points to the fact that God has overlooked much of the sins of His extravagant servants and has not taken them to account except for what He does not approve of in any way, as He said: ﴿And He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾ [al-Zumar: 7], and that had He not overlooked much of it, God would have afflicted them with severe harm in this world and the Hereafter.

This is a passage from Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 10, verse 108.

Page 308

﴿Say, "O mankind, the truth has certainly come to you from your Lord. So whoever is guided, it is only for [the benefit of] his own soul that he is guided; and whoever goes astray, it is only against it that he goes astray. And I am not over you a guardian."﴾

This is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), serving as a conclusion (dhayl) to what preceded in the whole surah and as a summation (hawsala) of what had occurred of argumentation, disputation, warning and encouragement. Therefore, what this sentence contains is a comprehensive statement and a decisive farewell.

Its opening with "Say" (qul) is to draw attention to the fact that this is a communication from Allah, Exalted is He, so it is worthy of being received.

The opening of the speech with the vocative (nida') is to gather their attention because of the importance of what is about to be said to them. The address is to all people, believers and disbelievers alike, though its primary intended audience is the polytheists; for this reason I have dwelt at length on their situation. The guided ones are mentioned alongside them as an honour to them.

He emphasised the statement with the particle qad, to record against them that what contains the truth has been conveyed to them, and to affirm that it is indeed truth.

Al-haqq (the truth) is the religion that the Qur'an brought, and he described it with "from your Lord" to highlight that it is a clear truth, which no falsehood or doubt mixes with, and so it is protected from that.

The choice of describing the Lord, attributed to the pronoun of the people, rather than using the name of majesty (Allah), is to draw attention to the fact that this is guidance from the One who loves the welfare of His servants and calls them to what benefits them, which is the manner of one who is a rabb (lord), that is, one who governs and manages.

The linking of the clause "So whoever is guided" to the clause "the truth has certainly come to you" is to indicate that the arrival of clear truth entails that following it is a gain for its follower, and not a favour he bestows upon Allah. Thereby it is inferred that whoever turns away from it has wronged his own soul, and has made the consequence of turning away fall upon it.

Page 309

The lam in His saying "for his own soul" indicates that being guided is a blessing and a sufficiency, and that turning away is a harm to its possessor.

The reason for using the two forms of restriction (qasr) in "it is only for [the benefit of] his own soul that he is guided" and "it is only against it that he goes astray" is to refute the polytheists, who would make excessive demands, saying, "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth" (Al-Isra: 90), and similar things, implying that they would confer a favour upon him if they embraced Islam. Some of them would show that they were angering the Prophet ﷺ by remaining in disbelief. So the restriction conveys that his being guided is limited to its connection with the sense of the lam in His saying "for his own soul", that is, for the benefit of his own soul, and does not extend beyond it to a connection with my benefit. And that his going astray is limited to the connection with the sense of "against", that is, to its harm, and does not extend beyond it to a connection with my harm.

The clause "And I am not over you a guardian" is coordinated with the clause "So whoever is guided", so it falls within the scope of the consequence (tafri') and completes what was consequently derived. For when the guidance of the one guided is for his own soul, and the straying of the one who strays is against his own soul, it becomes established that the Prophet ﷺ was not commanded by Allah to do more than convey the message, and that his own soul gains nothing from their guidance nor is harmed by their straying. Therefore they should not suppose that his eagerness is for benefiting himself or averting harm from himself, so that they would make demands and set conditions; and that he is a sincere advisor to them and a conveyor of what in following him is good for them, while turning away from him is harmful to them.

The use of the nominal negated sentence indicates the continuance and permanence of the negation of that ruling in all circumstances.

The meaning of wakil (guardian) is one to whom the accomplishment of a matter is entrusted. "Over you" (alaykum) carries the sense of "over your guidance", so the preposition has entered upon the essence while the intended meaning is some of its states, by the indication of the context.

[p. 310]

﴿And follow what is revealed to you, and be patient until Allah judges; He is the best of judges.﴾

This is coordinated with "Say" (قُلْ), meaning: convey that statement to the people. ﴿And follow what is revealed to you﴾, i.e., follow in yourself and in your companions what is revealed to you. ﴿And be patient﴾, i.e., patient in the face of those who oppose you and do not believe. This is indicated by the limit expressed in His words ﴿until Allah judges﴾, for it is a limit to this specific patience, not to patience in general.

Since judgment requires two parties, the object of the verb has been omitted, relying on the context. The meaning is: until Allah judges between you and them.

The clause ﴿and He is the best of judges﴾ is a praise and a concluding statement for what it contains of generality, meaning: He is the best of judges between every two disputants in this matter and in others. The definite article in "al-hākimīn" (الحاكِمِينَ, "the judges") is for comprehensiveness (lil-istighrāq), as indicated by the concluding statement.

Khayr (خَيْرُ) is a comparative/superlative form; its original form is akhyar (أخْيَرُ), and the hamza was dropped due to frequent use. The superiority of Him among judges is the superiority of fairness in giving rights. It is here a metonymy for punishing the wrongdoer, because the command to be patient implies that the one commanded has been wronged. Thus, in the information that Allah is the best of judges, there is an implication that Allah supports His Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers against those who denied and opposed them. This is a comprehensive statement, in which lies the excellence of the conclusion.

[p. 311]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Sūrat Hūd

It is called Sūrat Hūd in all the codices (maṣāḥif) and books of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) and Sunnah, and no other name is known for it. This name was also reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās: "Abū Bakr said: O Messenger of Allah, you have grown gray. He said: Hūd has made me gray, and al-Wāqiʿa, and al-Mursalāt, and ʿAmma yatasāʾalūn, and idhā al-shamsu kuwwirat." Narrated by al-Tirmidhī with a good chain in the Book of Tafsir, in the section on Sūrat al-Wāqiʿa. It has been narrated through other routes with similar wording, some of which add to others.

It is named after Hūd because his name is repeated in it five times, and because what is related about him in it is longer than what is related about him in other places, and because ʿĀd are described in it as the people of Hūd, in His saying: ﴿Surely, a distance for ʿĀd, the people of Hūd﴾ [Hūd: 60]. A different reason for the naming was mentioned in the naming of Sūrat Yūnus, which applies to this one as well, namely that it distinguishes it from among the sūrahs that begin with "Alif-Lām-Rā".

It is entirely Meccan according to the majority. This was reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Zubayr, and Qatāda, except for one verse: ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day﴾ [Hūd: 114], up to His saying: "for those who remember." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it is Meccan except for three verses that were revealed in Medina. These are His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So perhaps you will leave some of what is revealed to you﴾ [Hūd: 12]; His saying: ﴿Is one who has a clear proof from his Lord﴾ [Hūd: 17], up to His saying: ﴿those believe in it﴾ [Hūd: 17], which is said to have been revealed concerning ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām; and His saying: ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day﴾ [Hūd: 114], the verse, which is said to have been revealed concerning the story of Abū al-Yasar, as will come. The more correct view is that all of it is Meccan, and that what has been reported of occasions of revelation concerning some of its verses is a mistake arising from confusion in using them as evidence in a story that they were revealed at that time, as will come. Moreover, it is clear that the first of these three verses is Meccan.

This sūrah was revealed after Sūrat Yūnus and before Sūrat Yūsuf. It is counted as the fifty-second in the order of the revelation of the sūrahs. Ibn ʿAṭiyya related in the course of his tafsir of this sūrah that it was revealed before Sūrat Yūnus, because the challenge in it occurred with ten sūrahs, while in Sūrat Yūnus the challenge occurred with one sūrah. This will come with explanation.

Its verses are counted as one hundred and twenty-one in the last Medinan count. In the first Medinan count, its verses were counted as one hundred and twenty-two. It is likewise in the count of the people of Syria, while in the count of the people of Basra and the people of Kufa it is one hundred and twenty-three.

* * *

Its purposes: it begins by alluding to the challenge to match the Qur'an, by what the disjointed letters at the beginning of the sūrah point to.

Then it connects with glorifying the Qur'an.

And with prohibiting the worship of other than Allah, the Exalted.

And that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is a warner to the polytheists of the punishment of a great day, and a bearer of good news to the believers of good enjoyment until a specified term.

And the affirmation of the gathering (to judgment).

And the information that Allah is aware of the hidden matters of people.

[p. 313]

And that Allah is the manager of the affairs of every living thing on the earth.

And the creation of the worlds after they were not.

And that the return of people is to Him, and that He did not create them except for recompense.

And the steadying and consoling of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning what the polytheists say and what they propose of signs according to their own desires, ﴿saying: Why has not a treasure been sent down to him, or an angel come with him?﴾ [Hūd: 12].

And that the sufficient proof for them is the verse of the Qur'an with which He challenged them to match it, and they were unable to match it, so their humiliation became clear, and they deserve loss in the Hereafter.

And the striking of an example for the two groups of believers and polytheists.

And the mention of their counterparts among the perished nations: the people of Noah and the detailed account of what befell them, and ʿĀd, Thamūd, Ibrāhīm, the people of Lūt, Madyan, and the mission of Mūsā, by way of allusion to the lessons in all of that and what should be guarded against, for those people were not benefited by their gods which they called upon.

And that in those reports there is an admonition for those who follow their ways.

And that the root of the misguidance of the misguided is their not fearing the punishment of Allah in the Hereafter; so there is no doubt that the polytheists of Arabia are heading toward what those people came to.

This sūrah uniquely details the event of the Flood and its subsiding.

Then it alludes to comforting the Prophet (ﷺ) and consoling him regarding the disagreement of the people of Mūsā about the Book given to him: so the Messenger and his followers have nothing to do but to be upright in what Allah has commanded, and not to incline toward the polytheists; and upon them is to establish prayer, be patient, and persist in calling to righteousness, for there is no destruction with righteousness.

Admonitions and lessons are interwoven throughout all of that, along with the command to establish prayer.
